en: The Middle Way Treatise of Nāgārjuna,
accompanied by the commentary titled *Prasannapadā* composed by the master Candrakīrti. 1.
The First Chapter, titled "An Examination of Conditions.
Homage to the noble Mañjuśrī, the Youthful!
He who has shaken off all dwelling in the two extremes, and whose birth was obtained from the ocean of the wisdom of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Out of compassion, he has declared the profound nature of the waters of the True Dharma, exactly as he himself has realized it. // 1 //
The splendors of whose vision even today burn away the fuel of the doctrines of opposing disputants, as well as the mental darknesses of the world. // 2 //

Whose volleys of arrows—his words of peerless wisdom—destroy the entire army of the enemy that is existence, bestowing the glory of sovereignty over the three realms upon the world of disciples, including the gods. // 3 //
Having prostrated before that Nāgārjuna, I shall compose a commentary on his *kārikās*, bound with clear and excellent methods of exposition, undisturbed by the winds of sophistry, and lucid. (4)
In this regard, the treatise to be explained beginning with "Not from self, nor from another, nor from both," and so forth, is the subject at hand.
To the question, "What are its connection, subject matter, and purpose? [it is replied:]

Beginning with the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*)— which is adorned with non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), preceded by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), and serves as the cause for the arising of the Tathāgata’s gnosis— and following the method established in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, [this work] concludes with the composition of this treatise by the master Nāgārjuna, who understood the unerring system of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), out of compassion for the sake of awakening others.
Such, then, is the connection of this treatise:
that which instructs you regarding all enemies in the form of the afflictions and protects you from miserable rebirths and cyclic existence—
because of its quality of instruction and its quality of protection, this is a "treatise" (śāstra), and this [quality] does not exist in other doctrines.
Thus, the Master himself, demonstrating the subject matter and purpose of the entire treatise that is about to be explained,

and manifesting the majesty [of the Buddha] by way of his unerring illumination of that [subject], desires to perform a prostration to the Tathāgata— the Supreme Guru— who abides inseparably from that very nature, as the occasion for composing the treatise:
"Neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal..."
It has no manifold meaning and no diverse meaning; it is without coming and without going.
"Dependent origination," and so forth. Herein, dependent origination as characterized by the eight attributes beginning with "non-ceasing" is the subject matter of the treatise;
and nirvana, characterized by the quiescence of all conceptual proliferation and auspiciousness, is indicated as the purpose of the treatise.
"I pay homage to him, the best among speakers"—
by this, prostration is expressed.
Such, then, is the collective meaning of these two verses.
The meaning of the individual components is now analyzed:
therein, *nirodha* means cessation;
momentary destruction is called cessation.
Arising (*utpāda*) means bringing into being;
it signifies the emergence of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). Annihilation (*uccheda*) means cutting off.
The meaning is the cessation of continuity. "Eternal" (śāśvata) means constant;
it means remaining as a pillar at all times.
"Single object" (*ekārtha*) means one and the same object, that is, an undivided object; it means not separate. "Diverse objects" (*nānārtha*) means different objects.
"Separately" (pṛthak) is the meaning.
"Coming" (āgati) is arrival;
it is the movement to a proximate location by those situated in a distant location.
"Nirgati" means departure;
it is the movement to a distant location by those situated in a proximate location.
The root "i" has the sense of going.

The prefix *prati* has the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*), because the meaning of a verbal root is transformed by the influence of a prefix; as it is said: "The meaning of a verbal root is forcibly led elsewhere by a prefix."
Just as the sweetness of the waters of the Gaṅgā [is lost] by the water of the ocean.
In this context, the word *pratītya* ends in the suffix *-lyap* and signifies "reaching" or "depending.
The root *pad*, preceded by the prefixes *sam* and *ut*, means "manifestation"; thus, the word *samutpāda* signifies "arising.
Consequently, the meaning of *pratītyasamutpāda* is the arising of entities in dependence upon causes and conditions.
Others, however, say: *iti* means going or destruction; those things which are conducive to *iti* are called *ityāḥ*;
*prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).

Having thus derived the word *ittha* as ending in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), they explain that there is the "arising of those things that perish individually" (*prati prati ityānāṃ vināśināṃ samutpādaḥ*).

For them, in contexts such as "O monks, I shall teach you dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpādaṃ vo bhikṣavo deśayiṣyāmi*) and "He who sees dependent origination sees the Dharma," this derivation would be superior, because the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) is possible and a compound (*samāsa*) can indeed exist.

But here, in contexts such as "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises," where a specific meaning is directly accepted, how can the word *pratītya*—in the phrase "dependent upon the eye"—have the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), given that the arising of a single consciousness is intended even when the cause is the single faculty of the eye?
However, the sense of "reaching" (*prāpti*) is possible even for the word *pratītya* when no specific meaning has been accepted: namely, "having reached, [consciousness] comes into being."
Regarding the term "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
even though a specific meaning has been accepted, it is possible [to interpret it as] "depending on the eye" or "reaching the eye."
Because of the explanation that "the eye and form are required," and because in the word *itya*—

which ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*)— in the phrase "visual consciousness arises depending on the eye and forms," the word *pratītya* lacks the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and because no compound exists there, when the case-ending is heard, [it is understood as] "depending on the eye."
The expression "consciousness and forms" would have to be a fixed compound (nipāta);
however, this is not the case.
Therefore, one must accept that the derivation belongs specifically to the indeclinable (avyaya) form ending in the suffix -lyap.
But as for the one who [says]: "Because the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*),
because the root *eti* has the sense of reaching (*prāpti*),
and because the word *samutpāda* has the sense of occurrence (*sambhava*),"

Having cited the explanations of others— namely, that "some say dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) means arising (*samutpāda*) having reached those various conditions (*pratyaya*)," and "others say it is the arising (*utpāda*) of things that perish individually (*prati prati*)"— he sets forth a refutation;
yet, first of all, his lack of skill in accurately restating the opponent's position is itself evident.
What is the reason?
For he who explains the word *pratītya* as having the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*) does not explain *prati* as having the sense of "repetition" (*vīpsā*).
Nor does it mean "going toward" (eti) for the sake of reaching; rather, it means "reaching" (prati) for the sake of reaching,
and he explains the word *pratītya* as signifying reaching alone when combined [with the prefix *pra-*].

Now, if by the term *pratītyasamutpāda*— which has been etymologically explained as "arising having reached"— there is intended a reference to all things that arise without exception, then the distributive connection is made such that "arising having reached this or that totality of causes and conditions" is *pratītyasamutpāda*.
Alternatively, if there is an intention to refer to a specific instance, [the same applies].
In that case, the connection would not be with the distributive repetition (vīpsā) "the eye [reaches] forms."
Thus, first of all, there is the teacher's lack of skill in restatement.
This, moreover, is illogical.
Furthermore, it is illogical to say: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises."
Regarding the objection stated here— that two meanings are impossible—
that too is not tenable.
What is the reason?
How can it be possible for that [attainment] to occur by this alone? Because it is a mere assertion lacking supporting reasoning.

Now, if the intention were this: "Because consciousness is formless (*arūpin*), there is no attainment of it by the eye, since attainment is observed only in the case of things possessing form (*rūpin*)," [then the following applies].
This too is not tenable, because even in the case of the statement, "this monk has attained the fruit," attainment is admitted.
Furthermore, since the word *prāpya* is a synonym for the word *apekṣya*,
the Master Ārya Nāgārjuna intended the very meaning of "attainment" in the word *pratītya*; thus,
whatever has arisen in dependence upon this or that [condition] has not arisen by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because this is accepted [as a premise],
others maintain that even the refutation [of the opponent's position] is not tenable.
And furthermore, your own established position is: "What then?
When this exists, that comes to be;
with the arising of this, that arises."
As for the claim that "the meaning of 'this-conditionality' (idaṃpratyayatā) is the meaning of 'dependent origination' (pratītyasamutpāda)," that too is untenable,
because the specific meanings of the two words *pratītya* and *samutpāda* have not been individually explained.
And because the exposition of that [subject] is intended.
Furthermore, even if one were to accept the term *pratītyasamutpāda* as a conventional (rūḍhi) word— just as one speaks of "forest sesame" and so forth— that too is not tenable,
because the Master [Nāgārjuna] has explained *pratītyasamutpāda* precisely as that which conforms to the meaning of its constituent parts.
Because it is accepted that whatever has arisen upon reaching this or that [condition] is, by its own nature, unarisen; for example,
when "this being, that becomes," as in the case of "long" existing when "short" exists.
If it is explained in this way, does it not follow that you have indeed admitted [the very point in question]: namely,
that [the long] exists in dependence upon the short,
having reached the short?
"Long exists in dependence upon short.
Consequently, it is not logical that one accepts exactly what one intends to refute;
so, enough with this digression.

Thus, by elucidating the arising of entities as dependent upon causes and conditions, the Blessed One has refuted the notions that entities arise without a cause, from a single cause, or from discordant causes, as well as the view that they are produced by themselves, by another, or by both. By means of this refutation, the conventional nature of conventional entities, as it truly exists, is revealed. Now, because this very conventional dependent origination is unarisen by way of intrinsic nature, with respect to noble gnosis, there is no cessation in it, up to and including no departure in it; thus, by means of these eight attributes beginning with non-cessation—*anirodha*, etc.—it is characterized.
It is distinguished by its six aspects;
and how cessation and the other [characteristics] do not exist in dependent origination, he will demonstrate throughout the entire treatise.
Although there exist infinite qualifications of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), only these eight are taken up because they constitute the primary factors of dispute.
Since, when dependent origination is seen as it truly is, the proliferation (*prapañca*) characterized by the expressible and so forth ceases entirely for the Noble Ones (*ārya*),
that very dependent origination is called the "cessation of proliferation" (*prapañcopaśama*), in the sense that "in this [dependent origination], there is the subsiding of proliferations."

Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors do not arise therein, and because the conventional discourse of knower and known has ceased, it is "auspicious" (*śiva*) due to being free from all afflictions such as birth, aging, and death without exception.
Dependent origination, characterized by the aforementioned attributes, is designated as the "object" (*karman*) because it is that which is most desired to be expressed through the act of teaching.
Neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal, not a unity nor a plurality, without coming and without going. // 1 //
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, who taught dependent origination—the auspicious cessation of conceptual proliferation. (2)

Furthermore, by understanding dependent origination as it has been described, and seeing that only the Tathāgata alone is a speaker of non-perverted truth while recognizing all other doctrines of outsiders to be like the prattle of children, the Master, filled with extreme faith,
further distinguishes the Blessed One, calling him "the best among speakers."
And here, the penetration of cessation is mentioned first in order to demonstrate that there is no established state of priority or posteriority between arising and cessation.
For it will be said:
"If birth were to exist first, and old age and death were to follow after."
Birth would be without old age and death, and one would be born immortal.
Thus, there is no such rule that arising must necessarily occur first and cessation afterwards.

Now, desiring to demonstrate dependent origination as characterized by non-cessation and so forth, and considering that the negation of cessation and the rest is easily accomplished through the negation of arising, the Master begins with the negation of arising itself;
for arising, as it is conceptualized by others, must be conceptualized either from itself or from another.
It might be conceptualized as arising from both [causes] or from no cause at all;
having determined that it is not tenable in any way whatsoever, he says:
Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause, do any entities ever exist anywhere as having arisen. (3)
In this context, "jātu" means "at any time.
The word *kvacana* expresses the locus (*ādhāra*) and is a synonym for *kvacit*; the word *kecana* expresses the located (*ādheya*) and is a synonym for *kecit*.
Consequently, the connection [of the words] is as follows: "Entities are never found to have arisen from themselves at any time."
In some cases, some [people] [hold such views];
in this manner, the three propositions should likewise be applied.
But is it not the case that if it is determined that "they are certainly not produced from themselves," then the undesirable consequence follows that they are produced from another?
It does not follow, because an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is intended,
and because production from another will also be refuted.
And the reasoning by which production from self is not possible is as follows:
"Therefore, there is no advantage whatsoever in its coming into being; and it is simply not logical for that which is already born to be born again."
This and so forth should be understood by means of the *Madhyamakāvatāra* and other such works.
But the master Buddhapālita said: "Entities do not arise from themselves,
because their arising would be purposeless and because it would entail the fault of an over-extension."
For there is no purpose in the further arising of entities that already exist by their own nature; if that which already exists were to be born,
it would never not be born.

Regarding this, some offer the following criticism: "That is incorrect, because [the argument] fails to state a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and because it does not avoid the faults asserted by the opponent;

furthermore, since it is a statement of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), when the opposite of the intended meaning is established through the reversal of the subject and its properties, there would be no production from another, and thus the utility of birth would be lost. [End of fragment] Janmaniro... [text ends].
If it were to fall away, there would be a contradiction with the established conclusion.
We see that all this criticism is untenable. How so?
Regarding that which was first stated, namely, "because of the failure to state a reason and an example":
That is incorrect.
Why?
Because the opponent, while asserting production from self, [accepts it as follows]:
It is asked: [Does it arise] from itself as its cause, and yet that very same thing arises again?
We see no purpose in the re-arising of what already exists, and we see only an infinite regress.

Furthermore, you do not accept the re-arising of what has already arisen, nor do you accept an infinite regress as desirable. Therefore, your doctrine is entirely devoid of logical justification and contradicts your own admission.
When thus challenged, why would the opponent not concede, such that the employment of reasons and examples might bear fruit?
Now, if the opponent does not desist even when challenged with a contradiction of his own accepted tenets, then, due to his shamelessness, he would not desist even through reasons and examples;
and we do not engage in debate with a madman.
Therefore, in every respect, the Teacher reveals his own inclination toward inference, even by introducing inference in an inappropriate place.
Furthermore, for one who is a Mādhyamika, it is not proper to employ an independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*), because of the absence of any acceptance of an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*).
Thus it was said by Āryadeva:
Against one who holds no position such as "existent," "non-existent," or "both existent and non-existent," a criticism cannot be leveled even after a long time.
And it is said in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*:
"If I had any thesis, then for that very reason I would have a fault;
but I have no thesis, therefore I have no fault at all."
If I were to perceive anything at all, I would either affirm or deny it;
but since such objects do not exist through means such as direct perception, I am beyond reproach.

Thus, since the Mādhyamika does not state independent inferences (*svatantrānumāna*) in this way, how could there be an independent thesis (*svatantrapratijñā*) such as "the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatanas*) are not produced from themselves," against which the Sāṃkhyas might raise an objection? What is the meaning of this thesis: is it that [they] do not arise from themselves because they are of the nature of an effect (*kāryātmakatva*), or because they are of the nature of a cause (*kāraṇātmakatva*)?
What follows from this? If [the reason] is taken as having the nature of the effect, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If it is taken as having the nature of the cause, it is a contradiction (*viruddhārthatā*), because everything that possesses origination is produced precisely while existing in the form of its cause.
Since for us the reason "because of existing" cannot result in either the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or the fallacy of contradictory meaning (*viruddhārthatā*),
we shall make an effort to refute whichever case of *siddhasādhana* or *viruddhārthatā* might arise.
Therefore, because the faults alleged by others do not even apply, Master Buddhapālita need not describe their refutation.

Now, it might be argued: since the Madhyamikas do not state independent inferences because their own positions, reasons, and examples are unestablished, let there be no proof of the meaning of the thesis—the negation of intrinsic arising—by means of an inference established for themselves, nor the refutation of the opponent's thesis by means of an inference established for both.

Rather, the opponent's thesis must be countered by pointing out its contradiction with inference established for [the opponent] himself, using propositions and so forth that are free from the faults of position, reason, and example, as established for [the opponent] himself.
And because that [reason] was not stated, and because that fault was not avoided, that very same fault remains.
It is said in reply: this is not so.
What is the reason?

Because when someone asserts a particular point, they must demonstrate to others the very same reasoning by which that point was realized for themselves— desiring to produce in others a certainty identical to their own.
Therefore, this is the logical principle: that one must employ the very means of proving the thesis accepted by oneself as proposed by the opponent;
and this [person] does not [employ such means] against the opponent.

Because of the impossibility of providing reasons and examples, he resorts solely to the mere restatement of his own proposition as the proof for the point he has asserted; thus, by accepting a position devoid of justification, he merely deceives himself and is unable to produce certainty in others.

This alone is its most evident refutation, namely, its lack of capacity to prove the point it has itself asserted; what, then, is the purpose of raising the objection of sublation by inference (*anumāna*) in this case?
Even if one must necessarily point out the fault of contradiction with inference from [the opponent's] own perspective, that too has already been pointed out by the Master Buddhapālita.
If it is asked how so,
[it is because] "entities do not arise from themselves, because their arising would be purposeless," as it has been stated.
For here, by the word "that" (tad), there is a reference to that which exists by its own nature.
If one asks why,
it is because this explanatory sentence is a detailed elaboration of that concise statement previously mentioned.
"For there is no purpose in the re-arising of things that already exist by way of their own nature.

By this statement, there is the presentation of a corroborative example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) which is well-established for the opponent and which follows the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*).
In that context, by the phrase "of that which exists by way of its own nature," there is a reference to the logical reason (*hetu*).
By the phrase "because production would be purposeless," there is a reference to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
In that regard, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced;
being produced is seen to be impermanent, as in the case of a jar."

And likewise: "Sound is produced; therefore, because it is produced, it is impermanent. Here, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the reason (*hetu*) as manifested by the application (*upanaya*).
In the same way, here too: "Entities do not arise from themselves."
Because it is pointless for things already existing in their own right to arise again;
for here, a jar or similar object already existing in its own right and situated before one is seen to have no need for further arising.
Thus, if you consider that even in the state of a lump of clay and so forth, the jar and other objects exist in their own right, [then they would not need to arise].
Even then, there is no arising for that which already exists by way of its own nature.

Thus, by means of this reason—which is established through its own existence as manifested in the application (*upanaya*) and which is non-deviant in its negation of further arising—the Sāṃkhya’s own contradiction with inference has indeed been brought forth.
So why is it said that "this is improper because of the failure to state a reason and an example"?
Not only is it not possible that there is no statement of reasons and examples,
but it is also not possible that there is the fault of failing to avoid the defects stated by the opponent. How so?

For the Sāṃkhyas do not desire the manifestation again of a jar that already exists in a manifest form standing before one; and it is precisely such a thing that is taken here as an example, because its nature is already established.

Furthermore, since that which has an unmanifest form and exists in the state of a potentiality possesses a probandum characterized by the negation of its production, how can there be any suspicion of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
or how can there be any suspicion that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory? Therefore,

even when an objection is raised regarding an internal contradiction with inference, since the aforementioned defects do not exist, it is simply impossible to avoid the defects pointed out by the opponent.
Thus, it should be understood that this objection is entirely irrelevant.

Since the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "the jar and so forth" is intended to include all objects whatsoever that are about to arise, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) cannot possibly apply even on account of the potter and others.

Alternatively, here is another line of reasoning: those who assert that entities arise from themselves [claim] that things other than the person do not arise from themselves precisely because they already exist by way of their own nature.
Like a person;
this example is to be cited in this manner.

And although the negation of production does not constitute a refutation for the proponent of manifestation (*abhivyaktivādin*), nevertheless, by applying the term "production" to manifestation and because manifestation itself is designated by the word "production" on the basis of its similarity to non-perception before and perception after, this negation is not without refuting power.
If it is asked, "How then can this analytical investigation be obtained without the expression of the meaning as previously stated? it is replied:
Alternatively, the sentences were composed;
because they possess great significance, they proceed by encompassing the meaning as it has been explained.
And when these are being explained, they give rise to the very nature of the meaning as it has been described; thus, nothing that was not already included can be conceived here.
Furthermore, the consequence of a contrary meaning applies only to the opponent and not to us,
because we have no thesis of our own;
consequently, there is no possibility of contradicting our own established tenet.
Furthermore, we certainly accept that as many faults as may accrue to the opponent through the occurrence of consequences that contradict [his own] position;
for how indeed could the Master Buddhapālita, who follows the unerring doctrine of the Master Nāgārjuna, be said to employ statements that leave room for [such] objections?
How could an opponent find an opening against him?

When a proponent of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) applies a *prasaṅga* against a proponent of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), how could there be the consequence of the opposite meaning of that *prasaṅga*?
For words do not render the speaker powerless like policemen with nooses;
rather, they conform to the speaker's intention provided that there is the capacity [for expression].
Consequently, since the purpose of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is merely the negation of the opponent's thesis, there is no implication of a meaning contrary to the *prasaṅga*.
And thus the Master, for the most part, refuted the opposing position by means of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*). For example: "Space does not exist at all prior to the characteristic of space;
for if it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without characteristics."
If form were devoid of its cause, it would follow that form exists without a cause;
yet no object whatsoever exists anywhere without a cause.
First of all, nirvana is not an existent thing, for it would follow that it possesses the characteristics of aging and death;
indeed, there is no existent thing that exists without aging and death.

...and so forth. Now, if it is argued that because the words of the Teacher (Ācārya) are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), they possess great significance and thus may be conceived as the cause for the production of multiple interpretations, then why are the commentaries of the Teacher Buddhapālita not likewise conceived in that same way?
Or, if it should be said: "This is the rule for commentators..."
As for the claim that it is necessary to state the full details of the formal syllogisms (prayogavākya),
this too is not the case;
for even the Master, while composing his commentary on the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, did not state such formal syllogisms.

Moreover, it is observed that this logician— who, despite having accepted the Madhyamaka view, utters independent syllogistic arguments solely out of a desire to manifest his own extreme proficiency in the science of logic— is the locus of an exceedingly great multitude of faults.
How so?

In this regard, as for what was stated thus: "Here the formal argument (*prayogavākya*) is as follows: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikānyāyatana*) are not produced from themselves, because they already exist, like consciousness (*caitanya*)."

If it is asked: "For what purpose, then, is the qualification 'from the perspective of ultimate reality' (paramārthataḥ) employed here? For production accepted according to worldly convention (lokasaṃvṛti) is not being negated, and if it were negated, there would be the consequence of contradicting what has been accepted."
This is not tenable,
because even conventionally, arising from self is not admitted;
as it is said in the Sūtra:

“And this sprout, which arises with the seed as its cause, is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, nor is it produced without a cause; it does not arise from God, time, atoms, primordial matter, or inherent nature.
Thus: “While the seed exists, the sprout [arises]; yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout.”
It is neither other than that nor is it that very thing; such is the nature of phenomena, which is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Here too, it will be said:
"Whatever comes into being dependently is neither that very thing, nor is it something other than it;
therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal."
Thus it is said.
If it is argued that the qualification is made with respect to the ultimate [truth], that is incorrect; for even conventionally, we do not accept the establishment of such a thing.

For since the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) have indeed fallen away from the unerring vision of the two truths, it is only to be expected that a merit [is gained] as long as they are refuted in both ways.
Thus, even the employment of qualifiers with reference to the positions of others is not tenable.
Nor does the world accept that things arise from themselves, such that the qualification [“from self”] would be purposeful even in relation to that view.
For the world, without engaging in such investigations as whether [things arise] from self or from another, accepts merely this much: that an effect arises from a cause.
In this way, the Teacher also established [the position];
thus, it is determined in every respect that the qualification is indeed futile.
Moreover, if this qualification is employed by one who wishes to refute arising from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛti),

then there would either be a fault of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) consisting in a substratum unestablished for oneself (svato 'siddhādhāra), or a fault of the reason (hetudoṣa) consisting in an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi).

If it is argued that there is no fault because, while from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) the sense bases such as the eye are not admitted, they do exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*),
then for whose sake is the qualification "from the perspective of ultimate reality" intended?

If it is argued that the qualification "ultimately" (paramārthataḥ) is used in the negation of arising because the conventional eyes and so forth are negated as arising from the perspective of ultimate reality, then one should simply state it thus: "There is no arising of the conventional eyes and so forth ultimately.
Yet, it is not stated in this way.

Even if this were stated by others, since they accept only the eyes and so forth as substantially existent (*vastusad*) and do not accept them as conceptually existent (*prajñaptisat*), the thesis would suffer from the fault of having a locus (*āśraya*) unestablished for the opponent; therefore, this [position] is not tenable.
Now, it might be argued: just as in the case of "sound is impermanent," only the generalities of the property and the property-bearer are apprehended, not their specific particulars;
for if the particulars were apprehended, there would be an absence of the conventional usage of inference and the object of inference.
To explain: if sound were apprehended as being composed of the four great elements (*cāturmahābhautika*), [the inference would fail].
That [reason] is unestablished for the opponent;
if, on the other hand, it is taken as a quality of space,
it is unestablished for the Buddhist himself.

Likewise, for a Vaiśeṣika who asserts the non-eternality of sound, if sound is apprehended as being produced (*kārya*), that is unestablished for the opponent; or if it is apprehended as being manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
That [reason] is unestablished for himself;
likewise, depending on the circumstances, if destruction were also caused,
it would be unestablished for the Buddhist himself.
If, on the other hand, it were causeless, it would be unestablished for the opponent;
therefore, in this case, only the generalities of the property and the subject are taken.
If it is argued that here too, the mere substratum (dharmin) will be accepted with its qualifications set aside,
this is not so;
because at the very moment the negation of arising is intended here as the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), [the qualification cannot be disregarded].
At that very moment, he himself has admitted the disappearance of the substratum—the locus—whose existence is acquired merely through error.
For error and non-error are indeed distinct; thus, when by means of error that which is non-existent is grasped as existent, [the substratum vanishes].
Just as one with cataracts perceives hair and the like,
how then could there be the perception of even a trace of a truly existent entity?
And when, due to the absence of error, that which is unreal is not superimposed— just as one free from cataracts does not perceive hair and the like— [then what reality remains]?
In that case, how could there be the perception of even a trace of an unreal entity, by virtue of which conventional reality (saṃvṛti) might exist at that time?
For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Master:
"If I were to perceive anything at all, I would either affirm or deny it;
but since such objects do not exist through means such as direct perception, I am beyond reproach."

Since error and non-error are thus distinct, there can be no possibility of error in the non-erroneous state of the wise; therefore, how could there be a conventional eye that could serve as the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition?
Thus, the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*)—namely, that its basis is unestablished (*asiddhādhāra*)—is not avoided.
Or else, the reason is subject to the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*);
thus, this is not a valid rebuttal at all.
There is also no similarity in the illustrative example (*nidarśana*).
For in that case, both parties possess the generality of sound and the generality of impermanence, with their specific distinctions left unexpressed.
However, a generality of the eye is not accepted in this way by either the proponent of emptiness or the proponent of non-emptiness, neither conventionally nor ultimately.
Thus, there is no similarity with the illustrative example.

And this same method for exposing the fault of the thesis having an unestablished locus (asiddhādhāra) should also be applied to exposing the unestablished nature of the meaning of the reason "because of existence" (sattvāt).
And this is indeed so,
for even this logician himself has accepted the aforementioned point:
that there certainly do exist causes and other factors that produce the internal sense-bases.
Because it has been taught by the Tathāgata in such a way;
for whatever has been taught by the Tathāgata as being thus is indeed so,
just as, for example, "nirvāṇa is peace."
Regarding this proof put forward by the opponent, the following refutation has been stated by him: "What is intended by you here as the meaning of the reason (*hetu*):
is it because the Tathāgata taught it in such and such a way conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), or is it ultimately (*paramārthataḥ*)?"
If [it is argued] from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*),
then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) in itself; if [it is argued] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [the same fault applies].
When a phenomenon that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent does not arise—
since the status of an effect as being existent, non-existent, or both has been refuted—
then how can a cause be productive? For only in such a case would it be logical.

The meaning of the sentence is that this [cause] is not at all a producer. Consequently, since from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ) the relationship between the produced and the producer is unestablished, the reason (hetu) is either unestablished in its object or contradictory.

Since, by this very reasoning, he has himself admitted that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), therefore, in all inferences where the reason is presented as a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), all means of proof (*sādhana*) are undermined because the reason and other factors are unestablished from his own perspective.
For example: "In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no arising of the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) from those conditions (*tatpratyaya*) which are other [than themselves]."
Because they are external,
just as, for example, a cloth [is not its own cause].
Alternatively, it is understood that conditions which produce the internal sense-bases such as the eye are not intended to be "other" in the ultimate sense.
Because it is extrinsic,
just like threads and so forth; however,
in this case, the state of being extrinsic and so on is itself unestablished.

Furthermore, this was stated by him [Nāgārjuna] wishing to expose the unestablished nature (*asiddhārthatā*) of the reason propounded by the opponent— namely, that "internal entities have indeed arisen because they perform specific conventional designations regarding their objects"—

in order to prove that for a yogi in meditative equipoise who perceives the true nature of things with the eye of wisdom, production, motion, and so forth do exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
In that case, the reason— "because it effects a qualified conventional usage regarding that object"— is unestablished (asiddha),
since motion itself is negated precisely by the negation of arising.
Thus, even in the proof formulated by oneself, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that which has not been traversed is never being traversed.
Because of the reason "being a temporal path," like a path already traversed; thus, the lack of established meaning for the reason "being a temporal path" should be applied by its very nature.
From the perspective of ultimate truth, the homogeneous eye does not see form,
because it is an eye-faculty, just like its non-homogeneous counterpart.
Likewise: the eye does not perceive form, because it is composed of the elements, like form;
nor is the earth of a solid nature.
Because they are [already] established as real, just like the "nirla" and so forth, the non-establishment of the reason and other factors should be applied by oneself in these cases.
Furthermore, this reason, "because of existence," is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) from the perspective of the opponent.

[The opponent asks: "Is it because of existence that the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) arise from themselves like consciousness (*caitanya*), or rather do they arise from themselves like jars (*ghaṭa*) and so forth? If it is argued that there is no inconclusiveness because jars and the like are equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*), [we reply:]...
This is not so, because it is not stated in that way.

But surely, just as a refutation has been stated regarding the inferences of others, so too, when the aforementioned refutations apply to one's own inferences as well, that very same fault— such as the unestablished locus (*asiddhādhāra*) or the unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*)— would follow; and thus, that which is a fault for both parties, [should not be raised].
"By that [reasoning], not even a single objection arises; thus, all this criticism turns out to be untenable.
It is replied:
"This fault arises for those who assert an independent inference (*svatantra-anumāna*)."
We do not employ independent inference, because our inferences have as their result the negation of the opponent's thesis.
For instance, the opponent maintains that "the eye sees";
he is refuted by means of an inference established solely according to his own [tenets]: "You accept that the eye has the property of not seeing itself."
And it is accepted that there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) between the non-perception of one's own self and the perception of another;
therefore, wherever there is no perception of one's own self, there also is no perception of another,
as in the case of a jar.
Furthermore, since the eye does not perceive itself, it likewise lacks the perception of others.

Consequently, the perception of "blue" and other external objects—which contradicts its own failure to perceive itself—is contradicted by an inference established by [the opponent] himself. It is merely this much that is raised by our inferences; so how could there be any fault in our position?
Why would there be an equality of fault?
Furthermore, is there not sublation of inference even by an inference established for only one of the two parties?
There is; and that occurs precisely through a reason established for oneself alone.
It is not by means of what is established for the opponent, because it is seen thus from the world itself;
for sometimes in the world, victory or defeat occurs by the word of a witness who has been accepted as authoritative by both the plaintiff and the defendant.
Sometimes [a decision is reached] by one's own statement;
however, by another's statement, there is neither victory nor defeat.
And as it is in the world:
The same applies to the *Nyāya* system as well, because it is precisely worldly convention (*laukika-vyavahāra*) that is the subject under discussion in the *Nyāya* treatises.
For this very reason, some have stated: "There is no sublation of inference by the force of what is established from another [source]."
Because it is precisely what is established for the opponent that one intends to refute.
As for the one who thinks: "Only he whose argument is certain for both parties [is entitled to] employ a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or a refutation (dūṣaṇa),"...
It does not state that which is established for only one party or that which is doubtful;
therefore, even by one who follows worldly convention, the very same principle as stated above must be accepted regarding inference.
For indeed, there is no sublation by means of a scripture established for both parties; rather, [sublation occurs] even by means of that which is established for oneself alone.
In the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), however, in all instances, one's own established conviction alone is more important,
not the conviction established by both parties.
For this very reason, the formulation of a definition of *tarka* (reasoning) is purposeless.
According to the reasoning established for each [system], the Buddhas act out of compassion to favor those disciples who are not yet proficient in that [particular system].
Thus, enough of this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand.
Entities do not arise from another either; this is because of the very non-existence of another,
for the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities is not found in conditions and the like.
This he will demonstrate hereafter.
Consequently, precisely because of the non-existence of another, things do not arise from another either.
Furthermore: if indeed another were to exist in dependence upon something else...
In that case, there would be abundant darkness from a flame;
moreover, everything would indeed arise from everything,
because "otherness" is equal in respect to all things, even those that are not its producers.
By such passages from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, the refutation of arising from another is to be understood.

The master Buddhapālita, however, explains: "Entities do not arise from another, because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could arise from everything. The master Bhāvaviveka offers this critique: "In this case, since it is a statement of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), one must reverse the probandum and the probans;
[therefore, the conclusion is that] entities arise from themselves, from both, or without a cause."
Because something arises from something else,
there is a contradiction with the previous position;
otherwise, since everything would result from everything, this [objection] falls outside the scope of proof and refutation and is therefore irrelevant.
This too is irrelevant in meaning;
since it has already been established and because it falls within the scope of the refutation of the opponent's proposed thesis, this is merely trivial, and no further effort is expended upon it.
Entities do not arise from both [causes] either, because this would entail the faults stated for both positions individually, and because each lacks the capacity for production.
For it will be said:
Suffering might be created by both, if it were created by each one individually. Thus [it is said].
Nor do they arise from no cause; for if a cause were absent, neither effect nor cause would exist,
as this would entail the faults that will be stated hereafter.
Furthermore, the world could not be perceived at all if it were devoid of a cause,
just like the color and fragrance of a lotus in the sky.
And because of the consequence of such faults as these.
The master Buddhapālita, however, said: "Entities do not arise without a cause, because it would follow that everything could arise from everything at all times.

To this, the master Bhāvaviveka stated a refutation: "In this case as well, since it is a statement of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), if the meaning of the sentence is intended to express the opposite of the probandum and the probans,"
By this, the following is meant: entities arise from causes,
because something arises from something at some time,
and because the commencement [of an action] is fruitful.
"This interpretation is not tenable because of the faults previously mentioned";
to this, others reply: "That is incorrect, because of the refutation already stated."
Furthermore, even if it were for the sake of including Īśvara and others, that too would not be correct;
for Īśvara and the rest are included within one's own position, the opponent's position, or both, according to how they are accepted.
Therefore, it has been established that there is no arising;
and because arising is impossible, dependent origination characterized by non-arising and so forth is proven.

Here it is said: If dependent origination is thus established by you as characterized by non-arising and so forth, then what of that which was stated by the Blessed One—"conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces"—and likewise, "they are impermanent"?
Formations are subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
for having arisen, they cease, and their subsiding is bliss.
Likewise: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains constant;
there is one phenomenon for the maintenance of beings, namely the four nutriments;
two phenomena protect the world, namely moral shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya)," and so forth.
Likewise, the coming here from the next world and the going from this world to the next—
thus has dependent origination, characterized by cessation and so forth, been taught by the Blessed One;
how could that not be [the case]?
Why is it being obstructed?
Precisely because cessation and the other [characteristics] are perceived within dependent origination,
for this very reason the Master composed this Madhyamaka-śāstra in order to demonstrate the distinction between sūtras of interpretable meaning (neyārtha) and those of definitive meaning (nītārtha).

In this regard, those [characteristics] such as arising and so forth that have been stated concerning dependent origination are not from the perspective of the nature of the object of untainted cognition, which is free from the cataracts of ignorance; rather, they are from the perspective of the object of knowledge belonging to the eye of cognition whose vision is impaired by the cataracts of ignorance.

With reference to the vision of reality, however, the Blessed One said: "O monks, this indeed is the supreme truth, namely, Nirvana, which has the nature of non-deception; and all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) are false and have the nature of deception.
Likewise: "In this, there is neither suchness nor non-falsity."
This too has the nature of deception; this too has the nature of dissolution;
this too is false.
"This is an illusion that deceives the foolish. Likewise:
"Form is like a mass of foam; sensation is like a bubble;
perception is like a mirage; mental formations are like a plantain tree."
"And consciousness is like an illusion," so it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun.
"Beholding phenomena in this way, a monk who has initiated vigor— whether by day or by night— being clearly comprehending and mindful,
shall penetrate the peaceful state, the auspicious stilling of all conditioned formations. Thus it is said.
And because phenomena are devoid of self, and so forth.

For one who might have doubt due to not understanding the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of such a teaching— thinking, "Which of these teachings here is of definitive meaning (*tattvārtha*), and which indeed is intentional (*ābhiprāyikī*)?"—
and who, owing to dull intellect, understands a teaching of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) as being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
For the sake of both these classes of disciples, the Teacher composed this treatise by means of reasoning and scripture in order to eliminate doubt and false knowledge.
In that regard, the reasoning is set forth by the passage beginning with "not from itself."
"That which has the nature of deception is false," so the Blessed One has said;
and since all conditioned phenomena have the nature of deception, they are therefore false.
"The prior limit is not known," said the Great Sage;
for saṃsāra is indeed without beginning or end, having neither a first nor a last.
And in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" were refuted by the Blessed One, who clearly discerns both existence and non-existence.
By such passages as these, scripture (āgama) has been described.
And it is said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Which sūtras are of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and which are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
Those sūtras that are taught for the purpose of entering the path..."
These are called of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);
those discourses (*sūtrānta*) which are taught for the sake of entering into the fruit are called of interpretable meaning.

To the extent that those discourses (sūtrānta) which teach emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of formative activity, non-arising, non-birth, non-existence, selflessness, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a living soul, the absence of a person, the absence of ownership, and the gateways to liberation— these are called "definitive in meaning" (nītārtha).
This, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is called "reliance on discourses definitive in meaning."
"Not relying on discourses of interpretable meaning."
And so it is said in the *Āryasamādhirājasūtra*:
"One knows the distinction of sūtras of definitive meaning as emptiness taught by the Sugata;
furthermore, one knows all phenomena in the [sūtras] where persons, beings, and individuals [are mentioned] to be of interpretable meaning."
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the teaching of arising and so forth has a false meaning, the Master began the investigation of dependent origination.

But surely— if, in the absence of arising and so forth, the Master has undertaken this [treatise] for the purpose of demonstrating that all phenomena are false— then it follows that what is false does not exist; thus, unwholesome states do not exist,
and in their absence, the miserable destinies do not exist,
nor do wholesome actions exist.
Due to the absence of that [reality], there would be no happy destinies; and because of the non-existence of both happy and miserable destinies, there would be no cyclic existence (saṃsāra);
thus, every undertaking would indeed be rendered futile.
It is said:

In consideration of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), we establish the falsity of things as an antidote to the world’s adherence to the notion that "this is true. However, the Noble Ones (*āryas*), having accomplished what was to be done, do not perceive anything at all that could be either false or non-false.
Moreover,
for one who has fully realized the falsity of all phenomena, do they still possess karma,
or does saṃsāra exist for them?
Nor does this [mind] perceive the existence or non-existence of any phenomenon whatsoever.
As the Blessed One said in the noble *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*:
"For the mind, Kāśyapa, when thoroughly sought, is not found."
That which is not obtained is not perceived;
that which is not perceived is neither past, nor future, nor present.
That which is neither past, nor future, nor present—
That which has no intrinsic nature has no arising.
For that which has no arising, there is no cessation.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
But he who, due to following after perversion, does not understand falsity and adheres to the intrinsic nature of dependent entities,
being thus attached through his adherence to these phenomena as being true, also performs actions.
He wanders even within saṃsāra;
because he remains in a state of perversion, he is not capable of attaining nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, even things whose intrinsic nature is false serve as the basis for affliction and purification;
just as an illusory maiden serves those who do not know her true nature, and a magical creation of the Tathāgata serves those who have accumulated roots of merit.
For it is said in the *Dṛḍhādhyāśaya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:

"Son of good family, it is just as when a theatrical performance by a magician is underway, and someone whose mind is overcome by passion, seeing a woman created by the magician, might rise from his seat and depart out of fear of embarrassment before the assembly;
having departed, he would then contemplate that very same woman as impure."
One should attend to it as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self;
such is the detailed explanation.
And in the Vinaya,
it is said that a mechanical maiden made by a machine-maker, though devoid of a real maiden, appears in the form of a real maiden and becomes a basis for sensual desire for that painter.
Likewise, although phenomena are false by nature, they serve as the basis for the affliction and purification of the foolish.
Likewise, in the *Āryaratnakūṭasūtra*:
"Then indeed, those five hundred monks, not entering into, not plunging into, and not having faith in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma, rose from their seats and departed.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One [went] by the path on which these monks were going."
On that path, he manifested two monks.
Then those five hundred monks approached the path by which those two created monks were going.
Having approached them, they asked, "Where, venerable sirs, will you go? The two created monks replied, "We shall go to the forest retreats."
There we shall dwell in the abodes of the contact of meditative bliss;
for whatever Dharma the Blessed One teaches, we do not enter into it, we do not plunge into it, and we do not have faith in it— we tremble and fall into great terror.

Then those five hundred monks said this: "Venerable sirs, we too do not enter into, do not fathom, and do not have faith in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma; we are terrified, we are greatly afraid, and we fall into a state of terror.
Therefore, we shall dwell in forest retreats, living in the pleasant contact of meditative absorption."
The two emanated monks said: "In that case, venerable sirs, we shall recite together and not dispute;
for non-dispute is the supreme quality of a śramaṇa.
For the sake of abandoning what, venerable sirs, have you set out?"
They replied, "We have set out for the sake of abandoning passion, hatred, and delusion.
The two emanated beings asked, "But, venerable sirs, do passion, hatred, and delusion actually exist within you, such that you would exhaust them?
They replied, "They are not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."
Nor do they arise as unimagined.
The two emanated beings said: "Therefore, venerable sirs, do not imagine;
do not conceptualize."
And when, venerable ones, you do not conceptualize and do not discriminate,
then you will neither be attached nor be detached.
And he who is neither attached nor detached—
He is said to be "peaceful.
Venerable ones, ethical discipline does not transmigrate nor does it attain final nirvana;
so too, venerable ones, are concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
It neither transmigrates nor enters final nirvāṇa;
and by these dharmas, O Venerable Ones, nirvāṇa is indicated.
Furthermore, these dharmas are empty and by nature secluded.
Venerable ones, abandon this notion, namely, that there is "parinirvāṇa.
Do not form a notion regarding a notion, and do not fully comprehend a notion through a notion.
For whoever thoroughly understands perception within perception,
that very perception becomes his bondage.
Venerable sirs, enter the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling!
We declare that for a monk who has attained the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, there is nothing further to be done.
Then, the minds of those five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
With their minds thus liberated, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to those monks: "Venerable sirs, where have you gone, or from where have you come? They replied: "Venerable Subhūti, the Dharma has been taught by the Blessed One such that there is no going anywhere and no coming from anywhere. He asked: "Who, venerable sirs, is your teacher?"
They said: "He who has not arisen and will not pass into parinirvāṇa.
He asked: "How have you heard the Dharma?
They replied: "Neither for bondage nor for liberation."
He asked, "By whom have you been disciplined? They replied, "By him who has neither body nor mind. He asked, "How have you applied yourselves?"
They said: "Neither for the sake of abandoning ignorance, nor for the sake of producing knowledge.
He asked: "Whose disciples are you?
They replied: "Of one by whom nothing has been attained and nothing has been fully awakened to."
He asked, "Who are your fellow practitioners of the holy life?
They replied, "Those who do not wander within the triple world.
He asked, "After how long will you venerable ones attain final nirvana? They replied, "When the emanations of the Tathāgata attain final nirvana."
He asked: "Have you done what was to be done?
They replied: "By means of the full understanding of 'I-making' and 'mine-making'.
He asked: "Are your afflictions exhausted?"
They said: "Because of the ultimate exhaustion of all phenomena.
He asked: "Has Māra been defeated by you?
They replied: "Because the Māra of the aggregates is not to be apprehended."
He asked: "Has Māra been defeated by you?
They replied: "Because the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra) is not perceived.
He asked: "Has the Teacher been served by you?"
They said: "Neither by body, nor by speech, nor by mind.
He asked: "Has the ground of those worthy of offerings been purified by you?
They replied: "By way of non-grasping and non-receiving."
He asked: "Have you crossed over saṃsāra?
They replied: "Neither through annihilation nor through permanence.
He asked: "Have you entered the ground of those worthy of offerings?"
They said: "Because of being completely liberated from all grasping.
He asked: "Where are you going, venerable ones?
They said: "We go wherever the emanations of the Tathāgata go."

Thus, as the venerable Subhūti was questioning and those monks were responding, in that assembly the minds of eight hundred monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging, and the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye was purified in thirty-two thousand beings. Thus it was.
Thus, by means of these two monks created as emanations of the Tathāgata, who were of a false nature, the cause for the purification of five hundred monks was established.
And it is said in the *Āryavajramaṇḍā-dhāraṇī*:

"For example, Mañjuśrī, depending upon a piece of wood, depending upon a fire-drill, and depending upon the exertion of a man’s hands, smoke appears and fire is produced. Yet that heat of the fire does not depend on the piece of wood, nor does it depend on the fire-drill, nor does it depend on the exertion of the man’s hands."
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, for a person who is deluded by unreal misconceptions, there arises the fever of passion, the fever of hatred, and the fever of delusion;
yet that fever does not abide internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, as for that which is called "delusion," for what reason is it called "delusion"?
Because, Mañjuśrī, it is utterly liberated from all phenomena; therefore, it is called "delusion."
"Mañjuśrī, likewise, all phenomena have hell as their entrance; this is the dhāraṇī phrase.
He asked, "Blessed One, how is this the dhāraṇī phrase?
He replied, "Mañjuśrī, hells are fabricated by the false inversions of foolish common people; they arise from one's own conceptual construction."
He asked: "Blessed One, where do the hells converge?
The Blessed One replied: "Mañjuśrī, the hells converge in space.
What do you think, Mañjuśrī: do the hells arise from one's own conceptual construction, or do they arise from an intrinsic nature?"
He said: "O Blessed One, it is solely through their own conceptual constructions that all foolish common people perceive the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama.
And by superimposing what does not exist, they experience painful sensations and undergo suffering within all three miserable states."
And just as I, Blessed One, see the hells, so too do I experience the suffering of hell.
It is just as if, Blessed One, some man who has fallen asleep were to perceive himself in his dream as having gone to hell;
he would perceive himself there cast into an iron cauldron, many fathoms deep, boiling and blazing.
There he would experience harsh, bitter, intense, and painful sensations;
there he would perceive a mental burning, and he would become terrified, falling into a state of panic. Upon waking from that state, he would think: "Oh, what suffering!"
"Alas, what suffering!
he would cry out, grieve, and lament.
Then his friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives would ask him: "By what means do you have this suffering?"
He would speak thus to those friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives: "I have experienced the suffering of hell.
He would revile and reproach them, saying: "While I am indeed experiencing the suffering of hell, you ask me further, 'By what means did this suffering of yours come about?'"
Then those friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives would say this to that man: "Do not fear, O man!
You are indeed asleep;
you have not gone out from this house anywhere."
Then, mindfulness arises in him again: "I was asleep;
this was falsely imagined by me.
He then regains a state of mental well-being.
"Just as, Blessed One, that man, through the superimposition of what is non-existent, while asleep and having entered a dream, perceives himself as having gone to hell;
even so, Blessed One, all foolish common people, obscured by the portion of the unreal, conceptualize the sign of a woman.
Having conceptualized the sign of a woman, they perceive themselves as sporting together with them."
To that foolish ordinary person, it occurs thus: "I am a man;
this is a woman; she is my wife."
With his mind obsessed by that desire and attachment, they direct his mind toward the pursuit of wealth.
On that account, he gives rise to quarrels, strife, and disputes;
and for him whose faculties are corrupted, enmity is born.
Having died because of that perversion of perception, he perceives himself as experiencing painful sensations in the hells for many thousands of eons.
It is just as if, Blessed One, the friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives of that man were to say to him: "Do not fear, do not fear, O man!
For you are asleep."
"You have not come from anywhere, nor have you been grasped from here.

In this very way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma to sentient beings who are deluded by the four perversions: "In this there is no woman, no man, no sentient being, no life-force, no person; all these phenomena are unreal."
All these phenomena are non-existent;
all these phenomena are fabricated; all these phenomena are like an illusion.
All these phenomena are like a dream;
all these phenomena are like a magical creation;
all these phenomena are like the moon reflected in water.
Thus it is said in detail:
having heard this Dharma teaching of the Tathāgata, they perceive all phenomena as free from passion;
they perceive all phenomena as free from delusion, being without intrinsic nature and unobstructed.
They pass away with their minds fixed in space;
having passed away, they attain final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In this way, Blessed One, do I see the hells. Thus he spoke.
And it is said in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*: "I have shown the terrors of hell, and many thousands of beings have been struck with awe;
yet there is not a single being here who, having died, goes to a dreadful state of woe."
There are no makers or causes by which the swords, spears, and weapons were created;
yet, through the power of conceptual construction, one perceives those weapons falling upon the body in that state of woe.
Wondrous and delightful, with flowers arrayed, golden palaces shine forth, enchanting;
yet there is no creator whatsoever for them here, for they too are established by the power of a *kalpa*.
The world is conceptualized through the power of conceptual construction; the fool is conceptualized through the grasping at notions.
Yet that grasping is non-grasping and unreal, for conceptual constructions are like illusions and mirages.
Thus, it is established that these entities, being devoid of intrinsic nature and constructed by their own misconceptions, serve as the causes of affliction for the foolish within saṃsāra.
And how things whose nature is false can nevertheless serve as the causes for affliction and purification is to be understood in detail from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.

Here it is asked: If there is no arising of entities from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause, then how is it that the Blessed One stated, "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"? It is said in reply:
This is merely conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), not ultimate truth (*tattva*).
What is to be said regarding the establishment of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)? The establishment of conventional reality is accepted through mere conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatāmātra*);
it is not, however, by accepting any of the four positions, for that would entail the consequence of asserting the existence of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvavāda*).
And because that [position] is illogical:

for when one accepts the mere conditionality of "this" (idaṃpratyayatāmātra), since cause and effect are mutually dependent, there is no establishment by way of intrinsic nature; thus, there is no doctrine of intrinsic nature (sasvabhāvavāda).
Therefore it has been said:
Logicians maintain that suffering is self-created, created by another, created by both, or produced without a cause; but you have stated that it arises dependently.
Here too, he will say: "The agent proceeds in dependence on the action, and the action proceeds in dependence on that agent; we see no other cause for their establishment."
The Blessed One has also stated only this much: "In this regard, this is the conventional designation of phenomena (dharmasaṃketa): namely, when this exists, that comes to be;
with the arising of this, that arises."
Namely: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises, and so forth.
Regarding this, some raise an objection: "Is the certainty that 'entities are unarisen' born of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it not so born?
If it is held to be born of a means of valid cognition, then this must be stated: how many means of valid cognition are there, what are their characteristics, and what are their objects?"
Are they produced from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause?
Alternatively, if they are not born from any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaja*),
that is not tenable.

Since the comprehension of an object of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), an object not yet comprehended cannot be comprehended without the means of valid cognition. Therefore, if there is no comprehension of an object due to the absence of the means of valid cognition, how can this "correct certainty" exist? Thus, it is not tenable to say that "entities are unestablished."

Or, since this certainty of yours will be that "entities are unarisen," for that very reason my position will also be that "all entities exist. And just as this is your certainty— that all phenomena are unarisen— [so too is mine].
In exactly the same way, the arising of all things will also occur for me.

Now, if you have no certainty that all things are unarisen, then, because it is impossible to convince another when one is oneself uncertain, the undertaking of this treatise would be utterly futile; therefore, all things exist as they are not refuted.
It is said: if we were to have what is called a "certainty," it would have to arise either from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or from what is not a valid means of knowledge;
however, such a thing does not exist.
What is the reason?
For here, only when non-determination is possible could there be its opposite, determination, which depends upon it;
but since for us there is not even non-determination at all, [how can there be its opposite?]
In that case, how could there be a certain cognition of what is both contradictory and non-contradictory to it, given its independence from any other related entity,
like the shortness or length of a donkey's horn?
And since such a certain cognition is thus absent, [how can there be any determination?]
In that case, for whose sake shall we postulate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
From where will their number, definition, or object arise—whether their origination is from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause? All of this need not be discussed by us.

If there is no such certainty in every respect, how then is this statement of yours, which has a definitive form—"entities do not arise from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause"—perceived? It is replied:
This statement is certain for the world by means of a reasoning established for itself, but not for the Noble Ones (āryas).
Is it then that noble ones have no rebirth?
By whom has it been said that they either exist or do not exist?
For the ultimate reality for the noble ones is silence.
Therefore, how could there be the occurrence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) therein, such that there might be either its logical establishment or its non-establishment?
For if the Noble Ones do not describe logical establishment, by what means indeed will they now awaken the world to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Indeed, the Noble Ones do not describe logical proof by means of worldly convention;
rather, having accepted for the sake of instructing others that very proof which is well-established from the worldly perspective itself, they instruct the world by means of that very same [proof].
For just as those possessed by passion do not perceive the impurity of the body even though it exists— because they are overcome by perversion—
and instead become afflicted by superimposing an unreal aspect of beauty upon it,
[the Buddha] manifested an emanation of a Tathāgata for the sake of their detachment.

Or, as a god might describe the defects of the body that were previously concealed by the perception of beauty— starting with "In this body there are hairs," and so forth— so that those people, being freed from that perception of beauty, might attain detachment; even so here, the Noble Ones [describe] how beings, because their mental eyes are impaired by the cataract of ignorance, superimpose a perverted intrinsic nature upon things that are in every respect unapprehendable as a self, and further exaggerate some particular quality in certain instances.
Ordinary people suffer;
now the Noble Ones awaken them by means of an argument based precisely on what is commonly accepted by them:
namely, that it is not admitted that an existing jar arises from clay and other such materials.
Thus, since that which already exists prior to its arising continues to exist, let it be concluded that there is no arising.

And just as it is accepted that the sprout does not arise from things that are other, such as flames or embers, so too let it be concluded that it does not arise from the seeds and so forth intended here either.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "This is our experience. But this too has been refuted, because this experience is false.
Because it is an experience,
like the experience of two moons and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia;
therefore, since experience itself is equal to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*), it is not proper to raise an objection based upon it.
Therefore, the first chapter is commenced as an antidote to the superimposition of an erroneous intrinsic nature, namely that "entities are unproduced.
Now, the remaining chapters are commenced for the purpose of refuting whatever specific qualities have been superimposed in various instances.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no distinction whatsoever—such as the goer, the destination, or the act of going—in dependent origination.
Now, it might be argued: "This very worldly convention of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*) has been described by us in our treatise.
In that case, the purpose of this description must be stated;
for that [convention] has been destroyed by fallacious logicians through their formulation of erroneous definitions.
If it is argued that we have correctly stated its definition,
this too is untenable;
for if the world’s perception of the object to be defined were indeed rendered erroneous by sophists through the formulation of a contrary definition, [then our definition would be valid].
For that purpose, the effort would have to be fruitful;
but this is not the case.
Therefore, this effort is indeed futile.

Moreover, if the comprehension of the objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition, then by such questions as "by what are those means of valid cognition themselves determined?", the fault established in the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* remains;
since that has not been refuted, there is no correct indication of their defining characteristics either.

Furthermore: if two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been stated in accordance with the two characteristics—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—does that which possesses these two characteristics exist, or does it not?
If it exists, then since there is another object of cognition (*prameya*), how can there be only two means of valid cognition?
Now, if the characterized object does not exist, then the characteristic also does not exist, being without a basis; how then can there be two means of valid cognition?
For it will be said:
And when the characteristic does not arise, the characterized object is not tenable;
and when the characterized object is not tenable, the characteristic itself is impossible. Thus it is said.

Now, it might be argued: "A *lakṣaṇa* is not that by which something is characterized (*na lakṣyate 'nena*); rather, having applied the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object according to the rule *'kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam'* [Pāṇini 3.3.113], it is a *lakṣaṇa* because that [object] is characterized by it (*lakṣyate tad*)."
Even so, since it is impossible for this [object] to be perceived by itself, the same fault remains because the instrument by which it is perceived must be a distinct entity from the object.
Now, it might be argued: "Since cognition is the instrument [of perception] and it is included within its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), this fault does not arise. To this we reply:
Here, the specific characteristic of entities is that which is their own unique nature, not shared by others;
for example, solidity in the case of earth, the experience of objects in the case of sensation (*vedanā*), and the distinct representation of objects in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Therefore, on the grounds that it is characterized by that [object], and having set aside the etymological derivation that follows common usage, he accepts it as a passive construction (*karmasādhana*).

And by stating "by one who understands the instrumentality of consciousness," it is implied that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is the object (*karman*), while another particular characteristic is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
