Neither a sentient being nor a life-force nor a person is to be found; these phenomena are like foam and the plantain tree.
They are like an illusion, like lightning in the sky, like the moon reflected in water, and like a mirage.
No person whatsoever, having died in this world, transmigrates to or goes to another world;
yet no action ever perishes when performed, for it yields fruit—whether dark or bright—as one wanders through saṃsāra.
There is neither eternalism nor annihilation, nor again is there an accumulation of karma, nor its persistence;
nor does one who has performed an action experience it again, nor does another who has not performed it experience it.
There is no transition, nor is there any returning; nothing exists, yet again, nothing does not exist.
Here, there is neither the purity of seen places nor of movement, nor is there the conduct of beings, for their course is perfectly tranquil.
For the three realms of existence are like a dream—insubstantial, fleeting, broken, and impermanent; they are equal to an illusion.
They have not come from anywhere, nor have they arrived here; the continuums are always empty and signless.
Non-arising, peace, the signless state—this is the domain of the Sugatas, the qualities of the Jinas;
the powers, the dhāraṇīs, and the strength of those with the ten powers—this is the supreme sovereignty of the Buddhas.
It is a collection of the qualities of excellent, pure dharmas; it is the supreme power of retaining qualities and knowledge;
it is the supreme method for the practice of miraculous transformations; and it is the way to attain the excellent five supernormal knowledges.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Examination of Going and Coming," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Faculties of Sight and so forth is the third chapter.

Here it is said: Even though going, the goer, and the destination do not exist, nevertheless, with regard to the established tenets of the teaching (*pravacana*), one must admit the existence of the seer, the seen, the seeing, and so forth.
And so it is stated in the Abhidharma:
"Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind—these are the six faculties; their respective objects are the visible and so forth. (1)
Therefore, it is said that seeing and the other [faculties] exist by way of their own-being; we reply:
they do not exist.
For in this context, "vision" (darśana) refers to the eye because it sees; and visible form (rūpa) is taught as its object. // 1 //
Demonstrating how the visual faculty does not see form, he says:
For the visual faculty does not see its own self;
since it does not see itself, how will it see other things? (2)
In that regard, that very seeing does not see its own self, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
Consequently, due to not seeing its own self, it does not see blue and so forth, just like the auditory faculty and others.
Therefore, seeing does not exist. // 2 //
Even though vision does not see itself, it will nevertheless see other things, just like fire.
For instance, fire burns only other objects and not itself.
Thus, it follows that vision will see only others and not itself; this is highly unreasonable. For:
"The analogy of fire is not sufficient for the establishment of vision."
This example of fire which you have presented for the sake of establishing seeing is not sufficient, not capable, not competent, and is not tenable; this is the meaning. Because:
"That [fire] along with seeing has been refuted by [the analysis of] the being-traversed, the traversed, and the untraversed. (3)
That which exists together with seeing is "with-seeing" (*sadarśana*).

This example of fire (*agni-dṛṣṭānta*) which you have adduced for the sake of establishing [the existence of] seeing has also been answered— that is, refuted— along with the object of the example (*dārṣṭāntika-artha*), by means of its being "with-seeing."
He asks, "By what [means]? and says: "By means of the traversed, the untraversed, and the being-traversed.

Just as that which has been traversed is not being traversed, nor is that which has not yet been traversed, nor is that which is currently being traversed, so too it should be stated in the same way: by fire, that which has already been burned is not being burned, nor is that which has not yet been burned being burned, and so forth.
And just as that which has been traversed, that which has not yet been traversed, and that which is currently being traversed are not being traversed, so too:
first, the seen is not seen; the unseen is certainly not seen;
and that which is being seen, being free from both the seen and the unseen, is not seen.
Such [arguments] are to be stated, etc. // 3 //
And just as it was stated that "the goer does not go so long [as he has not yet gone]," etc.,
so too should it be said that "the burner does not burn so long [as he has not yet burned]," and so forth.

Thus, by means of the analogy of fire together with the examples of the seer and the act of seeing, the refutation is equal for both the "being traversed" (*gamyamāna*), the "traversed" (*gata*), and the "untraversed" (*agata*).
Therefore, it is not tenable that vision is established in the same way as fire.
Consequently, this is proven: like its own self, vision does not see other things either. // 3 //
When there is no seeing whatsoever, then that which sees does not exist;
how, then, is it logical to say that "seeing sees"?
And when, seeing thus, no seeing whatsoever occurs, then—
since for one who does not see there is no possibility of being "seeing," as in the case of a pillar or similar objects—
the designation "seeing" in the sense of "one who sees" is not tenable.

Although the reading "darśanaṃ paśyati" occurs immediately after the word "darśana" for the sake of conforming to the metrical structure of the verse, nevertheless, at the time of commentary, it should be read as "paśyatīti darśanam," for how else would this be logically consistent? // 4 //

Furthermore, regarding the statement "it sees here" (*iha paśyati*), if this is called "seeing" (*darśana*), one must conceive of a connection between the act of seeing and either the eye that has the nature of seeing or the eye that does not have the nature of seeing.
Since neither case is tenable, he says:
Vision does not see at all, nor does non-vision see at all.

First of all, for that which has the nature of vision and is already endowed with the activity of seeing, a further connection with "sees" and so forth is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of two activities of seeing and the consequence of two visions.
Furthermore, non-vision also does not see, because it is devoid of the activity of seeing, like the tip of a finger; this is the intended meaning. When...
Vision does not see at all, nor does non-vision see;
how then can it be logically consistent to say that "vision sees"?
The connection is with this very [word] alone.
But as for those who think: "This mere phenomenon (dharmamātra), being devoid of activity, arises as it arises," [they are wrong];
nothing at all sees any object, because of the absence of action (kriyā).
Therefore, it is established that "seeing does not see," and this is what is being proven here. To this, it is said:
if action were not a constituent part of conventional discourse, [the following would occur].
In that case, even a mere phenomenon (dharmamātra) would not exist, because it would be devoid of activity,
like a flower in the sky; so how could there be a mere phenomenon devoid of activity?

Therefore, if conventional truth is accepted, then action must also be admitted just as the mere phenomenon (dharma) is; but if this is an inquiry into ultimate reality, then you must admit that even the mere phenomenon does not exist, just as action does not.
As it is said in the *Śataka*:
"One who possesses activity is not eternal; there is no activity in that which is omnipresent.
One devoid of activity is equal to a non-existent; why is selflessness not dear to you?"
Therefore, this rule does not subvert the opponent's position, nor do we incur the fault of proving what is already established.

To this, he says: "Indeed, we do not accept that 'seeing' (*darśana*) is a term denoting the agent (karmadhāraya), as in 'that which sees'; rather, it is a term denoting the instrument (karaṇasādhana), as in 'that by means of which one sees. Consequently, the aforementioned fault does not apply."
And he who sees by means of this vision acting as an instrument is the seer; and this exists, whether it be consciousness or the self.
And since the agent exists, seeing is also established. It is said in reply: "By means of seeing itself, the seer should also be understood as explained. (5)

Just as the refutation of seeing was stated by means of the passage beginning with "seeing does not see itself," so too should the refutation of the seer be understood to be like that of seeing. That is to say:
the seer does not at all perceive his own self by means of seeing.
When one does not perceive oneself, how will one perceive others?
Such things should be stated.
Therefore, it is established that, just like seeing, the seer also does not exist. // 5 //
Here it is said: The seer indeed exists, because of the existence of his object and instrument;
for in this world, that which does not exist has neither an object nor an instrument, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, there exists for the seer an instrument, namely seeing, and an object of action, namely that which is to be seen;
therefore, just like a cutter who possesses both an object and an instrument, the seer indeed exists.
To this it is replied:
For neither the object of vision nor the act of seeing exists;
how then could there be a seer? For the object of vision and the act of seeing are dependent upon a seer.
And when that is examined:
"There is no seer apart from seeing, nor is there a seer who is not apart from seeing.
If, in this context, there were some such thing as a "seer," [it would have to exist either apart from or not apart from seeing].
It must either depend upon perception or be independent of it.
In that regard, if it is dependent upon perception, then is this dependence on perception desired while disregarding whether perception itself is established or unestablished?
If it depends on perception, does it depend on a perception that is already established or one that is not yet established?
In that case, the seer is already established and does not depend upon seeing.
What need would there be for a seer who is already established to again depend upon seeing?
For that which is already established is not established yet again.
Now, if the unestablished [seer] were to depend [on seeing],
then because it is unestablished, it would not depend on seeing, just like the son of a barren woman.
Thus, for the time being, there is no seer who exists by depending on seeing while disregarding it.
It has been stated previously that [the seer] exists even when disregarded, because [the act of seeing] is independent of being observed.
Thus, whether the act of seeing is disregarded or not disregarded, when the seer does not exist— then:
Since the seer does not exist, how can there be that which is to be seen and the act of seeing?
If the seer does not exist, the object of seeing and the act of seeing cannot occur, as they would be without a cause; how then could a seer be established through the existence of those two?
To this, it is said: the object of seeing and the act of seeing do indeed exist, because their effect exists. In that regard—
Just as the arising of a son is said to occur in dependence upon the mother and father, so too is the arising of consciousness said to occur in dependence upon the eye and visible form. (7)
Thus, consciousness arises dependent upon the object to be seen and the act of seeing;
from the coming together of these three, there is tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*),
and from contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises simultaneously.
"Craving has that as its condition.
Thus, all four members of existence (bhavāṅga) exist with the seen and the seeing as their causes.
Therefore, because the effect exists, the seen and the seeing must exist. 7.
It is said: these two might exist if there were only the fourfold group beginning with consciousness;
however, because of the absence of the object to be seen and the act of seeing, the fourfold group beginning with consciousness [does not exist].
Regarding the statement "it does not exist," it has been said that because the seer is absent here, both the object of vision and the act of seeing also do not exist.
Therefore, how could there be the fourfold set beginning with consciousness— namely, consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving?
Therefore, consciousness and the other [aggregates] do not exist.
Here it is said: these [factors] certainly exist because their effects exist.
In this context, by the statement "clinging has craving as its condition" and so forth, clinging, becoming, birth, aging, death, and the rest arise from the fourfold beginning with consciousness;
therefore, consciousness and the others exist because their effects exist.
It is said:
Appropriation and the other [links] would exist if the fourfold set beginning with consciousness itself existed;
however, when the fourfold set beginning with consciousness does not exist at all because of the absence of the seen and the seeing, then—
How, moreover, will appropriation and the subsequent factors come to be? // 8 //
The meaning is that grasping and the other [links] do not exist. // 8 //
Now, for the purpose of extending the explanation by analogy to the remaining sense bases (*āyatana*) as was done for the eye, he says:
"Having explained seeing, one should understand hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind—along with the hearer, the audible, and so forth—by means of the explanation of seeing itself. (9)
Thus it is said.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"The eye does not see form, nor does the mind know mental objects;
this is the supreme truth, wherein the world does not penetrate."
"Where the Leader reveals vision through the totality [of conditions], the wise one calls that the ground of conventional designation for the ultimate truth. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
Depending upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises here;
yet the form does not reside in the eye, nor is there any transfer of the form into the eye.
These phenomena are selfless and impure, yet within them the notions of "self" and "purity" are imagined;
this perverted and unreal conceptualization gives rise to visual consciousness as well.
The yogi perceives consciousness as arising from cessation and as having consciousness as its fuel;
he sees it as empty and like an illusion, neither gone anywhere nor come from anywhere.
And so it is said in the *Ācāryopālipṛcchā*:
"The eye sees everything when it is in conjunction; therein, that which lacks the necessary conditions does not see.
Yet the eye does not see form at all; therefore, there is the conceptual construction of conjunction and disjunction."
The eye perceives forms that are beautiful, variegated, and distinguished, depending upon light;
yet by that very [light] through which the eye depends on yoga, the eye never perceives at all.
And even that pleasant sound which is heard has never entered into the interior;
no transition of it is found, yet by the power of conceptual construction, the sound arises. Thus it is said.
Thus it is sung: "Neither song nor dance, nor the sound of musical instruments, should be grasped; for sensual pleasures are like dreams and are delusions for the ignorant.
The ignorant, greedy for their own mental constructions, meet with destruction here; why then should I become like a foolish person, a slave to the afflictions?"
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Examination of the Faculties such as the Eye," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Aggregates, Chapter Four.
Here it is said: If, in this way, the sense-faculties such as the eye do not exist, nor do the aggregates, [then...]
"Since there is no prohibition, the sense-faculties are included therein;
therefore, they too will exist. To this it is said:
It would indeed be so, if the aggregates (skandhas) existed. With reference to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), it is said:
"Form is not perceived apart from the cause of form;
nor is the cause of form seen apart from form. (1)
In that regard, matter is derivative;
its cause consists of the four great elements.
Apart from those, no separate matter—known as visible form, sound, odor, taste, or the tangible—is perceived, just as a cloth is not perceived apart from a jar.
Even as something distinct from form, no cause of form is perceived that is not itself devoid of form. // 1 //
Desiring to establish these two propositions, he says:
If form were devoid of its cause, it would follow that form is without a cause;
yet no object whatsoever exists anywhere that is without a cause. (2)

Just as a cloth, being a distinct entity from a jar, is not caused by the jar, so too, if material form (*rūpa*) were held to be distinct from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are its cause, it would not be caused by those elements.
And there is no object whatsoever anywhere that exists without a cause.
Therefore, because it would entail the fault of being causeless, one must not accept that form exists apart from its causes. // 2 //
Now, demonstrating how there can be no cause of form even when it is separated from form, he says: "If, however, there were a cause of form that was separated from form..."
If the cause of form were to exist as something distinct from the form that is its effect,
then,
just as a bowl (kuṇḍa) established separately from a jar (ghaṭa) is not caused by that jar, [so too would it be].
Thus, if a cause were asserted to exist as something separate from its effect,
that cause would be without an effect;
it would be without a basis.
For the activity of an effect is the proof for a cause's status as a cause;

and since the activity of an effect does not exist as something established independently from a cause that is independent of an effect, a cause that lacks an effect does not exist at all—like the horns of a man, a snake, or a horse—because it would be without a basis. Thus he says:
And there is no cause that does not have an effect. // 3 //
Thus [ends section] 3.
Now, if this cause of form is asserted, is it asserted as a cause when form exists or when it does not exist?
It is untenable in either case; thus he says:
"When form already exists, a cause of form is not tenable."
When form does not exist, a cause for form is not tenable. // 4 //
If form already exists, what need is there for a cause of form?
If form does not exist and is not present, what need is there for a cause of form,
or for whom is that cause imagined?
Therefore, even if form does not exist, a cause of form is not tenable. // 4 //
Now, it might be argued: "Even if such a cause for form is not possible, nevertheless, the effect—form—is found to exist; therefore, because of its existence, the cause must also exist."
It might be so, if form were an effect;
but it is not,
because form without a cause is simply not possible at all.
It has already been explained how the cause of form does not exist.
Since there is no cause, how could there be a causeless effect, namely form?
By means of this double negation with emphasis—"not at all, not at all"—he demonstrates that its being causeless is utterly undesirable.
And since form, when examined in every way, does not exist in this manner,
therefore the yogi who perceives reality—
One should not conceptualize any conceptual constructions pertaining to form. // 5 //

The meaning is that one should not conceptually construct any [notions] based on the object of form—such as the distinctions of being with resistance or without resistance, visible or invisible, past or future, blue, yellow, and so forth. // 5 //
Furthermore, if this cause of form is asserted to produce an effect, would it produce an effect similar [to itself] or dissimilar?
Since it is untenable in either case, he says:
"It is not tenable that the effect is similar to the cause."
It is not tenable that an effect can be dissimilar to its cause. // 6 //
In this context, the cause of form (*rūpa*) consists of the essential natures of solidity, fluidity, heat, and mobility.
Derived form (*bhautika*), however, is twofold: internal, consisting of the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the basis for the five visual consciousnesses and so forth;

and external, consisting of the sense bases (*āyatana*) such as visible form, which are characterized by being the objects of apprehension for visual consciousness and the rest, and do not possess the nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Therefore, because they possess distinct characteristics, there is no similarity whatsoever between cause and effect, just as there is none with nirvāṇa; thus, it is logically untenable that an effect is similar to its cause.
Furthermore, a mutual relationship of cause and effect is not observed among things that are similar, such as rice seeds and the like; for this reason—
It is not tenable that the effect is similar to the cause;
nevertheless, it is also not tenable that the effect is dissimilar to the cause.
The intention is that [it] is like nirvāṇa precisely because its characteristics are distinct. // 6 //
And just as this form is not tenable in any way when analyzed,
so too are feeling and the others; pointing this out by extension, he says:
The sequence for feeling, mind, perception, and mental formations is in every respect exactly the same as that of form; indeed, the process is identical for all phenomena whatsoever. (7)
All [factors] beginning with sensation (vedanā) are likewise to be applied equally through the analysis of form (rūpa).
For just as the emptiness of a single phenomenon is intended to be established by the Mādhyamika, so too is that of all phenomena. // 7 //
Therefore:

"Whoever should offer a rebuttal during the formal analysis (vigraha) once emptiness has been established—for him, everything remains unrebutted, as it becomes identical to that which is yet to be proven. (8)
In this context, "refutation" (*vigraha*) refers to the criticism of the opponent's position.

When the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvavāda*) has been refuted by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) acting as the reason—namely, that form (*rūpa*) is devoid of intrinsic nature—if the opponent should offer a rebuttal, saying: "Sensation (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates certainly exist," [then one must respond].
In the same way, [the argument] that "form also exists" remains entirely unrefuted by him;
for the existence of feeling and the other [aggregates] should be understood as being equal to the existence of form, which is the very point to be proven.
Just as form is non-existent when analyzed in terms of its identity with or difference from its own causes, so too is feeling conditioned by contact,
and perception co-arising with consciousness.

Formations have ignorance as their condition, and consciousness has formations as its condition; yet when examined in terms of identity or difference from its own causes, such as contact and so forth, it is found not to exist. Thus, all of this is "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*). Just as feeling and the other factors are equal to the probandum, [so too is this].

In this way, all categories of entities—such as the characterized and the characteristic, cause and effect, whole and parts, and so forth—are likewise equal to the "probandum" (sādhya) in terms of their nature. How, then, could there be any possibility of refuting the opponent?

The Master teaches that since every statement of his is "equal to the probandum," the Mādhyamika must not accept the status of being "equal to the probandum" even when attempting a refutation throughout the entire treatise. // 8 //
And just as this method was prescribed for refuting the positions of others, so it is also at the time of exposition; thus he says:
"If someone should offer a criticism during the exposition when [the opponent] has spoken in terms of emptiness..."
Everything [stated] by him becomes unrefuted and equal to that which is to be proven. // 9 //

Even at the time of explanation, if one who is like a student should raise an objection or a censure, that objection or censure of his should also be understood as being "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*), just as before. As it has been said:
"He who is the seer of one entity is traditionally held to be the seer of all."
"The emptiness of one thing is indeed the emptiness of all things. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Āryagaganagañjasamādhisūtra*:
"By means of a single dharma, one comprehends all dharmas as being like an illusion or a mirage."
Ungraspable, void, hollow, non-eternal, and impermanent—he goes to the seat of awakening before long. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*:
"Just as the notion of self is known [to be empty], so too is the intellect applied everywhere;
all phenomena are of that same nature—pure and like space."
"By means of one, he knows all; by means of one, he sees all.
Even after cultivating this to a great extent, pride does not arise in him.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Examination of the Aggregates," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Elements: The Fifth Chapter.
Here he says: The elements (dhātu) exist because there is no negation [of them].
And it was said by the Blessed One: "O Great King, this person (puruṣapudgala) consists of six elements," and so forth.
Therefore, from the reading of the scripture, the aggregates (skandha) and sense-bases (āyatana) must likewise exist, just like the elements.
It is said: the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas) would exist if they were indeed the elements (dhātus).
How so? It is said:
No space exists whatsoever prior to the characteristic of space;
for if it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without characteristics. (1)
In that regard, six elements have been mentioned, namely: earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
With respect to space among these, the refutation is stated by way of defining its essential nature.
Here, non-obstruction is said to be the characteristic of space.

Since space would have to be the characterized object (*lakṣya*) prior to its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)— namely, non-obstruction— it follows that, because the characteristic has not yet arisen, there is no space in the form of a characterized object prior to that characteristic of non-obstruction.
And when this is the case—
No space exists whatsoever prior to the characteristic of space;
for if it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without characteristics.
For instance, let that which is without characteristics (alakṣaṇa) proceed; yet, in its absence, space would not exist, like a flower in the sky. Thus he says:
"Nowhere does any entity without characteristics exist anywhere."
Thus it is said. Here [the opponent] says: "The application of a characteristic must occur in relation to a characterized object;
because of the existence of that [characteristic], the characterized object also exists.
This too is not so, because—
If an entity lacks the characteristic of existence, where could a characteristic possibly apply? (2)

It has been stated that prior to its characteristics, an entity devoid of characteristics does not exist. Therefore, since an entity that is non-existent, unapprehendable, and lacking characteristics does not exist, where indeed would characteristics now operate? Thus, there is no operation of characteristics. // 2 //
Furthermore, when this characteristic (lakṣaṇa) functions, does it function with respect to that which possesses a characteristic or with respect to that which lacks a characteristic?
It is untenable in either case; thus he says:
"The functioning of a characteristic does not occur in that which lacks a characteristic, nor does it occur in that which possesses a characteristic."
Nor does it proceed elsewhere than from that which possesses characteristics and that which lacks characteristics. // 3 //
In that regard, there is no occurrence of characteristics in that which lacks characteristics, just as in the case of a donkey’s horn.
Nor is the occurrence of characteristics tenable even in an entity that possesses characteristics, because it would serve no purpose.
For what further function could characteristics perform for an entity that already possesses characteristics and is thus established?
In this way, there would be an infinite regress and an over-extension;
for that [entity] could never be without its characteristic, and thus the application of characteristics would result in being eternal.
And this is not desired.
Therefore, even with respect to an entity that possesses characteristics (*salakṣaṇa*), the application of a characteristic is not possible, because there is no purpose for it.
To this, one might say: "It will apply elsewhere, to something other than that which possesses characteristics and that which lacks characteristics. It is replied:
It does not apply elsewhere, even from that which possesses characteristics and that which lacks characteristics.
What is the reason? Because of non-existence.
If it possesses characteristics, it is not without characteristics.
Now, if it is without characteristics, it is not with characteristics;
therefore, to say that it is both with characteristics and without characteristics is a contradiction,
and what is contradictory cannot exist.

Therefore, precisely because it is impossible, the operation of a defining characteristic is not tenable with respect to that which possesses a defining characteristic nor with respect to that which lacks one. // 3 //
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if the application of characteristics does not occur, nevertheless the characterized object exists. This too is not the case; because:
"And when the characteristics do not occur, the characterized object is not tenable."
When the very occurrence of a characteristic does not exist, how could there be a characterized object?
The intended meaning is that it is simply not possible.
To this, he says: "The occurrence of a characteristic has been negated by you, but not the characteristic itself."
And therefore, the characterized object exists, because the characteristic exists. It is said:
"And in the absence of the characterized object, the characteristic is also impossible. (4)

And it has been established that when the characteristic does not occur, the characterized object is not tenable. Thus, when the characterized object is untenable, the characteristic itself is also impossible, because it would lack a basis. (4)
And when such a characteristic does not exist, then that which was said—that the characterized exists because of the existence of the characteristic—is not tenable; and since this is so:
therefore, the characterized does not exist, nor indeed does the characteristic exist.
Thus is the conclusion.

Here it is said: Even if the characterized and the characteristic do not exist, space nevertheless exists; and since space is an existent entity (*bhāva*), it must be either the characterized or the characteristic.
Therefore, both the characterized and the characteristic must exist.
To show that this too is incorrect, he says:
"An entity (bhāva) that is devoid of both the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) does not exist at all. (5)
How neither the object of definition nor the definition exists has been explained previously;
when these two are absent, [the following applies].
Then, because it is devoid of both the characterized and the characteristic, space does not exist, like a flower in the sky. // 5 //
If space is not an existent entity, then let it be a non-existent;
yet even this is not the case, because:
And when an existent thing does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?
When space is not an existent thing, then, in the absence of an existent thing, of what could non-existence be conceived?
For it will be said: "If an entity is not established, then non-existence is certainly not established;
for people describe non-existence as the alteration of an entity."
Therefore, since existence and non-existence do not exist, even as a non-entity, space cannot come into being.
Space is established as the absence of form (*rūpa*);
for if form were present, then space could only be defined as the absence of that form.
And when, according to the reasoning already stated, form itself does not exist, then of what absence could space be the designation?
To this, he says: "Existence and non-existence indeed do exist."
Because of the existence of an examiner of that [matter].
And you are indeed an examiner of both existence and non-existence, since you yourself have said:
"If existence does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?"
Thus [it is said]. Therefore, because you, the examiner of existence and non-existence, exist, both existence and non-existence—which are the objects of examination—also exist.
To this it is replied: even this is untenable, because—
And who, possessing a nature distinct from both existence and non-existence, could perceive existence and non-existence?
If existence and non-existence were to exist,
then the examiner of those two would have to be either an existent or a non-existent.
If it is held that he is an existent, then of that...
"Free from both the characterized and the characteristic, even an entity does not exist"—
this is the refutation that has been stated.
Now, as for non-existence:
And if an entity does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?
This objection has already been stated here.
Furthermore, there exists no third category of thing that possesses properties dissimilar to both existence and non-existence.
"There is no one who understands these two, nor any examiner of existence and non-existence.
For this very reason, the Blessed One said:
"He who understands both existence and non-existence is never attached to any phenomena."
"He who is never attached to any phenomena practices the signless concentration.
Likewise:
"Even he who contemplates phenomena as empty is weak and has entered upon a wrong path."
The phenomena proclaimed as syllables are empty; they are both beyond syllables and yet spoken of as syllables.
One who contemplates phenomena as peaceful and utterly tranquil—even that contemplation has never arisen as a real entity.
All mental discursive thoughts are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); awaken to phenomena as subtle and inconceivable.
Thus is the detailed exposition. // 6 //
Now, concluding the point thus established, he says:
Therefore, space is neither an entity nor a non-entity, neither the characterized object nor the characteristic.
Thus: "And just as space is, so too are the five other elements equal to space. (7)

The meaning is that the five remaining elements, beginning with earth, should also be fully understood as being like space—devoid of existence and non-existence, the characterized and the characteristic, and the nature of conceptual construction. // 7 //

Thus, while the intrinsic nature of things is established in this way, those of small intelligence— whose mental eyes are impaired by the cataracts of ignorance, who have practiced throughout beginningless saṃsāra, and whose vision is distorted regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth— have strayed from the true path that leads to nirvāṇa through the vision of the non-intrinsic nature (naiḥsvabhāvya) which is free from error; they perceive both existence and non-existence.
They do not perceive the auspicious pacification of the objects of vision among all phenomena. // 8 //

They do not perceive that which is to be seen as tranquility, characterized by auspiciousness (*śiva*), free from the entire web of conceptual construction, whose nature is the cessation of both knowledge and the object of knowledge—the auspicious (*śiva*) ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svabhāva*).

Because of their dull intellect, they do not see the ultimate, which is undecaying, immortal, non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*), nirvāṇa, and whose nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*), remaining instead attached to existence and non-existence.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*:
The nihilist goes to an evil rebirth, while the non-nihilist goes to a happy rebirth;
through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, one who relies on non-duality attains liberation. Thus it is said.
And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"Both 'it exists' and 'it does not exist' are extremes; 'purity' and 'impurity'—these too are extremes.
Therefore, having avoided both extremes, the wise person does not take a stand even in the middle."

"This is a dispute over 'it exists' and 'it does not exist'; this is a dispute over 'purity' and 'impurity. Through the attainment of dispute, suffering is not stilled; through the attainment of non-dispute, suffering is ceased. Therefore, it is simply impossible that nirvāṇa is realized by means of a worldly path. // 8 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Examination of the Elements," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The sixth chapter: An Examination of Passion and the Passionate One.
Here it is said: The aggregates (skandhas), sense-bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) do indeed exist.
Why? Because the affliction (saṃkleśa) based upon them is perceived.

In this case, that which does not exist cannot have the perception of a basis for affliction, just as the son of a barren woman cannot have the perception of a basis for the daughter of a barren woman;
yet the afflictions such as attachment and so forth, which are the cause of affliction, do exist.

As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, the foolish, unlearned worldling, following after conventional designations, having seen forms with the eye that are conducive to joy, becomes attached to them.
Being attached, he gives rise to passion. Being impassioned, he performs actions born of passion, hatred, and delusion, through body, speech, and mind," and so forth in detail.
It is said:
the aggregates, bases, and elements would exist if afflictions were nothing other than desire and so forth.
Here, when this desire is conceptually constructed by foolish ordinary people, would it be constructed in relation to a person who possesses desire, or in relation to one who does not?
And since it is not tenable in either case, he says:

If the one who is impassioned were to exist prior to passion, being devoid of passion, then passion would arise in dependence upon him; thus, passion would exist only when the impassioned one exists. (1)
In this context, passion (*rāga*), attachment (*sakti*), determination (*adhyavasāna*), clinging (*saṅga*), and fixation (*abhiniveśa*) are synonyms. One who is impassioned is the locus of passion.
If that impassioned one were, prior to passion, devoid of passion and excluded from passion, [then he would not be impassioned].
In that case, passion would arise dependent upon one who is already impassioned and obscured by passion;
thus, it would follow that passion exists within the impassioned person.
But this is not possible.
If one who is free from passion were to be impassioned, it would follow that even Arhats are impassioned. // 1 //
If this is so, and there is no passion when the one who is impassioned does not exist, then let there be passion even when the one who is impassioned does not exist.
To show that this too is untenable, he says:
Furthermore, if the one who is impassioned does not exist, how indeed will passion come to be?
When there is no passion even when the one who is impassioned exists, then how will passion— which lacks a basis— be established when the one who is impassioned does not exist?
For indeed, in the absence of a fruit, its ripening is not possible.
Here he says: Even though passion has been refuted by you, nevertheless, the impassioned one exists,
because he has not been refuted.
Furthermore, it is not logical for one to be impassioned without passion;
therefore, this [passion] also exists. To this, it is said:
If there were passion, then there would be one who is impassioned.
Since this impassioned person who is sought must be conceptualized either as existing when passion exists or as existing when it does not exist—it is not tenable in either case; thus he says:
Whether passion exists or does not exist, this same sequence applies even to the one who is impassioned. // 2 //
In that regard, if one were to conceive of a person as "attached" while passion exists,
then this very same sequence of the impossibility of passion just mentioned applies equally to the "attached" one as well:
if the attached one were to exist prior to passion, he would have to be devoid of passion.
And so forth. Now, if one who is impassioned (*rakta*) is asserted to exist even when passion (*rāga*) is absent, this too is illogical. Because:
"Furthermore, if passion is absent, how indeed could there be one who is impassioned?"
Thus, therefore, even the one who is impassioned does not exist.
And because of the non-existence of both passion and the impassioned one, the aggregates and so forth also do not exist. // 2 //

To this, he says: Indeed, there is no occurrence of passion (*rāga*) and the impassioned (*rakta*) in a temporal sequence such that this refutation would apply; rather, passion and the impassioned arise simultaneously.
For it is by means of passion, which is co-existent with the mind, that the mind becomes impassioned.
And that [desire] is "red" (attached).
Therefore, passion and the impassioned one certainly exist.
To this it is replied: even so—
Furthermore, it is not logical for passion and the impassioned one to arise simultaneously;
even simultaneous production is not logical for passion and the impassioned one, because they would then exist independently of one another. (3)
The intention is that [they cannot exist] because they coexist, like the left and right horns of a cow. // 3 //
Furthermore, regarding this passion and the one who is impassioned, would their coexistence be conceived as identity or as difference?
In that regard, if it were identity, that is not tenable; because:
There is no coexistence in identity;
why is that? He says: "For a thing does not exist together with itself."
For one's own self, being non-different from passion, is not designated as "together with passion."
Now, he states that even in the case of separateness, there can be no coexistence:
"Furthermore, how could coexistence possibly exist in the case of separateness? (4)
For indeed, the coexistence of light and darkness, or of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, when they are separate entities, has never been observed. // 4 //
Furthermore:
If coexistence were to exist in identity, it would exist even without a companion;
if coexistence were to exist in difference, it would exist even without a companion. (5)
If coexistence were to exist in identity, then wherever there is identity, there would be coexistence; consequently, even a single entity would possess coexistence.

Likewise, if coexistence were asserted to exist in difference, then wherever there is difference, there would be coexistence; thus, a solitary cow, standing apart and distinct from horses and other animals, would possess coexistence.
It may be so. // 5 //
Furthermore:

If there were coexistence in separateness, what would be established regarding passion and the impassioned one? For how could there be coexistence between those two if their existence were separate from each other? (6)
If the coexistence of passion and the impassioned one is postulated,
is their separate existence established?
Is the impassioned one established independently of passion, such that there could be a coexistence between the two?
For coexistence is observed only between a cow and a horse, which are established as separate entities;
however, passion and the impassioned one are not established as separate entities in this way, and thus there is no coexistence between these two. // 6 //

Alternatively, considering that there can be no coexistence for two things that are not established as distinct from one another— if you nevertheless postulate a separate existence for passion (*rāga*) and the impassioned (*rakta*).
He asks: "What is the point now of postulating a simultaneous existence (sahabhāva) that accomplishes nothing?"— "Why do you postulate a simultaneous existence of those two? (7)
For the sake of establishing passion (*rāga*) and the impassioned one (*rakta*), their coexistence (*sahabhāva*) is postulated.
Since that coexistence does not exist between two things that are not established separately, you must therefore admit that they are established separately.
But if this is so, since they are already established, what is the purpose of their coexistence?
Now,
if you desire their coexistence on the grounds that they are not established separately—
thinking that since passion and the impassioned one are not established individually, you therefore wish for these two to exist together— then:
And since that [conjunction] does not exist between two things established separately, you desire separateness once again for the sake of establishing their coexistence. (8)
But if this is the case, and a state of mutual dependence remains established, then upon the establishment of which one now could there be the establishment of the other? // 8 //
Furthermore: Since separate existence is not established, coexistence is not established either.
In the presence of what kind of separate existence do you desire coexistence? (9)

That separate existence which is independent of co-existence does not exist at all; since it is impossible for the establishment of co-existence to occur when such a separate existence exists, [the author], expressing this impossibility, says: "In what kind of separate existence do you desire co-existence to exist? (9)
Thus, concluding that passion and the impassioned one are not established through the consideration of the aforementioned analysis, he says:
"In this way, the establishment of passion by means of the impassioned one occurs neither simultaneously nor non-simultaneously.
And just as there is no establishment of passion and the impassioned one either through temporal sequence or through coexistence, [so it is with all things].
Extending this principle to all entities, he says: "In the same way as passion, the establishment of all phenomena occurs neither simultaneously nor non-simultaneously. (10)

Thus, the non-establishment of those who are hostile through hatred or deluded by ignorance is to be applied in the same manner as [the non-establishment] of those who are impassioned by passion. // 10 //
Therefore it was said by the Blessed One:

"He who would be impassioned, or that wherein he would be impassioned, or that whereby he would be impassioned; he who would be corrupted, or that wherein he would be corrupted, or that whereby he would be corrupted."
Whoever might be deluded, or that wherein one might be deluded, or that by which one might be deluded— he does not perceive that phenomenon, he does not apprehend that phenomenon.
Not perceiving and not apprehending that phenomenon, being without attachment, without hatred, and without delusion, with a mind free from inversion, he is said to be "composed."
He is called one who has crossed over and reached the further shore;
he is called one who has attained security;
he is called one who has attained fearlessness.

He is called one whose taints are exhausted; he is free from defilements, has attained mastery, is well-liberated in mind, well-liberated in wisdom, a noble thoroughbred, highly fortunate, one who has accomplished what was to be done,
completed his task, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is well-liberated through perfect knowledge.
One who has attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states is called a *śramaṇa*;
such is the detailed explanation.
Likewise: Those who,

having understood that passion, hatred, pride, and delusion are by nature produced by the cause of conceptual construction and proceed falsely, neither conceptualize them nor seek detachment from them here— those for whom all states of existence have been clearly discerned, [attain liberation] swiftly.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Examination of Passion and the One Who is Passionate," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Conditioned, the Seventh Chapter.
Here it is said: The conditioned natures do indeed exist, because the aggregates, bases, and elements possess the characteristics of the conditioned, such as arising and so forth.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
Of the conditioned, monks, arising is discerned, and passing away is also discerned."
Regarding the phrase "there is also the alteration of duration":
that which is non-existent, such as the horn of a donkey, does not possess characteristics such as birth and so forth.
Therefore, because the characteristics of the conditioned are taught, the aggregates, bases, and elements must indeed exist.
It is said:
According to your own view, the aggregates, bases, and elements would indeed have a conditioned nature,
provided that their characteristic were solely birth and so forth.
In this context, this arising (utpāda), which is intended as a characteristic of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa), is itself intended to be either conditioned or unconditioned. Regarding that:
if arising is conditioned, then the triad of characteristics is applicable there.

The collection of the three characteristics is the "triple characteristic" (*trilakṣaṇī*). Since this [triple characteristic] is by nature inseparable from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), as it consists of the collection of arising, duration, and cessation, if one were to conceive that arising itself is conditioned,
then the triple characteristic would necessarily follow even in the case of arising.
Consequently, origination would be a characterizable entity (*lakṣya*) like form and so forth,
rather than being a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, if the triad of characteristics is not admitted even for origination itself, [then it cannot be a characteristic].
Then, because it would lack the three characteristics, its status as a conditioned characteristic would be lost, like space; thus he says:
"Now, if arising were unconditioned, how could it be a characteristic of the conditioned? (1)
Thus, the intention is that this is not a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). // 1 //

Furthermore, these [characteristics] such as arising (utpāda) and so forth, when being conceived as the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛta), would they be conceived as characteristics either individually or separately, or collectively or simultaneously? It is said that neither way is tenable: api ca / ime utpādādayaḥ saṃskṛtasya lakṣaṇatvena parikalpyamānā vyastā vā pṛthagvā lakṣaṇatvena parikalpyeran, samastā vā sahabhūtā vā? ubhayathā ca na yujyata ityāha—

The three [characteristics] beginning with arising, when taken separately, are not capable of performing the function of defining the conditioned; yet how could they exist together in one place at one time? (2)
In that regard, taken individually, they are not applicable to the function of characterization.

If stability and destruction were absent at the time of arising, then arising would be impossible as a characteristic of the conditioned, like space, which is devoid of both stability and destruction.
Furthermore, if arising and destruction were absent at the time of stability, [the same fault would follow].
In that case, there would have to be the persistence of something devoid of those [characteristics];
yet, since an entity devoid of arising and ceasing does not exist at all, it is not logical for such a non-existent thing to persist, like a flower in the sky. Furthermore:
Furthermore, for that which is endowed with stability, there could not subsequently be a connection with impermanence as well, because it would be overcome by a property contradictory to it.
Now, it might be argued: "Having first been eternal, it later becomes non-eternal."
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to be both eternal and non-eternal; therefore, there can be no persistence for that which is devoid of arising and ceasing.
Likewise, if persistence and arising were absent at the time of cessation, then even destruction would not exist for something like a sky-flower, which is unarisen and lacks persistence.
Thus, taken individually, origination and the others are not capable—that is to say, not sufficient—for the function of defining [the conditioned].
Now he says that even all [the alternatives] together are not tenable:
"How could they all exist in one place at once?"— that is,
in a single entity.
The intention is that at one time, because they are mutually contradictory— like passion and dispassion, or like light and darkness— they are not logically possible [to coexist].
What conscious person would accept that at the very moment an entity arises, it simultaneously exists and perishes?
Therefore, all [three] characteristics, such as arising and the rest, lack the capacity to function as the characteristics of a conditioned phenomenon. // 2 //
Now, as for what was said, "If arising is conditioned," and so forth—
if by that the three characteristics are obtained or necessarily follow for arising and the others, then what is the fault?
If it is argued that there is no fault even if [the unconditioned] is unconditioned, it is said in reply:
"Arising, abiding, and ceasing are the characteristics of the conditioned."
If it exists, there is an infinite regress; if it does not exist, then they are not conditioned phenomena. // 3 //
"But surely the fault has already been established in both positions;
what, then, is the purpose of stating it again? True, the fault was indeed mentioned, but it was certainly not by the Teacher.
What then [is the view] of the commentator?
Alternatively, the Master has stated it once again for the sake of clarifying the very same point previously asserted by means of stating further refutations:
"If another set of characteristics of the conditioned, such as arising and so forth, is desired for arising, duration, and destruction..."
In that case, there would be one for them, and another for those, and yet another for those, resulting in the fault of infinite regress.

And since there would be the fault of infinite regress, what could exist prior [to another] such that something else might arise at a subsequent time? The intention is that because there is no such established order, the arising and so forth of things are impossible.
Alternatively, because arising is primary, its refutation was stated first.
But now, [it is said] "in general. If these do not exist, they are not conditioned; this meaning has already been explained. // 3 //
On this point, the Sāṃmitīyas say: There are indeed productions and so forth of production and the other characteristics,
yet there is no consequence of infinite regress,
because the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) are mutually productive of one another.
Because here, when a conditioned phenomenon—whether wholesome or afflicted—is arising, it arises as the fifteenth element including itself:
that phenomenon, its arising, its possession (*samanvāgama*), its duration, its aging, and its impermanence.
If that phenomenon is afflicted, [it arises with these fifteen factors].
For that [latter], there is false liberation;
but if it is wholesome, for that there is right liberation.
If it is conducive to liberation, it possesses the quality of being conducive to liberation; if it is not conducive to liberation, it possesses the quality of not being conducive to liberation.
Such is this retinue.
Now, regarding the arising of arising, and so on up to the non-leaving-nature of the non-leaving-nature—this is the retinue of the retinue.
In that regard, this primary arising, excluding itself, produces fourteen other factors.
However, the secondary characteristic known as "the arising of arising" produces only the primary arising itself.
Likewise, up to the quality of non-emancipation (*anairyāṇikatā*), it does not cause the fourteen factors to attain emancipation;
the meaning is that it does not lead them to that nirvana.
However, the non-leaving nature of that which is not conducive to leaving does not lead to liberation.
Thus, avoiding the fallacy of infinite regress regarding origination and so forth, he says:
"The origination of origination is merely the origination of the primary origination."
Furthermore, the primary arising of arising gives rise to the arising of arising. // 4 //
For origination is twofold:
one is primary origination,
and the other is that which is designated as the "origination of origination."
This is because it is the arising of arising.
In that regard, this arising which is designated as the "arising of arising" is solely the producer of the primary arising.
Now, if the primary origination (*maula-utpāda*) produces that origination which is designated as "origination-of-origination" (*utpādotpāda*),
then, because they are thus mutually established, the three characteristics of origination and so forth do indeed exist.
And there is no consequence of an infinite regress. // 4 //

To this it is replied: If, according to you, the "arising of arising" is the arising of the primary arising, how will that [secondary arising], which has not been produced by the primary, produce it? (5)

If it is your view that the "arising of arising" is the producer of the "primary arising," then how, being itself unproduced by the primary arising, will the "arising of arising" now produce the primary arising? // 5 //
Now, if you think that once the "arising of arising" has been produced by the primary arising, it will in turn produce the primary [arising], this too is incorrect; thus he says:
"If that [arising of arising], having been produced by your primary [arising], produces the primary..."
How can that which is primary and has not been produced by it produce it?

If that production called "the production of production" (utpādotpāda), having been produced by the primary production (maula), were to produce the primary production, then how could that primary production— which has not yet been produced by the "production of production" and is therefore non-existent— produce the "production of production"? Therefore, it is not tenable to say that the "production of production," having been produced by the primary production, produces the primary production.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of the relationship between that which is produced and that which produces in mutual dependence, that very same consequence of infinite regress follows; thus, there is no arising. // 6 //
To this it is said: "The primary origination (*mūlotpāda*), while itself originating, produces the origination-of-origination (*utpādotpāda*);
that very origination-of-origination will then bring about the primary origination. We reply:
"Granted, this [primary origination], while originating, might produce this [origination-of-origination]."
If this unborn one were able to produce this [unborn thing].
If the arising consisting of desire, while itself being produced, were to produce another arising,
it would be so provided that this very [arising], being unborn, were capable of producing another unborn [arising].
For that which is called "being produced" is indeed the future.
The intention is that it is not logical to ask how that which is unborn can produce [anything]; the same should be said regarding the "production of production" as well. // 7 //

To this, he says: Indeed, there is no further arising of arising such that an infinite regress would result. What then? Just as a lamp illuminates both itself and others, so too arising brings about both itself and others. (8)

Just as a lamp, by virtue of having illumination as its intrinsic nature, illuminates both itself and objects such as a jar, so too arising, by virtue of having arising as its intrinsic nature, will bring about the arising of both itself and the other. // 8 //
It is said: This might be so if the lamp were to illuminate both itself and others;
but it is not so. For:
There is no darkness in the lamp, nor where it is situated.
What does a lamp illuminate? For illumination is indeed the destruction of darkness.
In this context, illumination is the destruction of darkness.
And darkness cannot exist within the lamp's own self because of their mutual contradiction; for how could that which destroys darkness possess the nature of illuminating its own self?
Furthermore, there is no darkness in the place where a lamp stands, such that the lamp could possess the quality of illuminating others by destroying that darkness.
For this reason as well, the lamp does not possess the capacity to illuminate both itself and others.
And since this is the case, then—just like a lamp—the production of arising as that which produces both itself and others will not be possible;
thus, this [position] is untenable. // 9 //
Here it is said: As for what was stated—that there is no darkness in a lamp—it is indeed proper to say that only when darkness has been destroyed;
for it is by the very arising of the lamp that darkness is dispelled.
In that case, it is logical that there is no darkness in the lamp, and where the lamp is, there too there is no darkness.
If darkness were not destroyed by the lamp,

then even when the lamp has arisen, jars and other objects would not be perceived— just as when it has not yet arisen— because there would be no destruction of the darkness, remaining in the same state as before.
Therefore, the lamp indeed possesses illumination characterized by the destruction of darkness, and that [illumination] is produced by this lamp as it arises. To this it is replied:
How can darkness be destroyed by a lamp that is in the process of arising?
For when a lamp, while not yet having arisen, reaches the darkness... (10)
In this case, because light and darkness cannot exist simultaneously, there is no meeting between them.
And since there is thus no meeting, how is it now logical to conceive that darkness is destroyed by a lamp that is currently arising? In what manner could such a thing be possible?
And since a lamp, as it is thus arising, does not reach darkness, it should be concluded that, precisely because it does not reach it, the lamp does not illuminate anything at all. // 10 //

Now, if you think that just as knowledge destroys ignorance without reaching it, just as the eye sees form without reaching it, and just as a magnet attracts iron without reaching it, so too a lamp will destroy darkness without reaching it— this also is without substance, as he says:
Or if darkness were destroyed by a lamp without even reaching it, then a person staying here would destroy the darkness residing throughout the entire world. (11)
If darkness were destroyed by a lamp without even reaching it,
then a lamp situated here would destroy the darkness located throughout the entire world.
The intention is that because it has not yet been reached, it is as if situated nearby.
By this principle, ignorance is destroyed by knowledge,
just as form is perceived by the eye.
Just as iron is attracted by a magnet, such examples and others like them should be understood as being "equal to the point to be proven" (sādhyasama).
If it is argued that even though there is no contact, objects such as magnets and the like will perform their respective functions only when situated in a suitable location,
that too is not tenable; for if there were no contact, they would behave the same toward an object situated at a distant place as they would toward one situated at an adjacent place.

Since they have not been attained, it is not logical for even those situated in a suitable location to possess the state of being situated in a suitable location; how, then, will the performance of their own effects by those situated in a suitable location be established?
If it is argued that this is observed in the world, it is not so.
For it is not as you imagine that things are seen in the world;

because people in the world do not first engage in reflections on attainment and non-attainment regarding such objects as lamps, and then imagine that they possess the power of illumination and so forth. Rather, without engaging in the aforementioned analysis, [people simply observe] that "darkness has been destroyed by the lamp."
He maintains that there is the seeing of forms by the eye, the attracting of iron by a magnet-stone, and so forth;
or let the world view things in this way.
However, at the time of investigating reality (*tattva*), because the world [of conventional experience] lacks authority, it cannot effect a sublation [of the investigation].
Thus, for the time being, manifestation without reaching [the object] is untenable;
even if there is reaching, the grasping of the object and so forth remains untenable.
For attainment occurs when there is oneness;
and when there is oneness, then—just like its own essential nature—there is no seeing, drawing toward, or other such activities.

Although this investigation into acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth does not apply to worldly convention—since it is false in nature due to its lack of logical justification—it nevertheless must be introduced into the analysis of reality (*tattva*).
Let there be no acceptance of a position that lacks justification even from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); enough of this digression. // 11 //
And if you imagine that a lamp illuminates both itself and others, then you must also imagine that it conceals both itself and others, which are the very opposites of darkness; thus he says:
"If a lamp illuminates both itself and others..."
Darkness, too, will undoubtedly obscure both itself and others. (12)
Because it is an adversary, darkness, like a lamp, will perform an activity directed toward both itself and others; consequently, it will obscure itself just as it obscures others.
And if darkness were to obscure itself, [it would not be perceived].
There would be a non-perception of that very [form] because it is shrouded by darkness, just like a jar or other objects;
for this very reason, it is said in the *Āryopālipṛcchā*:
In this most delightful teaching, go forth into homelessness, casting off the mark of a householder;
you shall become fruitful, for this is the supreme instruction given by the Compassionate One.
Having gone forth and abandoned the marks of a householder, there will be the attainment of all fruits;
furthermore, by weighing the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there is the attainment of all fruits and of the fruits themselves.
They obtained the fruit and likewise the attainment; moreover, wonder arose within them: "Aha!
How exceedingly compassionate is the Lion among Men! The Victor has perfectly taught the method. Thus it was said.

Likewise, in the noble *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "Just as when a lamp has been lit for a long time in a dwelling by some man in his house, there is no darkness remaining there, [the Māra] thinks: 'I have been staying here for a long time; I will not depart from here.'"
The darkness has no power to avoid disappearing once a lamp is lit;
yet, depending upon the lamp, the darkness perishes. Both are empty, and neither conceives of anything at all.
Likewise, O Noble One, when pure knowledge arises in dependence [upon conditions], ignorance accumulated through the afflictions ceases;
there is never any contact whatsoever between that knowledge and the afflictions at any time.
Knowledge does not conceptualize; there would be no ignorance were it not for knowledge. Darkness perishes precisely through dependence upon knowledge.
Fear, too, is ungraspable, resembling a flower in the sky; likewise, both knowledge and ignorance, as well as fear, are empty. Thus. (12)
Furthermore: if this arising here were to produce itself,
would it produce its own self while already arisen, or while not yet arisen?
And since neither case is tenable, he says:
"How could this production, being unproduced, produce itself?
Or if it produces when already produced, what is produced again once it has been born? (13)
If arising that is unarisen were to produce itself, then even the crest-jewel of a frog’s hair would produce itself. Or, if it were already arisen that it were to produce [itself],...
What need is there for another production of that which has already been produced?
Thus, in the first place, production does not produce itself. (13)

Now, demonstrating how [an entity] does not produce another [entity] either, he says: In no way whatsoever is that which is presently arising, that which has already arisen, or that which has not yet arisen produced; this has been explained by means of the [analogy of] the traversed, the untraversed, and the being-traversed. (14)
For if anything were to arise, then arising would cause that [thing] to arise;
however, nothing arises, because arising is impossible throughout the three time periods.
And this has already been explained by means of the [analogy of] the being-traversed, the traversed, and the untraversed.
In that regard, just as that which has already gone is not being gone over,
because of the contradiction between the past and the present;
nor is that which has not yet been gone over being gone over.
Because there is a contradiction between the future and the present;
nor is the "being traversed" being traversed,
as it has been stated that no "being traversed" distinct from what has already been traversed and what has not yet been traversed is perceived.
In this way, an entity that is "presently arising" does not arise,
because there is no such thing as a "presently arising" state apart from what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, that which has already arisen does not arise.
Because there is a contradiction between the past and the present:
"has arisen" refers to one whose act of arising has ceased,
whereas "is arising" refers to one who is engaged in the present act of arising.
Furthermore, if it were said that "what has already arisen arises," there would be the simultaneity of the past and the present;
nor does "what has not yet arisen" arise,
because of the contradiction between the future and the present.
Therefore, it is not logical that arising gives rise to another arising. // 14 //
Here it is said: "That which is in the process of arising arises, not that which has already arisen, nor that which has not yet arisen.

Now, if you think that because an "arising" (utpadyamāna) is impossible apart from what has arisen and what has not yet arisen, therefore that which is in the process of arising does not arise—this is not so.

Since that which is endowed with the activity of arising is designated here as "that which is presently arising" (*utpadyamāna*), therefore, when arising exists, because the "presently arising" is established in dependence upon arising, it is the "presently arising" itself that arises;
and that "presently arising" brings about arising. To this, it is said:
When that which is in the process of arising does not proceed toward origination, how can it be said that "the process of arising" occurs in dependence upon origination? // 15 //
As it has been said: "Depending upon arising, that which is in the process of arising comes to be; and that [process] itself arises.
Now, [one might ask]: is this not so?
Specifically, this ought to be stated: "Depending on the arising of this, that which is called 'this' arises.
Yet it is not stated in this way;
for it is not possible to specifically determine that which is arising by saying, "This is that which is arising."
Because it is unarisen, there is no grasping of its causal signs;
and consequently, since that which is being produced is impossible, the act of production itself does not exist.
How, in the absence of production, could there be something being produced in dependence upon it?
Therefore, it is illogical to say that what is in the process of arising arises, and that this [arising] causes arising. // 15 //

Here he says: "Oh, alas! I am exceedingly afraid of you, who are an utter nihilist indifferent to both seen and unseen realities, and who, under the guise of explaining the teachings of the Tathāgata, merely displays your own skill in refutation while [denying] this ultimate truth characterized by conditionality and dependent origination as proclaimed by the Supreme Sage."
It destroys [the views] of the Tathāgatas.

Here, by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the reality of all phenomena has been revealed through the refutation of the proponents of a creator—namely, Prakṛti, Īśvara, Svabhāva, Kāla, Aṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Jaimini, Kaṇāda, Kapila, and other such non-Buddhist teachers—by means of the principle: "When this exists, that comes to be."

By revealing dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in its unerring form—namely, "with the arising of this, that arises; that is to say, conditioned by ignorance (avidyā) are the volitional formations (saṃskāra)," and so forth—you have, by offering refutations such as "it is neither being produced, nor produced, nor unproduced," committed nothing less than the murder of the Mother of the Tathāgatas, who is Dependent Origination itself. Enough!
"You, being a total nihilist"— to this it is replied:
"I do not destroy dependent origination, the mother who gives birth to all the Ten-Powered Ones."
But you, due to a lack of conviction in the most profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), have misapprehended its meaning and thus level this reproach against us alone.
Indeed, by stating "depending on this, that arises," the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, has clearly revealed the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all phenomena. For:
whatever arises dependently is, by its very nature, quiescent.
For whatever entity exists possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); by its own self, it maintains its own intrinsic nature as something imperishable.
Because it is already existing, it does not depend on anything else, nor does it arise.

Thus, since you yourself accept that entities possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatā*), when there is the admission of entities with intrinsic nature, how can there be dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Consequently, for one who accepts the intrinsic nature of entities, dependent origination itself is entirely subverted.
And thereby, even the vision of the supreme Dharma and the Buddha is subverted—[for it is said: "He who sees dependent origination sees the Dharma."

According to the scripture, "He who sees the Dharma sees the Buddha. However, by demonstrating that the cause called the seed and the effect called the sprout— which arise in dependence upon one another— are both peaceful, devoid of intrinsic nature, and dependently originated, I have in every way illuminated the Mother of all the Blessed Tathāgatas, which is dependent origination itself.
It is so; therefore, that which is arising is peaceful, and arising itself is likewise. // 16 //
Thus, let it be clearly understood. // 16 //
Here it is said: As it was stated—
“When that which is in the process of arising does not proceed toward arising,
how can one say that it arises in dependence upon arising?”
This is incorrect,
because it is only possible for this to be "arising" (utpadyamāna) in relation to its production;
for instance, a jar becomes "arising" in dependence upon the production of the jar.
And it is said that arising gives rise to that which is arising;
this too is incorrect, because:
if some unarisen entity were found anywhere at all.
If that [arising] were to arise, would an entity arise when that [arising] does not exist? // 17 //

If some thing called a "pot" that is unarisen were to exist anywhere prior to its arising, it would arise in dependence upon the action of arising; yet no such thing exists anywhere prior to its arising.
Since that pot does not exist, what is it that arises?

Now, it might be argued: even if the pot does not exist prior to its production, nevertheless, once produced, it will acquire the designation "pot"; thus, there is no fault on account of that future designation.
This too is incorrect;
for if the activity of arising were to proceed, then the entity, having become present, would acquire the designation "pot."

But when there is a non-occurrence of the action due to its lack of connection with the state of being future, how then can there be presentness? Or, if the action were to be commenced based on a non-pot as its locus...
This must be explained: that which is not a jar— is it capable of becoming a cloth, or is it nothing at all?
If the cloth is being produced, how could it, once produced, become a jar? Or if that is not the case at all, how then can activity proceed based upon it?
And how could it, having been produced, become a jar?
Thus, in every respect, even the conceptualization of [arising] as something already produced is untenable.
Therefore, it is established that arising, even while it is in the process of arising, does not cause [the thing] to arise. // 17 //

Moreover, even though such an arising is not logically tenable, we shall speak while provisionally accepting your position: If this [process of] arising were to produce that which is currently arising, then what further arising would produce that [primary] arising? (18)

Even if, according to your view, origination were to produce the entity that is currently arising, this must still be addressed: which other origination will now produce that [first] origination? (18)
Now, it might be argued that another production is postulated as the producer of this production;
in that case, there would be the fault of infinite regress. Thus he says:
"If another production were to produce this, there would be an infinite regress."
This has already been stated.
Now, if another arising of this [arising] is not admitted,
then it follows that arising arises without an arising.

Furthermore, demonstrating that even for those entities consisting of the "arising" and the "arisen," their production may occur even without [further] arising—because they possess the nature of being existent (bhāvatva), just like arising itself—he says:
"Now, if non-arising has arisen, then everything arises in that same way. (19)
Thus [ends the nineteenth].
Furthermore, regarding the position that arising produces both itself and others, we need not state a refutation at this point;
