for in this case, the refutation is already established: "The arising of what exists, as well as of what does not exist, is not tenable."
That it belongs neither to the existent nor to the non-existent has already been established. // 20 //
"A condition for an object that is neither non-existent nor existent is not tenable.

Since it has been stated previously in such passages as "When a phenomenon that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent is produced," production has indeed already been refuted.

And thus, since origination has been refuted in this manner, there is no possibility at all for the conceptualization that "origination produces that which is currently originating," or that it "produces both itself and another"; how, then, could it be established that "origination originates" or "that which is currently originating originates"?
And it produces both itself and another self. // 20 //
Furthermore: when this arising is being conceptualized here, is it conceptualized as belonging to an entity that is ceasing, which is thus subject to impermanence and is present;
or to one that is not ceasing, which is past or future and devoid of impermanence?
It is stated that it is untenable in either case:
The arising of an entity that is in the process of ceasing is not tenable;
nor is it tenable for an entity that is not ceasing to exist. (21)

In that regard, arising is not tenable for that which is ceasing, because it exists as a present phenomenon. Nor is there arising for that which is not ceasing—that is, for that which is devoid of destruction, such as the past or the future, or for that which lacks the characteristics of an existent entity, like a flower in the sky. Thus, [arising] does not exist. // 21 //
Having thus established the non-existence of the arising of entities, hereafter their stability is investigated.
Here it is said: The arising of entities certainly exists, because there is the presence of those dharmas that exist when they [the entities] exist;
for since stability is not possible for that which has not arisen, stability exists by virtue of the existence of arising.
Abiding is that which occurs when there is the state of arising;
therefore, arising also exists,
because of the existence of those phenomena that occur when that [arising] exists.
In this context, it is said that whatever does not exist cannot have the presence of a property that arises from its existence, just as, for example, there is no fragrance in a sky-flower.
There might be arising, if duration were indeed to exist as a consequence of that [arising];
but it does not. Thus—
An entity that has already come to rest does not rest; an entity that has not yet come to rest does not rest.
That which is currently resting does not rest; and what unarisen thing could possibly rest? (22)
That which is already situated does not remain, because the activity of remaining has ceased.
That which is in a state of non-remaining also does not remain, because it is devoid of remaining.
Even that which is currently remaining does not remain, because it would entail the fallacy of two acts of remaining.
Furthermore, because there is no state of "presently abiding" distinct from the already-abided and the not-yet-abided:
moreover, what unarisen thing could abide?
Since arising has been negated here, what such unarisen entity could exist that would abide? Thus, in every respect, there is no abiding. (22)
Furthermore, would this state of abiding belong to an entity that is ceasing or to one that is not ceasing?
Demonstrating that it is untenable in either case, he says: "The abiding of an entity that is ceasing is not possible."
Furthermore, that entity which is not undergoing cessation is not tenable. // 23 //
For an entity that is ceasing—that is, one facing cessation—abiding, which is its opposite, is not possible.
Furthermore, that which is not ceasing is not an entity at all; how then could there be abiding for it? // 23 //
Moreover, all things whatsoever are never abandoned by old age and death, even for a single moment.
Since this is so, there is no opportunity at all for the activity of "stability"—which is the opposite of old age and death—to occur among existing things; demonstrating this, he says:
"In all things that are always subject to the nature of old age and death..."
Which entities exist that are without aging and death? (24)
For what entities indeed, being devoid of aging and death, could have a persistence?
Therefore, the intended meaning is that persistence simply does not exist. // 24 //
Furthermore, if another state were postulated for the sake of the stability of this state,
or if it were to establish itself by its own self,
neither of these two cases is tenable; thus he says:
The abiding of abiding by means of another abiding, or by that very same [abiding], is not tenable;
just as the arising of arising occurs neither through itself nor through another. (25)
"Just as it has been stated in such passages as, 'How could this unarisen arising produce itself?', that arising does not produce itself,
so too it must be said that abiding does not abide itself."
If this stability is itself unstable, how could it establish its own self?
If it is already stable, then since it is already established, what more is there to be established once it is stable?
Thus it should be applied. And as it has been explained regarding arising: "If another [arising] produces this [arising], there would be an infinite regress. This same logic applies here.
The same should be explained regarding duration as well:
"If another duration establishes this duration, then there would be an infinite regress.
Thus, duration also is not tenable.
Therefore it was said by the Blessed One: "For these phenomena are non-abiding, and no stability is found in them;
non-stability, under the name of 'stability,' does not exist by way of intrinsic nature."
"Neither abiding nor arising was taught by the Lord of the World;
having understood the Lord of the World in this way, you should know this samādhi."
And it is said in the *Āryasaccaryagāthā*: "The wind rests upon space, and the mass of water rests upon that; this earth and the world rest upon that.
It is solely due to the cause of the karma of sentient beings that they enjoy [existence]. In this same way, the mind is established according to the nature of space; such is the meaning."
As far as this place has been described by me, so has it been spoken of by the Jina.
Thus is the detailed explanation. // 25 //
Here it is said: "Stasis and arising do indeed exist, because of the presence of the factors that accompany them.
In this case, conditioned phenomena possess impermanence which accompanies the characteristics of arising and stasis;
therefore, stasis and arising also exist."
It is said:
there would be stability and arising if there were only impermanence.
But it does not exist. How so? Because that which has not ceased does not cease, nor does that which has already ceased cease.
Nevertheless, as it is ceasing, is that which is ceasing something unborn? // 26 //
If impermanence were something existent,
it would have to belong either to an entity that has already ceased, one that has not yet ceased, or one that is currently ceasing.
In that regard, it is not logical to say that what has already ceased ceases.
Because there is a contradiction between the past and the present;
nor is it logical that it is unceased, because it would then be devoid of cessation.
Furthermore, because it is mutually contradictory to say that "that which is not yet ceased is what ceases";
nevertheless, this connects with the statement "that which is in the process of ceasing does not cease.
Even that which is in the process of ceasing does not cease, because there is no such thing as a "process of ceasing" [as a distinct entity]. (Pp_70)
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of two types of cessation.

Since, in this way, cessation is impossible in all three times, there is no such thing as cessation at all; how then could there be the possibility of existence and arising, which coexist with it? Moreover:
Since cessation prior to arising has already been refuted, cessation is simply impossible; thus he asks: "Is that which is unborn ceased? (26)
Furthermore, would this cessation belong to an entity that is stable or one that is unstable?
It is not tenable in either case; thus he says:
"First of all, the cessation of a stable entity is not possible."
For that which is abiding and opposed to cessation, there is no cessation;
nor does cessation occur for an entity that is not abiding. // 27 //
For that which is non-abiding, non-existent, and absent, there is no cessation;
thus, in every respect, there is no cessation. // 27 //
Furthermore: if cessation were to occur here, it would have to belong either to that very same state or to another state. Demonstrating that it is not tenable in any way whatsoever, he says:
Indeed, a state is not ceased by that very same state;
nor is a state ceased by a different state. (28)
First of all, that very state of milk is not ceased by that same state of milk,
because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
nor is the state of milk ceased by another state, namely the state of curd.
For if the states of milk and curd were simultaneous,
there could be a relationship of destroyer and destroyed between them;
however, the state of milk does not exist at the time of the state of curd.
And when it does not exist,
then what "existent woman of desire" could destroy it?
If it were to destroy it, [it would follow that]...
It might as well destroy the sharpness of a donkey's horn;
therefore, one state is not ceased by another state whatsoever. // 28 //
To this, he says: Even though that very state is not ceased by that same state, nor is one state ceased by another state,
nevertheless, there is still the cessation of the state of milk.
And thus, there would also be arising.
To this it is said:
Oh, how you reveal your own extreme dullness!
But surely, according to the reasoning previously stated, it has been said that in this way the arising of all phenomena is not tenable; so why is this being said again?
Then, in this way, the cessation of all phenomena would not be possible. // 29 //
Thus, it is established most clearly indeed. // 29 //
Moreover, if there were such a thing as cessation, it would have to belong either to an existing entity or to a non-existing one. In that regard,
first of all, the cessation of an existing entity is not tenable.
The cessation of an entity that has not fallen away from its intrinsic nature is not tenable;
because, in the case of identity, neither existence nor non-existence is possible. (30)
For cessation indeed means non-existence;
he who possesses that [cessation] does not exist at all.
Furthermore, by asserting that there is the cessation of an existing entity, one accepts the co-location of existence and non-existence within a single substratum.
If they were identical, both would be untenable; for if it were an entity at that time, [it could not simultaneously be its cessation].
In that case, because it is characterized by cessation— that is, by non-existence— an attribution of existence to it is improper.
Furthermore, if it were non-existence,
even that is not tenable for it.
Because it is never dissociated from a positive form that is the opposite of non-existence,
it follows that if existence and non-existence were identical, it would be logical to say that the entity is neither existent nor non-existent.
Alternatively, because they are mutually contradictory like light and darkness, if they were identical, it would be impossible for something to be both existent and non-existent.
Thus, first of all, the cessation of an existing entity is not logical. // 30 //
Now,
the cessation of even a non-existent entity is not tenable;
for there is no destruction of a non-entity that does not exist, just like the son of a barren woman.
Because it does not exist. For this very reason, he said:
"Just as there is no cutting off of a second head. (31)
Since a second head of a person—which is universally recognized as non-existent—is cited as an example, it was not mentioned [in the verse] because the illustration would have been incomplete;
thus, the cessation of a non-existent entity is not possible, nor is that of an existent one.
And that which is impossible in both ways—
By what nature does it exist?
Let it be understood that there is no cessation at all. // 31 //
Furthermore: if it is conceived that what is called "cessation" is the ceaser of entities, is another cessation now desired for that [cessation], or not?
If it is desired, that is not tenable.
There is no cessation by way of its own self, nor is there cessation by way of another self.
Demonstrating further how it does not exist, he says: "Just as the arising of arising is neither by way of itself nor by way of another. (32)
In this regard, as it has been stated: "How could this arising, being itself unarisen, produce itself?
and so forth, arising does not produce itself.
In the same way, cessation (*nirodha*) also does not cause its own self to cease. How so? It is said:
"How could this cessation, being itself unceased, destroy its own self?"
Now, if that which is already destroyed causes destruction, what is there left to be destroyed once it has been destroyed?
Thus it should be stated by way of simultaneous arising;
and in this way, there is no cessation by way of its own self,
nor now is there cessation by way of another self.
How so? In that regard, just as it was stated concerning arising—namely, "another causes this to arise," and so forth—it should likewise be said concerning cessation:
"If destruction were another [entity] that destroys this, there would be an infinite regress."
If this non-destruction has perished, then let everything of yours perish likewise.
Thus, since cessation is not possible even by means of another self, there is no cessation of cessation.
Now, if you think that there is no cessation of cessation itself, that is incorrect;
for if there were no cessation of cessation, [it would follow that cessation is permanent].
In that case, because it would lack cessation, it would forfeit the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, if the destruction of destruction is postulated, even so, destruction is not tenable;
yet, if it is not postulated, [the same fault follows].
Nevertheless, it is not tenable. But how, then, will destruction be tenable for the opponent?
Now, it might be argued: even so, when analyzed in this very manner, destruction is not tenable for you either.
Therefore, since a fault that applies to both parties cannot be used to challenge only one of them,
it is said in reply:
This objection does not apply to me.
Why?
Because those entities which are by their own nature devoid of intrinsic being—

And these [things], being indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), enter the path of worldly convention for the sake of the foolish who are attached to the notion that "this is real," by means of a logic established solely through non-investigation. Therefore, there is no application of the aforementioned investigation to them on our part; rather, like illusions, dreams, and cities of the Gandharvas, worldly objects, while lacking any logical justification, appear to the entire world whose mental eyes are impaired by the cataracts of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Having attained renown" means that they are merely accepted as having attained renown through mutual dependence alone, as is admitted by the foolish.
As it is said in the *Śataka*:
"By means of a whirling firebrand, a magical creation, a dream, an illusion, and the moon reflected in water..."
Existence is equal to mist, an echo within, a mirage, and clouds.
Therefore, when there is arising, there is that which arises; when there is that which arises, there is arising.
When there is cessation, there is that which ceases.
Since we accept worldly convention in the sense that "when there is something to be ceased, there is cessation," how could our position be subject to the same logical consequence?
As for one who, while accepting that destruction is causeless, asserts the momentariness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), [that person's position is flawed].

Since that [destruction] would be causeless, and because there would be an absence of destruction—like a flower in the sky—how could the momentariness of entities be established? And how could even the conditioned nature of things that are devoid of destruction be established? Thus, everything regarding him becomes entirely inconsistent.

By describing birth as the condition for aging and death, and by including [aging and death] within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) along with the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa), the Blessed One has clearly demonstrated that destruction possesses a cause. Furthermore, since this [destruction] depends solely upon birth, momentary disintegration (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is also easily established; thus, everything becomes well-founded.
Now, it might be argued: destruction is indeed non-existence;
and as for that which is non-existence, what can be accomplished by a cause for it?
Therefore, destruction is without cause.
But does this not lead to the consequence that existence (*bhāva*) as well would be without a cause?
For that which is called "existence" is, by definition, something that exists.
And for that which already exists, what is the purpose of a cause?
For that which has been produced is not produced again.
Therefore, since this would result in the absurdity of the absence of causes everywhere, this [position] is untenable.
Moreover, just as arising has a cause because it exists after having previously been non-existent, so too should destruction be accepted [as having a cause];
for destruction does not occur at all times.
Because it does not exist prior to its arising and exists after it;
and as for what is said— that "what can be done by a cause for that which is non-existent"— [it is irrelevant].
That is incorrect; for we do not maintain that anything is being produced by a cause of destruction,
but rather we describe it as the production of destruction itself.
If it is argued that, this being the case, destruction would also necessarily be an entity because it is something that is produced, we accept this very point;
for destruction is indeed an entity from the perspective of its own nature.
However, because its intrinsic nature is the cessation of phenomena such as form, it is not an existent entity.
Furthermore, death also brings about two types of effects: it establishes [the conditions for] existence and it effects the destruction of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
And since the scripture states that there is no cessation due to a lack of full comprehension, how could destruction not be caused?

Furthermore, by one who asserts that emptiness— characterized as the absence of the imagined— is actually of the nature of an existent entity, how is it that the state of being an existent has not been accepted for what is non-existent?
Furthermore, since it possesses existence (*bhāvatva*), how could emptiness (*śūnyatā*) be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Therefore, everything you have accepted is abandoned by you.
For this very reason, he will say:
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
For nirvāṇa is not conditioned, whereas existence and non-existence are both conditioned.
Thus, enough of this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand. // 32 //
Here it is said: Even if arising, abiding, and ceasing are refuted as belonging to the conditioned, nevertheless the conditioned exists, endowed with specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
For instance, hardness and so forth, as well as the dewlap and so forth, are taught as its specific characteristics.
Therefore, because the conditioned exists, its characteristic must also exist. It is replied:
this would indeed be so if the conditioned itself were a real entity.
Why? Because—since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, the conditioned does not exist;
for, by the reasoning already stated, arising, abiding, and ceasing themselves have been refuted.
In that case, how could there be a conditioned entity, or even its specific characteristic?
Here it is said: "The conditioned (saṃskṛta) certainly exists, because its opposite, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), exists. To this it is replied:
This might be so, if the unconditioned itself were established; however— And since the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be proven? (33)
In this regard, some conceive of space, cessation not through deliberation, and nirvāṇa as unconditioned;
others conceptualize emptiness, characterized as suchness, as unconditioned.
All of this is clearly demonstrated to be non-existent if the conditioned is not established. // 33 //
Here it is said: If it has been determined that arising, abiding, and ceasing do not exist, then what of this which was stated by the Sage, the possessor of unobstructed knowledge:
"O monks, the arising of the conditioned is also discerned;..."
"decay as well, and the alteration of duration as well," thus it was stated.
How is this to be understood? It is said:
Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as a city of the Gandharvas, so have arising, abiding, and ceasing been described. (34)

Just as illusions and the like, though unarisen by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and non-existent, are designated by words such as "illusion" and are accessible to the consciousnesses of illusions and so forth for the world,

so too these [phenomena] such as arising and the rest— though non-existent by way of intrinsic nature— are taught by the Blessed One merely in accordance with worldly convention, out of a desire to favor those disciples who are to be trained in such a manner.
Therefore it has been said:

Having formed the notion that "this is my wife" regarding this mere accumulation of skin, sinews, flesh, and bone, fools forcibly generate passion; they do not understand women for what they truly are—mere illusions.
Just as a maiden in a dream sees her son born and then dead—
exceedingly joyful at his birth and despondent at his death— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a city of Gandharvas, a mirage, an illusion, or a dream— know all phenomena to be like these, empty of intrinsic nature, yet consisting of the cultivation of signs.

These sages are secluded from both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; they possess no conceptual construction. Having attained the unconditioned within all realms of existence, they are forever secluded from views.
Always unattached, undeluded, and undisturbed, their minds are naturally concentrated;
he who understands these phenomena as empty possesses the power of samādhi and is truly strong. Thus it is said. // 34 //
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Examination of the Conditioned," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Action and the Agent, the Eighth Chapter.

Here it is said: Conditioned phenomena such as consciousness and so forth do indeed exist by virtue of having a conditioned intrinsic nature, because of the existence of the action and the agent which have them as their cause.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, this person, followed by ignorance, performs even meritorious formations, and even non-meritorious ones."
"He even performs immovable formative forces (*saṃskāra*)," and so forth; by such statements, the agent of actions is designated,
and the fruit of those actions— consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so on— is taught.
And whatever has an agent exists,
just as, for example, a jar.
That which does not exist has no agent, just as, for example, there is no maker of a cloak made of tortoise hair;
thus it is said.
Conditioned phenomena such as consciousness and the rest would exist if there were an agent and an action that produced them;
however, they do not exist. For this reason: "An existent agent does not perform an existent action."
Nor does an agent who is non-existent endeavor toward an action that is non-existent. // 1 //
In this context, "kāraka" means an agent (kartṛ), one who acts.
The designation "agent" applies only to one who is performing some action, not to one who is not acting.
Furthermore, that instrumentality (karaṇa) would have to be postulated either for an agent who is already existent, or...
Is it that which is non-existent, or that which is both existent and non-existent?
An object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent (*kartṛ*).
That [action] is also threefold:
existent, non-existent, and both existent and non-existent.
Among these, one proposition is that an existent agent engaged in action does not perform an existent object of action engaged in action.
Now, another proposition: even that which is non-existent, being devoid of action and agent, does not perform a non-existent action that is itself devoid of action. // 1 //
To establish the first [point] therein, he says:
"For that which is truly existent, there is no activity, and action would be without an agent;
for the designation of a 'kāraka' (agent) is dependent upon activity."
Only someone who is truly existent and engaged in an action receives the designation of a "kāraka" (agent).

Consequently, for such a person who has already received the designation of a kāraka by virtue of being the cause of an action, there is no further action by which they could perform an object (*karman*). And because of the absence of action, when the kāraka does not perform an object—
In that case, action would be independent of its factors and devoid of an agent;

yet an action devoid of an agent is impossible, like the making of a pot by the son of a barren woman. Thus, for that which is already existent, there is no activity, and action would be without an agent.
Thus, because of the consequence of these faults, an existent agent does not perform an action.
Now, demonstrating that even an existent action is not performed by an agent, he says:
"There is no activity for that which is existent, and the agent would be without an object. (2)

That which is called "existent" (sadbhūta) is an action (karman) endowed with activity (kriyā). Now, for that which has already acquired the designation of "action" by virtue of its connection with activity, there is no further activity by which it could be made to act.
Thus, in the first place, there is no activity for an action that is already existent.
When there is no further action, then the agent does not perform that truly existent action;
and when he does not perform it— because of the absence of a second action regarding the action— then (Pp_76)
Only that which is itself without an object—that is, only that for which no object exists—could be the agent (*kāraka*) of that [supposed] object;
and this is not evident.
For it is never observed that one who has not performed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*) can be the agent of such a transgression. // 2 //
Having thus established that a real agent does not perform a real action, he now explains how an unreal agent likewise does not perform an unreal action, saying:
"If an unreal agent were to perform an unreal action, the action would be without a cause, and the agent too would be without a cause. (3)
An agent that is non-existent is one devoid of action;

and since action is the cause for the designation "agent," an agent devoid of action would likewise be without a cause. Furthermore, an object of action that is non-existent would also be without a cause. (3)
Furthermore, he says that if one accepts the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), both effect and cause would be entirely negated:
"In the absence of a cause, neither effect nor cause exists.
For it is only when a cause is accepted as existing that whatever is produced by that cause is an effect.
And it is logical that whatever brings something into existence is its cause;
for example, clay is the cause of a jar, and the jar is the effect.
And for that [pot], the wheel and so forth are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*).

However, if one accepts the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), then because it would not depend on a cause, this pot would not exist—just like a pot made of the crest-jewel from the hair of a frog.
Since the pot does not exist, how could there be its cause? Thus—
In the absence of a cause, neither effect nor cause exists;
and consequently, in their absence, action, agent, and instrument do not exist. (4)
In the absence of that causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva), what action could possibly occur,
or in what action would the potter possess agency through his independence?
Nor is it logical for clay to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) through its identity with the action;
thus, in the absence of that [clay], neither the action, the agent, nor the instrument exists.
And therefore:
"Dharma and adharma do not exist when actions and so forth are impossible.

Here, when Devadatta, being an agent due to his autonomy regarding the action of abstaining from taking life, performs that action of abstaining from taking life by means of an autonomous effect serving as the instrument, [dharma arises].
Then, his merit arises.

This same logic should be applied to all ten wholesome paths of action—those accomplished through wholesome deeds—as well as to the undertakings of wholesome dharmas characterized by worshiping the Three Jewels, one's parents, and other venerable persons.

Likewise, regarding unwholesome actions characterized by killing and so forth, which are the opposites of the wholesome, one should point out the consequence that if there were an absence of agent, object, and instrument, it would follow that actions themselves do not exist.
And when dharma and adharma do not exist in this way, then their fruit also does not exist at all; demonstrating this, he says:
"When dharma and adharma are absent, the fruit born from them is not found. (5)
The desirable and undesirable fruits produced by dharma and adharma would not exist in the states of happy rebirth and miserable rebirth if dharma and adharma were absent. // 5 //
And therefore: if there were no fruit, the path would not lead to liberation, nor would it lead to heaven.

For if the fruits were indeed desirable or undesirable, then heaven— characterized by the attainment of meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti)— would be the fruit of the worldly path;
in that case, the cultivation of the worldly path for that purpose would be superior.
Furthermore, there would be the fruitfulness of abstaining from the paths of action that lead to evil destinies;
and if nirvana, characterized by liberation, were the fruit,
then there would be the fruitfulness of cultivating the supramundane noble eightfold path for its sake.
But when there is no fruit, then—
in the absence of a fruit— the path does not lead to liberation, nor does it lead to heaven.
Furthermore: if there were thus an absence of results, it would follow that all purposeful actions are rendered meaningless. (6)
For even those activities undertaken for the sake of a result— such as agriculture, trade, military service, or entering into employment—
all of them would be untenable if there were no result.

In this way, it follows that all ritual actions would be rendered meaningless for you; yet they are not meaningless. Therefore, considering that this [position] which denies heaven and liberation is like a field for the poisonous trees of every fault without exception, is the cause for falling into the great abysses of hell and other states of woe, and contradicts the principles of both seen and unseen causes and effects— [The rest of the passage continues: ...it is established that this [denial] is utterly baseless and devoid of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if one were to say: "If there is no self, then who experiences the fruit of these actions?"—this is not a valid objection. For the experience of the fruit occurs through the continuity of the stream (*saṃtati*) of consciousness, just as the ripening of a sprout occurs from a seed. Moreover, since the agent is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) for the collection of aggregates (*skandha*), there is no contradiction with the teaching of non-self (*anātman*). Thus, the doctrine of non-self is indeed the supreme truth. It is said: "Those who see the self do not see the Dharma; But those who see the Dharma see the selflessness of phenomena. Therefore, one should abandon the view of a self and cultivate the view of non-self. This concludes the section on the refutation of the self. Now, to refute the doctrine of the person (*pudgala*): some Vaibhāṣikas assert that the person exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*). They argue: "If the person did not exist, then for whom would the Buddha have taught the five aggregates of grasping? And who is it that transmigrates from this world to another? To this we reply: that is not so. If the person existed substantially, it would be either identical to or different from the aggregates. If it were identical, it would be subject to arising and ceasing, just like the aggregates; if it were different, it would be permanent, like space. Since neither of these is tenable, the person does not exist substantially. As it is said: "If the person were different from the aggregates, It would be permanent, like space. If it were identical to them, It would arise and perish. Thus, the person is merely a conventional designation for the collection of the aggregates, like the word "chariot" applied to a collection of parts. It is not a substantial entity. Therefore, the doctrine of the person is also to be rejected. This concludes the refutation of the person. Now, to refute the doctrine of primordial matter (*prakṛti*): some Sāṃkhyas claim that all things arise from a single, eternal, unchanging primordial matter. We ask: if this primordial matter is eternal and unchanging, how can it produce diverse effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and the elements? If it produces them, it must undergo change; if it changes, it cannot be eternal. Furthermore, if it is a single substance, how can it possess the three qualities (*guṇa*) of sattva, rajas, and tamas? These contradictions prove that primordial matter does not exist. As it is said: "If the cause is eternal and unchanging, How can it produce various effects? If it produces, it must change; If it changes, it is not eternal. Thus, the doctrine of primordial matter is also baseless. Now, to refute the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*): some Vaiśeṣikas assert that the world is composed of atoms. We ask: do these atoms touch one another or not? If they do not touch, there would be gaps between them, and the world would be porous. If they do touch, do they touch at a single point or their entire extent? If they touch at a single point, the atom would have parts and thus lose its nature as an atom. If they touch in their entirety, all atoms would merge into one, and the entire world would become a single atom. Since neither case is possible, atoms do not exist. As it is said: "If atoms touch, they must have parts; If they do not touch, there are gaps between them. If they touch entirely, everything becomes one; Thus, the doctrine of atoms is destroyed. Therefore, the doctrine of atoms is also to be abandoned. Now, to refute the doctrine of the creator god (*īśvara*): some Naiyāyikas claim that a supreme lord, omniscient and omnipotent, creates the universe. We ask: does he create by his own will or without a cause? If he creates by his own will, why does he not create all beings happy? Why does he create some in suffering? If he creates without a cause, he would be acting like a madman. Furthermore, if he is independent, why does he depend on karma? If he depends on karma, he is not independent. Since these arguments contradict his supposed sovereignty, the doctrine of the creator god is also false. As it is said: "If he creates by his own will, Why does he not make all happy? If he creates without a cause, He is like a madman. If he depends on karma, He is not independent. Thus, the doctrine of the creator god is also to be rejected. Now, to refute the doctrine of chance (*yadṛcchāvāda*): some Cārvākas claim that everything arises by chance, without cause or condition. We ask: if this were so, why is there order in the world? Why do certain seeds produce certain fruits, and not others? Why do specific causes lead to specific results? If everything were random, there would be no distinction between cause and effect, and the world would be chaotic. Since we observe regularity and causality, the doctrine of chance is irrational. As it is said: "If there were no cause, There would be no order in the world. Why do seeds produce their own fruits? Why do causes lead to specific results? Since we see regularity, The doctrine of chance is false. Therefore, the doctrine of chance is also to be abandoned. Now, to refute the doctrine of nihilism (*ucchedavāda*): some Lokāyatikas claim that there is no life after death, no karma, and no rebirth. We ask: if this were so, why do people practice virtue and avoid evil? Why do they seek liberation? If there is no future life, their efforts would be in vain. Furthermore, if there is no rebirth, the teachings of the Buddhas regarding the continuity of consciousness would be contradicted. Since we know through inference and scripture that there is a continuum of existence beyond this life, the doctrine of nihilism is false. As it is said: "If there were no future life, Virtue and evil would be meaningless. Why do people seek liberation? Since rebirth exists, The doctrine of nihilism is false. Therefore, the doctrine of nihilism is also to be rejected. Now, to refute the doctrine of permanence (*śāśvatavāda*): some claim that the self and the world are eternal. We ask: if they are eternal, how can they be perceived? If they are perceived, they must be subject to change. If they are not perceived, they cannot be known to exist. Furthermore, if they are eternal, there can be no liberation, as liberation implies the cessation of suffering. Since both perception and the possibility of liberation exist, the doctrine of permanence is false. As it is said: "If they were eternal, They could not be perceived. If they were perceived, They would be subject to change. Since liberation exists, The doctrine of permanence is false. Therefore, the doctrine of permanence is also to be abandoned. Now, to refute the doctrine of annihilation (*ucchedavāda*): some claim that the self is annihilated at death. We ask: if the self were annihilated, who would experience the fruit of past actions? Who would remember past lives? If there is no continuity, the moral law of cause and effect would collapse. Since we observe memory and the experience of results, the doctrine of annihilation is false. As it is said: "If the self were annihilated, Who would experience the fruit of karma? Who would remember past lives? Since memory and experience exist, The doctrine of annihilation is false. Therefore, the doctrine of annihilation is also to be rejected. Now, to refute the doctrine of the self as a mere collection (*samudāyavāda*): some claim that the self is nothing more than a collection of the aggregates. We ask: if the self is merely a collection, how can it be a single entity? A collection is multiple, whereas the self is conceived as one. Furthermore, if the self is the collection, it would arise and cease with each moment, making it impermanent. Since the self is considered to be a stable subject of experience, the doctrine of the self as a mere collection is false. As it is said: "If the self were a collection, It would be multiple and impermanent. Since it is conceived as one and stable, The doctrine of the collection is false. Therefore, the doctrine of the self as a mere collection is also to be abandoned. Now, to refute the doctrine of the self as a substance (*dravyavāda
The position that a non-existent agent performs a non-existent action along with [non-existent factors] is utterly inferior and must therefore be abandoned. // 6 //
Having thus established these two propositions, he now states that an agent who is of both natures does not perform an action that is of both natures:
"An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not produce that which is both existent and non-existent."

In this regard, that which is an unreal action—whether associated with activity or dissociated from activity—is not performed by an agent who is both real and unreal. Because: "For how could the real and the unreal, being mutually contradictory, exist as one? (7)
It is simply not tenable that a single entity at one and the same time should be both engaged in action and not engaged in action.

Consequently, the intended meaning is that an agent, whether existent or non-existent, does not perform an object of action, whether existent or non-existent, because such a thing is impossible. // 7 //
Having thus raised an objection against the symmetrical position, he speaks with the desire to refute the asymmetrical position as well:
"An existent thing is not produced by an existent agent, nor is a non-existent thing produced by a non-existent agent."

First, an action performed by an agent who is real and endowed with existence does not produce an object that is unreal and devoid of action; for in that case, all those very same faults would necessarily follow. (8)
For that which is truly existent, there is no activity, and action would be without an agent.
Thus, first of all, an agent that is truly existent does not perform an action,
nor is an action that is non-existent performed.
For an action that is non-existent would be without a cause; and consequently, when there is no cause, neither effect nor cause exists.
By such statements, every [alleged] refutation is rendered untenable.
Therefore, since this discordant position has already been refuted by the reasons previously stated, the reason is not employed again.
And just as it has been demonstrated that a real agent does not perform a non-existent action, so too...
Thus, it should be explained according to the path already described that a non-existent agent, being devoid of action, does not perform a real action. // 8 //

Having thus stated the refutation by examining each term individually within the case of the dissimilar position (*viṣamapakṣa*), he now states the refutation by examining each term in relation to a pair of terms:
"An agent does not perform an action that is non-existent, nor one that is existent, nor even one that is both existent and non-existent; this is for the very reasons previously stated. (9)
That agent, being truly existent, does not perform an action that is non-existent or both existent and non-existent.
How so? It says: "by the very reasons previously stated.
In that regard, it has been said: "There is no activity for that which is truly existent."
By such statements as these, it is shown that an existent agent does not act,
nor is a non-existent object acted upon; for "the action would be without a cause," and "when there is no cause, there is no effect."
Because of the fault already established by such arguments as these,
even an action that is both existent and non-existent is not performed;
for how could existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, exist as one?
Because of this statement, thus, first of all, an existent agent does not perform an action that is non-existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent. // 9 //

Now, it is said that even an unreal agent does not perform a real action, nor does he perform an unreal action: "Even an unreal agent does not perform a real action, nor indeed an unreal one, for the very reasons previously stated. (10)
An unreal agent would be without a cause;
because of the faults stated in such passages as "and when there is no cause, there is no effect," an unreal agent does not act.
Since it would follow that there is no action for that which is already existent and the agent would be without an object,
an existent action is not performed.
Furthermore, an action that is both existent and non-existent is also not performed.
For it is said: "How indeed can existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, be one and the same? (Verse 10)

Now, demonstrating how an agent who is both existent and non-existent—being of a dual nature—is likewise unable to perform an action that is either existent or non-existent and designated by distinct conventions, he says:
An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not perform an action that is existent, nor one that is non-existent, nor one that is both;
this should be understood through the very reasons previously stated. (11)
For it is said: "How can that which is both existent and non-existent be one and the same, being mutually contradictory?
Thus, an agent who is both existent and non-existent does not act.
There is no activity for that which is already existent, and the agent would be without an action.
Thus, by way of this consequence, an existent action is not performed;
nor is a non-existent action performed, because of the faults already stated in such passages as, "When there is no cause, there is no effect."
Since, in this way, the establishment of both the agent and the action is in every respect untenable— whether the sides [of cause and effect] are equal or unequal—

therefore, that which was stated, namely, "the conditioned phenomena such as consciousness and so forth do indeed exist, having a conditioned nature, because of the existence of their causes, actions, and agents," is incorrect.

To this he says: "Have you determined that these things do not exist? Certainly not. For you, who maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the negation of all things is possible because of the absence of intrinsic nature in those things.
We, however, do not perceive any intrinsic nature at all in any things, precisely because they have arisen dependently (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Whom, then, shall we blame?
As it is said in the *Ārya-ratnāvalī*:
"Thinking that this was water in a mirage, he came here..."
If one were to take that water thinking it does not exist, he would indeed be a fool.
For one who grasps at this world, which resembles a mirage, thinking "it exists" or even "it does not exist," this is delusion; and as long as there is delusion, one is not liberated.
"What was previously imagined through ignorance, when it no longer finds any existence upon the determination of the meaning of reality, then where is non-existence? (11)
Thus, since all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how could there be an establishment of them in the manner described?

Therefore, having accepted the worldly misconception, it is said that the establishment of conventional entities—which are like water in a mirage—occurs solely through the acceptance of their mere conditionality (*idampratyayatāmātra*), and not otherwise:
"Dependent upon the agent is the action; dependent upon that action is the agent."
Karma proceeds;
we see no other cause for its accomplishment.

In this case, for one who does not act and is independent of action, there is an absence of agency; therefore, it is only by depending on an action that an agent possesses agency. Furthermore, since nothing that is not being acted upon can possess the status of an object (*karman*), the designation "object" applies only to that which is being acted upon. Thus, we see no cause for the establishment of the object and the agent other than their mutual dependence, such that the object proceeds in relation to that agent. // 12 //
And just as the establishment of the action and the agent is mutually dependent, so it is for other entities as well; pointing this out by extension, he says:
"In this way, one should understand the appropriation [of the agent] from the relinquishment of the action."
By the phrase "and thus for the agent," he shows the immediately preceding designation of the object-factor (*karmakāraka*);
*upādāna* means appropriation (*upātti*).
And by this, he expresses the act of appropriation (*upāttikriyā*).
That act brings together its own means: the agent who appropriates (*upādātṛ*) and the object which is appropriated (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, the establishment of these two—the appropriated and the appropriator—which are mutually dependent, occurs just like that of the object and the agent; it is not intrinsic (*svābhāvikī*).
Why, then, is it not intrinsic? He says: "Because of the relinquishing (vyutsarga) of both the action and the agent.
The word "iti" refers to the reason.
Vyutsarga means complete relinquishment.

Consequently, this meaning follows: by those very same reasons for which the relinquishment of karma has been stated by us, it should be understood that the appropriator and the object of appropriation are likewise negated.

Furthermore, it should not be understood that the establishment of these two through their mutual dependence is to be determined solely by the negation of both agent and action; rather, one should discern all remaining entities by means of the agent and the action. // 13 //
The phrase "the wise one" (*prājña*) is the completion of the sentence.

Apart from the factors of action (*karmakāraka*), the object to be acquired (*upādeya*), and the acquirer (*upādātṛ*), there are other entities (*bhāva*)— namely, those characterized as the produced and the producer, the goer and the going, the seer and the visible, the defined and the definition, the generated and the generator— as well as, without exception, all entities such as parts and wholes, qualities and possessors of qualities, means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, and so forth.

Having refuted their existence by way of intrinsic nature through an investigation of agent and action, the wise person seeking liberation should contemplate that their establishment is merely mutual dependence, for the sake of release from the bonds of birth, aging, death, and so forth.
And a detailed investigation of these should be understood from the *Madhyamakāvatāra* and other such works.

But is it not the case that since the appropriated (upādāna) and the appropriator (upādātṛ) are already understood by the very statement "one should discern the remaining entities," it is improper to mention the appropriated and the appropriator again?
This is true;
nevertheless, in the investigation of reality, they are mentioned separately in order to indicate their primary importance.
For indeed, in the subsequent chapters, there will be further investigation primarily into these two very points.
Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*:
"I have shown the fear of hell to me, and many thousands of beings have been struck with awe."
And there exists no being here who, having passed away, goes to a terrible state of woe.
There is no agent nor any instrument by which the swords, spears, and weapons were made;
yet, through the power of conceptual construction, one perceives those weapons falling upon the body in that state of woe.
Variegated and delightful, with flowers arrayed, golden celestial palaces shine, enchanting;
yet among them, there is no creator whatsoever here, for they too are established by the power of *kalpa*.
The world is conceptualized through the power of mental construction; the fool is conceptualized through the grasping at notions.
Yet that grasping is non-grasping and unreal, for conceptual constructions are like illusions and mirages. Thus [it is said]. 13.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Examination of Action and the Agent," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Ninth Chapter: Examination of the Prior.
Here it is said: "Thus one should understand appropriation [to arise] from the relinquishing of action and of the agent. Thus it was stated.
That is incorrect; for it is said:
"Some indeed assert that he who possesses seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, exists prior to those [faculties]. (1)

The Sāṃmitīyas assert that the appropriator, for whom there exist seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and so forth, as well as feeling, contact, mental attention, and so forth, exists prior to these appropriations. // 1 //
What is the reason? Because:
"For how could seeing and so forth belong to an entity that does not exist?
Therefore, prior to those [actions], that entity exists as established. (2)

In this world, it is only Devadatta who exists that takes up wealth, not one who does not exist, such as the son of a barren woman. Likewise, if the person (pudgala) were not already established prior to seeing and the other [faculties],
he would not have performed the appropriation of seeing and so forth.

Therefore, that person exists prior even to the appropriation [of aggregates], just like Devadatta who exists prior to his wealth; he is the person who will perform the appropriation of these [aggregates] prior to seeing and the other [sensory activities]. // 2 //
It is said:
By what means, then, is that entity which existed prior to seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, designated? (3)
By what means is that person (pudgala) who is established as existing prior to seeing and so forth to be designated?
For seeing and so forth are the causes for the designation of a person.
If it is conceived that he exists prior to them, then he would be independent of perception, like a cloth is [independent] of a jar;
and the intention is that whatever is independent of its own causes is causeless, and like a creditor who is independent of wealth and so forth, such a person does not exist. // 3 //
Furthermore:
If that [self] were established even without seeing and the other [faculties], then there is no doubt that these [faculties] would also exist without it. // 4 //
If you think that prior to seeing and the other [faculties] there exists a so-called person (*pudgala*),
and that this person takes up seeing and the rest as its appropriation (*upādāna*),
then, this being the case, it follows beyond doubt that even these [faculties of] seeing and the rest would exist without the person.
For instance, Devadatta, having existed prior to his connection with wealth as something distinct from wealth, acquires that wealth which is indeed a separate entity established independently.
In the same way, for the appropriator as well, there would have to be an appropriation consisting of seeing and so forth, which exists as a separate entity distinct from his own self. (4)
But it is not possible; thus he says:
Someone is manifested by something, and something is manifested by someone.
How can there be someone without something, and how can there be something without someone? (5)
In this world, by means of a cause called a seed, a certain effect called a sprout is manifested;
and by that effect, a certain cause called a seed is manifested—such that one knows, "this is the cause of that" and "this is the effect of that.
Likewise, if some self-nature were manifested by some substrate such as vision and so forth, [one would know], "this is the appropriator of that."
By means of some self, some appropriation—such as vision and so forth—is manifested, such that one can say, "this is the appropriation of that.

At that time, there would be the establishment of the appropriation and the appropriator through their mutual dependence. However, when vision and so forth are accepted as established separately, without an appropriator, then being without a support, it is simply non-existent. Therefore, there is no establishment of either.
Thus, it is not tenable that there exists a grasper established as distinct from seeing and the other [faculties]. // 5 //
Here he says: regarding what was stated, "from seeing, hearing, and so forth," etc., this is now replied:
if it were admitted that [the self] exists prior to all [functions] such as seeing, then this fault would indeed arise; but when—
No single thing exists prior to all [the functions] such as seeing and so forth;
rather, it exists prior to each one individually.
And when this is the case, then—
Furthermore, at another time, it is manifested by something other than seeing and the rest.
When the "seer" is manifested by means of seeing, it is not then designated in dependence upon hearing and the other [faculties];
therefore, the previously mentioned faults do not apply. // 6 //

It is said: this too is not tenable, because it is impossible for that which is devoid of seeing and the other [faculties], which is without a basis (*anupādāna*), without a cause (*ahetuka*), and stainless (*nirañjana*) to exist.
Even if it is conceptualized thus: "If it does not exist prior to all [the faculties] such as seeing," even so—
How can that [self] exist prior to each individual [factor], such as seeing and the rest? // 7 //
For that which does not exist prior to all things does not exist even prior to each individual thing;
just as, for example, a forest does not exist prior to all the trees.

At that time, there is no oil even from each individual grain; and since there is an absence of oil production from all the grains of sand collectively, there is likewise no oil from each single grain of sand.
Furthermore:
For indeed, if someone is prior to each one individually, has it not been admitted that he is prior to all of them as well?
Because there is no "all" apart from each individual.
Therefore, it is not logical that [the cause] exists prior to each individual [effect]. // 7 //
For this reason as well, [the position] is not tenable— because:
if that very same one who is the seer is also the hearer and the feeler, then—
It cannot be rightly said that each [sense] would previously be the same as the seer or the same as the hearer;
for if that were the case, then even one who is devoid of the act of seeing would possess the status of a seer simply by being a hearer.
Even for a seer who lacks the activity of hearing, there would be the state of being a hearer.
But this is not observed: that one could be a seer while lacking the activity of seeing, or a hearer while lacking the activity of hearing. Therefore, he said:
And thus, this is not tenable. // 8 //
Thus [it is said]. And since there is a difference in the factors of action (kāraka) for every individual response, how could this be so? Demonstrating this, he says: "And thus, this is not tenable."
The master Buddhapālita, however, explains: "If the self were unitary, it would follow that the person could move from one sense organ to another, just as one moves from one window to another.

To this, the master Bhāvaviveka offers a refutation: "Since the self is omnipresent, there is no movement from one sense organ to another; therefore, the fault of the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅgadoṣa*) is untenable."
This is incorrect, because the refutation of the theory of a person (pudgalavāda) as conceived by our own fellow Buddhists is the subject at hand, and that [person] is not asserted to be omnipresent.
Therefore, the fault of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is indeed valid. // 8 //
Furthermore, if, out of a desire to avoid the aforementioned faults, it is postulated that the seer is one, the hearer is another, and the knower is yet another;
That too is not tenable; for if it were accepted in this way, there would be a hearer when there is a seer, and there would be a plurality of selves. (9)
For example, a horse is other than a cow; it is not the case that when the cow exists, the horse does not exist simultaneously.
Likewise, if the hearer were other than the seer, then even while the seer exists, the hearer would exist simultaneously.
And since this is not accepted, there is no distinctness [of the self].
Moreover, if this were the case, it would follow that there are indeed many selves, because one would have to admit the separate establishment of the seer, the hearer, the feeler, and so forth.
Therefore, prior to each individual act of seeing and so forth, there exists no such thing as a person (pudgala). // 9 //
Here he says: That self indeed exists prior to all [faculties] such as seeing and so forth.
Now, if it is thought that "if it exists, by what is it designated?"—to this it is replied:

In this context, prior to seeing and the other [sensory functions], the four great elements exist during the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because from them, in sequence, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—which have name-and-form as their condition—arise, such as seeing, hearing, and so forth.
Therefore, prior to seeing and the others, there exists only the appropriation of the four great elements. Even so:
seeing, hearing, and the rest, as well as feeling and the rest, [are likewise].
This [self] does not exist even in those elements from which those [qualities] arise. // 10 //

The intention is that even with respect to those great elements from which seeing and so forth arise, this [notion] based on the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the great elements is likewise untenable for the same reason stated previously.
In this regard, it is as was said before:
"How can there be something without something else? How can there be something else without something?"—this must be stated here in the same way.
For if the self were previously established through the appropriation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), [it would follow that it exists independently].
It would have to exist by depending upon the great elements;
but it is not so, because it would be without a cause.
And that which does not exist...
How could he grasp the great elements?
Thus, since the refutation regarding the grasping of the elements has already been stated—just as in the case of the grasping of views—it is not stated again. // 10 //
Here it is said: Even though the self has been thus refuted, nevertheless seeing and so forth do exist, because they have not been refuted.
Furthermore, there is no connection with seeing and so forth for things such as jars, which lack the nature of a self;
therefore, the self must indeed exist as that which possesses such connections.
To this, it is said:
If the self were to exist, it would have to be nothing other than seeing and the other [faculties];
yet they do not exist.
Since that for which seeing and the others are the substratum does not exist, [the self cannot exist].
It has been established that, since that self which is the appropriator does not exist, how could there be the existence of the appropriations consisting of seeing and so forth? Thus he says:
If that to which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth belong, does not exist, then these [functions] do not exist either. (11)
It has been stated that when that [self] for whom seeing and so forth are conceptually constructed does not exist, then it is clearly demonstrated that seeing and so forth do not exist either.
Consequently, due to the absence of seeing and so forth, the self simply does not exist. // 11 //
Here he asks: "Is it indeed certain to you that there is no self at all? Who has said this?
Has it not just been stated that because of the absence of seeing and so forth, the self also does not exist?"
This has been stated by us;
however, you have not correctly determined its meaning,
since you have conceptualized the self as being of the nature of an existent entity.
That does not exist by way of its own-being;
and I have uttered speech regarding it solely to turn back the adherence to its own-being, acting as an antidote to the misconception of what is unreal, but I have not imagined its non-existence.
For these two must be abandoned: attachment to existent things and attachment to non-existent things.
As Āryadeva has said:

That which is your self is not my self; therefore, because it is not subject to self-restraint, it is not [the self]. Indeed, conceptual construction arises only with respect to impermanent phenomena.
Thus [ends the eleventh].

Explaining this very point, he says: "That which does not exist prior to seeing and so forth, nor now, nor even later—regarding that, the conceptual constructions of 'it exists' and 'it does not exist' have ceased. (12)
First of all, the self does not exist prior to seeing and the other [faculties], for it is absent there;
nor does it exist as co-existent with seeing and the others.
Since two things that are not established separately cannot be observed to exist together— just as in the case of a hare’s horn and [the horn of] a rabbit—
and since the self and its appropriation are not established separately when they are independent of one another, they do not exist at present,
nor will they exist in the future.
For if seeing and the other [sensory functions] were to exist first, and the self were to exist at a later time, then it would have to come into being subsequently.
But this is not the case, because an action without an agent is unestablished.
And since such a self does not exist when examined prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with seeing and the other [faculties],
what wise person would now postulate the existence or non-existence of that whose nature is unperceived?
Therefore, it is established that the establishment of the relationship between the appropriated and the appropriator is mutually dependent, just like the action and the agent, and is not intrinsic.
Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One in the venerable *Ārya-samādhirāja*:
"At that time, the faultless Jina, the Daśabala, spoke this supreme samādhi:
'The entire world is like a dream; indeed, no one is born, nor does anyone die.'"
Neither a sentient being nor a life-force nor a person is found; these phenomena are like foam and the trunk of a plantain tree.
They are like an illusion, like lightning in the sky, like the moon reflected in water, and like a mirage.
No person whatsoever, having died in this world, transmigrates to or goes to another world;
yet the action performed never perishes, yielding its fruit—whether dark or bright—as one wanders through saṃsāra.
There is neither permanence nor annihilation, nor is there an accumulation of karma, nor does it remain;
having performed an action, one does not experience its result again, nor does another who has not performed it experience it.
There is no transition, nor is there any returning; nothing exists, yet again, nothing does not exist.
Here, there is neither purification through the stations of views nor the movement of beings, for their course is perfectly tranquil.
Non-arising, peace, the signless state—this is the domain of the Sugatas, the qualities of the Jinas;
the powers and the dhāraṇīs are the strength of those who possess the ten powers; this is the supreme, bull-like prowess of the Buddhas.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Examination of the Prior," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Fire and Fuel, the Tenth Chapter.

Here it is said: As for that which was stated—that therefore, just like the action and the agent, the appropriation and the appropriator also lack establishment by way of intrinsic nature—that is incorrect.
Because even things that are dependent are seen to possess intrinsic nature;
for instance, fire exists in dependence upon fuel,
yet fire is not devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because its effects, such as heat and the capacity to burn, which constitute its intrinsic nature, are perceived; thus,
fuel exists in dependence upon fire,
yet it is not devoid of intrinsic nature.

Because it has the nature of the four external great elements (*mahābhūta*), even though the appropriator (*upādātṛ*) is dependent upon appropriation (*upādāna*), he will exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and likewise, appropriation is dependent upon the appropriator. Thus, these two—the appropriation and the appropriator—will exist like fire and fuel.
It is said:
This might be so if fire and fuel were indeed [identical], but they are not.
How so? If fire and fuel were to exist here, they would necessarily be either identical or distinct.
Yet, in neither case is it tenable; thus he says:
If the fuel were the fire, there would be identity between the agent and the object;
if the fire were other than the fuel, it would exist even without the fuel. (1)
In this context, that which is ignited is the fuel, consisting of combustible materials such as wood;
its burner, the agent of burning, is fire.
In that regard, if it were first imagined that the fuel is indeed the fire itself,
then there would be identity between the agent and the object;
and this is not observed to be the case.
Because it would follow that the jar and the potter, or the cutter and the object to be cut, are one and the same, and that is not accepted;
or else, they would be different.
Even so, if fire were other than fuel,
then fire would be perceived independently of fuel;
for indeed, a cloth that is other than a pot is never seen to be independent of it.
And since fire would thus not be dependent on fuel, this [position] is not tenable. // 1 //
Moreover: If fire were other than fuel, then it would be eternally burning, as it would lack a cause for its ignition.
Furthermore, in such a case, rekindling would be useless, and it would be devoid of action. (2)
If fire were desired to exist as something distinct from fuel, it would be perpetually burning;
it would lack a cause for its ignition, and the act of starting it would be rendered useless.
This being the case, it would be entirely devoid of action. // 2 //
Desiring to establish this very point, he says:
"Because it would be independent of anything else, it would not have ignition as its cause;
furthermore, if it were eternally burning, the act of igniting it again would be rendered useless. (3)
Thus: in this context, that which is ignited is "ignition," namely the fuel;
that which has ignition as its cause is "caused by ignition. That which is not caused by ignition is "not caused by ignition" (*apradīpanahetuka*).
If fire were other than the act of kindling, then it would be independent of fuel;
for whatever is other than something else [is independent of it].
It is observed to be independent of that [fuel], just as a cloth is independent of a jar;
and consequently, because it is independent of anything else, it would lack the cause for its ignition.
For fire that depends on fuel for its ignition would indeed go out in the absence of that fuel;
however, when it is independent of fuel for its ignition,
it would remain perpetually burning due to the lack of any condition for extinction.
Furthermore, if fire were eternally burning, then the fanning of its fuel and so forth for the sake of preventing the fire from going out would be entirely useless;
and this being the case, fire would be an agent that performs no action.
Furthermore, one who lacks an object of action cannot possess agency, just like the son of a barren woman;
therefore, it is not tenable that fire is something other than the fuel. // 3 //
Here it is said: As for what was stated—
"If fire were other than fuel, it would exist even apart from fuel"—
that is incorrect.
Even though fire and fuel are distinct here, fire does not exist without fuel;
for that which is encompassed by flames and characterized as being combustible is the fuel,
and it is by depending upon that [fuel] that fire is perceived, not separately.
And since this is so, the designation "fuel" occurs only through its connection with fire,
and fire is perceived by depending upon fuel, not separately from it.
In that case, there would be no occasion at all for the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of faults such as "if fire were other than fuel" and so forth.
Yet, pointing out the irrationality of this position as well, he says:
"If it is argued that in this case, the fuel becomes what is being ignited..."
By what could that fuel be ignited, when it is merely of such a nature? //4//

If you think that the object characterized by being combustible, which is enveloped by flames, is the fuel, and that fire is its support—even when conceived in this way, it is not tenable to say that "fire burns the fuel. Why? Because:
By what could that fuel be ignited when it is merely of such a nature?
For when it is conceptualized here that "fire burns the fuel," the fuel to be consumed is that which is enveloped by flames;
and apart from this, we do not perceive any other fire by which the fuel might be burned.
Since only this much is perceived— namely, the mere combustible object enveloped by the flame—
and since there is no fire apart from this, then by what could that fuel be burned?
When it is said "this is merely that," the meaning is "this is merely that which is being ignited.
Therefore, fire does not burn the fuel, because there is no fire distinct from it.
And since this is so, how could there be the grasping of a flame by anyone? Thus, that very same fault does not waver. // 4 //

Moreover, if one accepts the distinctness of fire and fuel, since the designation "that which is being burned" would be absent, from where could there be fuel that is being burned, or how could fire burn the fuel? Demonstrating this, he says:
"If they were other, they would not meet; not meeting, it would not burn; and not burning, [it would not be fire]."
One who is not unextinguished will not attain nirvana, or else he will remain possessing his own characteristic.
If fire were other than fuel, then, because of that otherness, it would not reach the fuel—just as it does not reach darkness.
And it would not burn it, because of that non-reachment, being as if situated at a remote distance; such is the intended meaning.
And thus, it is not at all tenable that the fuel is being ignited;
consequently, there would be no extinction of the fire,
and [the fire], not being extinguished, would remain possessing its own characteristic marks.
The meaning is "blazing.
The word "vā" (or) should be understood as signifying emphasis or as having the sense of an alternative:
fire will remain possessing its own characteristic mark alone.

Or, if there is no otherness of fire from the fuel, or in the case of their conjunction: [if they were identical], the fire would not reach the fuel, it would not burn it, it would not go out, and it would remain possessing its own characteristic.
Therefore, it is illogical for fire to be something other than the fuel. // 5 //

Here it is said: "It is illogical that fire and fuel are different, because [if they were different], the fire would not reach the fuel; and not reaching it, it would not burn it; and not burning it, [it would not be called fire]," and so forth.
That is incorrect.
For it is observed that the meeting of a woman and a man occurs when they are distinct;
likewise, it will be the same for fire and fuel. It is said in response:
Fire would indeed meet with fuel only if it were something other than the fuel.
Just as a woman obtains a man and a man obtains a woman. // 6 //
This might be so, if the establishment of fire and fuel were independent of one another, as is the case with a woman and a man. // 6 //
But he says that it is not so:
"Fire would indeed reach the fuel if fire and fuel were distinct from one another and mutually independent. (7)
But it is not possible that fire should exist independently of fuel, nor that fuel should exist independently of fire;
therefore, the example is futile.
It would be logical to employ as examples only those things for which attainment is established despite their being mutually dependent for their arising and possessing distinctness;
however, since such things do not exist, it is not tenable to claim that attainment exists when there is distinctness. // 7 //
Here it is said: Even though fire and fuel do not have an establishment independent of each other like a woman and a man, nevertheless, there is at least mutual dependence between them.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of fire and fuel does indeed exist, because they are mutually dependent.
For indeed, a mutual dependence between the son and daughter of a barren woman, who do not exist, is never observed.
It is said in reply: even so—if fire exists in dependence on fuel, or if fuel exists in dependence on fire—
Which of these two is established first, such that fire would depend upon fuel?

If fire is established in dependence upon fuel, thinking "this fire is the burner and the agent of this fuel," and if fuel is [established] in dependence upon fire, thinking "this fuel is the object (karman) of this fire";
Of these two, which was established first:
is it the fuel, depending upon which fire would exist, or is it the fire, depending upon which there would be fuel?
In that regard, if it is conceived that the fuel is already established beforehand, that is incorrect,
because that which is independent of fire and not being ignited lacks the nature of fuel.
Because it would follow that everything, including grass and so forth, would be fuel;
furthermore, the claim that fire comes first and fuel afterwards is also untenable.
Because fire that is already established prior to the fuel is impossible,
as it would entail the consequence of being causeless; and because, if it were to exist after [the fuel], its dependence on it would be purposeless.
Therefore, there is nothing here that is established beforehand, in dependence upon which the establishment of the other could occur. // 8 //
Moreover, if you think that the fuel comes first and the fire afterwards— even so,
if fire depends upon fuel, it would be the establishment of a fire that is already established.
If it is conceived that fire exists in dependence upon fuel, then in that case, there would be a further proof of fire which is already established.
It is only for an existing entity, whose form is already established, that dependence is logical.
For indeed, Devadatta, being non-existent in the house, does not depend on anything;
likewise, if fire were not existent, it would not depend on fuel.
Therefore, O Agni, your existence must be accepted.
And in that case, what further need is there for this fuel?
For fire that is already established does not require fuel again.
It must be for the sake of that purpose for which the dependence upon fuel would be fruitful.
Therefore, it is not logical to say that fire exists in dependence upon fuel.
Furthermore, if it is postulated that fire exists in dependence upon fuel—
If this were so, then fuel would also exist without fire.
If fuel were unestablished,
it could not be depended upon by fire, because that which is unestablished cannot be the object of dependence.
Therefore, one must admit the establishment of fuel that is devoid of fire; yet since this is not the case, it is not tenable. // 9 //
Now, it might be thought: the establishment of fire occurs simultaneously with the establishment of fuel, and the establishment of fuel occurs simultaneously with the establishment of fire;
and thus, since not even one of them is admitted to be established prior [to the other].
In this regard, as for what was said—
