Furthermore, that which is dependent upon someone is also his own property, just as one's own servants or one's own wealth;
whereas that which is dependent on another is not his own property, such as a temporary loan or anything that is not independent.

Since, in this way, it is not accepted that something artificial and dependent on other factors can be an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for this very reason it is logical that heat is not the intrinsic nature of fire; because it is bound by causes and conditions, having not existed previously and arising later, it is something produced (*kṛtaka*).
And since this is so:

Therefore, that which is the fire’s own innate form, unchanging across the three periods of time, which does not exist after having previously been non-existent, and which does not depend upon causes and conditions— unlike the heat of water, or like "this shore" and "the other shore," or like "long" and "short"— is [the true nature].
It is designated as "having that as its intrinsic nature.
But does fire indeed have such an essential form?
It does not exist, nor is it non-existent by way of its own essential form.
Even though this is so, nevertheless, for the sake of removing the fear of listeners, we say that it exists by way of conventional truth, having superposed [the existence] upon it.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"What is the hearing of the dharma that is beyond syllables, and what is its teaching?
It is heard and it is taught through superimposition, though it is without syllables.
And here too, he will say:
"One should not say 'it is empty,' nor that 'it is non-empty,' nor both, nor neither; it is spoken of only for the purpose of designation."
If indeed you say that it exists due to superimposition upon that,
what is its nature? It is that which is called the "dharmatā" of phenomena.
That itself is its true nature.
Now, what is this "dharmatā" (the true nature) of phenomena? It is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena.
What is this intrinsic nature? It is primordial substance. And what is this primordial substance?
It is this very emptiness.
What is this emptiness? It is the absence of intrinsic nature.
What is this absence of intrinsic nature? It is suchness.
What is this suchness (*tathatā*)?
It is the state of being thus, immutability, and perpetual stability.
Indeed, the absolute non-arising of fire and so forth—due to their independence from other factors and their lack of artificiality—is called their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This is what is meant: that very nature by which the collection of phenomena, perceived through the power of the cataract of ignorance, becomes an object for the Noble Ones (āryas) who are free from the cataract of ignorance—by way of its non-appearance—is established as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
And this is its definition:
It should be understood that the masters established [the principle]: "Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed non-artificial and independent of anything else.

Furthermore, this intrinsic nature of phenomena, which consists in their non-arising, is in fact no intrinsic nature at all, because it is a mere absence due to its being nothing whatsoever; thus, it should be understood that there is no intrinsic nature of phenomena.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"He who understands things as both existent and non-existent never becomes attached to any thing.
He who never becomes attached to any thing touches the signless concentration."
Thus [ends section] 2.

Here it is said: Even if entities have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nevertheless extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) must exist, since that has not been refuted; and if extrinsic nature exists, intrinsic nature will also come to exist.
"Because the existence of other-nature (parabhāva) is not established in the absence of self-nature (svabhāva). It is said in reply:
"How can there be other-nature in the absence of self-nature?
For self-nature is indeed called the 'other-nature' of other-nature. (3)
In this world, indeed, it is an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) itself that is designated as "other" (para) in relation to another intrinsic nature.
For if heat were the intrinsic nature of fire,
it would be designated as an extrinsic nature (parabhāva) in relation to water, which has fluidity as its intrinsic nature.
But when, upon investigation by those seeking liberation, no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) whatsoever exists for anything, then how could there be "otherness" (paratva)?
And since otherness does not exist, it is established that intrinsic nature also does not exist. // 3 //
Here it is said: even if intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature do not exist, nevertheless, an entity (bhāva) must still exist,
since it has not been negated.
And that entity, in its process of becoming, must be either an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or an extrinsic nature (parabhāva);
therefore, both intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature will also come into being. To this it is said:
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, how could an entity possibly exist?
For an entity is established only when either intrinsic nature or extrinsic nature exists. // 4 //
For an entity, when being conceptualized, must be either intrinsic nature or extrinsic nature;
and these two do not exist according to the method previously explained.
Thus, since those two do not exist, it should be understood that existence itself does not exist either. // 4 //
Here it is said: although existence has been refuted by you, nevertheless non-existence exists,
because there is no negation of it.
And consequently, existence (bhāva) will also exist because of the presence of its opposite,
just like non-existence (abhāva). To this it is replied:
It might be an entity if it were indeed a non-entity; but since it does not exist, he says:
If existence is not established, non-existence is certainly not established;
for people say that the alteration of existence is non-existence. // 5 //
For in this case, if there were some such thing as an entity (*bhāva*),

its non-existence (*abhāva*) would follow from its alteration (*anyathābhāva*). Indeed, in the world, things such as jars, having fallen away from their present state and undergone alteration, become denotable by the term "non-existence."
But when these things such as pots are not established even as having the nature of existence, then how could there be a change in those whose intrinsic nature does not exist?
Therefore, non-existence also does not exist. //5//

Thus, since intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, existence, and non-existence are in every way untenable, those whose eyes of intellect are impaired by the cataracts of ignorance do not see the reality of the Buddha’s teaching— those who perceive [things] erroneously as intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, existence, and indeed non-existence. (6)
For those who, out of pride in their own non-erroneous explanations of the Tathāgata’s teachings, maintain that the nature of earth is solidity, the nature of feeling is the experience of objects,
and the nature of consciousness is the distinct cognition of objects—
Thus they describe the intrinsic nature of phenomena:
consciousness is one thing, and form is another.

Furthermore, they describe sensation as being something entirely other; thus they describe the nature of "otherness," while those who describe the present state of consciousness and so forth as being the [actual] entity itself.
Furthermore, by asserting that consciousness and the other factors, once they have passed into the past, are non-existent,
you do not describe the reality of the most profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
for the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), and so forth, is contradicted by the reasoning already set forth.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas do not describe the intrinsic nature of things in a way that contradicts reason,
because they have personally and unerringly awakened to the reality of all things in their entirety.
For this very reason, the wise declare that the word of the Blessed Buddhas alone is authoritative.
Because it is non-contradictory by virtue of being supported by logical reasoning;
and for this very reason, because it has come from authoritative persons (*āpta*) who have abandoned all defects,
or because it causes one to arrive at reality, or because it causes one to understand reality in its entirety.
Because it leads toward [the goal] or because the world proceeds to nirvāṇa by relying upon it, the word of the Fully Awakened One alone is established as *āgama* (scriptural authority).
However, other doctrines, being devoid of logical justification (*upapatti*), lack validity and are established as mere semblances of scripture (*āgamābhāsa*). // 6 //

And because these views regarding intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, existence, and non-existence are devoid of logical consistency and are therefore not realities, for this very reason, in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, [the Blessed One] taught both "it exists" and "it does not exist" to those disciples seeking liberation.
This was forbidden by the Blessed One, who discerns both existence and non-existence.
For it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryakātyāyanāvavādasūtra*:
"Kātyāyana, for the most part this world is attached to existence or to non-existence;
therefore, it is not liberated."
One is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
one is not liberated from the bondage of the prison of saṃsāra with its five destinies;
and one is not liberated from the suffering and anguish caused by the death of a mother.
"Because of the suffering and anguish caused by the death of his father," and so forth.
And this sutra is recited in all the schools (nikāya).

Therefore, based on this scripture and the reasoning as it has been described, a wise person ought not to maintain a view regarding the existence or non-existence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and extrinsic nature (parabhāva), for such a view is utterly contradictory to the words of the Tathāgata;
it has been rejected by the Blessed One.
By what kind of Blessed One?
By the one who discerns existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvavibhāvī*).
He is called *bhāvābhāvavibhāvī* because it is his nature (*śīla*) to discern both existence and non-existence.

Because he has thoroughly understood the non-erroneous intrinsic nature of existence and non-existence as they truly are, the Blessed One alone is called "the one who discerns existence and non-existence.

Since both existence and non-existence have been negated by that Blessed One who discerns existence and non-existence, it is therefore not logical to maintain that the view of existence and non-existence constitutes reality.
Likewise,
Kāśyapa, "it exists" is one extreme; "it does not exist" is another extreme, Kāśyapa.
That which is between these two extremes is formless, invisible, baseless, non-manifest, without abode, and without cognitive representation;
this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the authentic discernment of reality.
Likewise:
"It exists" and "it does not exist"—both are extremes; "purity" and "impurity"—these too are extremes.
Therefore, having avoided both extremes, the wise person does not take a stand even in the middle.
"It is 'it exists' and 'it does not exist'—this is a dispute; 'purity' and 'impurity'—this is a dispute.
Through the attainment of dispute, suffering is not pacified; through the attainment of non-dispute, suffering ceases.
To this, he says: "If, moreover, fire and the like were to exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva)..."
What fault would there be? The aforementioned fault:
"An intrinsic nature produced from causes and conditions would be something created," and so forth. // 7 //
Furthermore, if this were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these things such as fire and so forth, then that which exists as such could not undergo alteration; demonstrating this, he says:
"If existence were by way of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtyā*), there would be no non-existence of it."

If a thing such as fire exists by way of its intrinsic nature—that is, by its very essence—then there could be no further alteration of that intrinsic nature which already exists by way of its essence. For:
"An alteration of intrinsic nature is indeed never possible. (8)

If this very nature were the intrinsic essence (svabhāva) of these things such as fire and so forth, then, because an intrinsic essence is unchanging, it would never be possible for them to undergo alteration.
For the non-obstructiveness of space never undergoes any change;
likewise, there should be no further alteration of fire and other elements that exist by their very nature.
Yet you perceive their destruction, characterized by the cessation of the continuity of their alteration.
Therefore, because they are subject to transformation, like the heat of water, it should be understood that this [permanence] is not their intrinsic nature. // 8 //

Here it is said: If it is argued that these entities have no intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) because a change of state is impossible for that which exists by way of intrinsic nature, yet a change of state is nevertheless perceived, then even so—
since intrinsic nature does not exist for anything, how will there be a change of state?

Now, for what that does not exist by way of its own nature or intrinsic essence— like a flower in the sky— could there be a change of state? Therefore, since no change of state is observed in that which lacks an existing nature,
yet a change of state is indeed seen, [it follows that things do not arise from themselves].
"It exists as intrinsic nature (svabhāva). To this it is said:
If, according to your view, "nature" is so called because that which does not exist by way of its own nature lacks any alteration, yet alteration is nevertheless observed, even so—
And while what nature (prakṛti) exists, how could there be any alteration? // 9 //
Now, for what that exists by way of its own nature (*prakṛti*) and intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), which is indeed present, could there be alteration?
Therefore, for that which exists by way of its own nature, there is no alteration; thus, in every respect, alteration is simply impossible.
Consequently, it should be understood that there is no intrinsic nature of phenomena. // 9 //
As for what was also said— that there is no primal nature (prakṛti) because change is observed—
that too was stated with reference to the observation of change as it is established by others;
however, we have never at any time accepted the change of anything whatsoever.

Thus, since the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) does not exist at all, and since all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) do not exist, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), and since their alteration (*anyathātva*) also does not exist— then for one who now conceptually constructs the existence and non-existence of entities,
while thus conceptualizing, it is necessarily the case that:
"It exists" is the grasping at permanence; "it does not exist" is the view of nihilism.
The phrase "it follows [as a consequence]" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And because this view of permanence and nihilism causes obstacles on the path to heaven and liberation, it brings about great harm.
Therefore, the wise person should not rely upon existence or non-existence. // 10 //
Why, moreover, does the consequence of the views of eternalism and nihilism follow when there is the view of existence and non-existence? Because:
"That which exists by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not become non-existent"—this is eternalism.
"It does not exist now, though it existed previously"—this leads to the consequence of nihilism. (11)
That which is said to exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) never at any time does not exist, because intrinsic nature is imperishable;
thus, when one accepts the existence of an entity in this manner, one falls into the view of eternalism (śāśvatadarśana).

Furthermore, for one who previously accepted the essential nature of an entity during its state of existence and now subsequently accepts that it does not exist because it has perished, the view of annihilationism follows as a logical consequence.
However, for one for whom the very intrinsic nature of an entity is not established, there is no consequence of falling into the views of eternalism or annihilationism.
Because the intrinsic nature of entities is not perceived.

Now, one might object: for one who accepts that entities have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while the view of permanence may indeed not arise due to the absence of the perception of entities, the view of annihilation (*ucchedadarśana*) necessarily follows. This is not so; it does not constitute a view of non-existence.
For one who first accepts the intrinsic nature of an entity and subsequently takes its cessation as an object,

there would indeed be a view of non-existence due to the denial of that previously perceived intrinsic nature. But for one who, like a person free from cataracts, perceives nothing at all— just as one free from cataracts perceives nothing in the hairs seen by one with cataracts— [there is no such view].
If one were to say that something does not exist, one would have to say "nothing exists at all," because there would be no object to be negated.
However, for the sake of removing the false attachment of those who are deluded, we—like those free from cataracts—say: "All things do not exist.
And for us, who are thus speaking and are solely devoted to the welfare of others, there is no consequence of falling into the view of nihilism.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Blessed One, whoever first accepts the existence of passion, hatred, and delusion, and later says that the states of passion, hatred, and delusion do not exist—
he, O Blessed One, is indeed a nihilist."
Thus is the detailed explanation.

But for one who, having accepted the mere reality of dependent mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), avoids the view of existence because of the non-existence of their imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
yet avoids the view of non-existence because of the actual existence of the mere dependent reality which is the basis for affliction and purification—
how can such a person avoid the two extremes, given that both views of existence and non-existence apply, since the imagined is non-existent while the dependent is existent?

Furthermore, since it has been demonstrated that what is produced by causes and conditions is untenable by virtue of having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this [opponent's] explanation is indeed untenable.
Thus, it is only within the Madhyamaka view that the occurrence of the two views of existence and non-existence is avoided, and not in the views of the Vijñānavādins and others.
This is to be understood.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*:
"The Sāṃkhyas, the Ulūkyas, the Nirgranthas, and those who propound the person (*pudgala*) or the aggregates (*skandha*)."
Ask the world if it speaks of a transcendence of "is" and "is not."
"Know that the nectar of the Buddhas' teaching, which transcends 'is' and 'is not,' is called 'profound' because it is the dowry of the Dharma. Thus it is said.

However, it should be understood that the discourse on consciousness and so forth was taught by the Blessed One as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), rather than of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), because it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for those to be trained who require such instruction, and because he was under the influence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As it is said in the venerable *Āryasamādhirāja*:
He knows the distinction of the sūtras of definitive meaning— the emptiness as taught by the Sugata—
and he understands all phenomena in their interpretable sense, wherein there is no person, being, or individual.
And this should be understood in detail from such sources as the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*.

Having realized that saṃsāra persists for as long as there is the adherence to the two views of existence and non-existence, the virtuous who seek liberation should cultivate the Middle Way exactly as it is, by means of rejecting these two views.
This was stated by the Blessed One:
Knowledge discerns both existence and non-existence; all is inconceivable, all is unreal.
But those fools who follow the power of the mind suffer for hundreds of millions of births.
"He who understands things as both existent and non-existent is never attached to any phenomena;
he who is never attached to any phenomena touches the signless samādhi. Thus it is said. Furthermore:
I remember that in a past time, in an inconceivable eon, there arose a Great Sage, the supreme among men, who acted for the benefit of the world; his name was Abhāvasamudgata.
As soon as he was born, standing in the sky, he taught the non-existence of all phenomena;
accordingly, a name was given to him, and by that sound, all within the triple-thousandfold world system became aware.
All the gods also raised a cry: "He shall become a Jina who has transcended all existence;
he who, immediately upon birth, took seven steps and proclaimed the equality of all phenomena as being without inherent existence."
When the Buddha becomes the King of Dharma, the Sage who reveals all phenomena,
there will arise the sound of the non-existence of all phenomena— of grasses, shrubs, trees, herbs, rocks, and mountains.
"As many sounds as there are in that world-system, all of them are indeed non-existent; for there is not the slightest thing that exists.
So many indeed are the sounds that issue forth from that Tathāgata, the Guide of the World.
Thus, "existence" (*bhāva*) means being or substantiality.
Since the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all things does not exist, all phenomena are non-existent;
all phenomena are empty by virtue of the yoga of being without intrinsic nature, according to the reading of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, because the intrinsic nature of an entity is untenable.
Thus, there will be a sound regarding phenomena that are non-existent.
The meaning of the sūtra should be understood through these and other such passages.
"Whatever sounds there are in that world-system, all are indeed non-existent; for there is no existence whatsoever," and so forth.
Because the intention is to negate existence after it has come to be, the meaning of "existence and non-existence" is precisely the meaning of "the absence of intrinsic nature."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Examination of Intrinsic Nature," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Sixteenth Chapter: An Examination of Bondage and Liberation.
Here it is said: The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities certainly exists, because cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) exists.
In this context, "saṃsāra" refers to wandering; the transition from one state of existence to another state of existence is called saṃsāra.
If entities (bhāvas) lacked intrinsic nature (svabhāva), of what would there be a transition from one state of existence to another state of existence as saṃsāra?
For indeed, the transmigration of non-existent things, such as the conditioned phenomena of a barren woman’s son, is never observed.
Therefore, because transmigration exists, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities must certainly exist.
To this, it is replied:
There might be an intrinsic nature of phenomena if cyclic existence itself were to exist;
however, it does not.
In this case, if saṃsāra were to exist,
would it necessarily belong to the formative forces (saṃskāras) or to a sentient being (sattva)? And what follows from this?
And since there is a fault in both cases, he says:

"If it is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that transmigrate, they do not transmigrate as permanent entities; nor do they transmigrate as impermanent. This same sequence applies to a sentient being (*sattva*) as well. (1)
In that regard, if it is postulated that the formations (*saṃskāra*) transmigrate,
do they transmigrate as permanent or as impermanent?
In this case, they do not transmigrate as permanent, because they lack activity.
And because impermanent things such as jars are observed to possess activity;
whereas those which are inactive are indeed impermanent.
They perish immediately upon arising.
And as for those that have perished,
since they no longer exist, how could they go anywhere— any more than the conditioned phenomena of a barren woman’s son?
Thus, even for impermanent things, there is no cyclic existence.

Now, it might be argued: "The conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), though indeed impermanent, transmigrate by means of an uninterrupted succession through the continuous chain of the relationship between cause and effect, and by proceeding as a continuum (*saṃtāna*).
This too is not tenable.
Why? Because, first of all, that which arises as an effect...
For him there is no saṃsāra, because there is no coming from anywhere nor going anywhere;
and as for that cause which has perished, [it does not exist].
For him also, there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*),
because there is no coming from anywhere nor going anywhere;
for the past and the future are not established apart from mere conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is non-existent by virtue of being both destroyed and unarisen.
If it is argued that when the subsequent moment has arisen, the preceding one transmigrates,
this could only be so if there were identity between the preceding and subsequent moments.
But there is no identity because of the relationship of cause and effect;
nor does such identity exist among the eye, visible forms, and visual consciousness.
Furthermore, if identity were to exist, the very designation of "prior" and "subsequent" moments would be impossible.
For a single Devadatta is not designated as both "prior" and "subsequent" at one and the same time;
likewise here too, because of its oneness, there could be no designation of "prior" and "subsequent" moments.
Furthermore, it would not be the case that the prior moment has perished, because it is non-different from the subsequent moment.
It would not be the case that "the subsequent moment has arisen," because it is non-different from the preceding moment.
Alternatively, if there were transmigration, it would have to occur upon the existence of difference [between moments].
If this were the case, even Arhats would undergo transmigration,
because the arising of saṃsāra exists for other ordinary persons (pṛthagjana);
furthermore, it would follow that an extinguished lamp burns within another lamp.
Furthermore:
would the arising of the subsequent moment occur from a preceding moment that has perished, one that has not perished, or one that is currently perishing?
In this regard, if it is held to arise from what has perished:
An sprout would arise even from a seed burnt by fire,
and consequently, it would be without a cause. Or, [if you say it arises] from that which has not perished, [then...]
Even so, the sprout would arise even while the seed remains unaltered;
there would be simultaneity between cause and effect; and arising would be without a cause.
If it is argued that [destruction occurs] while it is being destroyed, no;

for there is no "being destroyed" apart from what has already been destroyed and what has not yet been destroyed, and as for those two— what has been destroyed and what has not been destroyed— [they are mutually exclusive].
Since it perishes while still being subject to the faults [of production], there is no arising;
how, then, could there be the established order of cause and effect, or the established order of preceding and succeeding moments?
And when the established order of preceding and succeeding moments and the established order of cause and effect do not exist, [how can there be any causal relationship?]
In that case, there would be no continuum either;
and because of its absence, for you there would be no saṃsāra—meaning that even for impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is no saṃsāra.
On this point, some explain as follows: "It is true that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) do not transmigrate because they lack the nature of arising;
rather, it is the sentient being (*sattva*) who transmigrates. To this, it is replied:
This same sequence applies to the sentient being as well.
When it is said that "the sentient being transmigrates," does this one transmigrate as something permanent,
or as something impermanent?
When this is investigated, the very same sequence by which the transmigration of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is untenable applies equally to a sentient being (sattva) as well;
therefore, even a sentient being does not transmigrate. // 1 //
To this it is said: Indeed, the sequence of the non-arising of the transmigration of sentient beings and their formative forces cannot be the same;
for it has been stated here that there is no transmigration of formative forces, whether they be permanent or impermanent.
And the self is not likewise either permanent or impermanent.
For just as its being neither identical to nor different from the aggregates (skandhas) is declared to be inexpressible, so too its being permanent or impermanent is established as inexpressible.
Therefore, it is argued that it is the self (ātman) itself that transmigrates, and thus the aforementioned fault does not follow. To this it is replied:
If the person (pudgala) transmigrates within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements...
When sought in five ways, this [self] does not exist; what is it that will transmigrate? // 2 //
If there were such a thing as a person (pudgala),
he would transmigrate;
however, no such thing exists.
Because [the self], when sought in five ways among the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, does not exist.
How so? Furthermore, fire is neither the fuel, nor is it other than the fuel.
Fire does not possess fuel; fuel is not in the fire; nor is the fire in them.
The sequence of the self and its appropriation has been explained by means of fire and fuel.
Thus, the self does not have the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements as its intrinsic nature;
nor is it distinct from them;
nor does it possess the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
The self does not exist within the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements;
nor do the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements exist within the self.
Thus, when sought in these five ways according to the reasoning previously stated, the self is not found to exist.
Since, when thus investigated within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, [the self] does not exist in any of the five ways,
how could it, being non-existent, transmigrate? In this way, there is no transmigration for the self either.
Because it is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman. // 2 //

Moreover: This self, migrating from one appropriation to another, would become non-existent; and being non-existent and without appropriation, who is it that will migrate, and what will it migrate? (3)

Let it be granted for the sake of argument that there is a cycle of existence (saṃsāra) for the self, provided that such a cycle of existence were logical for one who exists without appropriation (anupādāna).
However, demonstrating how its state of being without appropriation follows as a consequence, he says:
"Transmigrating from one appropriation to another, one would become non-existent.
For in this case, when going from the appropriation of a human to the appropriation of a deity, does one go having abandoned the human appropriation, or without abandoning it?
If it is said that one goes having abandoned it, [the following objection applies].
Then, due to the relinquishing of the prior appropriation and the non-appropriation of the subsequent one, there would be a state of dissolution (*vibhava*) in the interval between them.
Dissolution (*vibhava*) means that existence (*bhava*) has departed.
Existence consists of the five aggregates of appropriation (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*).
He would be devoid of that.
Furthermore, one who is non-existent and without appropriation would be causeless, because, being devoid of the aggregates, he would lack the causal basis for designation.
And that which is without appropriation (*anupādāna*), stainless (*nirañjana*), unmanifest (*avyakta*), and without cause (*nirhetuka*)—what is it?
It is nothing at all;
the meaning is that it does not exist at all.
And since that [appropriator] does not exist, because of its very absence, appropriation also does not exist as something without an appropriator; so what will transmigrate?
The meaning is that there is simply nothing which will transmigrate.
Alternatively, why is this [non-existence] a qualifier of the action of transmigrating?
And thus, because it does not exist, it will certainly not perform the action of transmigrating.
In this way, first of all, transmigration by means of abandoning a previous appropriation is untenable.
Now, even if it is by way of non-abandonment, that too is not tenable.
What is the reason?
Because there would be a dual nature for a single self due to the non-abandonment of the former and the grasping of the latter,
and this is not desired;
therefore, there is no transmigration even by way of non-abandonment.
Furthermore, because the aggregates of the intermediate state arise between the two states of existence— the prior and the subsequent—

and because those [aggregates] possess appropriation (*sopādāna*), it follows that even for one who is transmigrating, there is no consequence of being without appropriation (*vibhava*). This too is not tenable.

Because the same logical consequence applies even to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—the wandering through the aggregates (*skandhas*)—regardless of whether one has abandoned or not abandoned the previous existence.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the simultaneous relinquishing and taking up, it is said in reply:
Does one relinquish the previous appropriation with one part while transferring by means of one part to the appropriation of the intermediate state, or does one do so with the whole self?
In that regard, if it is conceived [to exist] by way of a part,
then there is the aforementioned fault because of the consequence of having a dual nature;
or if [it exists] by way of its entire self, [the same fault follows].
Even so, that same consequence of non-existence (vibhavatā) would follow.
However, this much is the distinction: in the transition between intermediate states (antarābhava), due to extreme proximity, one might be without appropriation for a subtle duration of time.
Yet, it is never observed that there is simultaneous relinquishment and appropriation of an entire object—that is, of a single, undivided entity—with respect to its whole.

For it is not possible for a single Devadatta, moving from house to house with his entire self, to simultaneously perform the two acts of abandoning and taking up. If, however, simultaneous abandoning and taking up are postulated by means of one foot abandoning one house while the other foot takes up another,
then in that case, the self would possess a dual nature, just like its two feet.
Since it would have to abide in the former [state] by one part and abide in the latter [state] by another part, the consequence of having multiple parts would follow.
Therefore, simultaneous relinquishing and taking up are also impossible; thus, this is not a valid resolution.

Consequently, even in the case of taking up an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), that same fault follows; therefore, in every respect, there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) for a self (*ātman*) either.
And when there is no cyclic existence for either conditioned phenomena or a self, it is established that cyclic existence does not exist at all. // 3 //
Here it is said: Saṃsāra indeed exists, because its opposite exists;
for that which does not exist here, [its opposite cannot exist].
No opponent exists for it,
just as there is none for the son of a barren woman;
yet, there does exist an opponent to saṃsāra, namely nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that cyclic existence exists.
It may indeed be that there is cyclic existence.
If nirvana were the opposite of that [conditioned existence], it would not exist; thus he says:
"The nirvana of conditioned phenomena is not possible in any way."
Nor can the nirvāṇa of a sentient being be established in any way whatsoever. // 4 //
If there were such a thing as nirvāṇa, when it is being conceptually constructed, would it be conceived as belonging to conditioned phenomena that are permanent or to those that are impermanent?
In that regard, what could nirvāṇa do for things that are permanent and unchanging?
"What nirvāṇa could there be for things that are impermanent and non-existent?"—this is entirely the same as what was said before.
"In no way whatsoever" means by no manner at all.
Now, if the nirvāṇa of a sentient being is postulated, that too— as before— is not tenable whether it belongs to something permanent or something impermanent.
Now, if it is postulated that [the self] is inexpressible in terms of being either permanent or impermanent,
then in that case, one would have to admit that the self exists even in nirvāṇa, just as it does in saṃsāra.
Furthermore:
The inexpressibility of a self that possesses appropriation (sopādāna) is logical; however, since there is no appropriation in nirvāṇa, how could such a self possess inexpressibility?
Or, let it be granted that the self is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates].
Furthermore, does this [self] exist in nirvāṇa or not?
If it exists, then because of its presence even in liberation, it would be eternal.
If, on the other hand, it does not exist, then the self would be impermanent.

Furthermore, just as [the self] is inexpressible in terms of being identical to or different from [the aggregates], it would follow that it is likewise inexpressible in terms of being permanent or impermanent.
Now, if you maintain that even in *nirvāṇa* the self is simply inexpressible in terms of existence or non-existence,
even so, is it cognizable or not?
If it were cognizable, then this self would not be without appropriation in nirvāṇa, because of its being cognizable, just as in saṃsāra.
But if it is not cognized, [then...]
In that case, because its nature is unknowable, it simply does not exist, like a flower in the sky; so how can it be "inexpressible"?
Thus, even nirvāṇa does not exist. Because of its non-existence, saṃsāra does not exist either.
Therefore, it is said in the *Bhagavatī Aṣṭasāhasrikā*: "Venerable Subhūti, even nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a dream;
the qualities of a Buddha, Venerable Subhūti, are like illusions, like dreams," and so forth.
If, son of good family, there were another dharma even more superior than nirvāṇa, I would say that it too is like an illusion and like a dream.
Likewise, in the venerable *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"Ultimate truth is equal to a dream; nirvāṇa likewise transcends the dream. When the mind thus transcends [them], the wise declare that this is the supreme restraint of the mind."
Likewise,
when a bodhisattva here transcends the truth of cessation as if it were a dream, and likewise the nature of sleep and even nirvana by means of speech— this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
Here it is said: Even though you have refuted both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, nevertheless, bondage and liberation do exist.
And bondage and liberation are not possible for a non-existent intrinsic nature of things.
Therefore, because bondage and liberation truly exist, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities must indeed exist.
To this it is replied: there might be an intrinsic nature of entities, [but...]
If bondage and liberation were indeed real, they would not be as they are; thus he says:
"Those characterized by the nature of arising and passing away are neither bound nor liberated."
Conditioned phenomena are as before; a sentient being is neither bound nor liberated. // 5 //
In this context, those afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, which are designated as "bondage" because they render those who are bound devoid of autonomy,

and by means of which ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are established as not transcending the three realms— this very thing conceived as bondage is impossible for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that possess the nature of arising and passing away; for these, being momentary, perish immediately after their production, and once destroyed, they lack existence.
Furthermore, liberation characterized by the severance of the bonds of passion and so forth is simply not possible, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), being impermanent, do not exist;
this is according to the previous method, meaning the manner previously explained.
And just as, by the previously explained method, bondage and liberation of conditioned phenomena are not possible, [so too is liberation impossible].
In this way, just as before, a sentient being is neither bound nor liberated; thus, both bondage and liberation do not exist. // 5 //

Here it is said: Even if there is no bondage of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) or of a sentient being (*sattva*), nevertheless, that which is called "clinging" (*upādāna*), consisting of passion and so forth, exists as a form of bondage;
because of its existence, bondage will also exist.
It is said:
there might be appropriation if it were to bind some entity, [but it does not].
But it does not bind.
Demonstrating how it does not bind, he says:
If grasping is the bondage, then one who possesses grasping is not bound; nor is one without grasping bound. In what state, then, is one bound? // 6 //
In that regard, one who possesses appropriation— that is, one whose appropriation is present—
is not bound as long as he is such a being.
For whoever possesses appropriation, [is not bound].
He is already bound;
what further use would the application of bondage have for him?
And as for one who is without appropriation and free from bondage, [what could bondage do for him?]
He too, being free from bondage, is not bound, just like a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is illogical to say that one who is without appropriation and free from bondage is bound, because these are mutually contradictory.
And when examined in this way, whether with or without appropriation, he is not bound.
In what state, then, could he now be bound?
The intention is that there is no other state whatsoever for him in which he might be bound.
And when, upon such investigation, bondage does not bind anyone at all, then how can there be the state of being a bond for appropriation—such as passion and so forth—which binds no one?
Therefore, even bondage does not exist. (6)
Moreover:
one might indeed bind a bond if it existed prior to that which is to be bound;
but that does not exist.

In this world, it is observed that a fetter such as an iron chain, being already established independently of the one to be bound, binds the person to be bound, Devadatta. Likewise, if passion and the like, as a fetter, were established prior to the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*)— which are the objects to be bound—
or prior to the person (*pudgala*), who is the one to be bound, then by means of that previously established fetter, there would be a binding of either the conditioned factors or the person.
Furthermore, this is not possible because passion and the like cannot be established without a basis;
and because it would be purposeless for a previously established bond to be subsequently connected with that which is to be bound.

Moreover, since that which is to be bound is already established independently of the bond, there is no need for it to depend on a prior bond; thus, the bond is not established prior to that which is to be bound.
Therefore, bondage does not bind anyone at all.
And since it is not logical for that which binds no one to possess the nature of a bond, bondage does not exist.
And because of the absence of bondage, it is established that the bound person also does not exist.
Furthermore, whatever remaining refutation exists here has already been stated by means of [the analysis of] the traversed, the untraversed, and that which is being traversed. // 7 //
Thus it should be understood;
by changing the reading of the verse:
"One who is bound is not being bound, and one who is unbound is likewise not being bound."
One who is liberated from both the bound and the unbound is not bound while being bound.
It is to be applied with these and other [verses]. // 7 //

To this, he says: Even though you have refuted bondage, nevertheless, for the sake of those sentient beings who are bound in the prison of saṃsāra and are without protection, the Tathāgatas, who possess great compassion, have taught the three aggregates consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; that which was taught for their sake, liberation, at least exists.
Furthermore, there is no liberation for a person who is not bound;
therefore, bondage also exists. To this it is replied:
There would be bondage if there were liberation itself.
In this case, when this liberation is being conceptualized, would it be conceptualized for one who is bound or for one who is unbound? What follows from this?
And since it is not tenable in either case, he says:
"One who is bound is not liberated, nor indeed is one who is unbound liberated;
if the bound were being liberated, there would be simultaneous bondage and liberation. (8)

In that case, liberation is not possible for one who is bound, because of being bound. Now, if it is argued that liberation occurs through a means after one has been bound, such that the very one who was bound is liberated, then one should not say that "the bound is liberated."
What then will be liberated? If it is argued that one is being liberated simply because of the proximity to the present moment, then liberation would have to be possible at some time or other.

In that case, proximity would only exist when liberation is intended for someone in some state whatsoever; however, since liberation is impossible for one who is bound, if it is intended to demonstrate the non-existence of liberation, then how can there be proximity to the present?
Thus, it is established that the bound is not liberated.
Now, even one who is not bound is not liberated;
for he is already liberated. What would further liberation do for him?

Furthermore, because those who are liberated—namely the Arhats—would still have an expectation for further liberation, they would remain bound; consequently, even an Arhat would be subject to bondage.
Now, it might be argued: "Since liberation is impossible for one who is not bound, only the bound person is liberated.

This being the case, if a bound person is conceived as being liberated, then because of both the state of being bound and the state of being liberated, there would be bondage and liberation simultaneously.
However, because they are mutually contradictory like light and darkness, bondage and liberation cannot logically occur at the same time.
And since liberation is thus impossible for both the bound and the unbound, it follows that liberation does not exist;
and because of its absence, bondage also does not exist— this is established.
Here he says: If both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have been refuted by you alone,
and both bondage and liberation have also been rejected,
then for those who desire to be liberated from this saṃsāra— [for whom] the true path is covered by the thick, long creepers of various false views and the dense darkness of ignorance— ...

For those who desire to cross over the great wilderness of the forest of saṃsāra—which is crowded with poisonous trees of latent tendencies that yield the fruit of vast and most undesirable ripenings in the form of various calamities such as birth and so forth; which is surrounded on all sides by the massive mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), towering with its twenty peaks; and which has the great moat of the river of craving flowing through the vast and extremely slippery ravines of the great slopes of hope for sensual pleasures—there is the wholesome and great aspiration for the Dharma (*mahādharmacchanda*), which provides supreme consolation.
When indeed shall I, free from grasping, enter parinirvāṇa?
When indeed will my nirvāṇa come to pass? Surely he generates such thoughts in vain.

If it is argued that even for those who have thus generated a vast and stainless desire for the Dharma (*dharmacchanda*)— and for whom there exists the sequence of attending upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), giving, ethical discipline, learning, reflection, and cultivation for the sake of attaining *nirvāṇa*—
that [sequence] would likewise be in vain, it is said in reply:

For one who [perceives] all things as being thus without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), resembling reflections, mirage-water, firebrands whirled into circles, dreams, illusions, and magical displays;

Because they follow after mere cognitive distortion regarding things that lack the intrinsic nature of a self or what belongs to a self, they produce that very view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) by grasping at it through the manifestation of "I" and "mine"—the notions of "I-making" and "mine-making"—and think:
"I shall pass away without clinging; Nirvana will be mine. For those who hold such a grasp, there is a great grasping of clinging (*upādāna*). (9)
"I shall attain nirvāṇa without grasping, free from all grasping;
and for me who has practiced in this way, nirvāṇa will come to pass"— for those seekers of liberation who hold such a view, [there is grasping].
Is it not the case that this very thing called the grasping at "I" and "mine"—the clinging to the view of a self-existent body—is their great obsession?
And for those who are intent upon such a great obsession, peace is not possible.
For the attainment of liberation occurs only through the abandonment of all obsessions without exception, as long as there is the clinging and intentness toward the grasping of "I" and "mine."

As long as there is the grasping and adherence that "nirvāṇa exists," and as long as there is the adherence to the relinquishing of grasping, all undertakings of those who seek nirvāṇa through non-expedient means will inevitably be in vain.
Therefore, all this must be relinquished by one who seeks liberation.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryadhyāyitamuṣṭisūtra*:
"Then the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: 'Because they do not see the reality of the four noble truths as it truly is, their minds are perverted by the four inversions.'"
"Sentient beings do not transcend this unreal saṃsāra in this way.
When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One teach: by grasping at what do sentient beings not transcend saṃsāra?
The Blessed One replied: "Mañjuśrī, it is because of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that sentient beings do not transcend saṃsāra."
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, for whoever perceives both self and other, for that person there are the formative activities of karma.
Mañjuśrī, the foolish, unlearned worldling, not understanding that all phenomena are ultimately unextinguished, perceives a self and another;
having perceived them, he becomes attached;
being attached, he becomes lustful, hateful, and deluded.
Being attached, hostile, and deluded, he performs threefold karma through body, speech, and mind.
Through the superimposition of what is unreal, he conceptualizes: "I am attached," "I am hostile."
"I am deluded.
When he has thus gone forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata, it occurs to him: "I am virtuous; I am a practitioner of the holy life."
I shall transcend cyclic existence; I shall attain nirvāṇa;
I shall be liberated from sufferings.
He discriminates thus: "These are wholesome phenomena;
these are unwholesome phenomena;
these phenomena are to be abandoned."
These phenomena are to be realized:
suffering is to be fully understood,
and its origin is to be abandoned.
Cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be cultivated.
He conceptualizes: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
"All conditioned phenomena are ablaze;
what if I were to flee from all conditioned phenomena?
As he contemplates in this way, there arises in him a mental attention accompanied by world-weariness and preceded by the signless.
It occurs to him: "This is that full comprehension of suffering, which is the full comprehension of these phenomena.
It occurs to him: "What if I were to abandon the origin?"
He feels aversion toward these phenomena, feels ashamed of them, rejects them, loathes them, and becomes terrified, thoroughly terrified, and falls into a state of terror.
It occurs to him: "This is the realization of these phenomena;
this is the abandonment of their origination, namely, this aversion and loathing toward these phenomena."
It occurs to him: "Cessation is to be realized.
Having conceptualized arising, he perceives cessation.
It occurs to him: "This is that realization of cessation."
It occurs to him: "What if I were to cultivate the path?
Going alone into seclusion, he attends to those phenomena and attains calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Through that mental attention accompanied by disenchantment, calm abiding arises for him.
His mind recoils from all phenomena, turns away from them, and retreats;
he feels aversion toward them and feels ashamed of them, and a mind of non-delight arises.
It occurs to him: "I am liberated from all sufferings;
there is nothing further for me to do.
I am an Arhat."
Thus he perceives himself;
at the time of the moment of death, he beholds his own rebirth,
and he experiences doubt and uncertainty regarding the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Having fallen into doubt, he passes away and falls into the great hells.
Why is that?
Because, having conceptualized all phenomena—which are in fact unarisen—he gives rise to doubt and indecision regarding the Tathāgata.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "But how, Blessed One, are the four noble truths to be seen?
The Blessed One replied: "Mañjuśrī, by one who sees that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are unarisen, suffering has been fully understood."
For one by whom all phenomena are seen as unarisen, origination has been abandoned;
for one by whom all phenomena are seen as utterly parinirvāṇized, [origination has been abandoned].
By him cessation has been realized;
by him who has seen all phenomena as absolutely empty,
the path has been cultivated.
Mañjuśrī, one who has thus seen these four noble truths does not conceptualize or discriminate, thinking: "These are wholesome phenomena; these are unwholesome phenomena."
These phenomena are to be abandoned;
these phenomena are to be realized;
suffering is to be fully understood.
The origin is to be abandoned, cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be cultivated.
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive that phenomenon which one might conceptualize;
however, foolish common people, conceptualizing these phenomena, become attached, hostile, and deluded.
He neither arranges nor dismantles any dharma whatsoever. Because he thus neither arranges nor dismantles, his mind does not cling to the triple world;
he perceives the entire triple world as unborn.
Thus is the detailed exposition. // 9 //
Therefore, from this very scripture, the ultimate truth is stated:
"There is no superimposition of nirvāṇa, nor any removal of saṃsāra. Where [is there] saṃsāra? What nirvāṇa is conceptualized there? (10)
For in the ultimate truth, since nothing is apprehended, there can be no such superimposition upon nirvana, nor any attribution of nirvana;
likewise, neither the removal of samsara nor the exhaustion of samsara is possible.
What is that saṃsāra which is conceptualized for the sake of its cessation, or what is that nirvāṇa which is conceptualized as the goal to be attained? Or rather:

since even by one who exerts effort, it is impossible to effect the removal of any sentient being from saṃsāra and the placement of them in nirvāṇa—because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are themselves unapprehendable—what is there to be conceptualized?
In that regard, what is conceptualized as nirvāṇa?
Indeed, it is not at all appropriate to conceptualize anything.
And for one who does not conceptualize, there will certainly be the transcendence of the wilderness and forest of saṃsāra as previously described, and the attainment of the city of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said in the *Āryamāradamana-sūtra*:

"Then, at that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta focused his attention in such a way that Māra the Evil One, bound by the fetters of Indra’s pillar and fallen to the surface of the earth, cried out: 'I am bound by tight fetters!'"

Mañjuśrī said: "O Evil One, is there a bond more firm than this bond by which you are eternally bound and yet are not bound again? What, then, is that? It is this: the bond of the inversion of the conceit 'I am,' and the bond of craving and views."
This, O Evil One, is a bond;
there exists no bond more firm than this bond.
By means of it you are eternally bound, and you are not bound again.
...and so forth.
He said: "O Evil One, would you be glad of heart if you were released?
He replied: "I would be glad of heart."
May I become supremely joyful.
Then the divine son Suyāma said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Release Māra, the Evil One!
Let him go to his own abode.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to Māra, the Evil One: "By whom have you been bound, O Evil One, that you release yourself?"
He said, "Mañjuśrī, I do not know by whom I am bound. He replied, "Evil one, just as you, though unbound, have the perception of being bound,
even so all foolish ordinary people perceive permanence in what is impermanent."
Perceiving suffering as non-suffering,
perceiving the impure as pure,
and perceiving the non-self as self.
Those who perceive form in the formless,
those who perceive feeling in the absence of feeling,
and those who perceive perception in the absence of perception.
Those who perceive conditioned phenomena in the unconditioned,
and perceive consciousness in the absence of consciousness;
moreover, O Evil One, [it is so].
"As for you who will be liberated, from what will you be liberated?
He replied, "I do not know from anywhere that I shall be liberated."
He said: "In the same way, O Evil One, even those who will be liberated will not be liberated from anything at all, except for that perception of what is unreal."
They fully understand that;
having fully understood it, they are said to be liberated. Thus it is said.

Therefore, based on this scripture, liberation (*vimokṣa*)—which is the severing of the bond consisting of the creeper of conceptual construction that is the error of [perceiving] the non-existent—is called *nirvāṇa*, just as the extinguishing of the flames of a fire perceived in a dream occurs through the wind and water [of that same dream].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Examination of Bondage and Liberation," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Karma and its Fruit, the seventeenth chapter.
Here it is said: Saṃsāra indeed exists, because it serves as the basis for the connection between karma and its fruit.

If, here, there were a transmigration of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) or of a self (*ātman*) by way of an uninterrupted sequence of the continuum, through a succession of births and deaths, and by means of the operation of the relationship between cause and effect, then there would be a connection between action and its fruit.

However, since transmigration does not exist as described, and because the mind perishes immediately after arising, the maturation (*vipāka*) does not exist at the time when the action is projected; thus, there would simply be an absence of any connection between action and its fruit.

However, since cyclic existence (saṃsāra) truly exists, because an action performed here has a connection with its ripened fruit even in another birth, the connection between actions and their fruits is not contradicted.
Therefore, cyclic existence certainly exists, because it serves as the basis for the connection between actions and their fruits.
Now, what are those actions, and what is that fruit? With the intention of explaining their specific classifications, this is said:
That mind which restrains oneself and benefits others, which is friendly—that is the Dharma; it is the seed of fruit both in this world and after death.
In this context, "ātman" refers to that in which the conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna) has been placed or produced;

it is called the "pudgala-ātman" when it is designated in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas). It is called "cetas" because it accumulates (cinoti), amasses, and determines the capacity for the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
"Citta," "manas," and "vijñāna" are synonyms for that very [mind].

It is called "ātmasaṃyamaka" (self-restraining) because it restrains itself, makes itself independent of sense objects, and prevents its engagement under the influence of afflictions such as attachment.
This wholesome mind, which is self-restraining, prevents engagement in acts such as the taking of life and sustains one from going to an evil rebirth; therefore, it is called "dharma."
In the sacred teaching, this term *dharma* is established in three ways:

in the sense of maintaining its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇa*), in the sense of preventing one from going to evil states of existence (*kugatigamana-vidhāraṇa*), and in the sense of preventing the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies (*pāñcagatika-saṃsāra-vidhāraṇa*).
Among these, in the sense of maintaining its own characteristic, all phenomena—both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—are called *dharmas*.
The ten wholesome paths of action and other such qualities are called "dharmas" in the sense that they prevent one from going to an evil rebirth;
one who practices the Dharma dwells in happiness in this world and in the next.
In the context of "going for refuge to the Dharma," the term *dharma* refers to Nirvana in the sense of preventing one from wandering through the saṃsāra of the five destinies;
however, here the word *dharma* is intended specifically in the sense of preventing one from going to evil destinies.
But is the mind that is solely for one's own restraint the only thing that constitutes *dharma*? No, he says.
What then? That mind which is both beneficial to others and characterized by loving-kindness (*maitra*)—that too is *dharma*.

In the word "maitram" (friendly), it should be understood that the word "ca" (and) is elided. In this context, "a mind that benefits others" (*parānugrāhakaṃ cetaḥ*) refers to that mind which is engaged in the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and engaged in protecting others from fear.
This too is a dharma:
that mind which is friendly, being non-hostile toward friends and toward all sentient beings, is a "friendly mind" (maitra-cetas).
That mind which is friendly is "friendly mind," or it is simply "friendliness" (maitra).
And this threefold mind that has been described is called *dharma*;
by its opposite, *adharma* is to be understood.
And this mind, which has been described with its various divisions,
is the seed of the fruit;
it is the uncommon cause for the actualization of the fruit.
That alone is called the seed;
for example, the rice seed is the seed of the rice sprout.
However, that which is common, such as the earth and so forth, is not the seed, though it is a causal condition.
Just as it is so in that case, here too, when the desired maturation is brought forth, the mind becomes a threefold seed;
whereas human effort and the like are merely causes.
At what time, then, does the seed produce its fruit? He says: "both after passing away and in this world.
"After passing away" means in an unseen birth;
"in this world" means in a seen birth—this is the meaning.
And this should be understood in detail from scripture. // 1 //

Thus, having first established that there is only one phenomenon whose nature is mind (*citta*), the Blessed One, the Supreme Seer (*paramarṣi*)— so called because of his vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)— has further declared action (*karman*) to be of two kinds: volition (*cetanā*) and what is performed after having willed (*cetayitvā*).

He is both supreme and a seer (ṛṣi), thus he is the Supreme Seer (paramarṣi); because he has reached the ultimate reality in every respect and because he is superior even to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the Fully Awakened One, the Blessed One, is the Supreme Seer.
By that Supreme Seer it was stated in the Sūtra: "Action is volition, and having willed, one performs action."
And regarding this two-fold action that has been mentioned, many varieties of its classification have been proclaimed. (2)
How so?
In that regard, what is called "volition" (cetanā) is known as mental action; and what is called "having willed" (cetayitvā) is both bodily and vocal action. (3)
That which exists in the mind (*manas*) is "mental" (*mānasa*).

Because it reaches its completion solely through the door of the mind and because it is independent of the activity of body and speech, volition (*cetanā*) associated specifically with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "mental action.
In this context, the word "therein" (*tatra*) is used for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*).
As for that which was stated as the second type, "action after having intended," that should be understood as both bodily and vocal action; namely,
that which is performed after having reflected with the mind, thinking, "In such and such a manner, I shall engage through body and speech."
That which is performed after having intended it is called "action" (karma);
furthermore, that is of two kinds: bodily and vocal.
Because it arises from body and speech, and because its completion occurs through those two, it is thus threefold: bodily, vocal, and mental. (3)
This threefold karma, when further divided, becomes sevenfold; thus has the Blessed One described the manifold classification of that karma. How so?
The movement of speech and those non-abstinences designated as non-informative, as well as other non-informative [factors] known as abstinences, are likewise [non-informative]. (4)
Merit resulting from enjoyment, demerit of the same kind, and volition—these seven factors are traditionally known as the manifestations of karma. // 5 //
In this context, speech (*vāk*) is the utterance of distinct phonemes;
movement (*viṣpanda*) is bodily activity.
Therein, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all speech characterized by abstinence or non-abstinence, which originates informative action (*vijñapti*), is generally understood as "speech."
In this way, movement—whether wholesome or unwholesome, characterized by abstention or non-abstention, and which gives rise to informative intimation—is understood in its general sense.
Just as there is this twofold division of informative representation (*vijñapti*),
so too is there for non-informative representation (*avijñapti*); for non-informative representations are characterized either by non-abstention or by abstention.

In that regard, non-informative [actions] (*avijñapti*) characterized by abstention are as follows: for instance, from the moment one undertakes an evil deed— thinking, "From this day forward, I shall maintain my livelihood by killing living beings or committing theft"— non-informative actions arise continuously and constantly, even when one is not performing those acts, caused by that undertaking of unwholesome karma.

Furthermore, the non-informative [karmas] (*avijñapti*) that arise in fishermen and others from the time they begin their work with nets and so forth— even for those who are not currently performing that action—

are called non-informative karmas characterized by non-restraint (*avirati*). Just as these exist, there are likewise other non-informative karmas characterized by restraint (*virati*), which have a virtuous nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).

For example, from the moment one completes the informative action (*vijñapti*) of body or speech by resolving, "From this day forward, I shall abstain from taking life and so forth," there subsequently arise non-informative actions (*avijñapti*) of the nature of accumulating merit, even while one is in a state of negligence or the like; these are called non-informative actions characterized by abstinence.
Although these have the nature of form and action, they are called "non-informative" (avijñapti) because, unlike informative [action], they do not inform others.
Likewise, there is merit resulting from enjoyment; "merit" is the meaning of "wholesome.
It is called "resulting from enjoyment" because its sequence follows from enjoyment.
Enjoyment (*paribhoga*) is the utilization by the Saṅgha and others of an object that has been relinquished.
Succession (*anvaya*) means following after;
the meaning is the accumulation of merit born within the continuum of the donor.
And likewise, there is demerit of that same kind, meaning that which results from enjoyment;
for example, the establishment of temples and the like.
In a place where sentient beings are killed— indeed, to the extent that living creatures are slain for the sake of its fame— to that same extent,
through the enjoyment of that temple and so forth, demerit resulting from such consumption arises within the mental continuum of its builders.
In this way, such [an action] becomes non-meritorious.
And volition is characterized by mental action that conditions the mind.
In brief, this action is of seven kinds: wholesome or unwholesome speech, wholesome or unwholesome movement, and wholesome [action] characterized as non-informative (avijñapti).
Non-informative (avijñapti) unwholesome [action],
merit resulting from enjoyment, and demerit resulting from enjoyment.
And volition.
And these seven factors are traditionally held to be characterized by action, being manifested as action and having action as their defining mark. // 5 //

In this regard, some raise an objection: "Does this manifold karma that has been described persist until the time of its maturation, or does it not persist because it perishes immediately after arising? If, first of all—
If the action remains until the time of ripening, it would attain permanence;
if it has ceased, being already ceased, how will it produce a fruit?

If it is postulated that once produced, an action persists in its own nature until the time of its maturation, then it would follow that this action is eternal for such a long duration, because it would be devoid of destruction.
If it is argued that it is not eternal because destruction occurs later, [the response follows].
This is not so;

for that which was previously devoid of destruction, like space and so forth, cannot subsequently have a connection with destruction. Furthermore, it would follow that what is devoid of destruction must be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, since no maturation (vipāka) of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) is observed, and because they would remain forever as non-maturation, the admission of permanence for karmas would indeed follow;
such, then, is the fault in the case of permanence.
Now, if it is accepted that actions perish immediately after arising, then in that case—
if it has ceased, being already ceased, how will it produce a fruit?
The intention is that an action which has become non-existent will not produce a fruit at all, because it lacks an existing intrinsic nature. // 6 //
In this regard, certain members of other schools offer the following rebuttal: "Since conditioned phenomena perish immediately after their arising, the fault of impermanence does not apply to us.
As for what was also said—"
"If it has ceased, being already ceased, how will it produce a fruit?"— to this objection we offer the following reply:
"That continuum which proceeds from the seed, beginning with the sprout..."
Therefore, the fruit does not arise without a seed, nor does that [seed] proceed without [the fruit]. // 7 //

In this case, although the seed is momentary, it ceases only after having become the cause for a continuum— designated as the sprout, stalk, stem, leaf, and so forth— which is endowed with a specific capacity to produce a particular future fruit of its own kind.
And this continuum, beginning with the sprout, proceeds from the seed.
Therefore, when there is a gradual deficiency of auxiliary causes, even from a very small cause a vast accumulation of fruit arises.
Yet, without a seed—that is, in the absence of a seed—that continuum beginning with the sprout does not proceed.

Thus, by the fact that it occurs when that [seed] exists and does not occur when it is absent, the seed-cause of the continuum beginning with the sprout, which is the fruit, has been demonstrated. // 7 //
Thus, since the continuum arises from the seed, and the production of the fruit arises from the continuum, the fruit is preceded by the seed; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. (8)

If, in this case, the seed were to cease without having produced the continuum of the sprout and so forth due to the proximity of opposing conditions such as fire or embers, then, because the activity of the causal continuum would not be observed there, the view of annihilation would arise.
And if the seed were not to cease, [the same fault would follow].
And if the continuum beginning with the sprout were to proceed,
then, because the non-cessation of the seed would be admitted, there would be the view of eternalism;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, there is no consequence of viewing the seed as either eternal or subject to annihilation. // 8 //

And just as this sequence has been described regarding the seed, so it is said: "The mental continuum which proceeds from that mind—its fruit arises from that; and without the mind, it does not proceed. (9)

Therefore, from that mental continuum which proceeds with that [mind] as its cause—a mind associated with specific wholesome or unwholesome volitions—and from that mental continuum permeated by wholesome or unwholesome volitions, when there is no deficiency in the presence of auxiliary causes, the desirable or undesirable fruit arises in the happy or miserable realms.
However, without that mind, and in the absence of the mind, it does not proceed at all. (9)
Thus, since the continuum arises from the mind and the production of the fruit arises from the continuum, the fruit is preceded by karma; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. (10)
If a wholesome mind were to cease without having become the cause for a future mental continuum— which proceeds in an uninterrupted succession of causes and effects like the final mind of an Arhat—
then that karma would be severed.
Alternatively, if it were to remain without falling away from its own nature by becoming the cause for the future continuum, [it would persist].
In that case, the action would be eternal;
yet this is not so.
Therefore, even when one accepts that action is momentary, there is no consequence of falling into the two views of nihilism and eternalism. // 10 //
Thus, in this explanation of the divisions of action as previously described, the ten wholesome paths of action have been explained. And these:
"The ten white paths of action are the means for accomplishing Dharma;
their fruit consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure, both hereafter and in this world. (11)
The meaning is that these ten wholesome paths of action are the means for accomplishing the Dharma, serving as the causes for its realization.
But what is this thing called "dharma," distinct from the paths of wholesome action, which is established as the means for accomplishing them? It is said:
it is a certain particular state of mind that is expressed by the word "dharma."
"By this [it is meant]: that which is a mind of self-restraint and one that benefits others is loving-kindness (maitra); that is Dharma. Alternatively:
These ten wholesome paths of action, when in their completed form, are designated by the term "dharma";
however, when in the process of being performed, they are designated as "wholesome paths of action.
Therefore, these ten wholesome paths of action are established as the causes for the accomplishment of that which has been described by the aforementioned characteristics.

But how, in this context of the classification of karma, are there ten paths of wholesome action? It is said: by the passage beginning with "vocal movement and those non-abstentions designated as non-informative," the three bodily paths of action and the four vocal ones have been explained.
By this [explanation of] volition (*cetanā*), the three mental [paths of action] known as covetousness (*abhidhyā*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) have been explained.
Thus, all ten wholesome paths of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) have been explained here;
and they serve as the causes for the accomplishment of the aforementioned Dharma.
And the nature of this dharma consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure, characterized by visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"In the hereafter" means in the unseen world beyond;
"and in this world" means in this present life.
The fruit is experienced. // 11 //
Thus, when the objection and its rebuttal have been described by those of the same school, others, pointing out a fault against them and describing a different rebuttal of the objection, say:
"Even this conceptual construction would entail many and great faults."
If this [object] does not exist by that [means], then this conceptual construction is not tenable here. // 12 //

If the avoidance of the two faults of the views of eternalism and nihilism were achieved through the analogy of the seed and the sprout regarding the mental continuum, then many faults— both numerous in number and great in magnitude— would accrue to the opposing position due to their contradiction with both what is seen and what is unseen. How so?
For if, by the analogy of the continuity of seeds, only the continuity of rice sprouts and so forth proceeds from a rice seed and not something of a different kind,
and only a rice fruit arises from the continuity of the rice sprouts and so forth, [then the same would apply here].
It is not a wood-apple fruit, because it belongs to a different species;
likewise here too, from a wholesome mind, there would only be a continuum of wholesome minds.
Because it belongs to the same class [of wholesome states],
there is no continuum of unwholesome or neutral minds,
as they belong to a different class.
In this way, from an unwholesome or neutral mind, there would be only a continuum of unwholesome or neutral minds and nothing else, because they belong to different classes.
From minds belonging to the desire, form, or formless realms, or from untainted minds, only similar minds belonging to the desire, form, or formless realms, or untainted minds, arise. (Pp 137)
It would be so, but not for those of different classes;
from a human mind, only a human mind would arise, and not the minds of others such as gods, hell-beings, or animals.
