Consequently, whoever is a god would remain a god forever.
Whatever is a human would remain only a human, and so forth.

Consequently, even for gods and humans who perform unwholesome deeds, there would be no diversity in their destinies, modes of birth, complexion, intellect, faculties, strength, physical form, enjoyments, and so on, nor would there be falling into the miserable realms;
yet all of this is accepted [as existing].

Since many such great faults would follow from the conceptualization of the continuity of the seed as being analogous [to a flame], therefore this conceptualization is not tenable in this context. // 12 //
Furthermore, I shall now proclaim this conceptual framework which is applicable here, and which has been extolled by the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. (13)
And what is this "conceptual construction"? He says:
Just as a promissory note is the non-perishing, so too is karma like a debt;
it is fourfold according to the realms, and it is by nature indeterminate. (14)
In this case, once a wholesome action has been performed, it ceases immediately after its arising; yet, when it has ceased, there is no consequence of the absence of a fruit.
For at the very moment that action arises, [it projects its result].

At that time, a dissociated factor (*viprayukta-dharma*) called the "non-perishing" (*avipraṇāśa*) arises within the continuum of the agent of that action, standing in the place of a promissory note. Thus, it should be understood that the non-perishing is like a document;
and for whomsoever this factor named non-perishing arises, [that person's action is not lost].
That karma should be understood as being like a debt.

Just as, because of the existence of a promissory note, a creditor does not suffer the loss of his wealth even when the money has been lent out, for he remains connected to it through the fifth category of wealth at a later time; so too is that karma.
Likewise, even when an action has perished, because another entity called "non-perishing" (avipraṇāśa) persists, the agent is indeed connected with the fruit caused by that [action].

And just as a debt-bond, having effected the arrival of wealth for the giver, becomes discharged and is no longer capable of bringing about the arrival of wealth— whether it remains existent or no longer exists— so too the non-perishing, once it has yielded its maturation, whether it remains existent or no longer exists, cannot again effect a connection with maturation for the agent, like a discharged bond.

Furthermore, this non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) which we have described, as mentioned in other sūtras, is fourfold according to its elements (*dhātu*): it is distinguished by belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and by being untainted (*anāsrava*);
and it is by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it is not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome, non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) is indeed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If it were unwholesome for unwholesome actions, then it would certainly not exist for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*).
And if it were wholesome among wholesome states,
it would not exist for those whose roots of merit have been severed.
Therefore, this is indeed neutral by nature. // 14 //
Furthermore:
from the perspective of abandonment, it is not to be abandoned, or rather, it is only to be abandoned by cultivation.
And this non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) is not to be abandoned through abandonment.

Ordinary worldly actions (*pārthagjanika-karma*) are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) itself, so that a noble one (*ārya*) does not come to be possessed of the actions of an ordinary person.

However, the non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) is not abandoned by the path of seeing even when those actions are abandoned; rather, its abandonment occurs through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative, meaning that [the object] is to be abandoned precisely by transcending the realms (*dhātu*).

And since, in this way, the non-perishing (avipraṇāśa) does not perish even when the action perishes, nor is it abandoned even when the action is abandoned, therefore the fruit of actions arises by means of the non-perishing. // 15 //

Furthermore, if this non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) were to undergo abandonment through the abandonment of that karma— whether by way of its relinquishment, its cessation, or its destruction— or if it were to perish through the transition of karma, the destruction of karma, or the manifestation of another karma, what fault would there be? It is said in reply:
If [the fruit] were to be abandoned through the abandonment [of the cause], or by the transference of karma, then faults such as the destruction of karma would follow. (16)
If the non-perishing (avipraṇāśa) were abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga), just like ordinary worldly karma, then there would be the actual destruction of karma.
And due to the destruction of karma, the ripening of the desired and undesired fruits of karma for the noble ones (āryas) would not have their prior karma as its cause.
The fruit would arise from an action that had never been performed;
furthermore, because one would see the absence of a fruit for an action, it would constitute a false view.
Thus, faults such as the annihilation of karma would follow if one accepts that the *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing) is something to be abandoned through abandonment.
The same should be applied even in the case of the transference of karma. // 16 //
At the moment of rebirth, among all the dissimilar and similar karmas belonging to those same realms, only one of them arises. (17)
Actions of different types are dissimilar (*viṣabhāga*);
those that are similar are homogeneous (*sabhāga*).

For all these actions, both homogeneous and dissimilar, at the moments of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the desire, form, and formless realms, there arises a single non-perishing phenomenon (*avipraṇāśa*) which completely subsumes all those actions.
And that [transformation] also arises only from those with similar elements (samānadhātuka), not from those with dissimilar elements (viṣabhāgadhātuka). // 17 //
That [result] arises in the present life from every kind of action; furthermore, it persists even when the two types of action have reached their maturation. (18)

And this phenomenon called *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing) arises for every single action—whether its nature consists of volition (*cetanā*) or what has been willed (*cetayitvā*), and whether it is divided into two types by way of being with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)—in the present life, that is, in this very birth; for each and every action, a single *avipraṇāśa* comes into existence.
Furthermore, this *avipraṇāśa* does not necessarily cease even when its maturation (*vipāka*) has already ripened.
And like a leaf that has already been consumed, even though it still exists, it is no longer capable of ripening again. // 18 //
It ceases either through the transcendence of its fruit or through death;
therein one should discern the distinction between that which is with-outflows and that which is without-outflows. (19)
In that regard, it ceases through the transcendence of its fruit, as it has been said: "It is to be abandoned only by cultivation.
It also ceases through death, as it has been said:
"At the moment of rebirth-linking, however, one [of these] arises among those possessing elements.

Thus, one should characterize this distinction: that which pertains to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is itself contaminated, and that which pertains to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is itself uncontaminated. // 19 //
Thus, emptiness and not annihilation, cyclic existence and not permanence, and the non-perishing of karma— this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha. (20)
Since an action, once performed, ceases and does not persist by way of intrinsic nature, therefore emptiness is established because of the non-persistence of action through intrinsic nature.
Nor does this lead to the consequence of a doctrine of annihilation due to the non-abiding of karma, because the ripening of karma exists through the inclusion of the "non-perishing" (*avipraṇāśa*).
For it is only in the absence of ripening that there would be a view of the annihilation of karma.

Because of the existence of the principle of non-perishing (*avipraṇāśadharma*) and because there is no conceptualization of a similarity to the continuity of a seed (*bījasaṃtāna*), the manifold cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the five destinies— which is divided by the distinctions of various realms of rebirth (*gati*), types of birth (*jāti*), matrices (*yoni*), and elements (*dhātu*)— is established. Furthermore, there is no consequence of falling into the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*).
Because it is not admitted that karma exists in its own essential form,
and because there is the non-perishing of karmas, due to the existence of this non-perishing.
Since this Dharma was taught by the Blessed One who has awakened through the complete departure from the sleep of ignorance,
therefore, as for what was previously stated by the opponent— that "if karma remains until the time of its ripening, it would follow that it is eternal"— [that objection does not apply].
"If it has ceased, being already ceased, what fruit will it produce?"—this [objection] does not apply to our position;
therefore, the conceptualization described by us alone is logical. // 20 //

To this it is said: Why, sirs, are you so excessively agitated by the fear that the ramparts of a city of Gandharvas might collapse, and why have you undertaken the laborious effort of guarding them—when you yourselves dispute over the cause of the fruit of an action whose very production is untenable?
For if the production of action were to occur by its own inherent nature alone, [it would not depend on causes].
If it were to persist until its ripening, it would be eternal;
if it were to perish [before then], there would be annihilation.
But when karma does not arise at all because it is empty of intrinsic nature, [neither of these faults applies].
In that case, from where could its persistence or destruction come, such that this reflection would even arise? To this, he says:
"Why does karma not arise?"
The Teacher said: "Because it is without intrinsic nature;
since action is without intrinsic nature, therefore it does not arise."
If indeed, because of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), karma does not arise,
then how was it said by the Blessed One: "Karmas do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons"?
"Having obtained the causal complex and the [right] time, [karmas] indeed bear fruit for embodied beings"?
It is said in reply:
"And because that [action] has not yet arisen, it does not perish. (21)
"Such is the intention of the Blessed One;
therefore, this rule does not pose an obstacle for us. //21//

This must necessarily be understood in this way: that action is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For otherwise— If action were to exist by way of intrinsic nature, it would undoubtedly be eternal.
Furthermore, action would be uncreated, for that which is eternal is not produced. (22)
For if action existed by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would undoubtedly be eternal,
because there can be no alteration of intrinsic nature.
Consequently, the action would be unperformed.
For that which is most desired by an independent agent through its activity is the object (*karman*);
and this [definition] is not tenable [in your case].
What is the reason?
Because that which is eternal is not produced;
for that which is called "eternal" is that whose existence is already established.
And since that which already exists cannot logically be produced, it does not depend on a cause at all. // 22 //
Since the maturation of the entire world would occur even though wholesome and unwholesome actions had not been performed, it follows:
"If action were uncreated, there would be the fear of encountering what was not done;
furthermore, the fault of not dwelling in celibacy would ensue in that case. (23)
For if action were uncreated,
then there would be the fear of encountering what has not been done;
for even by one who has not committed such acts as the taking of life, [the result would follow].
Even for that [person], since that karma exists even though it was not performed, there would be the fear of encountering what was not done because of the connection with that [karma].
Furthermore, in that position, one would incur a life of non-celibacy.
What is the reason?
If there were no one who dwells in the perfectly pure holy life, there would be no one for whom nirvana could occur. // 23 //
What follows from this? All worldly conventions would undoubtedly be contradicted;
furthermore, the distinction between the doer of merit and the doer of evil would not be tenable. (24)

For indeed, regarding these undertakings of action such as agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing which are commenced for the sake of a result, there would be the futility of their commencement because all of them would already exist even without being performed. [For example, one might say:
"Make a pot."
Furthermore, all worldly transactions such as "weave a cloth" and so forth would be contradicted,
because everything, including jars and the like, would already exist.
Furthermore, the distinction that "this one is a doer of merit" and "this one is a doer of evil" would not be possible.
Because merit and demerit exist individually for both [the agent and the recipient], even when neither merit nor demerit has been performed by either. // 24 //
Furthermore:
"If action were established by way of its own intrinsic nature, then that which has already ripened as its maturation would ripen once again. (25)
Even for karma whose ripening has already matured, there would follow the granting of ripening once again, because it has not fallen away from its own nature,
just as in the state when its ripening had not yet matured.
Thus, if you consider karma to be intrinsic (svābhāvika), [this consequence follows].
Since that action exists as something established, therefore, without doubt, the faults described above would follow if it possessed intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatva*).
Therefore, action is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
and since action is without intrinsic nature, [the aforementioned faults do not apply].
Therefore, for us who explain it in this way, the consequence of falling into the views of eternalism or nihilism does not occur at all. // 25 //
Here it is said: Action exists by way of its own-being (svabhāva), because of the existence of its causes;
for that which does not exist here [cannot have causes].
It has no cause, like a tortoise’s hair serving as a garment;
yet there is a cause for karma, namely the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Formations (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition.
...because of the statement, "Existence has grasping as its condition," it follows that action (karma) indeed exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
It is said: this is indeed illogical.
Why? Because—
This [world] consists of karma and afflictions, yet those afflictions do not exist in reality;
if those afflictions do not exist in reality, how could karma exist in reality? (26)
In this context, this karma consists of afflictions and has afflictions as its cause;
yet those afflictions do not exist in reality.
For it will be said:
"Those [afflictions] which arise in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the distortions do not exist by way of intrinsic nature; therefore, afflictions do not exist in reality.
Thus, first of all, afflictions do not exist in reality.
How could action caused by that [self] exist in reality at that time?
Therefore, action does not exist by way of intrinsic nature. // 26 //
Here it is argued: afflictions and karmas do indeed exist, because their effects are present;
for here, the effect of afflictions and karmas is perceived in what is called the body.
And that which has an observable effect exists, because no effect is observed for that which is non-existent, such as a sky-flower. To this it is replied:
There would be afflictions and karmas if their effects— the bodies— were found to exist;
however, they do not exist, as he says:
Karma and the afflictions are declared to be the conditions for bodies;
yet if karma and the afflictions themselves are empty, what can be said of the bodies? (27)
It has been demonstrated that just as karma and the afflictions are empty, so too,
when karma and the afflictions do not exist, [how could there be a self?]
In that case, what discussion can there be regarding the non-existence of those bodies which are its effects?
Since their non-existence was already established previously, the intention is that there is no further specific point to be stated. // 27 //
Here it is said: Action exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because there exists one who experiences its fruit;
for that which does not exist has no experiencer of its fruit.
It is just like the fruit of a celestial mango tree.
Furthermore, there is an experiencer of the fruit of karma:
that living being who is shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving.
He is the enjoyer, and he is neither different from the agent nor is he that very same person.

In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of knowledge (*ajñāna*), darkness (*tamaḥ*), and delusion (*saṃmoha*) are synonyms. One who is shrouded or covered by ignorance is called a "creature" (*jantu*), because they are born again and again within the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies.
"Sattva," "pudgala," and "prāṇin" are synonyms for that very [person]. "Tṛṣṇā," "rāga," "sakti," and "visakti" are synonyms; they are fetters and bonds.
"One who has craving as a fetter" (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) means one for whom craving is a fetter; that is to say, one bound by craving.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Beings are shrouded by ignorance and have craving as their fetter.
Furthermore, this evil karma was committed by oneself alone.
Because of the statement, "Its ripening must be experienced by oneself," that experiencer of the fruit of karma is not other than the doer.
And yet, it is not that very same [person], because it is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from it.
Therefore, since there exists a recipient of the fruit, karma certainly exists. // 28 //
To this it is replied: there might be an agent of action and an experiencer of the fruit of action if action itself were [the agent];
but it is not so. How so?
Since this action exists neither as something arisen from conditions nor as something not arisen from conditions, therefore the agent also does not exist. (29)
If there is no action and no agent, from where could the fruit born of action arise?
And if the fruit does not exist, how indeed will there be an experiencer? (30)
If there were such a thing as action,
would it be produced from conditions or not produced from conditions?
If, first of all, it is held to be produced from conditions, that is not tenable,
because the fault has already been stated in the examination of conditions.

Now, that which is not produced from conditions— that is, being without a cause— is also explained in detail in the "Examination of Action and its Factors" (*Karmakārakaparīkṣā*) by means of the passage beginning, "When a cause is absent, there is neither effect nor cause. And since this action, whether produced from conditions or not produced from conditions, is thus impossible, [it does not exist].
Therefore, even an agent of this action is not possible.
And when both the action and the agent are thus non-existent,
how could there be a fruit born of action that is without a cause?
And if the fruit does not exist, how indeed could there be an enjoyer of the fruit?
Thus, it should be understood that all this is simply non-existent by way of intrinsic nature.
Here it is said: If the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of phenomena is established in this way,
then that which was stated by the Blessed One— that the maturation of a deed performed by oneself must be experienced by oneself alone—
is entirely refuted by this reasoning.
"And because you deny the fruit of karma, you are a primary nihilist. To this it is said: "We are not nihilists."
By refuting the dualistic discourse of existence and non-existence, we illuminate the non-dual path leading to the city of Nirvana.
We do not say that action, agent, fruit, and so forth do not exist;
rather, we establish that these are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Now, if you think that because it is impossible for entities devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) to perform an activity, the same fault remains as before—
this too is not the case,
because activity is observed only in those things that possess intrinsic nature (sasvabhāva).

For it is observed that only those things which lack intrinsic nature possess functional activity; thus, indeed, jars and other such objects, while being devoid of intrinsic nature, are perceived in the world as performing their respective functions. (30)
Moreover, let this meaning be understood even more clearly from this analogy:
just as a Teacher, by means of his perfected supernatural power, creates an emanation, and that emanation in turn creates another emanation. (31)

For example: suppose the Teacher, the Buddha, the Blessed One, by means of his perfection of supernatural power and through the majesty of his psychic potency, were to create a single emanation; and that emanation, which was created by the Buddha, the Blessed One, were in turn to create yet another, further emanation.
In that regard, this emanated being who is the creator of another emanated being is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;
the meaning is that he is lacking the intrinsic nature of a Tathāgata.
And this other created being,
who was himself created by a created being,
is also empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that [the Tathāgata] is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as here, for things that lack intrinsic nature, there occurs the performance of an action lacking intrinsic nature and the designation of an agent and an object;
likewise, the form of an emanation (*nirmitaka*) is the agent, and that which is produced by it is the object.
Just as one emanation is created by another emanation, so it is [with this]. // 32 //
For whoever here is the agent of an action has the form of a magical creation and is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
And whatever action is performed by that independent agent who is empty of intrinsic nature,
that too is empty of intrinsic nature.
It should be understood as being just like a created being (nirmitaka) who has created another created being;
as it is said in the Āgama:
"When one speaks, all the created beings speak."
For when one person becomes silent, indeed, all become silent.
Therefore, how could there be a false view for the Mādhyamikas who propound non-duality?
And it is said in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"When the Sugata, the Protector, out of compassion, speaks his discourse to the people gathered in the streets..."
Having emanated Victors there, he emanates them and wanders among them, teaching the sublime Buddha-dharmas.

Hearing that, hundreds of thousands of living beings made a vow for the supreme, foremost wisdom of a Buddha: "When shall we obtain such wisdom as this? Knowing their aspiration, the Jina gave them a prophecy.
The King of Dharma emitted hundreds of thousands of immeasurable rays from the soles of his feet;
all the hells became cool, suffering was removed, and beings experienced happiness.
"When the Dharma spoken by the One Possessing the Ten Powers is proclaimed here, the eye of gods and humans becomes purified," and so forth.
At that time, some give rise to longing; they have obtained a supreme and inconceivable gain.
Those by whom the Jina, the Lord of Men, was invited—the limit of their offerings is not reached.
Such is the detailed exposition.
Likewise, in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*,

a manifested bodhisattva brought from the world-system Gandhasugandhā food that had been the remains of what was consumed by the Tathāgata Samantabhadra; it was provided with various condiments, edibles, and so forth, possessing distinct and manifold flavors within a single meal.

Having satisfied all that assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as the kings, royal ministers, domestic priests, women of the inner court, gatekeepers, caravan leaders, and the rest of the populace, he caused them to attain the great samādhi named "Aspect of Joy. Thus it is said.
And it is recited in the Vinaya:
"The Blessed One manifested an illusory monk who was an unrepentant evil monk;
by his word, even for one possessed of virtue, a communal residence based on a declaration of purity was ordained. (32)
And it is not only through the example of a magical creation that the demonstration of the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*) is established;
rather, showing that the lack of intrinsic nature of all things is clearly understood from these very examples, he says:
"The afflictions, actions, bodies, agents, and fruits [are like a magical creation]."
They have the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and are like a mirage or a dream. // 33 //
In this context, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are attachment and so forth, so called because they defile the mental continuums of sentient beings;
actions (*karman*) are the wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable.
"Bodies" refers to physical forms;
"agents" refers to selves;
and "fruits" refers to results such as maturation (vipāka), sovereign power (adhipatya), and outflow (niṣyanda).
These objects, such as the afflictions and so forth, should be understood to be devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), like a city of the Gandharvas and similar illusions.

Therefore, it should be known that for the Mādhyamikas alone, because they do not accept an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena, there is no consequence of falling into the two views of eternalism and nihilism.

Furthermore, regarding this investigation into the relationship between action and its fruit, the refutation of all remaining objections and challenges should be understood in detail from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.
As it is said in the noble *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*:

"And five hundred monks who had attained meditative concentration rose from their seats and departed, failing to understand, failing to enter into, and failing to have faith in this profound teaching of the Dharma."

The Blessed One said: "For it is thus, Kāśyapa, that these monks who are conceited do not enter into, do not plunge into, and do not have faith in this untainted purity of ethical discipline; they are afraid, terrified, and fall into a state of dread.
Profound, Kāśyapa, is the formulation of these verses, and profound is the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones."
It is not possible for beings who have not planted roots of merit, who are gripped by evil friends, and who abound in a lack of resolute faith, to have such resolute faith.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, these five hundred monks were formerly disciples of other sects during the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Having heard this teaching of the Dharma from that very Tathāgata Kāśyapa with the intention of finding fault, they attained a single moment of serene faith.
Then they spoke these words: "How wonderful! To what an extent the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is sweet and pleasing in speech!"
Having attained this single moment of serene confidence, they passed away and were reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
having fallen from there, they have been reborn here,
and for that very reason, they have gone forth in my teaching.

"Kāśyapa, these five hundred monks, who have fallen into [wrong] views, do not enter into, do not plunge into, and do not have faith in this profound teaching of the Dharma; they are terrified, they tremble, and they fall into a state of panic.
Nevertheless, they have already been prepared by this teaching of the Dharma."
They shall no longer go to a state of woe or downfall;
rather, they shall attain final nirvana with these very same aggregates.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti: "Go, Subhūti, and persuade these monks.
Subhūti said: "They are already contradicting what has been spoken by the Blessed One himself."
What need is there to mention me?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One created two monks on the very path by which those monks were traveling.
Then those five hundred monks approached the path by which those two created monks had gone.
Having approached them, they said this: "Venerable sirs, where will you go? They replied: "We shall go to the forest retreats."
There, we two shall dwell in the abodes of the contact of meditative bliss.

Those five hundred monks also said this to them: "Venerable sirs, we too do not penetrate, do not fathom, and do not have faith in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma; we are terrified, we are greatly afraid, and we fall into a state of terror.
Therefore, we shall dwell in forest retreats, abiding in the pleasant contact of meditative concentration."
The two created beings said: "In that case, venerable sirs, we shall recite together and not dispute;
for the supreme dharma of a śramaṇa is freedom from dispute.
As for this which is called 'parinirvāṇa' by the venerable ones—"
What is that phenomenon which will attain parinirvāṇa?
Furthermore, is there here any body, or self, or sentient being, or living soul, or creature, or nourisher, or person, or individual, or human, or youth who will attain parinirvāṇa?
"Or by the destruction of what is there parinirvāṇa?
They replied, "Parinirvāṇa is through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion.
The two emanated beings said, "But do you, venerable sirs, possess passion, hatred, and delusion which you would thus destroy?"
They replied: "They are not perceived internally, nor externally, nor in between the two; nor do they arise without being conceptualized...
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Examination of Action and its Fruit," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka-kārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Self, the eighteenth chapter.
Here it is said: If afflictions, actions, bodies, agents, and fruits—all this is not reality;
rather, it is merely like a city of Gandharvas and the like, which, though unreal, appears to the foolish in the form of reality.
What, then, is the reality here, and how does one enter into that reality? It is said:
it is the complete exhaustion of the notions of "I" and "mine" both internally and externally, through the non-apprehension of all internal and external things whatsoever.
This is the essential point here:
furthermore, the entry into reality consists in discerning with wisdom all afflictions and defects that arise from the view of a self-existent body.
Having understood both the self and its object, the yogi effects the negation of the self itself.
This should be understood in detail from the *Madhyamakāvatāra* through such passages as these:

observing that cyclic existence has its root in the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and seeing that through the non-apprehension of a self there is the abandonment of the view of a self-body, and through that abandonment the cessation of all afflictions, one first of all examines the self itself, [asking]:
"What is this so-called 'self'?"

That which is the object of the notion of "I"— this very object of the notion of "I," when being conceptually constructed, must it have the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) or be distinct from the aggregates?

Since the positions of [the self as] the support, the supported, or possessing those [aggregates] are also included within the positions of identity and difference, and since the intention is to speak concisely, he intends to begin the refutation of the self by means of the refutation of these two positions of identity and difference alone.
The Teacher said: If the self were the aggregates, it would be subject to arising and passing away; if it were other than the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates. (1)

But for what reason are five positions each presented in the other two examinations—namely, the examination of the Tathāgata and the examination of fire and fuel—whereas here, however, only two positions are presented? It is said:
because it is by that very same [method] that five positions each were indicated in those two contexts.
For this very reason, because they have been specified elsewhere, they are not specified here again;
rather, only two positions are presented in brief.
In that regard, if it is conceptualized that the aggregates are the self, then the self would follow as being subject to arising and passing away, both produced and perishable,
because the aggregates are subject to arising and passing away.
And this is not accepted, because it would entail the fault of the self being manifold; for he will say:
"Nor has it arisen having previously been non-existent, for a fault would follow in that case."
"The self would either be something created, or it would have arisen without a cause.
Likewise:
"The appropriation itself is not the self; that [appropriation] passes away and arises."
For how indeed could the appropriation be the appropriator?
Furthermore,
if the aggregates were the self, then because of their multiplicity, there would be as many selves as there are aggregates.
Furthermore, the self would become a substance, and as such, it would not exist in either the state of being active or in its opposite.

In [the view that] nirvana is the annihilation of the self, there would necessarily be destruction and arising in the moments prior to nirvana. Because of the destruction of the agent, there would be an absence of its fruit; furthermore, one person would experience the karma earned by another.
Since this position has already been established in detail through the analysis set forth in the *Madhyamakāvatāra* by means of such passages, it need not be elaborated upon again here at length.
Thus, first of all, the aggregates are not the self;
nor is it tenable that the self is distinct from the aggregates.
For if the self were other than the aggregates, [it would follow that it could exist independently].
It would possess the characteristics of what is not an aggregate (*askandhalakṣaṇa*).
For just as a horse, being other than a cow, does not possess the characteristics of a cow,
so too the self, if conceived as distinct from the aggregates, would possess the characteristics of what is not an aggregate.
In that regard, the aggregates (skandhas), being conditioned, arise from causes and conditions and are characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
If, according to your view, a self possessing the characteristics of a non-aggregate were to exist, it would necessarily be endowed with the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
And that which exists in such a manner—

Because it is non-existent or because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), like a sky-flower or like nirvāṇa, it does not at all receive the designation "self," nor is it logically consistent as an object of the conceit "I" (*ahaṃkāra*);
thus, a self distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) is also not tenable.
Alternatively, this is another meaning: if the self were distinct from the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates.
The five aggregates have as their characteristics respectively: transformation, experience, grasping signs, volitional formation, and cognition of objects.

Furthermore, if the self were held to be distinct from the aggregates—just as consciousness is distinct from form and the other aggregates—it would have to be established as having a distinct characteristic;
and being established with a distinct characteristic, it would be perceived separately, just as the mind is perceived separately from form and the rest. Yet it is not so perceived.
Therefore, it does not exist as something distinct from the aggregates either.

But surely the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) have conceived of a self distinct from the aggregates and describe it as having a different characteristic; therefore, this rule [of dependent origination] does not contradict them at all.
And just as the outsiders describe the self as having a different characteristic, so it is stated in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*:
The self is conceptualized by the non-Buddhists as being eternal in nature, a non-agent, an enjoyer, devoid of qualities, and inactive;
relying on various portions of the Veda, the systems of the non-Buddhists have reached a state of diversity.
To this it is said:

It is true that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) state the definition of something distinct from the aggregates; however, they do not describe its definition after having perceived a self by way of its own intrinsic nature (svarūpataḥ).
Rather, because they do not understand the conventional designation based on [aggregates] as it truly is, they fail to realize that the self is a mere name; out of fear,
they have fallen away even from conventional truth, and being deceived solely by fallacious inference through false conceptualization,
they imagine a self out of delusion.
And they describe its characteristic.

Furthermore, by asserting that the self and its appropriation are established through mutual dependence in the examination of action, agent, and so forth, a refutation has indeed been established even from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). And it has been said:
"Just as, depending upon a mirror, one perceives the reflection of one's own face..."
Indeed, that which appears is not anything at all in reality.
In the same way, the ego is perceived by depending upon the aggregates;
yet it does not exist in reality as anything at all, being like the reflection of one's own face.
Just as one's own reflection in a mirror cannot be seen without taking up the mirror, so too the notion of "I" cannot be perceived without taking up the aggregates.
Having heard such a teaching as this, the noble Ānanda himself attained the eye of Dharma and repeatedly declared it to the monks. Thus it is said.
Therefore, no further effort is undertaken to establish that [self].

Rather, it is precisely that which is designated dependently (*upādāya prajñapyamāna*)—serving as the locus for the adherence to a self among those followed by the distortions of ignorance—that is investigated by those seeking liberation:

"Does this [self], which appears as the basis of appropriation for this pentad of aggregates (*skandha-pañcaka*), possess the characteristics of the aggregates, or does it lack the characteristics of the aggregates?"

And when those seeking liberation investigate in every way, they do not perceive this [self] by way of its intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*). At that time, for them, since the self does not exist, how indeed could there be anything belonging to the self (*ātmīya*)?
Because the self is not perceived, they certainly do not perceive the five aggregates—the basis for the designation of a self—as "belonging to the self."
For just as when a chariot is burnt, its constituent parts are no longer perceived because they have been burnt,
even so, at the very moment yogins realize the selflessness of the self, they necessarily realize the selflessness of the entities of the aggregates belonging to the self.
As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"The aggregates arise from the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*); that ego-conception is unreal in reality. For that whose seed is unreal, how can its sprout be real?"
"Having seen the aggregates as unreal in this way, the conceit of 'I' is abandoned;
and from the abandonment of the conceit of 'I', there is no further arising of the aggregates. Thus it is said.

For just as, at the end of midday in the summer heat, rays of the blazing sun— having reached the middle of the cloudless sky and being about to traverse it, and having become intent upon scorching the parched surface of the earth like the widely scattered sparks of a fiercely whirling fire— depend upon those very rays, and reaching the parched region of the earth, and depending upon a distorted perception, are perceived by those situated at a great distance as having the form of water.
Just as [the water of a lake] produces the perception of an extremely clear, deep blue form for those who possess birth,
but not for those situated near it,
so too here on the path of saṃsāra, [ignorance] exists for those standing at a great distance from the vision of the reality of the self and the phenomena of "mine" as they truly are.

Because those currently existing [beings] follow after the distortions of ignorance, the superimposition of the aggregates—which is a mere false object—appears as real; however, it does not appear to those who stand near the vision of the true nature of things.
As it was said by the venerable Teacher:
A form seen from afar is perceived clearly by those nearby;
if a mirage were actually water, why would it not be apprehended by those close at hand?
Just as this world is seen for what it truly is by those who have moved far away,
so too it is not seen by those nearby, being signless like a mirage.
"Just as a mirage resembles water but is neither water nor [water] in reality,
so too the aggregates resemble a self but are neither selves nor [selves] in reality."

And for this very reason, the yogi who dwells near the vision of ultimate reality through the non-perception of self and what belongs to the self, necessarily becomes free from "mine-ness" and free from "I-ness" due to the tranquility of both self and that which pertains to the self. (2)
"Beneficial to the self" (*ātmanīna*) means that which belongs to the self; it refers to the pentad of aggregates (*skandha-pañcaka*), meaning "one's own."

Through the pacification, non-arising, and non-perception of the self—which is the object of the notion of "I"—and of the aggregates and other phenomena which belong to the self and are the objects of the notion of "mine," the yogi becomes free from "mine-ness" and free from the notion of "I."
But surely, that yogi who is thus free from the sense of "mine" and free from the sense of "I" must exist;
and since he exists, it is established that the self and the aggregates exist. This is not so, because:
That which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not exist either;
he who perceives that which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not perceive it. // 3 //

Since the self and the aggregates are in every way unperceivable in their own nature, how could there be another entity distinct from them that is "without the notion of 'mine' (nirmama)" and "without the notion of 'I' (nirahaṃkāra)"?
It should be understood that whoever perceives such a thing— which lacks an existing nature and is without "mine" or "I"— does not perceive reality.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"Behold the internal as empty; behold the external as empty.
There is not even anyone who meditates upon emptiness."
Likewise:
"Even he who contemplates phenomena as empty is a fool who has entered upon a wrong path;
for while phenomena are proclaimed to be empty through syllables, they are in truth beyond syllables, though expressed by syllables."

"O Śānta, he who contemplates phenomena as utterly tranquil—even that mind has never arisen at any time. All conceptual proliferations belong to one who speculates about the mind; therefore, awaken to phenomena as inconceivable.
Thus it is said:
The aggregates are empty and secluded by their very nature; awakening is empty and secluded by its very nature.
Even he who practices is empty by nature—this is for the wise, but not for foolish people.
Thus [ends the third].
Thus, when "mine" and "I" have perished both externally and internally, grasping ceases; with the destruction of that, there is the destruction of birth. (4)

It is stated in the Sūtra that all afflictions (kleśa) are rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), originate from the view of a self-identity, and have the view of a self-identity as their cause.
That view of a self-identity is abandoned through the non-perception of a self or anything belonging to a self;
and with its abandonment, the fourfold clinging—namely, clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self—is abandoned.
And from the exhaustion of clinging, there is the exhaustion of birth, which is characterized by renewed existence. // 4 //
Since this sequence for the cessation of birth has been established in this way, it follows that liberation results from the exhaustion of karma and afflictions.
For when grasping is exhausted, existence conditioned by it does not arise;
when existence has ceased, how could there be the occurrence of birth, old age, death, and so forth?
Thus, it is established that liberation occurs through the exhaustion of karma and afflictions.
In that case, it must be stated through the exhaustion of what do karma and the afflictions reach their total cessation? It is said:
Karma and the afflictions arise from conceptual construction; they [arise] from conceptual proliferation, but conceptual proliferation ceases in emptiness. (5)
For when an ignorant ordinary person conceptualizes form and so forth in an improper manner, afflictions such as passion arise; as it will be said:
"Passion, hatred, and delusion are said to originate from conceptual construction, for they arise dependent upon the distortions of the beautiful and the ugly."
And it is said in the Sūtra: "O Desire, I know your root; you are born, they say, from conceptualization (saṃkalpa). I shall no longer conceptualize you; therefore, you shall not exist for me."
Thus, first of all, karma and afflictions proceed from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And those conceptual constructions arise from the manifold proliferation (*prapañca*) characterized by beginningless habituation in saṃsāra— consisting of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the signifier and the signified, the agent, the action, the instrument, and the activity, as well as pots, cloths, crowns, chariots, form, sensation, woman, man, gain, loss, pleasure, pain, fame, infamy, blame, and praise.
And this worldly proliferation (*prapañca*) ceases without remainder when emptiness is realized—that is, when the emptiness of all intrinsic natures is seen. How so?
Because the web of proliferation as previously described would exist only if there were the apprehension of real entities.

For indeed, having not perceived the daughter of a barren woman as possessing beauty, charm, and youth, those possessed by passion do not enter into the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) concerning her.
Nor, without entering into that proliferation, do they enter into improper conceptualization (*ayoniśovikalpa*) regarding her.

And without entering into the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*), they do not give rise to the masses of afflictions rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through the dogmatic adherence to "I" and "mine."

Furthermore, without first producing the host of afflictions consisting of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they do not perform actions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
And without performing such actions, they do not experience the wilderness of *saṃsāra*, which is a single web of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.

In the same way, for the practitioner (*yogin*) in the state of seeing emptiness, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are not perceived as having any intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

And not perceiving the intrinsic nature of things, they do not introduce the conceptual proliferation (prapañca) concerning them; nor, without introducing that conceptual proliferation, do they introduce discursive thought (vikalpa);
nor, without introducing discursive thought, do they give rise to the mass of afflictions rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) through the attachment of "I" and "mine."
Furthermore, without having first produced the host of afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, one does not perform karmic actions;
and without performing them, one does not experience the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) known as birth, aging, and death.

Thus, by resorting to emptiness, which is characterized by the auspicious cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there occurs the disappearance of the entire web of conceptual proliferation.

From the departure from conceptual proliferation (prapañca) comes the cessation of discursive thought (vikalpa); from the cessation of discursive thought comes the cessation of all karma and afflictions (kleśa);
and from the cessation of karma and afflictions comes the cessation of birth.

Therefore, emptiness alone is called nirvāṇa because it is characterized by the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), as it is said in the *Śataka*: "The Tathāgatas describe the Dharma in brief as non-violence;
emptiness alone is nirvāṇa—these two are indeed one here."
But the master Bhāvaviveka, not accepting that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas realize the emptiness as it has been described,

explains it thus: For the noble Śrāvaka who contemplates the mere collection of conditioned factors— which arise from others and perish moment by moment— as being without self and without what belongs to a self, there arises the vision that, due to the absence of any entity consisting of a self or what belongs to a self, "this is merely phenomena that are born and die."
For the self is indeed the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*);
since that [self] is absent, that [notion] is also absent.

Precisely because of its absence, no internal or external entity exists anywhere; thus, due to the non-arising of the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*), there arises neither the state of being "mine-less" nor the state of being "I-less," and consequently, no ascertainment of one's own nature occurs.

Except for conventional linguistic designations, this is especially true for the great bodhisattvas who perceive all conditioned phenomena as unarisen and who dwell in the practice of non-conceptual wisdom. Therefore it is said:
"That which is without 'mine' and without 'I'—even that does not exist."

Therefore, this Master [Candrakīrti], just as he does not follow the opinion of the venerable Ācārya [Bhāviveka] regarding such a matter, has already demonstrated so in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*— specifically in the passage stating,
"But on the Dūraṅgamā stage, he is superior by way of wisdom"—
and thus no further effort is expended here to refute that position.
Therefore it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā Bhagavatī*:
"Subhūti, one who wishes to fully awaken to the enlightenment of a śrāvaka should train in this very perfection of wisdom;
Subhūti, one who wishes to fully awaken to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha should train in this very perfection of wisdom."
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should train in this very perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
And it is said: "Whoever desires, 'May I become a disciple of the Sugata, or may I become a Pratyekabuddha, or likewise a King of Dharma'—
if they do not resort to this patience, they cannot attain it, just as one who does not see the near shore cannot reach the further shore."
Thus [ends the fifth].

Here it is said: If it has been established that reality (*tattva*) consists in the non-arising of the web of conceptual constructions such as "I" and "mine"—both internally and externally—due to the non-perception of internal and external entities, then what of this which was stated by the Blessed One:
"The self is indeed the master of the self; for who else could be the master?"?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven.
For the self is indeed its own protector; what other protector could there be?
For the self is the witness of one's own deeds, both those well done and those ill done.
Likewise, in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"Black and white karma does not perish; having performed it oneself, one must experience its result.
There is no transference of the fruit of karma, nor does one experience it without a cause."
Such is the detailed account.
How, then, is this not contradictory? It is said:
Has this also not been stated by the Blessed One—
"There is no sentient being or self here; rather, these phenomena exist together with their causes.
For it is thus: form is not the self, nor does the self possess form, nor is the self in form, nor is form in the self...
and so on, up to: consciousness is not the self.
"The self does not possess consciousness; the self is not in consciousness; consciousness is not in the self.
Likewise: "All phenomena are without self.
How, then, would there be no contradiction between this scripture and the previous scripture?
Therefore, the underlying intention behind the Blessed One’s teaching must be investigated.

Generally speaking, however, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who are like the suns that never set, intent on awakening the lotus-ponds of the intellects of all beings to be trained throughout the world by means of the extensive distinctions between the provisional and definitive meanings within their teachings, and who possess the expansive rays of great compassion, skillful means, and primordial wisdom— have [spoken thus].
The Buddhas have designated "self," they have taught "non-self," and they have also taught that there is neither self nor non-self at all. (6)

And here the intended meaning is this: in this world, those whose entire eye of the intellect is shrouded by the cataract-film of the blindness of false views regarding the non-existence of a self—failing to perceive the multitude of entities that transcend the scope of ordinary, pure vision, yet remaining established within conventional truth (vyavahārasatya)—are intent only on describing the mere reality designated as earth, water, fire, and air; they are like the perception of drinking liquor, which arises from the specific transformation of substances such as rice-gruel, water, and fermenting agents, and is accompanied by the particular capacities for intoxication, fainting, and so forth.
Describing consciousness as arising solely from the maturation of the primary elements beginning with the *kalala* stage, they proceed to deny both the past and the future;
thus, they deny the next world and the self, asserting: "This world does not exist;
the next world does not exist."
"There is no ripening of the fruit of well-done or ill-done deeds;
there are no spontaneously born beings," and so forth.

Because they thus deny these [truths], they turn their backs on the attainment of the specific desired fruits distinguished by heaven and liberation; instead, they are constantly and perpetually engaged in the performance of unwholesome actions, facing a fall into the great abyss of the hells and other realms.

In order to eliminate those false views of theirs, [the Buddhas], who conform to the inclinations of the realm of sentient beings—which is divided into eighty-four thousand different types of mental conduct—and who are intent on fulfilling their vow to deliver the entire realm of sentient beings without exception; who are preceded by the equipment of wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion; who are incomparable, the sole kinsmen of the world; who have become great king-physicians for the treatment of the great disease of all afflictions without remainder; and who desire to rescue those to be trained according to whether they are inferior, middling, or superior—[act accordingly].
In order to turn away from unwholesome actions and the like those disciples who are devoid of shame and who perform unwholesome deeds, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
have in some instances designated even a "self" and established it in the world.
Furthermore, the refutation of the doctrine of causelessness is established through the examination of karma and its agent.
Nor do they arise without a cause; therefore, since this should be understood in detail from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, no further effort is exerted here for the purpose of refuting that [position].
But those who are bound by the very firm, very long, and very loose great cord of the view of a truly existent self— like birds that have flown even a great distance—

though they perform wholesome deeds and turn away from the paths of unwholesome action, they are unable to bypass rebirth within the existence of the three realms and reach the city of Nirvana, which is auspicious, ageless, and deathless.

For those disciples of intermediate capacity, in order to loosen their attachment to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and to generate a longing for nirvāṇa, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, desiring to show favor to those beings to be trained, have also taught that "there is no self."

However, having ascertained the specific degree of resolve (*adhimukti*) of those superior disciples—who, through the maturation of the seeds obtained by their conviction in the profound Dharma accompanied by the excellence of previous practice, have drawn near to Nirvana; who are free from attachment to a self; and who are capable of plunging into the reality of the meaning of the most profound teaching of the Lord of Munis—the Buddhas taught that "neither is there a self, nor is there any non-self whatsoever."
For just as the view of a self is not reality, so too the view of non-self, which serves as its antidote, is likewise not reality.
Thus, there is no self whatsoever.
Furthermore, it has been taught that there is no such thing as a non-self;
as it is said in the noble *Ratnakūṭa*:
"Kāśyapa, 'self' is one extreme."
"Selflessness"—this is the second extreme.
That which is the middle between these two extremes is formless, invisible, non-abiding, non-manifest, non-cognitive, and without abode; this is called [the Middle Way].
Kāśyapa, the middle way is the correct analytical contemplation of phenomena.
And it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*: "Neither a self nor a non-self is found in accordance with reality;
therefore, the Great Sage has set aside the views concerning self and non-self."

"What has been seen, heard, and so forth is neither true nor falsely spoken by the Sage; for from a position there arises its opposite, and both of these do not exist in reality. Since it is thus that the Dharma-teaching of the Blessed Buddhas proceeds—by means of the negation of self, non-self, and both, according to the diversity of the inclinations of disciples who are inferior, middling, or superior—[it is established].
Therefore, there is no contradiction with scripture for the Mādhyamikas.
For this very reason, the venerable Āryadeva said:
"In the beginning, there is the warding off of non-merit; in the middle, the warding off of the self."
"He who subsequently understands the warding off of everything is wise. Thus it is said.
Thus it was said by the venerable Ācārya:
"Just as a grammarian would teach even the alphabet,
so did the Buddha teach the Dharma to those to be trained according to their capacity."
To some he taught the Dharma for the sake of turning away from evil;
to some for the sake of accomplishing merit; and to some that which is determined by duality.
For some, it is independent of duality; for others, it is profound and terrifying to the fearful;
for some, the means of achieving awakening has emptiness and compassion as its core. Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, this is another meaning: the term "self" (ātman) was also designated by the Sāṃkhyas and others, having imagined that there would be no connection between action and its fruit for conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that perish moment by moment.
The term "non-self" (anātman) was also designated by the Lokāyatikas, who do not perceive a transmigrating self through reasoning:
"The person is only as far as the range of the senses."
O blessed lady, this which the learned call "the wolf's footprint" is indeed that.

By such statements as these, the Buddhas— like those free from cataracts who do not see at all the nature of objects such as self and non-self imagined by foolish people, just as those with cataracts do not see the hairs, mosquitoes, and so forth that they perceive— have taught that "there is neither self nor any non-self."
As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*:
Then the bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, 'quiescence, quiescence' is spoken of;
what is this that is called 'quiescence'?"
"And through the pacification of what is it called 'pacification'?
The Blessed One said: "O son of good family, 'pacification' is a designation for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
"The pacification of afflictions" is a designation for the pacification of conceptualization, discursive thought, and mental construction.
"The pacification of conceptualization, discursive thought, and mental construction" is a designation for the pacification of perception and mental attention.
"The pacification of perception and mental attention" is a designation for the pacification of cognitive distortions.
"The pacification of perversions" is a designation for the pacification of causes and objects.
"The pacification of causes and objects" is a designation for the pacification of ignorance, becoming, and craving.
"The pacification of ignorance, becoming, and craving" is a designation for the pacification of the notions of "I" and "mine."
"Quiescence of 'I-making' and 'mine-making'" is a designation for the quiescence of the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

"Quiescence of the views of annihilationism and eternalism" is a designation for the quiescence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Śāntamati, whatever afflictions arise in connection with objects, causes, and views, they all originate from the view of a self-identity.
From the subsiding of the view of a self-identity comes the subsiding of all views;
from the subsiding of all views comes the subsiding of all aspirations;
and from the subsiding of all aspirations comes the subsiding of all afflictions.
Śāntamati, it is just as when the root of a tree is cut, all its branches, leaves, and fruits wither;
in the very same way, Śāntamati, through the subsiding of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) subside.
Śāntamati, when the view of a self-identity is not fully understood, all forms of grasping and secondary afflictions arise.
Through the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity, all forms of grasping and secondary afflictions neither arise nor cause harm.
Śāntamati asked: "Furthermore, Blessed One, what is the full comprehension of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?

The Blessed One replied: "Śāntamati, the non-arising of a self is the full comprehension of the view of a self-existent body; the non-arising of a sentient being, the non-arising of a life-principle, the non-arising of a person, and the non-arising of views—this, Śāntamati, is indeed the full comprehension of the view of a self-existent body."
That view is established within, not established without;
that view is entirely non-established.
Śāntamati, that knowledge which understands that very non-abiding view as being non-abiding— this is the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Śāntamati, "full comprehension of the view of a self-identity" is a designation for emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That one does not grasp that view by means of the patience that accords with emptiness—
this too, Śāntamati, is the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
For "self-identity," Śāntamati, means that by the view of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of formative activity, non-arising, and non-production, one does not grasp that view.
This too, Śāntamati, is the thorough knowledge of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Śāntamati, "self-identity" is a non-body;
it does not move, it does not expand, it does not accumulate, and it does not pile up.
From the very beginning, that which was falsely conceptualized is unreal;
and that which is unreal and falsely conceptualized is not conceptualized, is not being conceptualized, and is not to be conceptualized.
That is not performed, not fabricated,
not raised up, and not determined;
that is called "quiescence."
Śāntamati said: "O Blessed One, it is said, 'tranquil, tranquil.
Through the subsiding of what is it called 'tranquil'?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāntamati, the mind blazes because of its objective referent (ālambana)."
That which one no longer takes as an object does not blaze; not blazing, it is said to be "stilled.
Śāntamati, it is just as fire blazes because of fuel.
It is extinguished through non-appropriation;
in the very same way, the mind blazes because of an object of focus and is extinguished through the absence of an object of focus.
In this regard, Śāntamati, this bodhisattva, skilled in means and purified by the perfection of wisdom, understands the equality of objects of focus.
And one pacifies the focal object that is the roots of virtue, and so forth. // 6 //
Here it is asked: If the Blessed Buddhas have not taught that there is a self, nor that there is no self, then what have they taught? It is said in reply:
When the range of the mind has ceased, that which is to be designated ceases;
for the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa. // 7 //
In this case, if there were some entity to be expressed, it would be pointed out;
but when that which is to be expressed has ceased to exist, [it cannot be shown].
When there is no object for speech, then nothing at all is taught by the Buddhas. Why, then, is it said that there is nothing to be expressed? He says: "Because the range of the mind has ceased."
The range of the mind is "cittagocara";
"gocara" means the objective field, that is to say, the focal object (*ālambana*).
If there were some object of the mind, then the activity of speech would occur by superimposing some sign upon it;
but when an object for the mind is itself untenable, [how could speech arise]?
In that case, where could there be the superimposition of a causal sign (*nimitta-adhyāropa*),
by which the activity of words might occur?
Furthermore, demonstrating why the object of the mind does not exist, he says:
For the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa.
Since the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena, the fundamental nature (prakṛti) of phenomena, is established as being unarisen and unceasing like nirvāṇa,
for that reason the mind does not operate therein.
And when the mind does not function, from what cause could there be the superimposition of signs?
In the absence of that, how could there be the functioning of speech?
Therefore, it remains established without exception that nothing at all was taught by the Blessed Buddhas.
And for this very reason, he will say:
"The cessation of all apprehension, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, is auspicious;
no dharma whatsoever was taught by the Buddha anywhere to anyone."
And this is so.

Alternatively, here is another prima facie argument: as it was stated that "proliferation (*prapañca*) ceases in emptiness (*śūnyatā*)," how, then, does the cessation of proliferation occur in emptiness? It is said:
because "that which is to be expressed has ceased," and so forth; this is to be explained as before.

Alternatively, regarding what was stated previously—that through the non-perception of internal and external objects, there is the perpetual exhaustion of the notions of "I" and "mine" both internally and externally—this is the reality here.
What is that like? To what is it comparable?

Or it can be said: "Therefore, that which is to be designated has ceased when the range of the mind has ceased"; in this context, the words "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
But what is the reason for stating that "that reality has ceased when the range of the mind has ceased"? He says:
"For the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa."
Thus, the previous explanation alone should be applied.

Therefore, it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, from the night the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until the night he will pass into final nirvāṇa without clinging..."
In this interval, not even a single syllable was uttered, pronounced, or will be pronounced by the Tathāgata.

How then was the teaching of the Dharma in its various forms taught by the Blessed One to the assembly of those to be trained—consisting of all the gods, asuras, humans, kiṃnaras, siddhas, vidyādharas, uragas, and others?

By the utterance of speech in a single moment alone, it removes the darkness from the minds of those respective beings, awakens the many-fold lotus groves of the Buddhas, dries up the rivers and oceans of old age and death, and emits a radiance like the rays of the seven suns at the end of the aeon.
"Of great splendor, like the dawn of autumn."
Thus it is said in the Sūtra: "Just as a musical instrument made of machinery is played when impelled by the wind,
and although there is no player here, sounds nevertheless issue forth."

Thus, because it is perfectly pure from the beginning, the speech of the Buddha proceeds, impelled by the dispositions of all sentient beings, yet for him there is no conceptual construction here. Just as the sounds of echoes and the like exist neither internally nor externally, so too is his speech.
"Even so, the speech of the Lord of Men is neither internal nor situated externally.
Likewise:
"The divine drum resounded, O Goddess, having arisen from the ripening of karma for the sake of the immortals."
"O King, having perceived that you were dwelling in negligence, the sound of a drum was released from the sky."

All desires are impermanent and non-eternal, fleeting, unstable, and like the nature of foam; all states of existence are like illusions and mirages, like the moon reflected in water, and like the nature of a dream.
Accompanied by Śakra and the Maruts, who were sounding drums, he entered the Hall of Dharma.
He delivers a discourse on the Dharma for the gods, a discourse that is conducive to peace and dispassion.
Thus, in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"When the Buddha becomes the King of Dharma, the Sage who reveals all phenomena,
there will arise the sound of the non-existence of all phenomena— of grasses, shrubs, trees, herbs, rocks, and mountains."
However many sounds there are in that world-system, all are indeed non-existent; for there is not a single existent thing.
Yet from that Tathāgata, the Guide of the World, as many voices as those very sounds issue forth.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Likewise:
"O Benefactor of the World, though your voice is but one, various sounds emerge according to the diverse inclinations [of beings].
The Jina has spoken each and every word; tell us for whose sake you have smiled."

On this point, some raise an objection: the Mādhyamikas are no different from nihilists, because they assert that wholesome and unwholesome karma, the agent, the fruit, and the entire world are empty of the intrinsic nature of entities (*bhāvasvabhāva*);
for nihilists also assert that these do not exist.
Therefore, it is not the case that Mādhyamikas are indistinguishable from nihilists.

Why? Because the Mādhyamikas are proponents of dependent origination; having encountered causes and conditions, they describe this world and the next as entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) because everything is dependently originated.

Those who speak according to the true nature of things are not nihilists at all; because things are dependently originated and empty of intrinsic nature, they do not maintain the non-existence of the next world and so forth.
Rather, having perceived the multitude of worldly phenomena as existing by way of their own nature, [they maintain] their coming from the next world to this one, and so on.

If it is argued that there is a similarity with this [other] view because those who perceive the transition from this world to another world deny other objects similar to the objects perceived in this world—even though they have nonetheless understood the non-existence of that which does not exist by way of its own nature as a real entity—we say:
no. Why? Because there is no equality, since the Madhyamikas accept existence conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*).

If it is argued that they are equal in reality, although non-establishment is indeed equal in terms of the actual state of things (*vastutas*), nevertheless, there is inequality due to the difference between the cognizers.
For example, suppose one man, having committed a theft, is falsely accused of it by an enemy who, without having correctly ascertained the facts, declares, "Theft was committed by him.
Another person, however, having seen it with his own eyes, refutes that claim.
In this case, although there is in reality no difference between the two [statements],...
Nevertheless, due to the difference between the cognizers, one among them is called a speaker of falsehood while the other is called a speaker of truth;
and when properly examined, it is the former— and not the latter— who is logically associated with infamy and demerit.

Likewise here too, although there is no difference in the nature of the object for the Madhyamikas who speak and understand it as it truly is, there is no equality between their cognition and designation and those of the nihilists who do not know the nature of the object as it truly is. For just as there is a difference between an ordinary person and an Arhat—both of whom may share a common state of indifference, yet one is indifferent without discernment and the other with discernment—or between a person blind from birth and one with sight, regarding a common perception of a treacherous precipice; so it is here.
The former masters [state] that just as there is a great distinction [between the two views], so too there will be a distinction between the nihilists and the Mādhyamikas.
Enough of this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand. // 7 //
Here it is said: Even though the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is thus unarisen and unceasing— like nirvāṇa—
and there is no activity of speech or mind within it, [how can there be teaching?]

Nevertheless, since this [truth] cannot be understood by people unless it is taught, there must necessarily be a sequence of teachings in relation to conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) in order to lead those to be trained (vineyajana) into it;
therefore, let that [sequence] be explained.
It is said:
In this regard, the sequence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for teaching the entry into the nectar of reality (tattvāmṛta) should be understood as follows:
"Everything is true, or not true, both true and untrue, neither untrue nor true—this is the instruction of the Buddhas. (8)
In this regard:
"Whatever was previously dear to someone, one should act accordingly toward them;
for one who is offended is in no way a fit vessel for the True Dharma. Thus it is said.
And thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"The world disputes with me;
I do not dispute with the world."
What is accepted in the world,
that is also accepted by me; what is not accepted in the world, [that is not accepted by me].
And because of the scriptural authority stating: "That is not approved even by me."
Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand through a different language,
so too the world cannot be made to understand without recourse to worldly conventions.
Thus, from the very beginning, for the sake of those disciples who have developed a desire to hear the distinctions and essential natures of the categories well-known to the Blessed One,

the Blessed One described that very collection of aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth— which is imagined as real and perceived by those afflicted by the cataracts of ignorance— as being "real" in consideration of their perspective.
It is for the purpose of generating respect for himself in the world:
"This Blessed One is omniscient and all-seeing;

he knows the entirety of the world's affairs, [including] this receptacle-world (bhājanaloka) which extends from the wind-circle up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra) and culminates in the element of space."

And he taught the unerring nature of the world of sentient beings— including its stability, arising, and dissolution— along with its manifold varieties, its causes, its fruits, its gratification, and its disadvantages. Thus, for those disciples who had developed the cognition of omniscience regarding the Blessed One, it was subsequently taught that all of that is not real.
In this context, "reality" (tathya) refers to that which possesses no alteration.
However, because conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) perish at every moment, there exists a state of alteration; therefore, due to the presence of this alteration, it is not reality.
The word "or" (vā) should be understood as having the sense of "and" (ca) for the purpose of combining the teachings:
"Everything is real, and yet not real."
For some, it has been taught that all this is both true and untrue.
In that regard, with respect to ordinary people, all this is true;
however, with respect to noble wisdom, all this is false.
Because they are not perceived in this manner.

However, for some who have practiced the vision of reality for a very long time, yet whose roots of the tree of obscurations have not been entirely uprooted, it has been taught that "it is neither unreal nor real.
For the sake of abandoning even that slight remaining obscuration, both [real and unreal] are negated, just as the fairness or darkness of the son of a barren woman is denied.
And this is the instruction of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: instruction is the establishing [of beings] on the right path by leading them away from the wrong path.
Thus, instruction is "instruction" (anuśāsana) because it follows a sequential order;
or alternatively, instruction is "instruction" because it conforms to the capacities of those to be trained.
All these teachings of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—who possess great compassion, skillful means, and wisdom—are established as means for entering the nectar of reality (*tattva*).
Indeed, the Tathāgatas do not utter words that are not means for entering the nectar of reality.
Like the administration of medicine appropriate to a specific illness, they teach the Dharma in accordance with what is suitable, out of a desire to favor those beings who are to be trained.
As it is said in the *Śataka*:
"Existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither—these are spoken of;
indeed, it is by the power of disease that something comes to be called 'wholesome medicine'."
Thus [ends the eighth].
