Furthermore, what is the characteristic of that reality for the purpose of introducing which the Blessed Ones teach these instructions?
This has been stated by us:
"That which is to be expressed ceases when the range of the mind ceases."
And since this is so, what else remains to be asked?
Even though it is thus, [one might ask:]...

Nevertheless, just as one accepts worldly reality and so forth in accordance with conventional truth (*vyavahārasatya*), let its characteristic also be stated by way of superimposition (*samāropa*). To this it is said:

Not dependent on another, peaceful, not proliferated by conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*), and without manifold meanings—this is the characteristic of reality (*tattva*). (9)
In this regard, "not dependent on another" (aparapratyaya) means that there is no reliance on another in this [state];
it is not to be reached through the instruction of another,
but rather must be realized by oneself— this is the meaning.

For just as those with cataracts, seeing the false forms of hair, gnats, flies, and so forth, are unable—even through the instruction of one free from cataracts—to realize the actual nature of the hairs as it truly exists by way of non-perception, like those without cataracts; rather, they understand from the instruction of the one without cataracts only this much: "This is false."

But when their eye of intelligence is anointed with the ointment of the vision of non-erroneous emptiness, which destroys the cataract [of ignorance], and they have thus given rise to the knowledge of reality,
they then personally realize that reality through the yoga of non-apprehension.
Thus, that intrinsic nature of phenomena which is not dependent on another is the reality (*tattva*).
And this [reality], being of a peaceful nature, is devoid of intrinsic nature—meaning it is like the non-perception of hairs by one free from cataracts.
For this very reason, it is not conceptualized by conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*);
for *prapañca* is speech.
It is called "proliferation" (prapañca) because it proliferates objects;
"unproliferated by proliferations" means it is not expressed by words.
And that is non-conceptual.
Conceptualization is the movement of the mind;
because it is devoid of that, reality is non-conceptual.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is ultimate truth? It is that wherein even cognition does not function."
How much more so, then, regarding syllables? Thus it is non-conceptual.
"Having manifold objects" means having manifold meanings, that is, having distinct meanings;
"not having manifold objects" (anānārtha) means not having manifold meanings, that is, having non-distinct meanings.
As it is said in the *Āryasatyadvayāvatārasūtra*:
A son of the gods asked, "Mañjuśrī, what then is right practice?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O son of the gods, that which is equal from the perspective of ultimate reality—suchness, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and absolute non-arising."

In the ultimate sense, those are equal to the five deeds of immediate retribution; what is equal to the five deeds of immediate retribution is equal to the views held by false doctrines; and what is equal to the views held by false doctrines is equal to the dharmas of ordinary worldlings.
What is equal to the dharmas of ordinary persons is equal to the dharmas of those in training;
what is equal to the dharmas of those in training is equal to the dharmas of those beyond training;
what is equal to the dharmas of those beyond training is equal to the dharmas of the perfectly awakened Buddhas.
That which is equal to the dharmas of the perfectly enlightened Buddha is equal to nirvāṇa;
that which is equal to nirvāṇa is equal to saṃsāra;
and that which is equal to saṃsāra is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, equal to affliction.
That which is equal to affliction from the perspective of ultimate reality is equal to purification from the perspective of ultimate reality;
that which is equal to purification from the perspective of ultimate reality is equal to all phenomena from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus, O Son of the Gods, a monk who is engaged in the equality of all phenomena from the perspective of ultimate reality is said to be "correctly engaged."

The son of the gods asked: "By what kind of equality, Mañjuśrī, is it that from the perspective of ultimate reality, purification is equal, and thus all phenomena are equal from the perspective of ultimate reality?

Mañjuśrī replied: "From the perspective of ultimate reality, all phenomena are equal through the equality of the non-arising of all phenomena; from the perspective of ultimate reality, all phenomena are equal through the equality of the absolute non-birth of all phenomena. For what reason is that?"
For, O Son of the Gods, from the perspective of ultimate reality, all phenomena are indeed non-different from nirvāṇa, by virtue of their absolute non-arising.
It is just as, O Son of the Gods, the space within an earthen vessel and the space within a precious jewel-vessel [are not different].
This is simply the element of space;
in the ultimate sense, there is no distinction whatsoever.
In the same way, O Devaputra, that which is affliction—
From the perspective of ultimate reality, it is absolute non-arising;
even that which is purification is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, absolute non-arising;
and even saṃsāra is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, absolute non-arising.
Even nirvāṇa,
from the perspective of ultimate truth, is absolute non-arising;
herein there is no distinction whatsoever from the standpoint of ultimate truth.
For what reason?
Because, from the perspective of ultimate truth, all phenomena are absolutely unarisen.
Thus, it should be understood that the characteristic of reality is its lack of manifoldness, because emptiness has a single flavor;
furthermore, here a successive explanation should be understood. // 9 //

Thus far has been described the characteristic of reality for the Noble Ones who have accomplished their task through the total exhaustion of birth, old age, death, and saṃsāra. Now, however, with reference to the worldly characteristic of reality, it is said:
Whatever arises dependently is certainly not that very same thing.
Nor is it anything other than that; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal. // 10 //

Whatever effect arises in dependence upon whatever cause— for example, a rice sprout is produced in dependence upon a rice seed and the collection of conditions such as earth— it cannot be said that the cause is itself the effect.
The seed is not identical to the sprout,
because that would entail the absurdity of the produced and the producer being one and the same;
consequently, even father and son would have to be one.
Furthermore, because of their non-difference, in the state of the sprout, there would be the apprehension of the seed just as there is of the sprout,
and likewise, there would be the apprehension of the sprout just as there is of the seed;
and in this way, the seed would be eternal.
Because [the seed] would have to be admitted as indestructible,

and consequently, due to the consequence of the doctrine of eternalism, there would be a mass of great faults resulting from the consequence that karma, its fruit, and so forth do not exist. Thus, for the time being, it is not tenable that the seed itself is the sprout.
Nor is it anything other than that;
nor is the sprout something other than the seed,
because it would follow that the sprout could arise even in the absence of the seed.
If it were the case that "one thing is other than another even without [depending on] the other," then,
according to this statement, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the seed is not destroyed even when the sprout exists;
and consequently, the fault of the theory of pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda) would follow.
And since this is so— that whatever effect arises in dependence upon whatever cause— that cause does not itself become the effect,
nor is that effect something other than its cause.
Therefore, it can be established that the cause is neither annihilated nor eternal.
As the venerable Āryadeva said:
"Because an entity arises, its annihilation does not occur."
"Because an entity ceases, it is not born as something eternal.
And it is said in the *Ārya-lalitavistara-sūtra*:
"Just as when there is a seed, there is a sprout, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout."
It is neither other than that, nor is it that very thing; thus is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Thus [ends the tenth].
Thus, by the reasoning as it has been described:
"Having manifold meanings yet not having diverse meanings, neither annihilated nor eternal—this is the nectar of the teaching of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World. (11)

[To those] whose circle of directions, extending to the limits of the realm of space, is covered without interval by the great cloud-banks of great compassion and skillful means; who are intent upon pacifying the scorching heat of the fire of the suffering of birth, old age, and death for the world tormented by the exceedingly fierce solar orb of the active defilements such as passion; and who, through the falling showers of the nectar of the true Dharma—the antidote to conduct—taught constantly, without cessation, and according to what is appropriate, desire to sustain and cause the increase of the medicinal herbs, fruits, flowers, and climbing vines of the roots of virtue in those beings to be trained, according to their respective capacities.

This nectar of the True Dharma belongs to the Great Nāgas who are the Perfectly Awakened Ones—who rain down a great shower of the nectar of the True Dharma, who provide protection to those without protection in this world, who are the protectors of the helpless, and who are the lords of the entire world.
This nectar of the True Dharma should be understood as having the nature of exhausting the suffering of existence within the entire triple realm;
according to the principle already described, it is devoid of identity and difference, and free from the doctrines of eternalism and nihilism.
For those disciples who have entered into this nectar of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) and proceed through the sequence of hearing,

reflection, and cultivation, there occurs the certain attainment of nirvana— which is by nature the exhaustion of old age and death— through the consumption of the nectar-essence consisting of the three aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom. Nevertheless, if, due to the fact that their roots of virtue are not yet matured, they should somehow hear even this nectar of the True Dharma here, [they will eventually attain it].
Although they do not attain liberation in this very life,
nevertheless, even in another birth, their certain accomplishment will inevitably be achieved solely by the power of their prior causes.
As it is said in the *Śataka*:
In this world, even if one who knows reality does not attain nirvāṇa [in this life],
they will certainly obtain it without effort in a future birth, just like the ripening of karma.
Thus [ends the section]. 11.
Furthermore, even if by some chance there were no appearance of perfectly awakened Buddhas and the Śrāvakas had further diminished,
the realization of the nectar of the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva) would not occur due to the lack of the condition of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who teaches the Noble Path.

Nevertheless, by the power of the cause consisting in having heard the reality of the Dharma in other previous births, the self-arisen knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from non-association, even without depending on worldly instruction, for them the conditions have been brought forth merely through the practice of seclusion. // 12 //
Physical and mental seclusion is non-association,
or alternatively, the failure to seek out virtuous friends.
Because of that cause of non-association, the realization of the reality of phenomena occurs for Pratyekabuddhas even in a time when no Buddha has appeared.

Therefore, it should be understood that the accomplishment of this nectar-medicine of the reality of the True Dharma, prescribed by the Great King of Physicians, the Perfectly Awakened One, is unfailing. And since this is so, a wise person ought to seek the reality of the True Dharma even at the cost of sacrificing their own life.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā Bhagavatī*:
"And how, Blessed One, was this perfection of wisdom sought by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita?
When this had been asked, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Elder Subhūti: "By the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita..."
In the past, while seeking the perfection of wisdom, the Mahāsattva sought it without regard for his body, indifferent to life, and independent of gain, honor, or fame.
While he was thus seeking the perfection of wisdom, having gone into the forest, he heard a voice from the sky: "Go, noble son, toward the eastern direction."
There you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom;
go in such a way that you do not give rise to thoughts of physical fatigue,
nor do you give rise to thoughts of sloth and torpor.
Do not give rise to thoughts of food, nor direct the mind toward anything at all, whether internally or externally;
and do not look to the left, O son of good family.
Go; do not go by the south, nor by the east, nor by the west.
Do not look toward the north, nor upward, nor downward, nor into the intermediate directions as you walk.

And so, noble son, go in such a way that you do not waver from selfhood, nor from the view of a real body; do not waver from form, nor from feeling, nor from perception, nor from mental formations, nor from consciousness.
For whoever wavers from this stands apart.
[From what does he stand apart?]
One stands apart from the qualities of a Buddha;
whoever stands apart from the qualities of a Buddha wanders in saṃsāra.
He who wanders in saṃsāra does not course in the perfection of wisdom,
nor does he attain it.
When the evil Māra had made the water disappear, this thought occurred to him: "What if I were to pierce my own body and drench this spot of earth with my blood?
For what reason?
Because this spot of earth is full of rising dust."
"Let not the realm of dust fall upon the body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. What shall I do with this physical form, which is inevitably subject to disintegration?
It would indeed be better for my physical form to be destroyed by such an act as this."
But it was not through such fruitless action.
For many thousands of my own bodies have been shattered again and again as I wandered through saṃsāra for the sake of sensual desires, with sensual desires as their cause;
yet never before in such places...

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having taken a sharp weapon, pierced himself all over and sprinkled that entire area of ground with his own blood, and so forth. Then, at the mere sight of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita obtained such happiness as that of one who has entered the first dhyāna.

For a monk whose mind is one-pointed, for such a monk, this is the teaching on the perfection of wisdom by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata: namely, that through the sameness of all phenomena, there is the sameness of the perfection of wisdom;
and through the solitude of all phenomena, there is the solitude of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the immovability of all phenomena, there is the immovability of the perfection of wisdom;
through the non-conceitedness of all phenomena, there is the non-conceitedness of the perfection of wisdom;
through the lack of arrogance in all phenomena, there is the lack of arrogance in the perfection of wisdom.
Because all dharmas have a single flavor, the perfection of wisdom has a single flavor;
because all dharmas are limitless, the perfection of wisdom is limitless;
because all dharmas are non-arising, the perfection of wisdom is non-arising.
Because all phenomena are non-ceasing, the perfection of wisdom is non-ceasing;
because space is limitless, the perfection of wisdom is limitless;
up to: because all phenomena are undifferentiated, the perfection of wisdom is undifferentiated.
Because all phenomena are non-apprehendable, the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehendable;
because all phenomena are equal in their lack of substantiality, the perfection of wisdom is equal in its lack of substantiality;
because all phenomena are inactive, the perfection of wisdom is inactive.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, it should be understood that the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Examination of the Self," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Nineteenth Chapter: An Examination of Time.
Here it is said: The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities certainly exists, because it is the cause for the cognition of the three times.
In this context, the Blessed One has taught that the times— past, future, and present— are based on the substratum (āśraya).
And those [times] are based on entities (bhāva),
because an entity-svabhāva that has arisen and ceased is designated as "past."
For that which has arisen but not yet ceased is the present,
while that which has not yet attained its own-being is the future;
thus, the times have been taught as being based upon the intrinsic nature of entities.
And those [causes] do exist; therefore, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities, which is based upon them, also exists. To this it is replied:
The intrinsic nature of entities might be the cause for the designation of the three times,
if the three times themselves were what you intend them to be;
however, they do not exist.
Demonstrating how they do not exist, he says:
"If the present and the future depend upon the past..."
The present and the future will exist within the past time. // 1 //
In this regard, first of all, if the present and the future were to exist,
would they exist in dependence upon the past time, or without depending upon it?
In that case, if they were established in dependence upon the past, then they would necessarily exist at a past time;
for that which is non-existent in a certain place [cannot depend upon it].
Therefore, it is not regarded by that [cause],
just as a barren woman is not regarded by her own son,
or the mālatī creeper of the sky by its own flower.
If it is argued that sand requires its own oil,
and even though darkness does not exist [independently], it is required by a lamp, and the lamp too is required by darkness as its counterpart; then:
This is not so, because this [position] is also equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*). Therefore,
in this case, if the past time is held to contain the present and future times, [the same fault follows].
If this were the case for the sake of establishing dependence, then because they exist in past time, they would possess the nature of the past, just like the past time itself.
Consequently, even the past would not exist;
for that which has transcended the state of the present is the past, while that which has not yet arrived is the future.
But when the present and the future are simply impossible, then how could there be the pastness of anything?
Therefore, even the past would not exist. // 1 //
Now, wishing to avoid the aforementioned fault: If the present and the future do not exist there [in the past], how could the present and the future exist in dependence upon it? (2)

In that regard, if it is conceived that the past time does not exist if the present and future times do not exist, even so, because they are non-existent therein, there can be no dependence, just like a sky-lotus. // 2 //
Now, it might be argued: "For those who propound time, time certainly exists; so what is the purpose of [further] dependence upon it?
To this, it is said: even so—
Furthermore, the establishment of those two [past and future] does not exist independent of the past;
therefore, neither the present nor the future time exists. // 3 //
The present and the future do not exist,
because they do not depend on the past,
like the horn of a donkey.
And since it is thus with the present and the future, it should be understood that time does not exist. // 3 //
And when, in this way, there is no establishment of the present and the future either by depending on or not depending on the past;

and likewise, when the non-establishment of the past and the future— either by depending on or not depending on the present— is intended, as well as the non-establishment of the present and the past— either by depending on or not depending on the future— then, for that very reason, [the establishment] of the present and the future would depend on the past.
Or, by way of extension (*atideśa*), showing that the refutation is equal through the sequence of non-establishment regardless [of the specific case], he says:
"By this very same [method], one should characterize the two remaining [alternatives] in their respective order—the superior, the inferior, and the middling, etc., as well as oneness, etc. (4).
How so?
For if the past and the future exist in dependence upon the present,
then the past and the future will exist within the present.
Furthermore, if past and future time do not exist therein,
how could past and future time exist in dependence upon it?
Furthermore, since their establishment does not occur without mutual dependence,
neither past nor future time exists as such.
This, first of all, is one transformation of time:
if the past and the present exist in dependence upon that which is unborn,
then while time is unborn, the future would also have to exist as both past and present.
If the past and the present do not exist there [in the future],
how could the past and the present exist in dependence upon it?
Furthermore, since their establishment does not occur without depending [on one another], that which has not yet arisen does not exist for those two;
therefore, neither past nor present time exists.
"This is the second turning of the wheel of time," so it is said in the *Vyākhyānakārikā*.
In this way, two turnings of the wheel of time are to be understood.
And since, upon such investigation, the three times do not exist, it follows that time does not exist;
and because of the absence of time, it is established that the existence of entities also does not exist.
Just as these three times have been examined, one should likewise characterize the superior, inferior, and intermediate, as well as oneness and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "superior, inferior, and intermediate," the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral are intended.
Arising, abiding, and ceasing;
the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit;
and the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.

All those categories of entities—beginning with those that are in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanaināśaikṣa), and so forth—as many as there are, which are established through their relations with the three [types of] categories, are all included.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "oneness and so forth," duality and plurality are understood; thus, it should be known that those very [categories] beginning with "highest" (*uttama*) and "oneness" (*ekatva*), etc., are explained by the explanation of the three times. // 4 //
Here it is said: Time certainly exists because it possesses dimension.
Whatever does not exist here has no possession of dimension, just as, for example, a donkey's horn.

Furthermore, time possesses the quality of being measurable, through its divisions such as the moment (*kṣaṇa*), the twinkling (*lava*), the hour (*muhūrta*), day, night, day-and-night (*ahorātra*), the fortnight (*pakṣa*), the month (*māsa*), the year (*saṃvatsara*), and so forth.
Therefore, because it is measurable, time certainly exists. To this, it is replied:
If there were such a thing as time, it would possess dimension;
however, it does not exist. For:
Time that is not abiding cannot be grasped; time that is abiding does not exist.
How can time be designated if it is neither being grasped nor has been grasped? (5)
In this context, if there were some entity called "time" existing as something distinct from moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth, it would be perceived as possessing magnitude by means of those moments;
however, there is no such thing as "time" that exists as a permanent, unchanging entity.
That which would be grasped by means of moments and so forth— thus, time is not grasped as something non-abiding; the meaning is that because it is non-abiding, it is not grasped.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "There exists an entity called time (*kāla*) which is indeed eternal and possesses a fixed nature;
it is manifested by means of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth. For it is said:
'Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.'"
"Time keeps watch while others sleep; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Thus it is said that whatever possesses such characteristics exists as something whose nature is stable.
To this, it is replied:
Even so, there exists no persisting time that could be perceived as being manifested by moments and the like.
Why, then, does no persisting time exist?
Because it is not perceived apart from moments and the like.
Furthermore, is this time, while existing, of a conditioned nature, or is it of an unconditioned nature?
Both [possibilities] have been refuted in the examination of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
When arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, the conditioned does not exist;
and when the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be established?

By this [it is shown]: thus, there is no established time that could be apprehended. And as for this present time which is not apprehended—because it is non-abiding and lacks an existing intrinsic nature—how can it, while being unapprehended, be designated in reality through [divisions] such as moments? To this he says: "And how is time, when unapprehended, designated?"
Therefore, time does not exist at all. // 5 //

To this, he says: It is true that there is no such thing as "time" (kāla) by name, which is eternal, distinct from form and the other [aggregates], and established by its own nature; rather, it is precisely those conditioned factors (saṃskāra), such as form and so forth, that, being designated in dependence upon them, become what is expressed as "time," such as a moment (kṣaṇa) and so on; therefore, there is no fault.
It is said: Even so—if time exists dependent upon an entity, how could there be time apart from an entity?
If you establish that time comes into being dependent upon an entity, [then this follows].
When, indeed, no entity exists, then it is certain that time, which is caused by that [entity], also does not exist; demonstrating this, he says:
"And there is no entity whatsoever."
Since this has already been established in detail previously and because of the refutation to be stated hereafter,
when no entity whatsoever exists in reality, then how could time exist? (6)

Furthermore, because time does not exist, the divisions of time such as moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and muhūrtas—which are its transformations—do not exist either. Therefore, how can time be established by virtue of possessing transformation?
Consequently, entities have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) at all.
For it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryahastikakṣyasūtra*:
"If there were any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among phenomena, the Jina together with his disciples would go right there.
If phenomena were immutable, there would be no nirvāṇa, and the wise man would never be free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)."
Likewise:

"The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas who have passed away, having spoken hundreds of thousands of dharmas—neither the dharma nor the syllables were ever exhausted; because there was no arising, they are therefore inexhaustible."
Likewise:
"At the time of the Tathāgata’s birth, he who shall here be named Maitreya will exist;
this earth shall then be covered in gold—whence could such a thing come now?"
For the five strands of sensual pleasure are deceptive, causing delusion and infatuation, and possessing the nature of theft;
they are just like the water in a mirage at midday in the summer heat.
For in one eon, the world indeed becomes like space, having the nature of the sky;
it undergoes burning and destruction.
From where do those terrifying things come, and where is their destination? Thus it is said.
For example:
"O monks, these five are mere designations, mere assertions, mere conventional usages, and mere relative truths; namely, the past time, the future time, space, nirvāṇa, and the person.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Examination of Time," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Complex of Causes, the Twentieth Chapter.
Here it is said: Time exists, because it serves as a cooperative cause in the production of a fruit.
That which does not exist cannot function as a cooperative cause,
like the son of a barren woman;
therefore, time exists.
Because of the nature of cooperative causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*).

Here, this sprout, which arises in dependence upon the totality of causes and conditions designated as seed, earth, water, fire, wind, and space, does not arise even when the totality of conditions such as the seed is present, due to the absence of a specific season.
And just as it is with external things, so it is also with internal things,
as stated by the Blessed One:
"Karmas do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. Thus it is said.
And because there is such a dependence on time,
therefore that which is called "time" exists, which serves as the auxiliary cause for the production of the sprout and so forth.
It is said:
Time might be a cooperative cause if there were indeed the continuous production of effects such as sprouts and so forth.
But it does not exist. How so?

When the arising of a fruit such as a sprout is postulated from the totality of causes and conditions such as a seed, one must postulate that the production occurs either from a fruit already established within that totality or from one that is not yet established.
And what follows from this?
If it is postulated that [the nature] is established [prior to the activity],
he says the following to demonstrate that this is not tenable:
If the fruit arises from the assemblage of causes and conditions,
and if that fruit already exists within the assemblage, how can it arise from the assemblage?
If, according to your view, the effect exists within the totality of causes and conditions, then since it already exists within that totality,
how can it be produced by it?
For curd already existing in a bowl is not produced by the bowl;
moreover,
that which exists does not require further production because it is already accomplished, just like a jar already completed and standing before one.
If it is argued that manifestation or grossness is produced for that which already exists in a subtle form, then regarding that position as well, it has already been stated:
"Fire does not come from elsewhere; fire is not found within the fuel."
The answer to this has been stated here. // 1 //

Now, if it is postulated that the effect does not exist at all within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), he says the following to demonstrate that this too is untenable: "If [the effect] were produced from the causal complex of causes and conditions..."
And since the fruit does not exist within the causal complex, how could it be produced by that complex? // 2 //
If that fruit does not exist within the assemblage of causes and conditions,
how then is the fruit produced by the assemblage of causes and conditions?
Because it is non-existent therein, just like oil [produced] from sand.
For this very reason, not considering [such a possibility], he says:
"There is no fruit in the causal complex; how could it be born from the causal complex?
The intended meaning is that the fruit is not produced from the causal complex. // 2 //
Furthermore:
If the effect exists within the assemblage of causes and conditions, it should indeed be perceived within that assemblage; yet it is not perceived within the assemblage. (3)
Whatever exists in a certain place is perceived there, just as curd is perceived in a bowl.
And whatever does not exist in a certain place is not perceived there, just as oil is not perceived in sand,
or a crest-jewel in the hair of a frog.
Now, it might be argued: even though objects exist, they may not be perceived due to extreme subtlety, extreme proximity,
or extreme distance.
Due to the impairment of the sense organs, due to the obstruction by a corporeal substance,
and due to the disappearance of the corporeal form.

If it is argued that [the mind] is not perceived because it does not remain stationary—like an atom; like a stick of ointment on the eye; like the movement of the sun; like a single hair seen by one with cataracts; like form, sound, and so forth, for those who are blind or deaf; like a jar or other objects obstructed by a wall; like the bodies of perfected beings, gods, piśācas, and so forth; or like another object when one is occupied with a different object—then:
What indeed is the mark for the existence of these [objects] when they are not being perceived, by virtue of which it could be said that they exist despite their non-apprehension?
If it is argued that their existence is established through inference, comparison, and scripture, then...
In that case, it should not be said that those [objects] are unperceived,
because they are perceived through inference and other means.
That which is graspable by the material sense faculties is not apprehended even though it exists, due to these causes.
If this is argued, it is replied:
Have we stated that what exists must be apprehended by means of the material sense-faculties?
On the contrary, we state this in general terms: "Surely it would be apprehended when the causal complex [is complete]."
Moreover, you might think: that which does not exist in something does not arise from it, just as oil does not arise from sand;
yet, the fruit arises from the causal complex (sāmagrī).
Therefore, it is by means of inference that the existence of the fruit within the causal complex [is established].
It is said: whatever exists in a certain place...
It does not arise from that, just as curd does not arise from a bowl.
Since its existence is also untenable by this inference, why is it not accepted that the effect simply does not exist within the causal complex?
Now, it might be argued: "Just as existence is not tenable because it contradicts inference for both positions, so too is non-existence.
To this, it is said:
We do not establish its non-existence; rather, we refute the existence of it as imagined by others. Likewise, we do not establish its existence.
Rather, we refute its non-existence as it is imagined by others,
because our intention is to establish the Middle Way by avoiding the two extremes.
And it has been said in the *Śataka* by the venerable Āryadeva:

"The decoration of pillars and so forth for the sake of a house is useless for one who maintains that the effect exists [prior to its production], and it is likewise useless for one who maintains that the effect does not exist. Thus,
in this way, the effect is not produced from a causal complex, because it would follow that what already exists must be perceived.
Thus it is established. // 3 //
Now, if you think that the effect does not exist at all within the causal complex, even so:
If the effect does not exist within the causal complex of causes and conditions, then those causes and conditions would be the same as non-causes and non-conditions. (4)

For just as a sprout does not exist within flames, embers, and so forth, and thus they do not serve as its causes and conditions, so too the seeds and other factors intended [as causes] would not possess the status of causes and conditions, since the sprout does not exist within them.
And it is not logical for an effect to arise from what lacks causes and conditions; therefore, there is no arising of an effect by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

To this it is said: Indeed, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not possess the capacity to produce the fruit, such that this consideration would arise—whether the fruit exists within the causal complex or whether it does not.
Rather, it is the cause that possesses the capacity to produce the fruit;
the causal complex merely provides assistance to the cause.
That cause ceases after having given its causal impulse for the sake of the arising of the fruit; and the fruit arises being sustained by that cause. To this it is said:

For there is no assistance whatsoever for a cause that has not yet arisen, nor can anything at all be done to that which is unborn, just as nothing can be done to the son of a barren woman; thus, this conceptualization is untenable. // 4 //
Moreover:
If the cause, having given its causal efficiency to the effect, were to cease, then there would be a twofold nature for the cause—that which was given and that which has ceased. (5)

If it is conceived that the cause ceases after having provided the causal factor for the arising of the fruit, then, this being the case, the cause would possess two natures: that which is given and that which has ceased;
and this is not tenable.
Because it would entail the consequence of being half-eternal, and because there is no unity between the eternal and the non-eternal, which are mutually contradictory. // 5 //

Now, in order to avoid the consequence of the cause having two existences, if it is maintained that the cause ceases in its entirety without giving anything at all for the sake of the arising of the fruit, even so: If the cause were to cease without having given anything to the fruit, then that fruit, having arisen when the cause has ceased, would be without a cause. (6)
If the cause were to cease in its entirety without giving anything at all to the fruit, then surely that fruit which arises once the cause has ceased would be without a cause;
yet there is nothing that is without a cause.
Thus, this conceptual construction is untenable. // 6 //

Here it is said: If there is thus a fault in the arising of the effect from the cause, then let the collection [of causes] that has arisen simultaneously be the producer of the effect, just as in the case of a lamp and its light.
Demonstrating that this conception also is not tenable, he says:
"If the fruit were to manifest simultaneously with the causal complex, it would follow that the producer and that which is produced are simultaneous. (7)

Furthermore, it is not observed that two things existing at the same time—such as the left and right horns of a cow, or the left and right hands or feet—stand in the relation of producer and produced;
therefore, this conceptualization is untenable, and thus [the opponent's] argument is incorrect. // 7 //
Regarding this, some say: "The arising of entities from what did not previously exist is indeed not logical, because it would entail the consequence of being causeless.
Therefore, that fruit was already established prior to the assemblage of causes and conditions, existing in its future state;
by means of the assemblage of causes and conditions, its present state is produced."
"But as for the substance, it is indeed established. To them it is replied: "If the fruit were to manifest prior to the causal complex,"
If it were free from causes and conditions, the fruit would be without a cause. // 8 //
If it were your intention that the effect exists in its own nature even prior to the causal complex,
then it would be independent of causes and conditions;
and consequently, it would be causeless.
Furthermore, the existence of causeless entities is not logical, because it would entail the absurd consequence that even things such as the horns of a donkey, a horse, or a serpent would exist;
moreover, for that which is already established, there is no purpose in depending again upon causes and conditions. Thus, this [position] is untenable. // 8 //

Others, however, describe it thus: the cause alone produces the fruit, not the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Nor does this entail the aforementioned fault, because the cause is not one thing and the fruit another.
For there might arise the inquiry: does the cause cease after having given its causal efficacy to the fruit, or rather without having given it?
But [the answer is]: the cause itself, having ceased, is established in the form of the fruit.
To this it is said: even so—
If the effect were to exist when the cause has already ceased, there would be a transmigration of the cause;
furthermore, it would follow that a cause already previously born would be born again. (9)
If, according to your view, the effect arises when the cause has already ceased,
and it is further conceived that this effect is of the very same nature as the cause,
then in that case there would be a transmigration of the cause.
Just as an actor merely shifts from one costume to another upon discarding the previous one, there would be only a transition of the cause,
and not the production of a previously non-existent effect;
consequently, the cause itself would be eternal.
Furthermore, the existence of eternal things is never found anywhere;
as it is said in the *Śataka*:
"The existence of anything, anywhere, at any time, without dependence [on causes] does not exist."
"Never, nowhere, does anyone exist; therefore, there is no eternal [self]."
Furthermore, according to this conception, it would follow that a cause already produced undergoes production once again.
And it is not logical for that which has already been produced to be produced yet again, because it would be purposeless and because it would lead to an infinite regress.
Now, if you think: "It is not born with that very nature by which it exists, nor is it born with that very nature by which it does not exist"—
this too is not logical.

Since it is impossible to prove the non-difference of substance merely on the basis of a difference in designation or a difference in state—given that the cause, whose intrinsic nature has not been abandoned, is designated as the "effect"—and because at the stage of the effect, that which has abandoned its causal nature is what is denoted by the word "effect," the claim that "the cause persists in the form of the effect" is nonsensical. // 9 //
Furthermore: if a cause were to produce an effect, would it produce it while having ceased or while not having ceased?
And as for the effect, would it be produced while already arisen or while not yet arisen?
Demonstrating that it is untenable in either case, he says:
"How could a cause that has ceased and passed away produce an arisen effect?
And how could a cause, even while persisting, produce an effect if it is held [by it]? (10)
If it is postulated that a cause which has already ceased and gone to its end produces an effect that has arisen and is currently existing, that is not tenable.
If one asks why:
How could a cause that has ceased and no longer exists produce an effect?
If it were to produce one, then even the son of a barren woman would produce a son.
Furthermore, how can a cause produce an effect that already exists and is independent of birth?
Now, if you think: "The ceased cause does not produce because it lacks capacity; rather, the cause will produce the effect while still persisting."
It is said:

Even while persisting, how could a cause that remains unchanged in form and is already occupied by—that is, connected with—an existing effect produce it? For in this case, a cause produces another effect only as it undergoes transformation.
Thus, for one who maintains the non-existence of a cause, the cause must necessarily undergo transformation;
however, that which does not undergo transformation is not at all endowed with the characteristics of a cause.
And how could that which is already connected with the fruit produce it?
Because the fruit already exists. // 10 //

Now, if you think that because it is impossible for an existing effect to be produced again, the cause will produce the effect while being unobstructed—that is, even while disconnected from the effect—this too is incorrect; thus he says: "If this [cause] is unobstructed by the effect, which effect would it produce?"
If it is maintained that the cause is entirely unconnected with the effect, then which effect would it now produce?
Or rather, because of its lack of connection, it would produce every single effect whatsoever.
Or rather, it would not produce anything at all, precisely because of its lack of connection; such is the intended meaning.
Furthermore: if a cause were to produce an effect, would it produce that effect having seen it, or without having seen it?
It is stated that neither case is tenable:
For a cause does not produce an effect either by not seeing it or by seeing it. // 11 //
In that regard, if it is conceptualized that the cause produces [the effect] after having seen it, that is not tenable;
because only that which already exists can be seen, not that which does not exist.
If it already exists,
it is not produced because it already exists;
thus, in the first place, the cause does not produce the fruit upon seeing it.
Even without being seen, it does not produce [an effect], because that would entail the absurd consequence that every cause produces every effect.
Now, what is this "seeing" (darśana), or what is "non-seeing" (adarśana)? It is said:
in the world, it is well known that perception (upalabdhi) is seeing.

But surely this is not possible in the case of seeds and the like, which are devoid of sense faculties. Let it be possible or not; this is not a challenge we pose, but rather one directed at the proponent of arising.

In this regard, if one who asserts [the theory of] arising should say, "It produces [the effect] after having seen [it]," he should be told: "It is not observed in the world that [the seed and so forth] see;
therefore, this conceptualization is untenable."
If, on the other hand, one were to imagine [an effect] by not seeing it,
then whatever unperceived thing might possibly exist would all be produced;
yet it does not produce them.
Therefore, it does not produce [an effect] even without being perceived.

For we examine the constructions of others by means of undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭāpatti*), as if [examining] the world that is beset by a garland of sufferings—the forest thickets, wildernesses, mountain caves, and precipices of *saṃsāra*.

And the Nirgranthas, who accept a creator such as *Puruṣa* as the cause of the world, do not escape the same logical consequence when they assert that seeds and so forth possess a single sense-faculty (*ekendriya*).
Therefore, there is no fault. // 11 //

Furthermore: if there were a conjunction characterized by the mutual approaching of cause and effect as you assert, then only at that time would there be between them the relationship of producer and produced.
For it is not observed that light and darkness, or saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, which are not mutually conjoined, possess the relationship of producer and produced.

Therefore, one who necessarily desires a relationship of producer and produced between cause and effect must accept a conjunction [between them]. Yet, when that conjunction is examined throughout the three periods of time, it is not possible.
Consequently, the cause does not produce the effect.
Demonstrating how there is no conjunction, he says: "For a past effect, there is never any conjunction with a past cause, nor with one that is unborn, nor with one that has already arisen. (12)
First, there is never at any time a conjunction of a past effect with a past cause,
because both are non-existent due to their being past.
Nor is there ever found a conjunction of a past effect with an unborn (future) cause.
Because both [the past cause and the present effect] are non-existent— since one has perished and the other has not yet arisen— and because they belong to different times,
it is not possible for there to be a connection between a past effect and a present cause that has already arisen.

Because they occur at different times, and because a fruit that has already perished does not exist—just as [an action] cannot belong to Devadatta by way of a barren woman’s son—this is the intended meaning. // 12 //

And just as there is never a conjunction of a past effect with a past, future, or present cause, so too there is no conjunction of a present effect with a cause belonging to the three times; demonstrating this, he says:
"For there is no [conjunction] of a born effect with an unborn cause."
There is never any conjunction with that which has passed away, nor with that which is yet to be born. // 13 //
There is no conjunction of a produced effect with a cause that is either unproduced or past, because they exist at different times;
nor is there a conjunction of a present effect with a present cause, because cause and effect cannot be simultaneous.
Furthermore, the conjunction of those two would be purposeless;
for what need is there for a further conjunction of two things that already exist independently of one another? Thus, no conjunction exists. // 13 //

Now, demonstrating that even for a future fruit there is no conjunction with a cause—whether past, future, or present—he says: "For a fruit that has not yet arisen, there is never any conjunction with a cause that has already arisen, nor with one that is unarisen, nor with one that has perished. (14)
For an unarisen fruit is non-existent;
it has no conjunction with a cause that exists at a different time—whether present or past—because they belong to different times. It also has no conjunction with a future cause.
Because both are non-existent. // 14 //
And when there is thus no connection whatsoever between cause and effect, then— given the absence of a connection— how can a cause produce an effect?
The intention is that a cause does not produce an effect at all, because a connection does not exist, just like the son of a barren woman.
Furthermore, it might be argued that a cause produces an effect only when there is a conjunction;
however, that too is not tenable,
because no such conjunction is perceived in any of the three times.
Furthermore, even if some kind of conjunction between cause and effect were to be imagined, even so—when such a conjunction exists, how could the cause produce the effect? (15)
The intention is that if the fruit were already present, rebirth would be purposeless; furthermore, it is illogical for there to be a conjunction of things that are not already conjoined. // 15 //
Furthermore: If the cause is empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect?
If the cause is not empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect? (16)
This which is accepted as the cause of the fruit, the producer of the fruit—
is it empty of that [fruit] or non-empty when it produces the fruit?
In that regard, a cause that is empty, being devoid of the fruit, does not produce the fruit.
Because it would be like a non-cause, being devoid of a fruit;
moreover, even a cause that is not devoid of a fruit does not produce that fruit,
because the fruit already exists.
Like Devadatta who already possesses a son;
thus, whether a cause is devoid of a fruit or not devoid of a fruit, it does not produce a fruit. // 16 //
Furthermore, as for the fruit that arises,
does it arise as non-empty or as empty?
Regarding that first point:
A non-empty fruit will not arise, and a non-empty [fruit] will not cease.
That which is non-empty would thus be neither ceased nor arisen. (17)
For a non-empty effect would be unarisen dependently and established by way of intrinsic nature;
such an effect would never arise, and because intrinsic nature is indestructible, it would not cease.
Consequently, that which you maintain to be non-empty would be both unceased and unarisen.
And this is not accepted;
therefore, that fruit is not non-empty, because the acceptance of its arising and cessation [is required]. // 17 //
Now, demonstrating that even that fruit, being empty, cannot possibly exist because it would follow that it possesses neither arising nor ceasing, he says:
"How will the empty arise? How will the empty cease?"
If it were empty, it would follow that it is neither ceased nor arisen. // 18 //
In this context, that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature is called "empty.
And how could that entity which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature ever arise?
Or how could it be ceased?
For the arising and passing away of things such as space, which do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), are never observed.
Therefore, even that fruit which is desired would follow as being neither ceased nor arisen, and thus [the result] would be empty. // 18 //
Furthermore: if the cause were to produce the fruit, would it produce it as something non-different from the fruit, or as something different?
And since neither case is tenable, he says:
"The identity of cause and effect is never tenable;
the difference between cause and effect is never tenable. (19)
Demonstrating that this is merely a mere assertion, he says: "If cause and effect were identical, there would be oneness between the producer and the produced;
if cause and effect were distinct, the cause would be equivalent to a non-cause. (20)
If there were identity between the cause and the effect, then one would have to accept the identity of the produced and the producer;
yet there is no such identity between these two.
Because it would follow that the father and son, the eye and visual consciousness, and the seed and sprout are identical;
thus, in this way, there is no identity between the cause and the fruit.
Now, even otherness does not exist.
What is the reason?
If, according to your view, there were an intended otherness between the cause and the effect, [it would follow that they could exist simultaneously].
In that case, because it would be independent of anything else, the effect would be independent of a cause;
yet this is not so.
Therefore, even the distinctness of the cause from the effect is not possible.
Furthermore, when two things are thus examined and found to possess neither identity nor difference, their relationship as producer and produced is never accepted;
therefore, a cause does not produce an effect at all. // 20 //
Furthermore: if the cause were to produce an effect,
would it produce that effect as something already existing by way of its own nature, or as something non-existent?
And since it is not tenable in either case, he says:
"How will a cause produce an effect that exists by way of its own-being? How will a cause produce an effect that does not exist by way of its own-being? (21)
In that regard, whatever fruit is truly existent by way of its own nature and exists by way of its own nature, that is not produced again because it already exists,
like an existing jar.
Furthermore, even a result that is non-existent by way of its own-being is not produced by a cause,
because it is non-existent by way of its own-being.
Like the horn of a donkey.
If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive because of a reflection,
let it be inconclusive; nevertheless, the lack of intrinsic nature of entities is established.
Consequently, there would be an abandonment of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (sasvabhāvavāda),
and it would merely be a restatement of our own position.

Since no entity whatsoever exists that possesses intrinsic nature, and because of the absence of its opposite, how could there be any inconclusiveness [in the argument] that even an entity lacking intrinsic nature does not exist?
For our reflection is neither with intrinsic nature nor without intrinsic nature,
because those two properties cannot exist in the absence of a substratum (dharmin).
Indeed, the Noble Ones do not perceive anything called a "reflection" as being either without intrinsic nature or with intrinsic nature.

In that regard, by means of the two preceding verses beginning with "The fruit will not first arise," the status of the fruit as the agent of the act of production was directly negated. Now, the causality of the cause—that is, its being the instigator of the act of producing the fruit—is being refuted. This should be understood as the distinction between this [present argument] and the previous one. // 21 //
To this it is said: although the causal agent's role in instigating the activity of producing an effect has been refuted, nevertheless, the cause still exists by way of its own nature;
and yet, in the absence of an effect, the causality of the cause is not established.
"Therefore, the fruit will also come into being.
It is replied: There might be a cause, if this [cause] could possess the status of a cause without producing [the effect].
And the status of being a cause is not tenable for that which does not produce [an effect].
Now, it might be argued: "Even if the causality of the cause is thus non-existent, nevertheless, the effect at least exists."
And since it is not logical for an effect to exist without a cause, it follows that because the effect exists, the cause must also exist.
To this it is said: when it has been stated that a cause which does not produce [an effect] lacks the status of being a cause, then—
And if the status of being a cause is untenable, whose fruit will there be? // 22 //
Thus, for this reason, the fruit also does not exist. // 22 //

Here it is said: "Indeed, the causal operation that produces the fruit does not belong to the cause alone; rather, the fruit is generated by the totality of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī). To this, it is replied:
Because it entails the faults already mentioned, this is not tenable.
Furthermore, if it is conceived that this collection of causes and conditions (*hetupratyayasāmagrī*) produces the effect,
does it first produce itself, or does it not?
If it is conceived that [the cause] produces [the effect], that is not tenable;
for it is never observed that something which has not attained its own existence can function as an instigator. Therefore, the causal complex must necessarily have attained its own existence.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which has already attained its own existence to act as the causal agent for the production of itself;
therefore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not produce itself.
And that which does not produce itself—
Explaining how that [causal complex] is able to produce an effect, he says:
"And since this causal complex does not produce itself by means of itself through the causes and conditions, how could it produce an effect? (23)
This collection of conditions and causes does not, by itself, produce itself,
because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself, and because production of what already exists would be purposeless.
And how can that which does not even produce itself in this manner produce a fruit?
For it is not logical that the daughter of a barren woman, being unable to produce herself, should produce a son.
In this way, it is also not tenable that a causal complex, which does not produce itself, produces an effect. // 23 //
Therefore, the fruit is not produced by the causal complex;
however, it might be argued: "If the fruit produced by the causal complex is not possible,"
If it is argued that, in that case, [the effect] must be produced by a non-complexity (asāmagrī), it is said:
there is no effect produced by a non-complexity.
When an effect produced by a complexity does not occur, [how could one be produced otherwise]?
In that case, how could that which is utterly contradictory be produced by a non-complexity of causes?
A fruit produced by a non-complexity of causes is not possible.
Now, it might be argued: although there is no fruit by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nevertheless the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*) does exist.
And since the collection of causes and conditions cannot occur without a fruit, the fruit must also come into existence.
It is said:
there might be a collection of causes and conditions if the fruit itself were to exist.
But when, according to the reasoning already stated, the fruit itself does not exist, then: "How indeed can there be a collection of conditions without a fruit? (24)
The intention is that when there is an absence of a fruit, the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*) is also non-existent because it would be without a cause.
For it is said in the *Ārya-lalitavistara-sūtra*: "Depending upon the throat, the lips, the palate, and the movement of the tongue, syllables resound."
Nor is it found in the throat, nor in the palate; each individual syllable is not perceived.
And that speech issues forth from the assembly of conditions by the power of mind and intellect;
mind and speech, being invisible and formless, are not apprehended either externally or internally.
When a wise person perceives the arising and passing away of the sounds,
cries, and tones of speech, they then see all words as momentary, insubstantial, and like an echo.
Likewise, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*:
"In this delightful teaching, go forth into homelessness, casting off the marks of a householder;
you shall become excellent ones who possess the fruit, as instructed here by the Compassionate One."
Having gone forth and abandoned the marks of a householder, there will be the attainment of all fruits;
furthermore, by weighing the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there is the attainment of all fruits and the fruits themselves.
"They obtained the fruit and likewise the attainment; moreover, wonder arises within them:
'Oh, how exceedingly compassionate is the Lion among Men! The Victor has perfectly taught the method.
Thus it is said in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom (*Ārya-prajñāpāramitā-aṣṭasāhasrikā*).
Therefore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor should not abide in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness;

he should not abide in the fruit of stream-entry, nor in the fruit of once-returning, nor in the fruit of non-returning, nor in arhatship, nor in the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor should he abide in the state of a perfectly awakened buddha. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Examination of the Collection," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Twenty-first Chapter: An Examination of Origination and Dissolution.
Here it is said: Time exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is the cause of origination and dissolution.

In this world, the arising of sprouts— the production of entities— occurs in dependence upon a specific time; likewise, their dissolution or destruction occurs in dependence upon a specific time, and not at all times.
Even though the collection of causes and conditions exists, time nevertheless exists because it is the cause of arising and passing away. To this, it is said:
Time might be the cause of arising and passing away if arising and passing away themselves existed;
however, they do not exist.
And as for how they do not exist:
Establishing this, he says:
"Indeed, disintegration does not exist either without or together with origination;
indeed, origination does not exist either without or together with disintegration. (1)
In this case, if origination and dissolution were to exist,
they would have to exist either through mutual coexistence or through mutual non-coexistence.
When examined in both ways, neither is possible.
How so?
First, in that regard, just as there is no dissolution or destruction without occurrence or arising, [so too is it with the other].
Demonstrating this, he says:
"How indeed could there be dissolution without origination?
There is death without birth; dissolution does not exist without emergence. (2)
Without origination, how indeed could there be cessation, that is, destruction?
By the phrase "how indeed," he demonstrates that such a thing is utterly impossible;
for how could it possibly come to be?
The intention is that this is simply not possible.
Furthermore, if disintegration were to occur without prior origination, what fault would there be? It is said in reply:
Death would occur even without birth;
there would be death for one who has not been born.
And yet, the death of one who has not been born is never observed.
Therefore, disintegration cannot exist without origination.
Here, the first half-verse constitutes the thesis, while the middle quarter-verse establishes a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*).
It should be understood that the conclusion is made by the final [member]. // 2 //
Having thus established that disintegration is not tenable without origination, he now establishes that disintegration is also not possible even with origination, saying:
"How could disintegration exist simultaneously with origination?
For birth and death are not found to occur at the same time. (3)
For if manifestation were simultaneous with origination, occurring at the same time,
then birth and death would occur simultaneously.
But this is not the case, as two mutually contradictory things, like light and darkness, do not exist at one and the same time.
Therefore, it is established that even with the possibility of coexistence, there is no proof of disintegration. // 3 //

And since, in this way, there is no establishment of disintegration either without or with origination, he says— demonstrating that likewise there is no establishment of origination either without or with disintegration:
"How indeed could origination exist without disintegration?"
For impermanence is never not found among existing things. // 4 //
For indeed, existence is not possible without dissolution;
because impermanence is never absent from entities that possess the nature of becoming and the nature of arising—it is rather always present. For it has been said:
"Among all entities that are subject to the nature of aging and death, which entities always exist without aging and death? Thus,
when all entities are in this way constantly followed by impermanence, [how could they be permanent?]
In that case, from where could there be any state that is devoid of destruction?
Therefore, there is no arising without disintegration.
Thus, for the time being, there is no occurrence without disintegration.
The remainder is not examined here, as it has already been investigated in the *Saṃskṛtaparīkṣā*.
But that destruction which has a cause,
because it possesses the characteristics of a conditioned phenomenon, is like arising.
Having thus presented the proof, he asserts that [the reason] is inconclusive due to the final moments of mind and mental factors;
however, he does not speak correctly,
because even their destruction has a cause— namely, birth as its condition— and because it is equivalent to the probandum, there is no lack of conclusiveness.
As for what was stated— that arising is said to be the very coming-to-be of an entity that did not previously exist,
and therefore, because arising is established as substantially real, there is the existence of an example from the perspective of conventional usage—
that too is not tenable.
Because it is accepted that reflections and the like, which lack substantial reality (*adravyasat*), possess causes;
as stated by the Master [Vasubandhu]:
"Those things whose arising is from a cause do not exist in the absence of that [cause]."
"How indeed could they not be clearly considered equal to a reflection?
From this scriptural authority (*āgama*), how can there be a failure to establish the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)?
And if [the example is not established] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*bhāva*), [then it is established conventionally].
That which cannot be described as being either identical to or different from reality is said not to exist even conventionally;
thus, even blue and so forth are said not to exist.
As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"Because form is merely an absence, space is a mere name;
and since there can be no form without the primary elements, even that which is a mere name does not exist."
Moreover, from where could the Mādhyamikas have an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) established as an existent entity, of which "arising" (*utpāda*) would be a particular state?
Therefore, the objection that the example is unestablished (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhatā*) is entirely untenable.
As for what was said—that destruction is not caused—[that too is incorrect].
Because it possesses indestructibility,
just like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for one who speaks thus, this reason becomes a great contradiction.
For just as this reason establishes that destruction is causeless, it likewise establishes the absence of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, it contradicts everything such as its inclusion within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and its inclusion among the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*); therefore, this view is not tenable.
Likewise,
consciousness does not cut off the intrinsic nature of an object, because it lacks the nature of consciousness [as a cutter].

Because all [phenomena] are negated by such statements as "like the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛtavat*), a great undesirable consequence follows for this [position]; therefore, this should not be accepted. // 4 //
Now, demonstrating how origination cannot be established along with destruction, he says:
How can origination exist together with destruction itself?
For birth and death do not exist at the same time. // 5 //
For if arising were indeed simultaneous with passing away, then birth and death would be co-temporal;
yet that is not possible.
Therefore, even by way of coexistence, there is no establishment of arising and passing away. // 5 //
Now, it might be argued: although there is no establishment of birth and death either through their identity or their difference, nevertheless, arising and passing away do indeed exist,
because they are expressible.
"Like consciousness," it is said;
[if] the establishment of these two is desired by way of being expressible, [then...]
Let it be accepted even for the son of a barren woman.
Moreover:
For those two things for which establishment neither together with one another nor without one another exists, how indeed can their establishment exist? (6)
There is no other alternative possibility devoid of both coexistence and non-coexistence from which the establishment of arising and passing away could occur.
If it is argued that their establishment will occur through inexpressibility, then what indeed is this so-called "inexpressibility"?
If there were a state of mixture, that would be untenable,
because those things which are not established as distinct from one another cannot undergo a process of mixing.
Since they cannot be determined as having an intrinsic nature, origination and dissolution do not exist at all, just like the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman.
And when origination and dissolution do not exist in this way, it is established that time, which is their cause, also does not exist. // 6 //

Furthermore, regarding this: when these two, arising and passing away, are being conceptualized, would they be conceptualized as belonging to an entity that is subject to destruction, or to one that is not subject to destruction?
Demonstrating that neither case is tenable, he says:
"There is no arising of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there any arising of that which is not subject to destruction."
There is no disintegration of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there disintegration of that which is indestructible. // 7 //
In that regard, the arising of destruction—which is characterized by decay—is not logical, because of the presence of opposing factors.
Furthermore, the arising of that which is indestructible is also not logical, as it is devoid of the characteristics of an entity, like the horn of a donkey.
Thus, there is no disintegration of destruction.
For that which is subject to destruction does not exist [independently]; therefore, its disintegration without a basis is not logical.
Likewise, disintegration does not belong to that which is indestructible.
For the inexhaustible dharma is indeed distinct from the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
Since it does not exist [in that sense], how could there be its destruction?
Furthermore, both arising and destruction do not belong to an entity that possesses the nature of exhaustion, nor to one that lacks the nature of exhaustion.
Those two do not occur;
thus, neither arising nor passing away exist. 7.
Here it is said: Arising and dissolution do indeed exist for entities, because of the existence of the substratum (dharmin) upon which they depend.
In this context, arising and dissolution have entities as their substratum.
And as long as that entity exists,
because of its existence, the two properties dependent upon it will also exist; to this,
it is replied:
These two properties would be dependent upon an entity if that entity existed;
however, when the entity does not exist, then—
Arising and passing away do not exist without an entity.
If it is asked why an entity does not exist [without them], it is because: "Arising and passing away do not exist without an entity. (8)
For arising and passing away are the defining characteristics of an entity,
and since these two do not exist by way of their own nature, they have been refuted.
And when those two are refuted in terms of their reality, [the entity itself is likewise refuted].
In that case, without arising and passing away—which are the characteristics of an entity—how could there be an entity distinct from the characteristics of an entity?
Furthermore, without an entity, arising and passing away do not exist.
Others, however, having made the first half the latter, explain it thus:
origination and destruction do indeed exist,
because they are properties of existing things (*bhāva*).
In this context, whatever does not exist lacks the nature of being an existent entity,
just as, for example, the crest-jewel of a frog’s hair.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence are the phenomena of arising and passing away; therefore, those two must indeed exist.
If, for someone, arising and passing away were to exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, [then existence and non-existence would follow].
It would be appropriate to call that an "entity" (bhāva);
yet those two do not exist,
for without both arising (saṃbhava) and passing away (vibhava), an entity is not found.
The meaning is that because the arising and passing away of an entity exist only when the entity itself exists;
and if that entity were non-existent, the reason [of the argument] would be unestablished. Likewise:
"Arising and passing away do not exist without an entity."
The intention is that because of the non-existence of the substratum, the dependent cannot be established. // 8 //
Furthermore: here, when these two—arising and passing away—are being conceptualized, would they be conceptualized for an empty entity or for a non-empty one?
Demonstrating that neither case is tenable, he says:
"Neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is empty."
The intention is that [arising and ceasing] are like a painting in the sky, because they lack a real substratum. Likewise:
"Neither arising nor ceasing is possible for that which is not empty. (9)
Since that which is non-empty does not exist, arising and passing away, being without a basis, are not tenable. // 9 //
Furthermore: if origination and destruction were to exist here, would they be identical or different?
Since neither case is tenable, he says:

It is not tenable that origination and dissolution are one and the same, because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory things, such as light and darkness, to be identical. Likewise, it is not tenable that origination and dissolution are different. (10)
Because the two are mutually non-deviant;
for indeed, the destruction of that which lacks origination is never seen, nor is the origination of that which lacks destruction ever observed.
Thus, because these two are mutually inseparable,
it is established that arising and passing away are not distinct.
Now, it might be argued: "What is the use of this subtle analysis?
For since ordinary people, even down to cowherds and women, perceive arising and passing away, therefore arising and passing away do exist."
For indeed, a son of a barren woman, being non-existent, cannot be seen. Even so, it might be argued:
"Both arising and passing away would be seen by you.
To this it is replied: this is inconclusive.
For it is not the case that whatever is perceived by the world exists;

for instance, people ranging from cowherds and women upwards perceive things such as a city of the Gandharvas, illusions, dreams, firebrands whirled into circles, and mirages—though these do not exist—due to the impairment of their sense faculties.
In the same way, he says that these two, arising and passing away, though non-existent, are seen only through delusion:
Both arising and passing away are seen only through delusion. // 11 //
Now, why again is this determined in such a way—that these two, arising and passing away, which lack an intrinsic nature, are seen by the world of beings only due to delusion?
For this is determined by reasoning.
What, then, is the reasoning here?
In this regard, if there were such a thing as an entity, it would necessarily arise either from an entity or from a non-entity;
likewise, if there were such a thing as a non-entity, [it would similarly have to arise from one or the other].
That [effect] too would have to arise either from existence or from non-existence;
yet in both cases, it is impossible for both. Thus he says:
"An existent does not arise from an existent, nor does an existent arise from a non-existent."
Non-existence does not arise from non-existence, nor does non-existence arise from existence. // 12 //
First of all, the arising of an entity called "existence" from an entity called "existence" does not occur,
because cause and effect cannot be simultaneous,
and because it is redundant for that which has already attained birth to arise again.
An entity does not arise even from non-existence.
What is the reason? For "non-existence" means dissolution or destruction.
And that [non-existence] is the opposite of existence.
Therefore, how could existence arise from that which is the opposite of existence?
If it were so, then even the son of a barren woman's daughter would exist.
And this is not so;
therefore, existence does not arise even from non-existence.
Now, non-existence also does not arise from non-existence.
