For non-existence (abhāva) has the nature of the cessation of becoming; therefore, how could it possess the capacity to produce an effect?
If it did, then even nirvāṇa would possess the capacity to produce an effect.
And if a non-entity were to arise from a non-entity, then even the son of a barren woman’s daughter would exist;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, non-existence does not arise from non-existence;
now, non-existence also does not arise from existence.
For non-existence is the opposite of existence.
How could it arise from existence? If it were to arise from existence,
then darkness would come from a lamp.
Since, when thus investigated, both arising and passing away do not exist, it should be understood that they are perceived by the world solely due to delusion.
Alternatively, here is another prima facie argument: for if origination and destruction were to exist here, they would have to be based either on existence or on non-existence;
yet, when existence and non-existence are examined in every way, they are not possible.
And therefore, from what source could arising and dissolution exist without a basis? For this reason, it should be understood that both arising and dissolution are seen only through delusion.
Demonstrating how both existence and non-existence are not possible, he says:
"An existent does not arise from an existent; an existent does not arise from a non-existent."
Non-existence does not arise from non-existence, nor does non-existence arise from existence.
The meaning of this is as before. // 12 //
Moreover, if there were such a thing as an entity (bhāva),
it would possess arising and ceasing, and thus would have both origination and dissolution.
Yet no entity exists by way of its own nature (svarūpa), because, like the horn of a donkey, it is unarisen by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
If it is argued that "the state of being unarisen is unestablished," that is established, because:
An entity is not born from itself, nor indeed is it born from another.
It is not produced from itself nor from another; how, then, could it be produced? // 13 //
And since this has already been explained in the very first chapter, it is not explained again here.
Furthermore, as for that which is born in the manner just described, from what does it now arise?
The intended meaning is that it does not arise from anything at all.
And this must necessarily be accepted: that in every respect there is no arising of an entity. // 13 //
Furthermore, he states that for one who follows the Buddhist doctrine, the acceptance of the real existence of entities leads to the fallacy of the views of eternalism and nihilism:
"For one who accepts an entity, the views of eternalism and nihilism follow as a consequence."
Because that entity must be either permanent or impermanent. (14)

For whoever, transgressing the established system of categories as they have been explained, accepts a view of the existence of entities, necessarily falls into the two views of eternalism and nihilism, which are utterly contrary to the teaching.
What is the reason?
Because that entity, when being conceptualized, must be either permanent or impermanent;
if it were permanent, then there would necessarily be the doctrine of eternalism.
If, on the other hand, it were impermanent, then there would necessarily be annihilation. // 14 //
Here it is said: For one who accepts the existence of entities, there is neither annihilation nor eternalism.
What is the reason? Because—
For existence (bhava) is indeed the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect. // 15 //
For that continuous succession of the arising and passing away of cause and effect is, for us, existence and saṃsāra;
in that regard, if the cause were to cease, [existence would not continue].
If the fruit caused by that [cause] were not to arise,
then there would be the fault of the doctrine of annihilationism;
and if the cause were not to cease, [the same fault would follow].
If it were to abide in its own essential nature,
then there would be the fault of the view of eternalism;
however, this is not the case.
Therefore, even when the existence of entities is admitted, there is no consequence of the two faults of the views of eternalism and nihilism.

That which is this very saṃsāra—the continuous succession of the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras), proceeding in an uninterrupted sequence of cause and effect—is what constitutes it. Consequently, we do not incur this fault. // 15 //
It is said:
If existence (*bhava*) is that continuum of arising and passing away of cause and effect, then even so—
It would follow that because expenditure does not arise again, there must be a total cessation of its cause. // 16 //

For if the causal moment, having functioned as the cause for the arising of the fruit, ceases—surely, since that causal moment which has undergone destruction does not arise again, you fall into the view of annihilationism.
If you ask, "How is this not a fault for you? [the response follows].
This fault applies to one who accepts existence;
however, I do not accept existence, because all phenomena are unarisen by way of intrinsic nature.
Whatever arises dependently upon something else is indeed not that very thing,
nor is it something other than it; therefore, there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
Thus it has been said; even there, by this same reasoning, the very lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of phenomena is established.
For otherwise, if the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of things were to exist, how could there not be a difference between the seed and the sprout?
Therefore, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not invalidate our position. // 16 //

Having thus demonstrated that for a cause that has already come into being, the consequence of the view of annihilation follows because it would not arise again, [the author] now states, pointing out the consequence of the fault in the doctrine of eternalism:
"The non-existence of that which exists by way of its own-being is not tenable;
for if the existence of the cause were by way of its own-being," [it would follow that it could never cease].
Thereafter, its non-existence could not occur, because intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is indestructible;
consequently, the consequence of the view of eternalism remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore:
At the time of nirvāṇa, there would be annihilation due to the cessation of the continuity of existence. (17)

Although the consequence of the views of eternalism and nihilism is avoided by means of the continuous progression of the stream of arising and passing away of cause and effect, nevertheless, where there is the non-progression of this stream once again—
that is, in nirvāṇa— one inevitably falls into the view of nihilism.
The Blessed One has stated that the view of annihilationism must be abandoned.

If you argue that such a view of annihilationism will not exist [in our system], then for what purpose would any other [view] exist for you? For it is because [all views] have as their objective support the cessation of existence.
The intended meaning is that it is like having the cessation of existence as its object at the time of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, as for what was said— "For existence is indeed the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect"— that too is not tenable.
How so? For here, the final existence is characterized by cessation, while the first is characterized by the reconnection of rebirth into a realm of existence.
In this context, the final existence (*bhava*), as it is ceasing, persists as the cause;
whereas the first existence, characterized by rebirth, persists as the nature of the fruit.
And the designation "saṃsāra" is applied to these two existences. // 17 //
And here this is investigated: as for this first existence which is established as having the nature of a fruit,
does it arise when the final existence has ceased, or when it has not ceased?
Or [does it exist] while ceasing,
from which there would be a cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) due to the continuous succession of cause and effect?
Demonstrating that it is not possible in any way when examined, he says:
The first existence is not tenable when the last has ceased;
nor is the first existence tenable when the last has not ceased. (18)
In that regard, if it is conceptualized that the first existence arises once the final existence has ceased,
then it would be without cause;
even a sprout would arise from a seed burnt by fire.
And this is not accepted;
therefore, it is not logical that the first existence occurs when the last has already ceased.
Now, even when the final existence has not yet ceased, a first existence is not tenable;
for if it were to exist, it would be without cause,
and a single sentient being would possess two forms.
There would be the manifestation of a previously non-existent being,
and there would be permanence for what is prior; furthermore, the sprout would arise even while the seed has not perished.
And this is not accepted as being so.
Therefore, it is established that: "The first existence is not possible when the last has not ceased. (18)
Now, demonstrating how the first existence is likewise untenable even when the final existence is ceasing, he says:
If the first were to arise while the final is ceasing, then that which is ceasing would be one, and that which is arising would be another. (19)
In this context, that which is "ceasing" is the present [moment], because it is denotable by a suffix expressing the present tense;
likewise, that which "is born" is also said to be the present, because it is denotable by the word "present.
Alternatively, "ceasing" refers to the agent of the action of ceasing.
And that which is born is also the agent of the action of being born; and these two, being conceived as existing at one time, exist indeed simultaneously.
Furthermore, that which is ceasing would be one existence and that which is being born another; thus, two existences would result simultaneously.
And it has already been stated that two existences cannot possibly belong to a single entity at once. // 19 //
Thus, by the method of investigation as previously stated:
If it is not tenable that the one being ceased and the one being born exist simultaneously, then in whichever aggregates one dies, in those very same aggregates one is born. (20)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction;
it brings together the phrase "each separately.
Thus, when the final [moment] has ceased according to the principle already stated, the first existence cannot possibly occur.
Even when the final existence has not ceased, the first existence does not occur;
nor does the first existence occur simultaneously with the final existence at one and the same time.
Therefore, would it then follow that one is born in those very same aggregates in which one dies?
That one dies in the very same aggregates in which one is situated and is born in those same ones is utterly contradictory;
for it is never observed that one who is dying is simultaneously being born. 20. Therefore—
Thus, in all three times, the continuity of existence favored by you is not tenable.

Since the first existence does not occur when the final existence has ceased, has not yet ceased, or is in the process of ceasing, there is no continuity of existence in any of the three times. How can that which does not exist in the three times be a continuity of existence? (21)
And that which does not exist in the three times—how could it exist with another self? Thus, in every respect, the continuity of existence (*bhava-saṃtati*) as conceived by you does not exist.
And therefore, as for what was said:
"For existence (*bhava*) is indeed the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect"—
this [assertion] is not tenable. Consequently, if you accept the existence of things (*bhāva*), that very same unavoidable consequence of the doctrines of eternalism and nihilism follows for you.
Therefore, it is established that there is indeed no arising of entities by way of their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
As it is said in the venerable *Ārya-samādhirāja*: thus—
Just as when a seed exists there is a sprout, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout;
it is neither different from it nor is it that very same thing—such is the nature of phenomena, characterized by neither annihilation nor permanence.
From a seal, an impression is seen, yet no transfer of the seal is perceived; it is not there, nor is it from anywhere else.
In this same way, conditioned phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Therefore, it was said by the venerable Āryanāgārjuna:
"The wise should understand that the reconnection of the aggregates occurs without transmigration, like a recitation, a lamp, a seal, a mirror, a sound, a sun-gem, a seed, or a mango tree."
Likewise, the Blessed One said:
"One is born and also passes away, yet for one who understands that there is neither birth nor passing away, this samādhi is not difficult to attain."
Likewise:
"Those people in the world who have understood that phenomena are inconceivable through their kinsmen are always well-happened;
they possess no conceptualization of dharma or adharma, for all mental proliferation has been eliminated."
Knowledge discerns both existence and non-existence; all is inconceivable, all is unreal.
Yet those fools who follow the power of the mind suffer for hundreds of millions of births.
Even one who contemplates phenomena as empty is a fool who has entered upon a wrong path;
for while phenomena are proclaimed to be empty through syllables, they are in truth beyond syllables, yet described by means of syllables.

One who contemplates phenomena as peaceful and utterly tranquil—even that mind has never arisen; all conceptualizations of the mind are proliferations (*prapañca*). Realize phenomena as subtle and inconceivable.
Thus [ends verse] 21.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Examination of Arising and Passing Away," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Tathāgata, the twenty-second chapter.
Here it is said: The continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati) certainly exists, because the Tathāgata truly exists.

For here, the Blessed One—upholding the non-duality of great compassion, skillful means, and wisdom; with a mind solely intent on the pacification of all sufferings such as birth for all sentient beings without exception throughout the entire triple world;

exerting himself through three or seven incalculable eons in an uninterrupted succession; by means of various unsurpassed and most diverse undertakings of meritorious deeds characterized by the sole activity of bringing about the welfare and prosperity of the whole world; and being devoted to the complete favoring of the entire world even more than that of a beloved only son—[has attained this state].

Under the influence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he brought himself to be enjoyed at will by sentient beings—like a great medicinal tree common to earth, water, fire, and wind—in various places of rebirth; thus, over a vast period of time, he attained the state of omniscience that discerns all aspects.

Because the Blessed One has thus attained the knowledge of omniscience and has understood the reality of phenomena exactly as they are established, without exception, he is called the *Tathāgata* due to his Buddhahood.
If there were no continuity of existence, then even a Tathāgata would not exist;
for it is not possible to attain the state of a Tathāgata in a single lifetime alone.
Therefore, the continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati) truly exists,
because of the actual existence of the Tathāgata. To this it is said:

Indeed, this very great ignorance of yours alone leads to the uninterrupted continuity and extreme longevity of the stream of existence; for even though the blinding darkness of your immense wealth of ignorance is being shattered by the various autumnal moonlights of reasoned knowledge, it is not yet destroyed nor does it cease, having increased through the expansion of habitual tendencies cultivated over an exceedingly long period of time.
For if there were such a thing as a Tathāgata by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then there would be a continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati) due to his manifestation over a long period of time;
yet no such thing as a Tathāgata is perceived by way of the intrinsic nature of an entity.

However, it is solely because your mental eye is impaired by the cataracts of ignorance that you perceive a so-called "Tathāgata" as something false by way of intrinsic nature— like a double moon, a hair, or a fly.
Demonstrating how the Tathāgata does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, he says:
The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them.
The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates; who, then, is the Tathāgata? // 1 //
For if there were some entity called a "Tathāgata" that was stainless and free from conceptual proliferation,
he would have to possess either the nature of the aggregates, or the nature of the five aggregates known as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Alternatively, it would either have as its intrinsic nature the five aggregates known as ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation,
or it would be distinct from them. In this investigation, only the former five aggregates are included because they are the basis for the designation of a "sentient being," and not the latter ones.
Because these [categories] are not all-encompassing, they have already been subsumed by the earlier ones.
Or if he were distinct from the five aggregates, then either the aggregates would exist in the Tathāgata, or he would exist in the aggregates.
Would the Tathāgata possess aggregates, like Devadatta possesses wealth?
When examined in every way, such a thing is not possible. How so?
In that regard, first of all, the aggregates themselves are not the Tathāgata.
What is the reason? For it has been said:
"If the fuel were the fire, there would be identity between the agent and the object."
The phrase "it would be" (bhavet) should be applied here as well:
"He is a Buddha who [sees] that the identity of the agent and the object is grasping. Thus:
It has been stated: "If the self were the aggregates, it would be subject to arising and passing away. This should also be applied here:
"If the Buddha were the aggregates, he would be subject to arising and passing away."
Thus, first of all, the aggregates are not the Tathāgata.
Now, it is not the case that the Tathāgata is other than the aggregates.
What is the reason? For it has been said:
"If fire were other than fuel, it would exist even without fuel."
Likewise:
"Because it does not depend on anything else, it would have no cause for its ignition;
furthermore, a renewed beginning would be useless, and thus it would be actionless while existing. Thus [it is said].
The same should be applied here as well:
if the Buddha were other than the appropriation, he would exist without appropriation;
likewise—

Because it is independent of anything else, it would have no cause consisting of appropriation; likewise, if it already exists, its renewed commencement would be purposeless, and it would be devoid of action.
Likewise:

"If he were other than the aggregates, he would possess the characteristics of non-aggregates. And because there is no otherness between the aggregates and so forth and the Tathāgata, [the Tathāgata does not exist as other].
The aggregates do not arise in the Tathāgata.
Nor is it tenable that the Tathāgata exists within the aggregates.

And this explanation of the two positions was stated in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*: "Because here [it is shown that] the self does not exist within the aggregates, nor do these aggregates exist within the self."
This conceptualization would indeed exist if there were a difference in reality; however, since that difference does not exist, this is merely a conceptual construction.
That the Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates is stated in that very same [text]:
"The self is not accepted as possessing form, because there is no self; for the application of the meaning of 'possessing' does not apply here."
In the case of difference, there would be "one possessing form" (rūpavān) like a cow; in the case of non-difference, neither identity nor otherness exists for the Self by virtue of its formlessness.
In reality, however, all five positions are actually included within the two positions of identity and difference.

It should be understood that the Teacher has described these five positions with reference to the activity of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). And thus, when examined in these five ways regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the Tathāgata does not exist.

"By what other self could he exist?"—in every way, the existence of a Tathāgata is simply impossible. Thus, not perceiving a nature of being (*bhāvasvabhāva*), the Master [Nāgārjuna] said: "Which Tathāgata is there here?
The intended meaning is that there is no such thing whatsoever whose nature of being consists in the discernment of all things within the three worlds.
And because the Tathāgata does not exist, it is established that the continuity of existence is also not a substantial continuity. // 1 //
On this point, some say: "We do not indeed assert that the Tathāgata is the aggregates, because that would entail the faults already mentioned;
nor do we assert that he is distinct from the aggregates."
Nor do we describe the Tathāgata as the untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandhas),
like a grove of trees on Mount Himavat;
nor do we [describe them] as being within the aggregates.
It is a lion in the very thicket of trees; nor do we describe it as having shoulders like a universal monarch endowed with the marks of excellence.
Precisely because we do not accept identity or difference;
rather, we establish the Tathāgata as inexpressible in terms of identity, difference, and so forth, by depending upon the stainless aggregates (*skandha*).
Therefore, this rule does not invalidate our position. To this, it is said:
If the Buddha, depending upon the aggregates, does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, how could he who does not exist by way of intrinsic nature exist by way of extrinsic nature? (2)
For if the Buddha, the Blessed One, is designated by depending upon the stainless aggregates as being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference,
then it clearly follows that he does not exist by way of intrinsic nature,
because he is designated by depending [upon those aggregates] like a reflected image.

And how can that which does not exist now by way of its own nature—that is, by way of its own essence—come to exist by way of another nature (*parabhāva*) based upon the aggregates, since it is non-existent by way of its own nature?
For it is not logical that the son of a barren woman, being non-existent, should come to be in dependence upon another nature. // 2 //

Now, it might be argued: "Just as a reflection, although non-existent by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), comes into being in dependence upon other entities such as a face or a mirror, so too the Tathāgata, though non-existent by way of his own nature, will exist by way of other entities (*parabhāva*) in dependence upon the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). Even so:
"That which exists in dependence upon other entities is established as being without self (*anātman*)."
And how can that which is non-self be the Tathāgata? // 3 //
If the Tathāgata is asserted to exist in dependence upon another entity, like a reflection, then it follows that this Tathāgata is likewise without self (*anātman*), just like a reflection;
it is not tenable [to say] that he exists by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This word "ātman" is a synonym for the word "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature).
And that which is non-self and devoid of intrinsic nature, being exactly like a reflection—
how could that be the Tathāgata by way of having the form of intrinsic nature?
The intention is that he will not proceed upon a path that is free from error. // 3 //
Furthermore, if the Tathāgata were to possess some intrinsic nature (svabhāva) here,
then, in relation to that intrinsic nature, the intrinsic nature of the aggregates would be an extrinsic nature (parabhāva); and depending upon that extrinsic nature, the Tathāgata would exist.
But when the Tathāgata has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) at all, how then could there be the otherness (paratva) of the aggregates? Demonstrating this, he says:
"If intrinsic nature does not exist, how could extrinsic nature (parabhāva) exist?"
And when intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature do not exist in this way, then, apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, who is that Tathāgata? // 4 //
For an entity, in existing, must be either its own nature (svabhāva) or the nature of another (parabhāva);
apart from these two, what other entity could there be?
Who is it that is established as the "Tathāgata"?
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not exist by way of intrinsic nature. // 4 //
Furthermore:
If some Tathāgata were to exist without depending upon the aggregates, he would now have to depend upon them; therefore, he would exist by means of dependence. (5)
If you think that the Tathāgata is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from the aggregates, and that he is designated in dependence upon the aggregates—
when would that be logical?
It would be logical if there were some entity called "Tathāgata" existing prior to and independently of the aggregates, without having grasped them.
He would have to take up the aggregates;

for just as Devadatta, who is already established as distinct from his wealth, takes up that wealth, so too, if there were some Tathāgata who existed without having taken up these aggregates, [that would be the case].
He would now have to take up the aggregates, and by taking up those aggregates, he would then come into existence. (5)
But when investigated in every way, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever who does not depend upon the aggregates,
because that would entail the consequence of being causeless.
And how can that which does not exist without grasping be grasped? // 6 //
The intention is that [the Tathāgata] does not exist [as a substantial entity].
And when, in this way, he does not grasp anything at all, then it is not tenable that there will be one called a "Tathāgata" by depending upon the aggregates (skandhas). // 6 //

And when the Tathāgata thus does not grasp anything because he does not exist prior to grasping, then it is established that even that grasping cannot possibly function as "grasping" since it is not being grasped by anyone; demonstrating this, he says:
"There is no such thing as a grasping that is not itself grasped."

And when, in this way, appropriation is not an appropriation because it is not appropriated by anyone, then, demonstrating that there is likewise no appropriator due to the absence of appropriation, he says: "And there is no Tathāgata whatsoever who is without appropriation. (7)
Thus [ends the seventh].
Thus, according to the reasoning established above:
"He who does not exist as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], and who cannot be found in five ways—how could that Tathāgata be designated by means of appropriation? (8)

For when the Tathāgata is investigated and sought in reality, he does not exist as identical with the aggregates, nor does he exist as different from the aggregates—that is, as separate from them; thus, because he is non-existent as either identical or different, he is not found when sought through the five modes of analysis: as the locus, the located, the possessor of those qualities, or the relationship between them.
How can that which does not exist—the Tathāgata who is absolutely non-existent—be designated by means of appropriation?
For this reason as well, there is no such thing as a "Tathāgata" by way of intrinsic nature. (8)
Not only does the Tathāgata not exist by virtue of this analysis,
but even this appropriation (*upādāna*) does not exist because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, this appropriation consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) known as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
That too does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, because it is dependently originated and because it has been refuted in detail in the "Examination of the Aggregates."

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though there is no appropriation by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nevertheless it will arise from an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) consisting of causes and conditions.
To demonstrate that even this is not tenable, he says:
And that which does not exist by way of its own-being, how could it exist by way of another-being? // 9 //
For indeed, the son of a barren woman, being non-existent by his own nature, cannot be designated through the existence of another;
therefore, even the appropriation does not exist.
Alternatively:

even this appropriation does not exist by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*), because it is dependent upon an appropriator, and because that which is independent of an appropriator lacks the status of being an appropriation; thus, there is no appropriation established by way of its own-being.

Now, even if it is granted that appropriation cannot exist as established by way of its own nature independently of an appropriator, let it then exist only in dependence upon such an appropriator. To this it is said: even so—
And that which does not exist by way of its own nature—how could it exist by way of another nature?
Since that appropriation which exists by way of intrinsic nature is not established, how could that which lacks an intrinsic nature come to exist for the appropriator by way of extrinsic nature?
Therefore, appropriation also does not exist. // 9 //
Now, demonstrating the very point as it has been established, he says:
"In this way, appropriation and the appropriator are empty in every respect.
When examined in every manner, appropriation is empty, being devoid of intrinsic nature.
The appropriator is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;
by means of that appropriation, which is itself empty, how can the Tathāgata—who is likewise empty—be designated? (10)
It is simply not possible that there could be a designation of a non-existent Tathāgata by means of something non-existent;
therefore, it is not tenable to say that the Tathāgata is designated in dependence upon the aggregates.

Regarding this, they say: "Alas! Our hope is utterly destroyed, for we have indeed [placed our trust] in those such as Kaṇabhakṣa, Akṣapāda, Digambara, Jaimini, and the Naiyāyikas—who are bound by the creeping-vine lattice of their own conceptual constructions and extremely harsh, base views; who have strayed from the path leading to the city of Nirvāṇa that is free from error; and who have not transcended the difficult wilderness of the forest of saṃsāra."

Having abandoned all longing for the founders of other sects— who pride themselves on teaching a path to heaven and liberation that is not free from error— he [the Buddha] is intent upon awakening the buds of the minds of various disciples, his rays of extremely sharp light of the teaching of the True Dharma pervading the faces of all directions, dispelling the darkness of the doctrines of all other non-Buddhist teachers without exception, and illuminating the unerring path that leads to heaven and liberation.

He is the stainless, singular eye for those who are vessels for the true meaning of the reality of things as they truly abide; he is the unique refuge for the entire world, possessing the stainless mandala of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he is the supreme charioteer of the Great Vehicle, the great path, whose chariot is yoked to the high-stepping horses of the seven factors of enlightenment and the foot-soldiers of the [eightfold] path; he is intent upon drying up the rivers of the wilderness of saṃsāra—characterized by birth, old age, and death—for all beings in the three worlds; and he is the victor in battle against the enemy Māra, having triumphed over the discharge of arrows from the four equal adversaries.

Those seeking liberation and desiring unsurpassed perfect enlightenment have taken refuge in the Tathāgata-Sun, who dispels the violent onset of the eclipse-grasper Rāhu— the false grasping of the entire world— and who eliminates the dense darkness of the thicket of ignorance;
and of him, by you—
Thus, grasping and the grasper are entirely empty;
how can a Tathāgata, who is himself empty, be designated by means of that which is empty?

By asserting through these and other statements that [things] lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), you have destroyed our hope for liberation—that is, our aspiration for the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, enough of you, who act like a great sun eclipsed by clouds, scattering a transient shower of wealth and grain, and who are like darkness to the world!
To this, it is said:

Our hope has been destroyed by such ignorant people as you, who, having indeed abandoned the doctrines of other sectarians out of a desire for liberation and having approached the Blessed Tathāgata— the unerring, supreme teacher— yet cannot endure the lion’s roar of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is most profound, unsurpassed, and not shared with the teachings of any other sectarians.

Like deer, due to their poverty of self-resolute confidence (*svādhimukti*), they enter that very path which follows the prison of the vast and most terrible wilderness of saṃsāra— a path crowded with the rows of serpents of various wrong views and pursued by people who are inverted.
For the Tathāgatas never at any time designate the existence of a self or of the aggregates (*skandha*).
As it is said in the Bhagavatī:
"Venerable Subhūti, even a Buddha is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the qualities of a Buddha, Venerable Subhūti, are like illusions, like dreams."
Likewise:
"The nature of phenomena is empty and secluded; the nature of awakening is empty and secluded.
Indeed, he who practices in this way has a nature that is empty, for one possessed of wisdom, but not for the foolish person. Thus it is said.
Nor do we assert that the Tathāgatas, who are entirely free from conceptual proliferation, are non-existent, such that we would incur the fault of deprecating them. // 10 //
Furthermore, a practitioner who, being intent on expressing the non-erroneous meaning, explains that the Tathāgata is indeed without intrinsic nature,
should not state in any way that he is "empty," nor that he is "non-empty," nor both, nor neither.
All of this should not be spoken by us; however,

since a cognizer is unable to comprehend the nature of things as they truly exist when it is not explained, we too, for the sake of conventional usage and in accordance with those to be trained, remain within the truth of worldly convention (*vyavahārasatya*) by means of superimposition.
We say it is empty, we say it is not empty, and we say it is both empty and not empty.
We say that it is neither empty nor non-empty; for this very reason, it is said: "But it is spoken of for the sake of conventional designation. (11)
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"All phenomena are empty by virtue of their lack of intrinsic nature;
all phenomena are signless by virtue of their signlessness."
All phenomena are wishless through the application of wishlessness;
all phenomena are naturally luminous through the purity of the perfection of wisdom. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere, it is stated that it is not empty:
"Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not take delight in past form.
But since, monks, past form does exist..."
"Therefore, the learned noble disciple does not delight in past form," and so on, "O monks, if there were no future [form]," etc.;
likewise, up to: "O monks, if there were no past consciousness," etc., as before.
Likewise, according to the Sautrāntika school, the past and the future are empty, while other things are non-empty;
and the non-associated representation (viprayukta-vijñapti) is empty.

Even in the Vijñānavāda, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty because it is not dependently originated (*apratītyasamutpanna*), like the vision of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia.
"Therefore, everything is described as neither empty nor non-empty;
because of its existence and its non-existence, that is the Middle Way."
The intention by which emptiness and so forth are taught should be understood from the "Examination of the Self" (*Ātmaparīkṣā*),
as it is said in the Sūtra:
You have shown that this world is like an illusion, resembling a theatrical stage or a dream;
there is no self, no sentient being, and no course of a living soul—phenomena are like a mirage or the moon reflected in water.
The world, not understanding that which is empty, peaceful, trackless, and unconditioned, wanders in delusion;
out of your compassion, you lead them across by means of hundreds of skillful methods, reasonings, and logical arguments.
Beholding the entire world terrified by hundreds of manifold diseases such as passion and the like,
you wander peerlessly like a physician, O Sugata, liberating hundreds of beings.
"The entire world revolves like a chariot wheel, having gone among animals, hungry ghosts, and in the hells;
deluded, without a guide, and fallen into helplessness—for them you reveal the supreme path.
Thus, all these conceptual constructions do not exist within the Tathāgata, who is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). 11.
Not only do the fourfold [attributes] such as emptiness and so forth not exist in the Tathāgata, but furthermore:

How could the fourfold [attributes] beginning with eternal and non-eternal exist in the peaceful one? And how could the fourfold [attributes] beginning with finite and infinite exist here in the peaceful one? (12)
In this regard, fourteen indeterminate points were taught by the Blessed One,
namely: "The world is eternal," and "The world is non-eternal."
"The world is both eternal and non-eternal," and "the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal"—
this is the tetrad.
The world is finite,
the world is infinite,
and the world is both finite and infinite.
"The world is neither finite nor infinite"— this is the second [view].
"The Tathāgata exists after death," [this is the third].
The Tathāgata does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
Thus is the third [view]:
"The soul is that body," or "the soul is one thing and the body another."
These fourteen points are called "unexpounded points" because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

In that regard, according to the principle already described, just as the fourfold set beginning with emptiness does not exist in the Tathāgata— who is by nature peaceful and devoid of intrinsic nature—
likewise, the fourfold set beginning with permanence and impermanence also does not exist here.

And precisely because of their impossibility, the Blessed One did not provide a categorical explanation for these four points regarding the world, just as he did not explain the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman.
Just as this tetrad does not apply to the Tathāgata, so too the [views of] finitude, infinity, and so forth, do not apply to the peaceful Tathāgata. // 12 //
Now, demonstrating that even the fourfold conceptualization beginning with "the Tathāgata exists after death" cannot possibly arise, he says:

"One who has grasped the dense apprehension that 'the Tathāgata exists,' while conceptually constructing 'he does not exist,' would likewise conceptualize [him] even when he has entered parinirvāṇa. (13)
For whoever has grasped a denser notion that "the Tathāgata exists" through great dogmatic adherence,
and has generated such a conceptual construction,
will certainly [be affected] when the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata does not exist after death;
after the time of death, he does not exist;
the Tathāgata is annihilated.
One should not conceptualize that "it does not exist. For one who conceptualizes in this way, there would be a dogmatic view (dṛṣṭikṛta). // 13 //
But for one who holds that, because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatva*), there is neither existence nor non-existence of the Tathāgata in any state whatsoever— in his position,
such a reflection is simply not tenable regarding that which is empty of intrinsic nature.
Or whether the Buddha exists after cessation, or does not exist. // 14 //
The intention is that this conceptual construction does not exist, just like the conceptualization of variegated forms in space. // 14 //

Thus, regarding the Tathāgata—who is by nature quiescent, devoid of intrinsic nature, and transcendent of all conceptual proliferation—those who, due to their dull intellect, proliferate him through such categories as eternal and non-eternal, permanent and impermanent, existent and non-existent, empty and non-empty, omniscient and non-omniscient, and so forth; they, being destroyed by conceptual proliferation, do not see the Tathāgata, who is beyond proliferation and undecaying. (15)
For conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) would be based on a real entity (*vastu*), yet the Tathāgata is without a real entity;
how, then, could there be the possibility for the occurrence of conceptual proliferations?
Therefore, the Tathāgata transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Because his nature is non-arising and because he does not undergo any change into another nature, he is imperishable.

Those who, with minds defiled by the impurities of their own imagined false conceptualizations, proliferate the Blessed Buddha—the Tathāgata of such a kind—by means of various unreal and particular conceptual constructions, [do so falsely].
Being destroyed by their own conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), they remain utterly remote from the abundance of the Tathāgata’s qualities.
Consequently, being like corpses, they do not see the Tathāgata within this teaching, just as those born blind do not see the sun.
For this very reason, the Blessed One said:
Those who saw me by my form, and those who followed me by my voice—
those people, being intent on false exertion, shall not see me.
The Buddhas are to be seen through the Dharma, for the Leaders are the Dharma-body;
yet the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unknowable—it cannot be fully comprehended.
Thus [ends verse] 15.
Thus, in this examination of the Tathāgata, the entire realm of sentient beings— including gods, asuras, humans, and so forth— has been examined.
And just as this realm of sentient beings is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*),
so too, demonstrating the lack of intrinsic nature of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*)— from the circle of wind up to the celestial palaces of the Akaniṣṭha heaven— he says:
Whatever is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata, that is the intrinsic nature of this world.
"This world" means the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*).
To the question, "What, then, is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata? he says:
The Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature; this world is without intrinsic nature. (16)
Thus it is said. And just as the world lacks intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), so it has been demonstrated through the examination of conditions (*pratyayaparīkṣā*) and other means.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtra:
The Tathāgata is eternally free from the nature of grasping, and all phenomena are similar to the Sugata;
yet those of childish intellect, through the grasping of signs, wander in this world amidst non-existent phenomena.
"For the Tathāgata is a reflection of wholesome, untainted phenomena;
herein there is neither suchness nor a Tathāgata, yet an image appears to the whole world.
And it is said in the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*:
Then those sons of the gods said this to the Venerable Subhūti the Elder: "Venerable Subhūti, are those beings like an illusion, or are they not an illusion?
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, those beings are like an illusion; sons of the gods, those beings are like a dream."
For thus, illusion and sentient beings are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity. For thus, dreams and sentient beings are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
O sons of the gods, all phenomena, moreover, are like illusions and like dreams.
Even the stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the fruit of stream-entry is like an illusion, like a dream. Likewise, even the once-returner and the fruit of once-returning are like an illusion, like a dream.
The non-returner is like an illusion, like a dream; the fruit of non-returning is also like an illusion, like a dream. The arhat is like an illusion, like a dream;
the fruit of arhatship is also like an illusion, like a dream.
Even a pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the state of a pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a dream;
even a perfectly awakened buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha) is like an illusion, like a dream.
I say that even perfect enlightenment is like an illusion and like a dream.

Then the sons of the gods said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, do you say that even a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha) is like an illusion and like a dream, and that even the state of perfect awakening (samyaksaṃbuddhatva) is like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti replied: "Sons of the gods, I say that even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream."
"What, then, is this other dharma?
The sons of the gods said, "Noble Subhūti, do you say that even *nirvāṇa* is like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti replied, "Sons of the gods, even if there were some other dharma more distinguished than *nirvāṇa*..."
I would say that even this is like an illusion and like a dream;
for indeed, illusion and nirvāṇa are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Examination of the Tathāgata," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Perversion, the twenty-third chapter.
Here it is said: The continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati) certainly exists, because its cause exists.
For in this world, karma proceeds from the afflictions (kleśa);
and with karma and the afflictions as its cause, the succession of birth and death arises. That is designated as the continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati).
And the primary cause of that [rebirth] is the afflictions (kleśas),
because for those whose afflictions have been abandoned, there is no continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati).
And those afflictions, such as attachment (rāga) and so forth, do exist.
Therefore, even though it is an effect, the succession of birth and death will continue as a stream of existence through an uninterrupted continuity.
To this it is said:
there may indeed be a stream of existence.
If those afflictions were to exist as its causes, they do not, however. How so?

In this regard, the Blessed Buddhas—who have destroyed the enemies that are the afflictions of all beings in the three worlds and have achieved victory in battle over the adversary of the four Māras—have declared: "Passion, hatred, and delusion arise from conceptual construction;
for they indeed come into being dependent upon the beautiful, the ugly, and cognitive errors. (1)
Volition is discursive thought;
because it originates from volition, it is "born of volition.
O Desire, I know your root: you are indeed born from volition.
I shall no longer form a conceptualization of you; therefore, you shall not exist for me.
Thus, from the statement of this verse, it is said that passion, hatred, and delusion originate from conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*);
because they are the root of all other afflictions (*kleśa*) and are the most prominent, only these three are mentioned.
And these three afflictions arise depending upon the errors regarding the beautiful and the ugly;
for therein, passion arises depending upon the aspect of the beautiful.
Aversion arises dependent on the unwholesome,
and delusion arises dependent on the perversions;
however, volitional construction is the common cause for the arising of all three.
But how is it that delusion arises from conceptual construction? It is said:
for it was stated by the Blessed One in the context of dependent origination: "Monks, ignorance, too, has a cause, has a condition, and has a source."
And what, monks, is the cause of ignorance?
Improper mental attention, monks, is the cause of ignorance;
turbid mental attention born of delusion, monks, is the cause of ignorance.
Therefore, ignorance arises from conceptual construction. // 1 //
And therefore:
Those afflictions which arise in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the distortions do not exist by way of intrinsic nature; therefore, the afflictions do not exist in reality. //2//
Thus, if passion and the other afflictions were established by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
they could not possibly arise in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*);
for intrinsic nature is uncreated and independent of anything else.
And since they arise in dependence upon the errors of the beautiful and the ugly,
they are therefore indeed devoid of intrinsic nature;
they do not exist in reality.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature. // 2 //
Moreover:
Since the existence or non-existence of the self is not established in any way whatsoever, how could the existence or non-existence of the afflictions be established without it? (3)
Just as existence and non-existence do not apply to the self, so it has been explained in detail.
And therefore—from that [self], how could there be existence and non-existence for the dharma that depends upon it? // 3 //

Now, it might be argued: "If existence and non-existence do not belong to the self, then what does this have to do with the afflictions (*kleśas*), such that they too lack existence and non-existence? It is said in reply:
For these afflictions belong to someone, yet that "someone" is not established; or rather, do the afflictions exist for no one at all, without anyone? (4)
In this world, these factors such as attachment and so forth depend upon a basis for their arising, just as a painting depends upon a wall or ripeness depends upon a fruit;
therefore, these belong to someone, and they do not exist without some basis.
Furthermore, that basis, when being postulated, must be either the self or the mind;
yet such a basis does not exist, as it has already been refuted.
And in the absence of any such basis, to whom would the afflictions belong?
They do not belong to anyone at all because that person does not exist; or rather, do the afflictions exist without anyone to whom they belong? (4)
To this, it is said: Indeed, no pre-established basis for the afflictions is admitted;
nor does there exist anything called a "self" (ātman) that could be established as their basis.
Because it is without cause, like a mango tree in the sky;
rather, the afflictions arise dependent upon a defiled mind,
and that mind arises simultaneously with those afflictions.
This also is not tenable; thus he says:
Just as in the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the afflictions do not exist in the afflicted in five ways;
just as in the view of a self-body, the afflicted also does not exist in the afflictions in five ways. (5)
One's own body (*svakāya*) is indeed a collection characterized by form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
The view of one's own body (*svakāyadṛṣṭi*) is the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) regarding one's own body, which functions by grasping at the aspect of "mine" (*ātmīyākāra*).
Just as this [view], when analyzed in five ways, is not found to exist within one's own body, so it is.
The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them.
The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates; who, then, is the Tathāgata here?
By this [argument], even when the afflictions (*kleśa*) are examined within that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), they do not exist in five ways.
In this context, "afflictions" are so called because they afflict, and "the afflicted" is that which is afflicted.
It is not tenable that what is afflicted is itself the afflictions, because that would entail the absurd consequence of identity between the burner and the fuel.
It is not tenable that the afflicted state is one thing and the afflictions are another,
because [the latter] are independent of anything else.
Because it would follow that there would be afflictions caused by non-afflicted factors;

and for this very reason, due to the absence of identity or difference, as well as the absence of the positions regarding the locus and the located or their possessor, there is no afflicted state within the afflictions,
nor are there afflictions within the afflicted state.
Nor is it defiled like the afflictions themselves.
Thus, when examined in these five ways, afflictions do not exist within that which is defiled.
And just as afflictions caused by a defiled source do not exist, [so too do they not exist otherwise].
In this way, when that which is afflicted— having afflictions as its cause— is examined in relation to the afflictions themselves, it cannot exist in five ways.
For the afflictions themselves are not the afflicted,
because that would entail the absurd consequence of the agent and the object being one and the same.
The afflictions are not one thing and the afflicted another,
for that would entail the consequence of their being independent;
nor do the afflictions exist in the afflicted, nor does the afflicted exist in the afflictions.
Defilements do not possess defilement;
thus, just as in the case of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), defilement does not exist in the five ways even within the defilements themselves.
And since this is so:
Therefore, even in terms of mutual dependence, there is no establishment of either the afflicted or the non-afflicted. // 5 //

Here it is said: Even though you have refuted the afflictions (*kleśa*), nevertheless their causes—the beautiful, the ugly, and the cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*)—still exist; and because these exist, the afflictions also exist.
It is said:
the afflictions would exist if there were only the distortions of the beautiful and the ugly.
To the extent that these also arise dependently, they are subject to the refutation to be stated hereafter;
and when they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then the errors regarding the pure and the impure do not exist by way of intrinsic nature.
Because they are dependently originated and because of the refutations to be stated later,
when those [afflictions] do not exist by way of intrinsic nature, then— depending upon what [objects] would the afflictions arise from the beautiful, the ugly, and the perverted? (6)
The intention is that afflictions do not exist at all, because of the absence of their causes: the inversion regarding the beautiful and the ugly. // 6 //
Here it is said: the afflictions (kleśas) certainly do exist, because their objective supports (ālambana) exist;
for in this world, that which does not exist—
It has no object of perception,
just like the son of a barren woman;
yet there exists a sixfold object of perception, namely those called visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Therefore, because their objective supports exist, the afflictions certainly do exist.
To this it is replied: This is true, as you have stated—
Visible forms, sounds, tastes, tangibles, odors, and mental phenomena—these sixfold objects are conceptualized as the basis for attachment, aversion, and delusion. (7)
In this context, "thing" (vastu) refers to the objective support (ālambana); or rather, it is so called because passion and the like abide within it, since they arise from it.
And that object of focus is sixfold, due to the mutual distinction among the six sense faculties which perform the function of delimiting [their respective objects]:
namely, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
In this context, it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is defined as "this is here" or "that is there," and because it possesses the quality of being formed (*rūpaṇā*).
It is called "sound" (*śabda*) because by means of that sound, objects are made known (*śabdyante*) or manifested.
They are called "odors" (*gandha*) because when encountered, they are smelled (*gandhyante*) and harmed (*hiṃsyante*), since they do not come from anywhere else.
It is called "taste" (*rasa*) because it is tasted (*rasyate*) or relished (*āsvādyate*). It is called "tangibility" (*sparśa*) because it is touched (*spṛśyate*).
They are called "dharmas" because they possess their own specific characteristics and because they support the supreme dharma of nirvāṇa.
These constitute six kinds of objects;
for what [do they serve]? For passion, hatred, and delusion.
In this context, *rañjana* (coloring) is passion (*rāga*), attachment (*rakti*), and fixation (*adhyavasāna*).
Or, it is called passion because by means of it the mind is colored;
corruption (*dūṣaṇa*) is hatred (*doṣa*).

*Āghāta* (malice) has as its object either sentient beings or non-sentient things; it is called *doṣa* (fault) because by means of it the mind is corrupted. *Moha* (delusion) is confusion or utter bewilderment, which is the lack of thorough knowledge regarding the true nature of things;
it is called *moha* because by means of it the mind is deluded.
Thus, for these afflictions, the sixfold object consisting of form and so forth serves as the objective support (*ālambana*).
In that regard, through the superimposition of a pure aspect, attachment arises toward form and the rest;
through the superimposition of an impure aspect, hatred [arises].
Delusion arises through the superimposition of such things as an eternal self. // 7 //

"This sixfold object is conceptualized as real by foolish people; however, it is merely that which lacks an existing intrinsic nature, yet is imagined by you to be the objective support for passion and the like—just as those with cataracts imagine non-existent hair, mosquitoes, flies, or a double moon. Demonstrating this, he says:
"Form, sound, taste, touch, smell, and mental objects alone [are thus imagined]."
"Kevalāḥ" (mere) means they are merely imagined; that is to say, they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
If they are devoid of intrinsic nature, how then are they perceived? It is said in reply:
They have the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and are like a mirage or a dream. // 8 //
Thus, these are perceived. // 8 //

Just as these things are like a city of the Gandharvas and so forth, perceived solely due to cognitive distortion, then— how could there be anything impure or pure in them, when they are like illusory persons and equal to reflections? (9)
Therefore, because they arise from a false basis, even the signs of the beautiful and the ugly are nothing but false. As it has been said:
"The aggregates arise from the ego-conception; that ego-conception is unreal in reality. For that whose seed is unreal, how can its sprout be real?"
Having seen the aggregates as unreal in this way, egoism is abandoned;
and through the abandonment of egoism, there is no further arising of the aggregates.
Thus [ends the ninth].
And it is not only because of the falsity of their basis that the signs of the beautiful and the ugly are false;
rather, demonstrating that these two are false by this reasoning as well, he says:
"Without depending on the beautiful, there is no ugly that we could designate."
Since that which is dependent upon the auspicious does not arise from the auspicious, the auspicious itself is therefore not established. // 10 //
In this case, if there were such a thing as "the auspicious," it would necessarily exist in dependence upon "the inauspicious," like the near and far shores.
It is like the seed and the sprout,
or like the short and the long,
because the auspicious depends upon other related entities.
Moreover, that which is to be depended upon—the unwholesome—does not exist without the wholesome.
The intention is that there is no unwholesome independent of the wholesome;
it is in dependence upon the unwholesome, having regard for the unwholesome, that we designate and establish what is wholesome.
By the word "which" (yat), there is a reference to the immediately preceding "impure" (aśubha);
by the phrase "we would designate" (prajñapayema), there is a connection to the subsequent "pure" (śubha).
And since, in this way, for the designation of the pure, no other related entity called "impure" need be required, [the pure is established independently].
Therefore, purity is not at all possible, just as "long" is impossible without "short," or as "this shore" is impossible without "the other shore"—this is the intended meaning. // 10 //
Now, demonstrating how even the impure does not exist, he says:
"Without depending on the impure, we do not designate the pure."
Since the impure exists dependently, therefore the impure does not exist at all. // 11 //
For if there were such a thing as the "impure," it would necessarily exist in dependence upon the "pure," like this shore and the far shore.
Or it is like "short" and "long," because the impure depends upon another related term;
and that which is to be depended upon— the pure— does not exist without the impure.
Without depending on the impure, the pure does not exist;
the intention is that without depending on the impure, the pure cannot come to be. It is by depending upon the pure, by relying upon the pure, that we designate the impure.
We shall establish the unwholesome;
here too, by the word "yat," there is a reference to the immediately preceding wholesome [state].
And by the phrase "we would designate," there is a connection to the subsequent [verse concerning] the impure.

Since, in this way, for the designation of the impure, another related thing called "pure" must be depended upon, yet no such distinct entity exists, therefore the impure does not exist at all. // 11 //
And since, in this way, there is no possibility of either the pleasant or the unpleasant, therefore:
When the pleasant does not exist, from where will attachment arise?
And when the unpleasant does not exist, from where will aversion arise? (12)

The intended meaning is that since attachment and aversion have the perception of the beautiful and the ugly as their cause, in the absence of such perceptions, they lack a cause and therefore cannot arise. // 12 //

Thus, having established the absence of passion and hatred through the non-existence of the signs of the beautiful and the ugly, he now states—demonstrating the absence of intrinsic nature in delusion as well by showing the absence of an intrinsic nature in the distorted views:
"If the grasping at the permanent in the impermanent is a distortion, Since nothing impermanent exists in emptiness, how can there be a grasp or a distortion? (13)
In this context, four inversions are taught.
Namely: the apprehension of the five aggregates—which are impermanent and subject to destruction at every moment—as being permanent, is an inversion. Likewise—
For that which is impermanent, suffering is certain; whatever is accompanied by suffering is not happiness.
Therefore, it arises that everything which is impermanent is suffering.
By this principle, that which is impermanent is suffering,
and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
therefore, regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), which are of the nature of suffering, the contrary grasping that they are "pleasure" [is to be abandoned].
This is another perversion: thus,
knowing that the seed is the union of semen and blood, nourished by feces and urine, and consisting of impure matter, why do you feel passion for it out of desire?
"He who would lie upon a heap of impurities covered by a skin moistened by their moisture—
he would lie within the lap of women," and so forth.
Thus, this body is by its very nature perpetually and entirely impure.
In this regard, that grasping and adherence which, out of delusion, perceives [the aggregates] as pure is a perversion (*viparyāsa*).

Likewise, the five aggregates are devoid of self (*nirātman*) because they are characterized by instability and the nature of arising and passing away, and thus they are empty of the intrinsic nature of a self (*ātmasvabhāva-śūnya*), being contrary to the characteristics of a self.
In that regard, whatever grasping at a self and attachment to what is not-self as being a self is a perversion;
these are the four perversions that serve as the cause of delusion.

Now, this is being investigated: if permanence and the perception of permanence are established as misconceptions regarding things that are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then indeed, since even impermanence does not exist in the aggregates (*skandha*) that are empty of intrinsic nature, impermanence is not found in the empty; how then can there be a grasping [at it] or a misconception?
For impermanence is established as a perversion only in relation to its opposite, permanence;
yet impermanence does not exist in the empty.
When there is an absence of impermanence, [how can permanence be established?]
The point is this: how then could there be its opposite, permanence, which is the inversion of constant perception?
Therefore, there is no inversion.
And just as impermanence is not possible in the empty—that which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of entities and is unarisen by way of intrinsic nature—[so too is permanence impossible].
In this way, even suffering is not possible; impurity does not exist;
and selflessness also does not exist.

And when suffering and so forth do not exist because they are empty of intrinsic nature, then how could their opposites— the distortions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self— come to be? Therefore, the distortions do exist by way of their own essential nature.
In the absence of that, how will ignorance arise?
Due to the absence of its cause.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
Ignorance never exists at all, nor does the arising of its causal conditions exist.
Since this ignorance does not exist in the world, it is for this reason that I have called it "ignorance."
Likewise:
"Blessed One, how is delusion a *dhāraṇī*-phrase?
The Blessed One replied: "Mañjuśrī, delusion is indeed utterly liberated."
Therefore, by means of such statements as "it is called delusion," and so forth, it is established as a cognitive distortion (*viparyaya*). // 13 //

Now, [the opponent] objects: "If this is so, then since a thing does not exist by way of its own-being (svabhāva), even the apprehension that it is 'impermanent' is impossible; why then is this too not established as a misconception (viparyāsa)? Demonstrating this, he says: "If the apprehension of the permanent in the impermanent is a misconception, why is the apprehension of even 'impermanence' not a misconception in the case of the empty? (14)
And when both the permanent and the impermanent are subject to error,
then there exists no other third thing apart from them that would not be erroneous. And when there is no absence of error, [how can there be liberation?]
In that case, with respect to what would there be error?
Therefore, by this reasoning as well, error does not exist;
and because of its absence, ignorance does not exist in terms of its own nature.
And just as the misconception that takes what is impermanent to be permanent is impossible, so too should it be applied to the impossibility of the remaining misconceptions.
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryadṛḍhāśayaparipṛcchā*:
The Blessed One said: "What does it mean, noble son, for one who seeks deliverance by means of the path?

Noble son, it is not that the Tathāgata has designated the abandonment of passion by avoiding things that provoke passion; likewise, it is not that the Tathāgata has designated the abandonment of hatred and delusion by avoiding things that provoke hatred and delusion."
For what reason?
Noble son, the Tathāgatas do not teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning or acquiring any phenomenon;
nor for the sake of full comprehension, nor for abandonment, nor for realization, nor for clear understanding, nor for wandering in saṃsāra.
It is not for the sake of going to nirvāṇa, nor for elevation, nor for differentiation.
For, noble son, the dharmatā of the Tathāgatas is not characterized by duality.
In this regard, those who course in duality—
They are not correctly engaged;
they should be said to be wrongly engaged.
And what, son of good family, is duality?
"I shall abandon passion"—this is duality.
"I shall abandon hatred"—this is duality. "I shall abandon delusion"—this is duality.
Those who are thus engaged are not correctly engaged;
they should be known as wrongly engaged.
It is just as if, noble son, some man were present at a magician’s performance and, seeing a woman created by magic, were to give rise to a mind of passion.
With his mind overwhelmed by passion, he might rise from his seat and depart out of fear of the censure of the assembly.
Having departed, he would then contemplate that very same woman as impure; he would contemplate her as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.

The Blessed One said: "In the same way, noble son, certain monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen are to be seen here who attend to unarisen and unborn phenomena as impure, and attend to them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
I do not speak of the cultivation of the path for those deluded persons;
they should be known as being engaged in what is false.
It is just as if, noble son, some man, while asleep, were to see the king’s wife in his own home in a dream; he might lie down with her,
and through a lapse of mindfulness, he might think, "I am guilty."
Terrified and trembling, he would flee,
thinking, "May the king not strike me;
may he not deprive me of my life."
"What do you think, noble son? Would that man, fleeing in fear and trembling because of the danger arising from the king’s wife, be released from it?
He replied, "No, Blessed One. For what reason?"
"For it was thus, Blessed One, that that man produced the perception of a woman toward what is not a woman and imagined what is unreal.
The Blessed One said: "In the same way, noble son, some monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen here are to be viewed in this light."

Those who, in that which is without passion, give rise to the perception of passion and, terrified by the fear of passion, seek the escape from passion; likewise, in that which is without hatred, give rise to the perception of hatred and, terrified by the fear of hatred, seek the escape from hatred; and in that which is without delusion, give rise to the perception of delusion and, terrified by the fear of delusion, seek the escape from delusion.
I do not speak of the cultivation of the path for those deluded persons;
they should be known as being wrongly engaged.
It is just as if, noble son, that man were to produce a perception of fear toward that which is not fearful through a false attribution.

In the very same way, noble son, all foolish common people, failing to understand the limit of passion (*rāga-koṭi*) and the limit of dispassion (*virāga-koṭi*), being terrified by the fear of the limit of passion, seek the limit of dispassion as their escape.

Failing to understand the limit of hatred (*doṣa-koṭi*) and the limit of nothingness (*akiñcana-koṭi*), being terrified by the fear of the limit of hatred, they seek the limit of nothingness as their escape.
Not understanding that the limit of delusion is the limit of emptiness, those terrified by the fear of the limit of delusion seek the limit of emptiness as an escape.
Noble son, I do not speak of the cultivation of the path for those deluded persons;
they should be known as being engaged in what is false.
Thus is the detailed exposition. // 14 //
Here it is said: although a misconception consisting of grasping the impermanent as permanent is not possible, nevertheless, this grasping does exist;
and what is called "grasping" is an act of seizing, having the nature of a positive entity.
And for that [action], there must necessarily be an instrument (*karaṇa*) as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), such as eternality and so forth;
there must also be an agent (*kartṛ*) who is independent, such as the eternal self or the mind;
and there must be an object (*karman*) which is the thing most desired by the agent, such as form and other sense-objects.
And if the existence of the instrument, the agent, and the object were established, then because everything would be established, our desired goal would be achieved.
To this it is replied:
this hope is false.
But indeed, according to the reasoning already described:
"That by which one grasps, the grasping, the grasper, and that which is grasped—all these are utterly stilled; therefore, no grasping exists. (15)

For here, it has already been demonstrated previously that it is impossible for a certain perceiver to perceive some object— such as a form or a sound— which serves as the object (*karman*), by means of a certain attribute such as permanence (*nityatva*) which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
How so?

It has been demonstrated that, as in the statement "if there is a grasping at the permanent in the impermanent, this is a perversion," and so forth, the status of permanence and the like cannot logically function as a cause.
Just as the grasper does not exist, so too the existence and non-existence of the self are not established in any way whatsoever;
this has been demonstrated by the following.
And that which is perceived also does not exist;
this is established by the statement: "Form, sound, taste, touch, smell, and mental objects are merely [isolated]."
And when the agent, the instrument, and the object are thus not established, how then can there be an apprehension that is without a cause? And therefore:
"That by which one apprehends, the act of apprehending, the apprehender, and that which is apprehended—"
The meaning is that all things are quiescent by their very nature because they are unarisen, and thus all are extinguished.
And since this is so—
Therefore, grasping does not exist.

Alternatively: since the absolute non-arising of all instruments, agents, and objects has been established through treatises such as the *Examination of Conditions* (*Pratyayaparīkṣā*), therefore all these are quiescent due to being devoid of the intrinsic nature of entities;
and for this reason, no grasping exists. // 15 //
Here it is said: misconceptions (viparyaya) do indeed exist, because their opposites exist.
For here, one named Devadatta exists who is followed by misconceptions.
And without the perversions, that which is accompanied by perversions cannot possibly exist;
therefore, the perversions do exist because of the existence of that which is perverted. To this, it is said:
In this context, we have established that because of the absence of instrument, agent, and object, there is in every way no grasping at all. And therefore:
When grasping does not exist, whether it be false or even correct, for whom could there be perversion, and for whom could there be non-perversion? (16)
Whether correct or incorrect, for one who does not grasp anything at all, how could there be either error or non-error?
Therefore, errors do not exist. // 16 //

Moreover, if these misconceptions are admitted to belong to someone, would they be conceived as belonging to one who is already mistaken, or to one who is not mistaken, or to one who is in the process of becoming mistaken?
Demonstrating that [erroneous perceptions] are not possible in any way whatsoever, he says:
"Furthermore, errors do not occur for one who is already mistaken, nor do errors occur for one who is not mistaken. (17)
Errors do not occur for one who is currently in error;
reflect for yourself as to whose errors could possibly occur. (18)
In that regard, for one who is already perverted, further perversions are not possible.
What is the reason?
Because he who is already perverted—
It is already erroneous;
what further connection with error could there be for it? For that would be purposeless.
Even for one who is not mistaken, errors are not tenable;
for otherwise, it would follow that even Buddhas—who possess the eye of awakened intellect—would be subject to error, since their sleep of ignorance and the cataracts of delusion have been stilled.
Likewise, even for that which is undergoing error, errors do not exist,
because there is no such thing as an entity that is undergoing error.
For what indeed is this other distinct entity?
What could there be that is called "the process of being mistaken" which is free from both the mistaken and the non-mistaken?
If you say it is "the process of being mistaken while half-mistaken," then what is called "half-mistaken" is that for which some part is mistaken and some part is non-mistaken.
In that regard, whatever of his is erroneous does not cause him to err, because it is already erroneous;
and as for that which is non-erroneous for him, [it likewise does not cause him to err].
Even that error does not cause one to err,
because it is itself non-erroneous.
Therefore, even for one who is currently erring, no errors are possible.

And since, in this way, neither the erroneous, the non-erroneous, nor that which is currently undergoing error are possible, you should now reflect for yourself with wisdom, remaining impartial, as to whose errors could possibly exist.
Thus, because there is no substratum, errors do not exist. (17–18)
Furthermore:
How indeed could errors that have not arisen come to be? If errors have not been born, how can there be one who has fallen into error? (19)
In this regard, an entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
since it is neither from self nor from another, how could one who has fallen into such views be subject to error? (20)
The meaning is: from what could there be a perversion?
Consequently, that which was stated—that perversions exist because of the existence of those who have fallen into perversion—is not tenable. (19–20)
Even for one who accepts that the fourfold set of inversions exists in some way, it is nonetheless impossible to maintain that such a person is inverted.
Why? Because:
If the self were pure, eternal, and blissful, then it would not be a misconception; yet such a self does not exist.
If the self were pure, eternal, and blissful, then there would be no error. (21)
If these— self, purity, permanence, and pleasure— are established as being inversions,
do they exist or do they not exist?
