If they do exist, then they are not errors, because of their existence, like selflessness and so forth. // 21 //

Now, if they do not exist, then because they are non-existent, not only is there no state of perversion (viparyāsatva), but since there is also an absence of the counter-correlates to perversion, even the non-perversions such as selflessness (anātman) and so forth would lack existence; demonstrating this, he says:
If neither a self, nor purity, nor permanence, nor happiness exists, then neither non-self, nor impurity, nor impermanence, nor suffering exists either. (22)
If you think that neither a self nor purity nor permanence exists because of the impossibility of cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*), then,

since the self and so forth would likewise be non-existent, if this [notion of] non-self and so forth were grasped as being free from cognitive distortion, [it would follow that it too does not exist].
In that case, even that [negation] must be abandoned,
because in the absence of an object to be negated, there can be no negation. And when, as it is thus, the non-self and so forth do not exist, [how can they be negated]?
In that case, since that [object] also does not exist by way of its own nature, just like the self and so forth, how could it not be a misconception?
Therefore, those who desire liberation from the bondage of the prison of saṃsāra—consisting of birth, old age, and death—must abandon all eight of these misconceptions. // 22 //

And demonstrating the great significance of this aforementioned investigation into the inversions (*viparyāsa*) by way of its being the cause for the abandonment of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, he says:
"In this way, ignorance is ceased through the cessation of the inversions.
When ignorance has ceased, the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and the rest are ceased. (23)
When this yogi does not perceive the inversions by means of the method as previously described,

then, through that non-perception of inversions, ignorance— which has them as its cause— is ceased. And from the cessation of that [ignorance], the factors beginning with formative forces (saṃskāra) and ending with old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, which have ignorance as their cause, are ceased.
For ignorance is the cause of the entire mass of afflictions as well as the suffering of birth and so forth.

Just as all the material sense-faculties, which have the body-faculty as their cause, cease when the body-faculty ceases, so too the factors of existence beginning with formative forces (*saṃskāra*), which have ignorance as their cause, necessarily cease when ignorance has ceased while they are proceeding. Demonstrating this, he says:
When ignorance has ceased, the formative forces and the rest cease. Thus it is said.
Here it is said: If ignorance is ceased through the cessation of error, then ignorance must exist, such that its cessation occurs through the cessation of error.
It is not the case, however, that there is a search for a means of abandonment for something non-existent, such as a mango-creeper in the sky.
Therefore, ignorance certainly exists,
because there is the actual search for the means to its cessation;
and consequently, the afflictions such as attachment and so forth, which have that as their cause, exist.
And because afflictions truly exist, there is indeed the continuity of existence within saṃsāra.
To this it is said:
Indeed, in this matter, the opponent’s "expertise" in what is utterly disadvantageous is truly great!

Indeed, it is truly remarkable that virtuous ones— who have bound themselves to the arising of the welfare of others— do not merely stand by with assistance while this poison-tree of affliction, which yields a continuous succession of blossoms and fruits within the utterly miserable, exhausting, and improper cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), is being uprooted without remainder by the great force of the winds of wisdom and skillful means.

Furthermore, you— who stand as a great mountain of the doctrine of the real existence of things (bhāvasadbhāvavāda), acting like a massive boulder against those who, like men of immense strength, seek to uproot that very tree— out of sheer arrogance, despite being its most formidable adversary, zealously provide water for the growth of that very tree of afflictions (kleśa), which has as its sole fruit the spreading suffering of birth, old age, death, sorrow, and exhaustion, by means of the flowing waters of attachment to the existence of things.
Moreover, if the abandonment of the afflictions such as ignorance were possible,
there would be a search for the means to abandon them;
however, their abandonment is not possible.
If it were to exist, would it exist as something possessing the nature of reality (*tattva*), or as something lacking it? And what follows from this?
In that regard, if the abandonment of afflictions that exist by way of their own intrinsic nature is asserted, that is not tenable.
Why? Because:
If any afflictions indeed existed for anyone by way of their own intrinsic nature, how could they ever be abandoned? For who can abandon an intrinsic nature? (24)
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities that exist by way of their own nature cannot be overturned;
for instance, the solidity and other such natures of earth and the rest do not cease.
Likewise, if these afflictions (*kleśas*) were truly existent by way of their own nature, [they could not be abandoned].
"Of some" refers to ignorance and the other [afflictions];
"of someone" refers to a person (pudgala).
How indeed might they be abandoned?
Indeed, those [defilements] could not be abandoned by anyone in any way whatsoever.
Why, then, are they not abandoned? He says: "Who would abandon intrinsic nature? because it is impossible to turn back intrinsic nature.
The intended meaning is that it is like the impossibility of removing the non-obstruction of space. // 24 //
Now, if it is conceptualized that [the afflictions] do not exist by way of their own-being (*svabhāva*), even so, the abandonment [of them] is impossible; thus he says:
"If any afflictions whatsoever were non-existent by way of their own-being for anyone..."
How indeed could they be abandoned? Who will abandon that which does not exist? // 25 //
Even afflictions that are unreal, being non-existent by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are simply impossible to abandon.
For it is not possible to remove the coldness of fire when it does not exist;
likewise, if these afflictions do not exist for anyone by way of intrinsic nature, [they cannot be abandoned].
Who will abandon them? No one at all will abandon them.
Thus, since abandonment is impossible in either case, there is no abandonment of the afflictions.
And since there would be no abandonment [of anything], how could there be a search for the means to abandon the afflictions?
Therefore, as for what was said— that ignorance and the other afflictions must indeed exist because one searches for the means to abandon them— [that is refuted].
That is incorrect;
as it is said in the *Ārya-samādhirāja*:
"He who would be attached, or that wherein he might be attached,"
That by which one might be attached;
he who would be corrupted, or that in which one would be corrupted,
or that by which one would be corrupted.
Whoever might be deluded, or that wherein one might be deluded, or that by which one might be deluded—
he does not perceive that phenomenon.
One does not apprehend that phenomenon.
Not perceiving and not apprehending that phenomenon, one is said to be without attachment, without hatred, without delusion, with a mind free from inversion, and concentrated;
one is said to have crossed over and reached the further shore.
He is said to have attained security.
Thus it is said in detail: likewise,
she gazes upon her well-adorned face in a mirror or in the bowl of oil.
Having conceived passion for it, the fool ran forth, searching for objects of desire.
"When no reflection of a face exists, a face is never found in the image;
just as a fool might conceive a passion for it, know all phenomena to be like that," and so forth.
Likewise—
Awakening was shown through form, and form was shown for the sake of awakening;
the supreme Dharma was taught by means of a voice that transcends all parts.
By means of sound, the subsequent form is profound by its very nature;
the form is equal to awakening, and no diversity is found therein.
Just as profound nirvāṇa is fully revealed by means of sound,
yet nirvāṇa is not found, and that sound is not found—
both the sound and nirvāṇa, these two, are not found.
Thus, within all phenomena that are empty, nirvāṇa is fully revealed.
Nirvāṇa is indeed cessation, yet nirvāṇa is not to be found;
for the non-occurrence of phenomena is the same as it was before.
All phenomena are by their very nature equal to and like nirvāṇa,
known by those who are devoted to the essence of renunciation for the sake of the awakening of a Buddha.
Thus—with wisdom I know the emptiness of the aggregates; having known it, I do not dwell with the afflictions.
Indeed, I speak by means of mere verbal expression; being parinirvṛta, I move through this world.
Likewise,
those heroes have attained final nirvana in this world, who, having known all phenomena by their very nature,
move among the qualities of sensual desire without attachment; having abandoned clinging, they discipline sentient beings.
Thus [ends the twenty-fifth].
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Examination of Errors," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Noble Truths, the twenty-fourth chapter. Here it is said:
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away.
It would follow that for you, the four noble truths do not exist. // 1 //

If it is argued that all this collection of external and internal entities is established as empty on the grounds that it is not logically tenable, then indeed, many and great faults would accrue to you. How so?
If all this were empty, then that which is empty does not exist, and that which does not exist—
Because that [intrinsic nature] does not exist, like the son of a barren woman, it neither arises nor ceases;
thus, there is no arising or passing away of any entity whatsoever.
And due to the absence of that, the non-existence of the four noble truths follows for those proponents of emptiness.

How so? Here, indeed, the five aggregates of clinging, produced by prior causes and arisen dependently, are called "suffering" because they consist of suffering-as-suffering, suffering-as-change, and suffering-as-conditioning,
and because they function as an adverse state through their very nature of affliction.

And this suffering is perceived as "suffering" only by the noble ones (āryas) when their cognitive distortions have been abandoned; it is not so perceived by the non-noble ones, because they are still possessed by those distortions.
And because the nature of things is established according to how they are perceived:

for instance, when those whose sense organs are deranged— such as those afflicted by diseases like fever— perceive even sweet substances like molasses and sugar as bitter, then from the perspective of that cognition, the bitterness alone is real and not the sweetness.
Because that entity is not perceived as having such a self-nature,
so too here, although the five aggregates of clinging are by nature suffering,
nevertheless, those who perceive these as being of the nature of suffering—
Suffering is established for those very [beings], and not for those who perceive it otherwise due to following after perversions.
Therefore, since the nature of suffering is a reality only for the noble ones (ārya), it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
But is it not the case that non-noble ones discern painful feeling as "suffering"?
If so, how is it that suffering is a truth only for the noble ones? This is true;
however, it is not the case that the Truth of Suffering consists solely of painful feeling.
Rather, all five aggregates of clinging are [the truth];
therefore, because it is true only for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), it is established as the "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*). As it has been said:
"Just as a single hair placed upon the palm of the hand is not [perceived]..."
That very same thing, when worn by men, produces both restlessness and pain when it enters the eye.
"A child, like the palm of the hand, does not perceive the eyelash of the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā);
but the wise man, like the eye, is deeply distressed by that very same thing.
Therefore, since this is a truth of suffering only for the Noble Ones (āryas), it is established as the "Noble Truth of Suffering" (duḥkha-āryasatya).
And when is that suffering, the noble truth, appropriate?
When the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena occur;
but when, due to emptiness, nothing at all arises and nothing at all ceases.
At that time, there is no suffering.
And if suffering does not exist, from where could the truth of the origin arise?
For that cause from which suffering originates—
that is, arises— is called the "origin," characterized by craving, karma, and the afflictions.
But when the truth of suffering, which is the fruit, does not exist, then since it is impossible for that which is devoid of a fruit to possess a cause, the origin also does not exist.
The disappearance of suffering and its non-arising again is called cessation (*nirodha*).
But when suffering itself does not exist, then of what would there be cessation?
Therefore, the cessation of suffering is also not possible;

for if suffering does not exist, there is likewise an absence of the truth of cessation. And if the cessation of suffering does not exist, how could there be the practice that follows the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering? Thus, the truth of the path also does not exist.
Thus, for one who asserts the emptiness of all things, it follows as a logical consequence that the four noble truths do not exist. // 1 //
And so, what is the fault? It is said:
Full comprehension, abandonment, cultivation, and realization would not be possible due to the non-existence of the four noble truths. (2)

If it follows that the four noble truths do not exist, then this thorough knowledge of the truth of suffering through its aspects such as impermanence, the abandonment of the origin of suffering, the cultivation of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, and the realization— that is, the direct witnessing— of the cessation of suffering [would all be impossible].
That is not tenable. // 2 //
If, in the absence of the Noble Truths such as suffering and the rest, there is no thorough knowledge and so forth, then what is the fault? It is said:
Because of their absence, the four noble fruits also do not exist.
In the absence of the fruit, there are neither those abiding in the fruit nor those who have entered the path. // 3 //
If those eight types of persons do not exist, then the Saṅgha does not exist; and due to the non-existence of the Noble Truths, the True Dharma also does not exist. (4)
When the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha?
And when, in this way, the full comprehension of suffering and so forth do not exist, then—
If this [path] does not exist, the fourfold fruit—known as the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship—is not possible. How so?
Because here, the abandonment of the afflictions is attained as a unified whole designated as "fruit."

For example, when the three fetters have been abandoned, that abandonment of afflictions which occurs at the sixteenth moment of the path—the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—is the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).

Furthermore, regarding the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), there are nine types; these are divided into the categories of superior, medium, and inferior, each of which is further subdivided into superior, medium, and inferior varieties.

In that regard, the abandonment occurring on the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) upon the destruction of the sixth category of afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). The abandonment of those very same afflictions of the desire realm occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions is the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). As for the afflictions belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*)—those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*) which are divided into nine categories in each respective stage (*bhūmi*)— [The text continues: ...the abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the first dhyāna is the fruit of the non-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the second dhyāna is the fruit of the once-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the third dhyāna is the fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpannaphala*). The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the fourth dhyāna is the fruit of the once-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the first *dhyānāntara* is the fruit of the non-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the second *dhyānāntara* is the fruit of the once-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the third *dhyānāntara* is the fruit of the stream-enterer. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the fourth *dhyānāntara* is the fruit of the once-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the first *ārūpya* is the fruit of the non-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the second *ārūpya* is the fruit of the once-returner. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the third *ārūpya* is the fruit of the stream-enterer. The abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the fourth *ārūpya* is the fruit of the Arhat (*arhattvaphala*). This is because it is the abandonment of all afflictions. Furthermore, the abandonment occurring on the path of liberation upon the destruction of the ninth category of afflictions in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the fruit of the Arhat. This is because it is the abandonment of all afflictions. It should be understood that the fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established in this manner according to the sequence of the destruction of the afflictions. Why is this? Because the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the destruction of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), while the fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the attenuation and the destruction of the afflictions, respectively. Therefore, the fruit of the once-returner is established based on the attenuation of the afflictions, and the fruit of the non-returner is established based on their destruction. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the destruction of all afflictions. Thus, the fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of the afflictions. The fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the distinction of the number of fetters destroyed. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). For these reasons, the four fruits are established. What is the reason for establishing the fruits based on the distinction of the number of fetters destroyed? Because there are three types of fetters: those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), and those that are neither. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the destruction of the fetters to be abandoned by seeing. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the destruction of the fetters that are neither. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the number of fetters destroyed. What is the reason for establishing the fruits based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows? Because there are two types of outflows: those with outflows and those without outflows. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of outflows with outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of outflows with outflows. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of outflows without outflows. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. What is the reason for establishing the fruits based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows? Because there are two types of outflows: those with objects and those without objects. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of outflows with objects. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of outflows with objects. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of outflows without objects. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. What is the reason for establishing the fruits based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows? Because there are two types of outflows: those that are internal and those that are external. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of internal outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of internal outflows. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of external outflows. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of manifest outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of manifest outflows. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of latent outflows. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of coarse outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of coarse outflows. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of subtle outflows. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of inferior outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of inferior outflows. The fruit of the Arhat is established based on the exhaustion of superior outflows. For these reasons, the four fruits are established based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows. What is the reason for establishing the fruits based on the distinction of the exhaustion of outflows? Because there are two types of outflows: those that are worldly and those that are supramundane. Among these, the fruit of the stream-enterer is established based on the exhaustion of worldly outflows. The fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner are established based on the distinction between the attenuation and the destruction of worldly outflows. The abandonment that occurs on the path of liberation when the ninth category of afflictions belonging to the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exhausted— that is the fruit of arhatship.
These, then, are the four fruits.
How are these [four truths] logically consistent?
If the full comprehension of suffering is possible, as is the abandonment of its origin...
There is the realization of cessation and the cultivation of the noble path;
however, when the noble truths such as suffering do not exist, there is no full comprehension of suffering and so forth.
At that time, those four fruits do not exist.
Since the four fruits are absent, those four noble persons (āryapudgala) established within them—the ones who abide in the fruits—do not exist.
For this very reason, the four noble persons who are still entering the path (pratipannaka) are also not found.
For here, prior to the sixteenth moment of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) on the path, there are fifteen moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
Namely: during the clear realization of suffering in the three realms, there are four moments of receptivity and knowledge having the truth of suffering as their object.
In that regard, what are the four moments of receptivity and knowledge during the clear realization of suffering in the three realms?

Namely: it is the antidote to the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm—namely, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, false view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and observances, doubt, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance—which are to be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering;

it arises with the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; it has the truth of suffering of the desire realm as its object; it is characterized by the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga); and it is the single moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti).

And the second moment is the moment of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣaṇa*), which has that very same object and aspect and is characterized as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Likewise,

the third is the moment of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe anvayajñānakṣāntikṣaṇa*), which has the truths of suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness as its object, serves as the antidote to the eighteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) mentioned immediately above excluding hostility (*pratigha*), and arises with the aspects of suffering and so forth, being characterized as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
And the fourth moment, characterized as the path of liberation, has that very same object and aspect as the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*).

Just as there are these four moments of patience and knowledge during the clear realization of the truth of suffering pertaining to the three realms, so too is there [a moment] characterized by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), which arises with the aspects of cause, origin, production, and condition; which has as its object the truth of the origin of suffering pertaining to the desire realm; and which serves as the antidote to the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely, false view, adherence to views, doubt, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance—that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering pertaining to the desire realm.

The first moment is the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*). And the second is the destruction of the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣaya*), which has that same object and aspect and is characterized as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

Likewise, it has the truth of origination belonging to the form and formless realms as its object and serves as the antidote to the twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) mentioned immediately above, excluding those associated with aversion (*pratigha*).

The third moment is the receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding the origin (*samudaye 'nvayajñānakṣānti*), which arises with the aspects of the truth of origin and is characterized by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).

The fourth moment is the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin (*samudaye 'nvayajñāna*), which has the very same object and aspects as that [receptivity] and is characterized by the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Thus, these are the four moments in the clear realization of the truths of suffering and origin pertaining to the three realms.

Just as these four moments occur during the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths of suffering and its origin pertaining to the three realms, so too there is one moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), characterized by the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*). This moment has as its object the truth of the cessation of suffering belonging to the desire realm; it serves as the antidote to the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) mentioned in relation to the origin [of suffering] which are to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering in the desire realm; and it arises with the aspects of cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation.
And the second moment is the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*), which has that same object and aspect and is characterized by the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

With these very same aspects, the third moment is the receptivity to subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe anvayajñānakṣānti*), which has the truth of the cessation of suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness as its object, serves as the antidote to the twelve underlying tendencies excluding hostility, and is characterized by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
And the fourth moment is the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe anvayajñāna*), which has that same object and aspect and is characterized by the path of liberation.
Thus, these are the four moments in the clear realization of the truth of the cessation of suffering pertaining to the three realms.

Thus, having added the eighth, *śīlavrataparāmarśa*, to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) described in relation to cessation among those to be abandoned by the vision of the path leading to the cessation of suffering in the desire realm, there is one moment characterized as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*). This consists of the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*), which serves as the antidote to the eight underlying tendencies, arises with the aspects of being the path, the right method, the achievement, and the definitive departure, and has as its object the path leading to the cessation of suffering in the desire realm.
And the second moment, the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārge dharmajñāna*), has precisely that same object and aspect as the characteristic of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

With those very same aspects, the third moment—the receptivity to subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*)—has as its object the path leading to the cessation of suffering in the realms of form and formlessness; it is characterized by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and serves as the antidote to the fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) excluding hostility.
Thus, these fifteen moments are designated as the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Established in this way, the noble one is called "one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
But when he abides in the sixteenth moment of the path, the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), he is called a "stream-enterer" (*srotaāpanna*).

These eighty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are called "to be abandoned by seeing" (darśana-prahātavya) because they are abandoned by the mere vision of the truths, without depending on cultivation (bhāvanā).
However, those which are abandoned later through the cultivation of the aspects (ākāra) of the truths as they have been seen are "to be abandoned by cultivation" (bhāvanā-prahātavya);
and these consist of ten underlying tendencies.
The desire-realm [afflictions] are attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance;
the form-realm [afflictions] are those same three excluding aversion;
and the formless-realm [afflictions] are likewise these three. Thus, there are ten.
And these, according to the principle already stated, are divided ninefold in each stage:
in the desire realm, in the four meditations,
and in the four formless attainments.

For the sake of abandoning each individual type of affliction (*kleśa-prakāra*), two moments of knowledge (*jñāna-kṣaṇa*) are established through the distinction between the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), corresponding to the reversal of the moments of affliction.
For the most intense of the intense types of affliction is abandoned by the weakest of the weak paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation;
continuing in this manner, the weakest of the weak types of affliction is abandoned by the most intense of the intense moments of knowledge.
For it should be understood that gross impurity is removable by little effort, whereas subtle impurity is removable only by great effort, according to the analogy of a washerman cleaning clothes.

In this context, the noble one who abides in the moments of knowledge prior to the moment of knowledge known as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), which serves as the antidote to the sixth category of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*)— that is, subsequent to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—
is called a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka*).
He is called a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmī*) because, having come to this world only once more, he attains final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*).
One who has entered upon the path for the sake of that fruit and is established in the stage of application is called "one who has entered upon the fruit of once-returning";
however, at the sixth moment, one is called a "once-returner."

An Ārya who exists during the moments of knowledge prior to the moment of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*)—which occurs upon the abandonment of the ninth category of afflictions after the sixth moment—is called one "practicing for the fruit of Non-returner" (*anāgāmiphalapratipannaka*).
Because he will not return to this world but will attain final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) right there, he is called a "Non-returner" (*anāgāmī*).
One who is established in the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the sake of that fruit is called one "practicing for the fruit of Non-returner."
But in the ninth moment, one is called a non-returner (anāgāmin).

An Ārya who, from the moment following the ninth moment of the path of liberation regarding the desire realm up until the moment of the path of liberation that abandons the ninth category of afflictions belonging to the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, abides in the moments of knowledge, is called one "practicing for the fruit of Arhatship.
Because he is worthy of worship from the world including its gods, humans, and asuras, he is called an "Arhat."
One who has entered for the sake of that fruit and is established in the path of application is called "one practicing for the fruit of Arhatship.
However, by abandoning the ninth category of afflictions belonging to the peak of existence, one established in the ninth path of liberation becomes an Arhat.

These four individuals who have entered the path and the four who abide in the fruit— these eight constitute the great persons (mahāpuruṣapudgala) described by the Blessed One as being most worthy of offerings.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"He was questioned by Śakra, the King of the Gods who wields power,
regarding those living beings who plow and perform sacrifices while desiring merit."
For those who always perform meritorious deeds based on material things with faith and conviction,
I shall describe to you that excellent field wherein what is given yields great fruit.
"The four who have entered the path and the four who abide in the fruit—
this is the Saṅgha worthy of offerings, by virtue of its perfection in knowledge and conduct.
If the Four Noble Truths do not exist, nor the thorough cognitions of them, [then this is impossible].

At that time, because the fruits obtainable through the vision and cultivation of the truths would be non-existent, there would likewise be an absence of those individuals who abide in the state of being a candidate for or have attained those fruits.
Consequently, the Saṅgha would not exist.

In that case, the Saṅgha—which is defined by the attainment of the Dharma and by the direct realization of the Dharma such that it cannot be divided even by all the Māras due to having gained verified faith in the Blessed Buddha—would not exist.
If those eight types of persons do not exist.
And because of the non-existence of the noble truths, the true Dharma (saddharma) also does not exist.
The Dharma of the virtuous noble ones is the true Dharma.
In that regard, the truth of cessation is the Dharma as fruit.
The truth of the path, however, is the dharma that leads to the attainment of the fruit;
this, first of all, is the dharma of realization (*adhigamadharma*). The teaching that elucidates it is the dharma of scripture (*āgamadharma*).

If all these noble truths do not exist, they are non-existent; and because the noble truths are non-existent, the True Dharma also does not exist. When both the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha?
For if the Dharma were as previously described,

then it would be logical that one becomes a Buddha through the realization of that Dharma by means of the perfect awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects; and if the Saṅgha were to exist [in that way],...

Then, with the equipment of knowledge being accumulated through those instructions, and the equipment of merit being accumulated through that giving, honoring, taking refuge, and so forth, one will gradually become a Buddha.
Alternatively, if the Saṅgha did not exist, there would be an absence of those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

And without attaining the state of one who is practicing for the fruits and so forth, Buddhahood cannot be attained. For the Blessed One must necessarily have been established in some fruit previously.
And in that regard, the Blessed One, being established in the fruit, is indeed included within the Saṅgha;
for in the absence of a Saṅgha, there can certainly be no Blessed Buddha.
Moreover, since the Blessed One is also included among those beyond training (aśaikṣa), he is likewise included within the Saṅgha.
And because of the expression "the community of monks headed by the Buddha," some describe the Blessed One as being included within the Saṅgha itself.
According to their view, this is clearly implied by the statement: "In the absence of both Dharma and Saṅgha, how could there be a Buddha?"

Furthermore, those who teach the *Madhyoddeśika* explain that by the system of stages taught in the *Mahāvastu*, a bodhisattva established on the first stage who has produced the path of seeing is included within the Saṅgha.
If they say this, then since the Saṅgha would not exist [for them], the bodhisattva also would not exist; how then could there be a Buddha? This is quite clear.
Thus, by speaking in this way, you deny all three Jewels. (5)

By speaking thus of "emptiness," you reject the Three Jewels known as the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for they are rare, appearing only at certain times, and because they are unattainable by those of little merit, they possess great value like precious gems. (5)
Furthermore:
By [asserting] emptiness, you contradict the existence of the fruits [of action], both non-dharma and dharma, as well as all worldly conventions. (6)
This is connected with the phrase "proclaiming emptiness.
If all this is empty, then when everything indeed does not exist, [how can there be arising and ceasing?]

At that time, because everything is included within [the ultimate], neither dharma nor adharma, along with their causes and their desired or undesired fruits, can exist. Furthermore, all these worldly conventions— such as "do" and "cook"— [cease to exist].
Eat, stay, go.
Expressions such as "come" and so forth are also not tenable, because all phenomena are included within "all," and because all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, the reasoning described above is not the superior one. // 6 //
To this we reply: You do not understand the purpose of emptiness, nor emptiness itself, nor the meaning of emptiness; therefore, you are thus frustrated. (7)

By means of your own conceptual construction alone, you have superimposed a perversion— namely, that non-existence is the meaning of emptiness— and by voicing this criticism, "If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away," and so forth, you have fallen into great distress regarding us;
the meaning is that you are excessively afflicted and struck down by various real [but false] conceptual constructions.
The meaning of emptiness that you have grasped was not the one described by us here in this treatise;
and since you do not understand the meaning of emptiness, you do not even know emptiness itself,
nor do you understand the purpose for which emptiness exists.

Consequently, due to your failure to understand the true nature of things as they actually exist, you have described many things that are improper and entirely disconnected from our own interpretation.
Now, what then is the purpose of emptiness?
This has already been stated in the *Ātmaparīkṣā*: "Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and afflictions; karma and afflictions arise from conceptual construction."
They [arise] from conceptual proliferation; however, conceptual proliferation ceases within emptiness. Thus it is said.
Therefore, emptiness is taught for the purpose of the complete cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
thus, the cessation of all proliferation is the purpose of emptiness.
You, however, by imagining non-existence to be the meaning of emptiness, merely increase the web of conceptual proliferation and do not understand the purpose of emptiness.
Now, what again is emptiness? That too has been stated in that very same place:
"Not dependent on another, peaceful, and not proliferated by conceptual proliferations."
"Free from conceptual construction and without manifold objects—this is the characteristic of reality.

Therefore, since emptiness has the nature of the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), how could there be non-existence within it? Thus, you do not even understand emptiness itself. Furthermore, regarding the referent (*artha*) upon which the word "emptiness" is based for its application:
We shall demonstrate that very point right here:
"That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness;
it is a dependent designation, and it is itself the middle way. Thus.
That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn; for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature.
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty; he who understands emptiness is heedful.
Thus, from these words of the Blessed One in verse:
whatever is the meaning of the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda), that alone is the meaning of the term "emptiness" (śūnyatā).
Furthermore, the meaning of the word "non-existence" is not the same as the meaning of the word "emptiness.
You reproach us by superimposing the meaning of the word "non-existence" onto the meaning of "emptiness";
therefore, you do not even understand the meaning of the word "emptiness."
And you, not knowing this, by thus leveling this reproach, will certainly be frustrated. // 7 //
And who among us offers the aforementioned criticism?
It is one who does not understand the non-erroneous distinction between the two truths as taught in the Blessed One’s word,
but is merely intent on the study of the mere text.

Therefore, out of compassion, for the sake of dispelling others' understanding of the meaning of false teachings, the Master first addresses the very establishment of the two truths as taught in the Blessed One’s doctrine, saying:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth that is ultimate. (8)
For here, the teaching of the Dharma by the Blessed Buddhas proceeds by relying upon two truths.
What are these two truths?
They are the conventional truth of the world (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Among these:
"The world is said to have the aggregates as its self, for the world is dependent upon them.
According to this statement, the *pudgala* (person), which is designated in dependence upon the five aggregates, is called "the world. *Saṃvṛti* is a complete covering or concealment.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) because it completely obscures the true nature of all phenomena.
Alternatively, *saṃvṛti* means mutual arising, in the sense of being dependent upon one another. Or else, *saṃvṛti* means convention (*saṃketa*), that is, worldly discourse (*lokavyavahāra*).
And that which is characterized by the signifier and the signified, knowledge and the object of knowledge, and so forth, is *saṃvṛti* in the world;
it is "worldly *saṃvṛti*" (*lokasaṃvṛti*).
But does a non-worldly *saṃvṛti* also exist, such that it is distinguished as "worldly *saṃvṛti*" in this way?
This is a restatement of things as they actually exist;
no such deliberation applies here.
Or alternatively:

Those who possess a state of distorted perception due to sense faculties impaired by cataracts, jaundice, and so forth, are "non-worldlings" (aloka); their conventional truth is "non-worldly convention" (aloka-saṃvṛti).
Therefore, it is distinguished as "worldly convention" (loka-saṃvṛti).
This has been explained in detail in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, from which it should be understood.
That which is true by way of worldly convention is "worldly conventional truth" (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*).
This entire range of worldly discourse—including the designator and the designated, knowledge and the object of knowledge, and so forth—is called worldly conventional truth without exception.
For these conventional expressions do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth; for therein—when the object of the mind has ceased, that which is to be expressed has ceased;
for the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like nirvāṇa: unarisen and unceasing.
Thinking thus, how could there be any activity of words there in that ultimate reality (paramārtha), or how could there be any activity of cognition?
For that ultimate reality is not dependent on another, it is peaceful, to be personally realized by the noble ones (āryas), and transcends all conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
It is neither taught nor cognized.
For it was said previously:
"Not dependent on another, peaceful, not proliferated by conceptual proliferations, free from discursive thought, and without manifold meanings— this is the characteristic of reality."
That which is both supreme (*parama*) and an object (*artha*) is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
That alone is the truth; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The detailed distinction between these two truths should be understood from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.
Relying upon these two truths, the Dharma teaching of the Blessed Buddhas proceeds.
This being the established order of teaching,
those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths—
They do not understand the profound reality within the Buddha's teaching. // 9 //
Here it is asked: If, then, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is by nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), let that alone be so;
what is the purpose of this other teaching concerning the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, the noble truths, dependent origination, and so forth, which is not the ultimate reality?
For that which is unreal must be abandoned.
And as for that which is to be relinquished, what is the use of teaching it? It is said:
This is indeed true;
however, without accepting worldly convention characterized by the signifier and the signified, knowledge and the object of knowledge, and so forth—
Demonstrating that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is indeed impossible to teach, and that it cannot be realized if it is not taught,
and that without realizing the ultimate truth one cannot realize nirvāṇa, he says:
Without relying upon conventional practice, the ultimate truth is not taught;
without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvāṇa is not realized. (10)

Therefore, because it is the means for attaining nirvāṇa, conventional reality (saṃvṛti) as it actually exists must necessarily be accepted at the very outset, just as one who seeks water must first accept the vessel. // 10 //
Thus, for that person who, having rejected the established distinction between the two truths characterized as the conventional and the ultimate, describes emptiness in such a manner—
that kind of individual [is destroyed];
"emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys one of dull intellect."
Like a snake poorly grasped, or like knowledge improperly mastered. // 19 //

For conventional truth is produced by mere ignorance and is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); the yogi, realizing its emptiness as the characteristic of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), does not fall into either of the two extremes.
Thinking, "What was there that now no longer exists?"—since he has not previously perceived the intrinsic nature of entities—he likewise does not subsequently perceive non-existence.
And because worldly convention, which takes the form of reflections, is not sublated, he does not sublate even karma, the fruit of karma, dharma, adharma, and so forth.
Nor does one superimpose ultimate reality upon things by way of their having an intrinsic nature,
because we observe the existence of karma, its fruit, and so forth only in the case of entities that are devoid of intrinsic nature, and not in the case of those that possess an intrinsic nature.
But he who, failing to see this distinction between the two truths, perceives the emptiness of conditioned phenomena— such a person,
while seeking liberation through the perception of emptiness, would either conceptualize the non-existence of conditioned phenomena,
or else conceive of emptiness as some kind of real entity.
And for the sake of its substratum, one might even conceptualize an intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*);
in either case, emptiness wrongly perceived will certainly destroy him.
How so?
If one were to conceive that all this is empty and that nothing exists at all, then one falls into a false view. As it has been said:
"This Dharma, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of little wisdom."
For one sinks into this [view] which is defiled by the view of non-existence.
Now, if one does not wish to resort to a universal denial [of all things],

then it necessarily follows that one must reject emptiness— how indeed could these entities, which are perceived by the entire world of gods, asuras, and humans, be empty? Therefore, the meaning of emptiness is not the meaning of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Having thus rejected [the teaching], by means of that evil karma conducive to the ruin of the true Dharma, one is destined for the miserable states of existence (*apāya*).
As it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*:
"Furthermore, another fool, through ignorance of this [teaching], considers himself a scholar."
"One whose self is destroyed by repudiation goes headfirst to the Avīci hell.
Thus, emptiness, when grasped as non-existence, destroys the grasper.
Now, suppose one were to conceptualize emptiness as existence.
And because of the existence of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that serve as the basis for those [views],

even so, due to being mistaken regarding the path leading to *nirvāṇa*, one becomes bewildered by the teaching on emptiness. Thus, emptiness, when grasped even as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), destroys the grasper.
Now, is it not the case that whatever is beneficial, if performed otherwise, does not lead to its fruit— just as a seed sown at the wrong time does not result in a crop,
whereas one sown at the proper time leads to the attainment of great fruit?
In the same way, a snake being subdued by means of jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, brings about a vast heap of wealth through the seizing of the crest-jewel.
Moreover, because it provides a livelihood for snake-catchers,
when it is seized by disregarding its designated purpose, it destroys the very person who seizes it.

Just as a mantra, when accomplished according to the instructions, benefits the practitioner, but when practiced while deviating from the instructions, destroys the practitioner himself; so too here, the great mantra of emptiness, when accomplished and grasped according to the instructions— by way of rejecting the grasping at existence, non-existence, and so forth— [brings about liberation].

The Middle Way joins the grasper with the supreme rain from the cloud of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which has as its sole flavor the extinguishing of the fire of suffering such as birth, old age, and death; yet,
when grasped through the absence of the specific instructions [of the teacher], it inevitably destroys the grasper himself by the very logic already described.
Since emptiness, when wrongly grasped, destroys the grasper,
and since it cannot be correctly grasped by those of dull intelligence, the Sage’s mind turned back from teaching it.
Having considered that this Dharma is difficult for the dull-witted to fathom.

Because this dharma characterized by emptiness destroys beings of dull intellect and meager wisdom through their grasping at perversions, the Blessed Buddha— the Sage endowed with the excellence of great skillful means and knowledge— having realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment, observed the realm of all sentient beings, and considered both the extreme profundity of the dharma and the fact that it is difficult for the dull-witted to fathom, turned his mind away from teaching the true dharma.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Then, not long after his full enlightenment, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: 'I have realized a Dharma that is profound, appearing as profound, beyond ratiocination, outside the sphere of ratiocination, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise and the learned.
If I were to proclaim it to others...'"
And if others were not to understand me,
that would be a hindrance for me; it would be a weariness for me.
"There might be a lack of mental arousal.
Suppose, rather, that I should dwell alone in a remote forest, having attained a state of dwelling in happiness in the present life," and so forth. // 12 //

Thus, since this is so, the fault you further attribute to us by overemphasizing emptiness— due to not understanding the non-erroneous establishment of the two truths— does not apply to us regarding the empty. (13)
This great consequence of error which you have cast upon us—

beginning with "If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away," and so forth— is advanced by one who, while being [supposedly] knowledgeable in the establishment of the two truths, has failed to correctly understand emptiness, the meaning of emptiness, and the purpose of emptiness.
Therefore, that [fault] is not applicable to our doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*) within emptiness.
And because it is not applicable,
whatever logical consequence of fault you have raised against emptiness— by which you effect a denial, a disparagement, a refutation, and a rejection of emptiness— is [unfounded].
Therefore, that objection of yours does not apply to us; for you have raised this consequence by superimposing upon the meaning of emptiness the meaning of non-existence,
whereas we do not explain the meaning of emptiness as having the sense of non-existence.
Rather, [it is] for the sake of dependent origination;
therefore, this refutation of the vision of emptiness is not tenable. // 13 //
And not only does the aforementioned consequence of faults not apply to our position, but rather,
he says— demonstrating that the entire systematic arrangement of the truths and so forth is all the more tenable:
"Everything is logical for him for whom emptiness is logical."
For him for whom emptiness is not tenable, nothing at all is tenable. // 14 //
For one to whom this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is logical,
for that person all this as it has been described is logical. How so?
For we explain that dependent origination is indeed emptiness: "That which is born from conditions is unborn; it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature.
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty; he who understands emptiness is heedful."
Thus, from the statement of the verse:
"All phenomena are empty by virtue of being devoid of intrinsic nature," so it is declared in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, for whomsoever this emptiness is logical, pleasing, and acceptable,
for them dependent origination is logical;
for whomsoever dependent origination is logical, [for them all phenomena are logical].
The four noble truths apply to that [dependent origination]. How so?
Because suffering is indeed dependently originated, not non-dependently originated.
And that [suffering] is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
When suffering exists, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering are logically possible.
Consequently, the full comprehension of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path are also logically possible.
And when there is the thorough knowledge of the truths such as suffering and so forth, the fruits are logically established;
and when the fruits exist, those who abide in the fruits are logically established; and when those who abide in the fruits exist, those who are entering toward them are logically established.
And when those who have entered the path and those who abide in the fruits exist, the Saṅgha is established.
And when the Noble Truths exist, the True Dharma is also established.
And when the True Dharma and the Saṅgha exist, the Buddha is also established.
And thus, all three jewels are logically established;
all mundane and supramundane entities, as well as all specific realizations, are logically established;
dharma and adharma, their results, happy and miserable rebirths, and all worldly conventions are logically established. It is thus:
Everything is tenable for him for whom emptiness is tenable;
for him for whom the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is tenable, all this that has been stated is tenable.
The meaning is that [it] is accomplished.
However, for one for whom emptiness as it has been described is not tenable,
nothing is tenable because of the absence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
And he will demonstrate in detail how it is not tenable. // 14 //

Thus, while our own position— being thoroughly purified, consistent with all established principles, and firmly settled— is thus situated, you, who fail to perceive the merits and defects as they truly exist in your own extremely crude, overly proximate, and contradictory position which is fraught with faults, cast upon us the very defects that belong to yourself.
Having mounted the horse itself, you have forgotten the horse itself.
For it is just as when someone, having mounted a certain horse, forgets that very horse and blames others for the fault of its being stolen.
In the very same way, you, though mounted upon the horse of the vision of emptiness characterized by dependent origination, revile us because you fail to perceive it due to extreme distraction. 15.
What, then, are those faults of the opponent, which he fails to perceive and instead levels only against the proponent of emptiness? Explaining these, he says:
If you perceive the existence of things by way of their intrinsic nature, then you perceive those things as being without causes and conditions. (16)
If you perceive entities as existing by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),

then, because intrinsic nature is independent of causes and conditions, you yourself would thus perceive external and internal objects— distinguished by various divisions— as being without causes and conditions, that is, as having no existing causes or conditions. (16)
Moreover, if you accept the absence of causes, you deny the effect and the cause, as well as the agent, the instrument, and the action;
you deny arising and ceasing, and the fruit. (17)
How so?

If you imagine that the pot exists here by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then what would be the purpose of causes and conditions such as clay for that which already exists by way of its own intrinsic nature? Consequently, those [causes and conditions] would be non-existent.
Furthermore, an effect called a pot cannot arise without a cause.

And in the absence of this [effect], there would be an absence of arising and cessation, due to the non-existence of the instruments such as the wheel, the agent— the potter— and the act of producing the pot.
If arising and cessation were non-existent, how could there be a fruit?

Thus, by accepting that things possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), you contradict all of this—such as the effect and so forth. Therefore, for you who accept that things possess intrinsic nature, nothing at all is tenable. (17)
But for us, who maintain that the intrinsic nature of things is empty, all of this is logically consistent.
Why?
Because we—
That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness;
it is a dependent designation, and it is itself the middle way. (18)
This dependent origination— the manifestation of sprouts, consciousness, and so forth, in dependence upon causes and conditions— is non-arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
And that which is the non-arising of phenomena by way of intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As the Blessed One has said:
"That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn; it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty; he who understands emptiness is heedful. Thus it was taught.
Likewise, in the *Ārya-Laṅkāvatāra*: "Mahāmati, with reference to the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), I have taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty."
Thus it has been explained in detail.
In the *Dvayardhaśatikā*: "All phenomena are empty by virtue of being devoid of intrinsic nature."
This very emptiness of intrinsic nature is a designation based upon [something else];
that very emptiness is established as a designation based upon [something else].
Just as a chariot is designated based upon its constituent parts, such as the wheels and so forth.
That designation which is based upon its own constituent parts is,
by its very nature, non-arising;
and that which is non-arising by its very nature is emptiness.
That very emptiness, characterized by the non-arising of intrinsic nature, is established as the middle way.
For that which has no arising by way of intrinsic nature lacks existence.
And because there is no disappearance for that which is unarisen by its own nature (*svabhāva*), there is an absence of non-existence. Therefore,

because it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, emptiness— characterized by the non-arising of all intrinsic natures— is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*), the middle path.
Thus, these are specific designations for dependent origination itself: emptiness, dependent designation, and the middle way. // 18 //
And when investigated in every way:
no phenomenon whatsoever exists that has not arisen dependently;
therefore, indeed, no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is non-empty. (19)
For whatever phenomenon is not dependently originated does not exist,
as it has been said in the *Śataka*:
Nothing exists anywhere at any time without depending [on something else];
therefore, nothing whatsoever exists as eternal anywhere at any time.
"Ordinary worldlings imagine space and so forth to be eternal;
yet even by means of worldly [reasoning], the wise do not perceive any real objects in them.
And it was said by the Blessed One:
The wise person, having realized phenomena through dependent origination, does not rely on extreme views;
they understand that phenomena arise with causes and conditions, for there is no such thing as a nature that exists without cause or condition.
Thus,
no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not dependently originated;
and that which is not dependently originated is empty.
Therefore, there is no phenomenon that is non-empty;
since this is so, for us all phenomena are empty.
Nor does the consequence of the faults stated by others apply. // 19 //
But for you, who maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvavādin*): if all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
then, necessarily, given the absence of both arising and passing away—
It would follow that the four noble truths do not exist for you. // 20 //
What is the reason? Because:
How could there be suffering that has not arisen dependently?
For it is said that suffering is impermanent; indeed, it does not exist in the state of having an intrinsic nature. (21)
For that which possesses intrinsic nature does not arise dependently;
and that which is not dependently arisen, [does not exist].
That is not impermanent;
for a sky-flower, being non-existent, cannot be impermanent.
And it has been stated by the Blessed One that what is impermanent is suffering: "That which is impermanent is suffering."
And so it is said in the *Śatakaśāstra*:
"For that which is impermanent, suffering is certain; that which is accompanied by suffering is not happiness.
Therefore, it arises that whatever is impermanent is all suffering."
And that which is impermanent does not exist when the intrinsic nature and substantial existence of entities are admitted. // 21 //
Thus, first of all, if things possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatva*), suffering is not tenable.
Furthermore, it is not only suffering that is untenable;
demonstrating that even the origin (*samudaya*) is untenable when the acceptance of intrinsic nature is maintained, he says:
What more could possibly arise from that which already exists by way of its own nature?
Therefore, for one who contradicts emptiness, there is no origination.
Here, that from which suffering arises is called "origination" (samudaya) because it is the cause of suffering.

Therefore, for one who rejects the emptiness of this suffering and accepts suffering as having intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), since its re-arising would be purposeless, the postulation of a cause for it is likewise purposeless;
thus, for one who rejects emptiness in this way, even the "origin" (*samudaya*) is not tenable for you. (22)
Demonstrating that for one who accepts suffering as being merely intrinsic, even the cessation of suffering is not tenable, he says:
"There is no cessation of suffering that exists by way of its own nature;
because you maintain the persistence of intrinsic nature, you contradict cessation. (23)
For if suffering were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then, because an intrinsic nature is indestructible, how could it be subject to cessation?
Thus, by fixating on intrinsic nature through such conceptual entanglements, you obstruct the very cessation of suffering by grasping at intrinsic nature. (23)
Now, demonstrating how even the Noble Path is untenable for one who maintains the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he says:
"If the Path possesses intrinsic nature, its cultivation is not tenable;
but if that Path is cultivated, then intrinsic nature does not exist for you. (24)

For if things were to possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), then the path (*mārga*) would likewise possess intrinsic nature; and since it would already exist in that uncultivated state, what further use would there be for its cultivation? Thus—
If the path possesses intrinsic nature, its cultivation is not tenable.
If, however, you accept the cultivation of this path,
then in that case, the noble path would lack intrinsic nature.
The intended meaning is "because it is an effect. // 24 //
Moreover, the cultivation of the path is intended for the sake of attaining the cessation of suffering and for the sake of abandoning its origin;
however, according to the reasoning previously stated, for you who maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvavāda*),
when suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not exist—
Since the path is the cessation of suffering, what will it bring about? (25)
That cessation of suffering does not exist at all,
which the cultivated path would reach by means of its cessation;
therefore, even the noble path is likewise untenable.
Thus, for one who maintains the doctrine of intrinsic nature, the non-existence of the four noble truths follows. // 25 //
Now, demonstrating how even the full comprehension of suffering and so forth is not possible for another [the opponent], he says:
"If its non-comprehension is by way of intrinsic nature, how could it [ever] occur again?"
Is it not indeed the case that thorough knowledge is established as its very intrinsic nature? // 26 //
If it is conceived that suffering, whose nature was previously unknown, is subsequently fully understood, that is incorrect.
What is the reason?
For indeed, it is said that intrinsic nature is firmly established;
for whatever is intrinsic nature, that, it is said,
is firmly established in the world.
It does not undergo alteration, just as heat is inherent in fire;
and when there is no alteration of intrinsic nature, [it remains as it is].
In that case, since suffering whose nature was previously unknown could not be known later either, the full comprehension of suffering would likewise be impossible. // 26 //

And when even this full comprehension of suffering is not possible, then for you, abandonment, realization, and cultivation are likewise untenable, as are the four fruits [of the spiritual life]. (27)
This abandonment of the origin and the realization of cessation—
these two, namely abandonment and realization— as well as this cultivation of the path,
are likewise untenable because the full comprehension of suffering is impossible.
Since that which has not been abandoned by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot lose that nature, its subsequent abandonment is likewise untenable.
This same reasoning should be applied to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not only thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) and so forth that are impossible under the doctrine of intrinsic nature; moreover—
Furthermore, the four fruits [of the spiritual life] would not be tenable as objects of full comprehension (*parijñā*).
Just as it is not logical for there to be a full comprehension of suffering that is not already fully comprehended by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
so too, for that which does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, it is impossible for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) to exist previously and then come into being later.
Just as it is with the fruit of stream-entry, so too should the non-existence of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship be understood. // 27 //
And it is not only that these fruits are untenable like thorough knowledge (*parijñā*);
rather, demonstrating that their realization (*adhigama*) is also untenable, he says: "How, moreover, can a fruit that is not realized by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [be realized]?"
It would be possible to attain [it] for one who grasps at an intrinsic nature. // 28 //

For one who accepts the doctrine of the intrinsic nature of entities because intrinsic nature is by its very character non-deviating, the subsequent realization of those natures that were not previously realized is not tenable. // 28 //
And therefore:
If there were no fruits, there would be neither those established in the fruits nor those entering toward them;
if those eight types of persons did not exist, there would be no Saṅgha. // 29 //
And because the noble truths do not exist, the True Dharma also does not exist; when the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha? (30)
And the meaning of these two verses should be understood as before. // 29–30 //

Moreover: If the existence of intrinsic nature were accepted, it would follow for you that enlightenment occurs even without depending [on causes], and it would follow for you that enlightenment exists even without depending on a Buddha. (31)

For if there were some entity called a "Buddha" by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he would exist even without depending upon or in relation to awakening (*bodhi*), which is the knowledge of omniscience;
for intrinsic nature is unconditioned and independent of anything else.
Because of this statement, enlightenment could exist even without a Buddha; that is, enlightenment would exist independently, without relying upon a Buddha. // 31 //
Furthermore:
"Moreover, one who is by nature unawakened, even though striving for awakening, will not attain awakening through the conduct of a bodhisattva. (32)

For in this case, if a person were of an unenlightened nature prior to Buddhahood, then even while engaged in the conduct of a Bodhisattva and striving for the sake of enlightenment, enlightenment would never occur;
because that which is of an unenlightened nature cannot be altered. // 32 //
Furthermore:
"Moreover, no one will ever perform either dharma or adharma. What can be done with that which is non-empty? For intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not something that is produced. (33)
For if one accepts the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the production of merit and demerit is not tenable.
What indeed is there to be produced for that which is non-empty?
For a cause for an intrinsic nature that is non-empty is not tenable, because it already exists. (33)
Furthermore: "Apart from dharma and adharma, a fruit indeed exists for you;
yet a fruit caused by dharma and adharma does not exist for you. (34)
If this desirable or undesirable fruit, which is caused by merit and demerit, exists by way of its own intrinsic nature,
then it would exist even without merit and demerit.
And when you hold that the fruit exists without dharma and adharma,
then it is impossible for your fruit to be born from dharma and adharma;
there would be the futility of acquiring dharma and adharma.
"And for you, a fruit caused by merit and demerit does not exist.
Now, if it is postulated that the fruit has merit and demerit as its cause, then that fruit is not non-empty; demonstrating this, he says:
Or if you hold that there is a fruit caused by merit and demerit, how can that fruit produced from merit and demerit be non-empty for you? (35)
This is indeed empty,
because it is dependently originated,
like a reflection.
This is the intended meaning. // 35 //
Moreover, all these [actions], such as "go," "do," and "cook," are indeed [of this nature].
"Read!",
"Stand!", and so forth— such worldly conventions are dependently originated.
If you maintain that these possess intrinsic nature, [then...]

In that case, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) would be subverted by you; and because of that subversion, all worldly conventions (vyavahāra) would likewise be subverted. Demonstrating this, he says:
"And you contradict all worldly conventions."
In that you deny emptiness as dependent origination. (36)
The word "yat" (which) is an adverbial modifier;
it is connected with the phrase "yad bādhase" (that which you obstruct). // 36 //
Furthermore:
For one who rejects emptiness, there would be nothing that ought to be done, action would be uninitiated, and an agent would exist without acting. (37)
For if things were not devoid of intrinsic nature (svarūpa),
they would indeed possess an inherent nature (sasvabhāva);
in that case, because an inherent nature would already exist, nothing whatsoever would need to be produced by anything.
For the non-obstructiveness of space is not produced by anything;
yet [if it were so], there would be an action that is not being performed,
and there would be the status of an agent for one who does not perform an action.
And this is not so;
therefore, entities are not non-empty. // 37 //
Furthermore:
The world would be unarisen, unceasing, and immutable; it would be devoid of intrinsic nature despite its various states. (38)

[For those who maintain that the world is empty of intrinsic nature: If the world were created by its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being fashioned through various states and produced by intrinsic nature alone— thus not having arisen dependently (*apratītyasamutpanna*)— then, for those who propound the emptiness of intrinsic nature, if entities were indeed possessed of intrinsic nature by way of their very intrinsic nature,
then because intrinsic nature is uncreated and immutable, this entire world would be neither born nor ceased.
Because it would be neither born nor ceased, the world would be immutable (*kūṭastha*).
For those who maintain that the world is non-empty, the world would be independent of causes and conditions, devoid of diverse states, and not dependently originated.
As it is said in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*:
If there were anything non-empty, the Jina would not have given its prediction;
for it remains established in its own respective state, immovable and unchanging, with neither increase nor decrease. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Āryahastikakṣyasūtra*:
