"If there were any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among phenomena, the Jina together with his disciples would go right there.
If phenomena were unchanging (*kūṭastha*), there would be no nirvāṇa, and a wise person would never be free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). (38)

Furthermore, he says this to demonstrate that not only do mundane conventions fail to be tenable if one accepts the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), but even supramundane ones likewise fail to be tenable:
The attainment of what has not yet been attained, the action that brings an end to suffering, and the abandonment of all afflictions—none of these exist if [all things] are not empty. (39)
For if all this were non-empty and possessed of intrinsic nature, then that which has not been attained would remain unattained;
thus, there would be no attainment of a fruit that has not yet been attained.
In that case, since the cause for bringing suffering to an end did not exist previously, it would likewise not exist now;
and since the abandonment of all afflictions did not occur previously, their abandonment could not occur later either. (39)
Thus, since all this is untenable when the doctrine of intrinsic nature (sasvabhāvavāda) is accepted, therefore:
He who sees dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) sees this: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path itself. (40)
For whoever correctly perceives the emptiness of intrinsic nature, which is the characteristic of the dependent origination of all phenomena,
they perceive the four noble truths as they truly are in reality.
As it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīparipṛcchā*:
Mañjuśrī, by whom the non-arising of all phenomena is seen, by him suffering is fully understood;
by whom the non-existence of all phenomena is seen, [by him suffering is fully understood].
His origin has been abandoned;
by him who has seen all phenomena as utterly extinguished, cessation has been realized.
Mañjuśrī, he by whom the non-existence of all phenomena has been seen,
by him the path has been cultivated.
Thus is the detailed exposition.
And it is said in the *Āryadhyāyitamuṣṭi-sūtra*:

"Then the Blessed One said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: 'Mañjuśrī, because they do not see the four noble truths as they really are, the minds of sentient beings are inverted by the four perversions; thus they do not transcend this unreal saṃsāra.'"
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows: “May the Blessed One explain: by grasping at what do sentient beings not transcend cyclic existence?
The Blessed One replied: “Mañjuśrī, it is by grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that sentient beings do not transcend cyclic existence. For what reason?”
Mañjuśrī, for one who perceives both self and other,
there is the formation of karmic actions.
Mañjuśrī, the foolish, unlearned worldling, not understanding that all phenomena are utterly parinirvāṇized, apprehends both self and other.
Having apprehended [an object], one becomes attached; being attached, one becomes lustful, hateful, or deluded.
Being lustful, hateful, and deluded, one performs threefold karma by means of body, speech, and mind.
Through the superimposition of what is unreal, he conceptualizes: "I am lustful," "I am hateful," and "I am deluded."
Having gone forth in the teaching of that Tathāgata, it occurs to him: "I am virtuous; I am a practitioner of the holy life; I shall transcend cyclic existence."
"I shall attain nirvāṇa; I shall be liberated from sufferings.
He conceptualizes: "These phenomena are wholesome."
"These phenomena are unwholesome;
these phenomena are to be abandoned;
these phenomena are to be realized."
Suffering is to be fully understood; its origin is to be abandoned; its cessation is to be realized.
The path is to be cultivated;
he conceives that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and all conditioned phenomena are ablaze.
"What if I were to flee from all conditioned phenomena?
As he reflects in this way, there arises in him a mental attention accompanied by world-weariness and preceded by the signless.
It occurs to him: "This is that full comprehension of suffering."

Regarding this full comprehension of these phenomena, it occurs to him: "I shall indeed abandon the origin. He feels aversion toward all phenomena, feels ashamed of them, recoils from them, feels disgust for them, and becomes terrified, thoroughly terrified, and falls into a state of terror.
It occurs to him: "This is the realization of these phenomena;
this is the abandonment of their origin, namely, the revulsion toward these phenomena."
It occurs to him: "Cessation is to be realized.
Having conceptualized arising, he perceives cessation.
To him it occurs thus: (Pp 226)
This is that realization of cessation.
It occurs to him: "What if I were now to cultivate the path?
Going alone into seclusion, he attends to those phenomena in his mind and attains calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Through that mental attention accompanied by disenchantment, tranquility arises for him.
His mind does not become absorbed in any phenomena; it recoils, turns back, and shrinks away from them, feeling aversion and shame toward them.
A mind of non-rejoicing arises;
he thinks to himself: "I am liberated from all sufferings;
there is nothing further for me to do."
He perceives himself as "I am an Arhat.
At the time of death, he sees his own rebirth among the gods.
Consequently, doubt and uncertainty arise in him regarding the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Having fallen into doubt, he passes away and falls into the great hells.
Why is that?
Because, having conceptualized all dharmas which are unarisen, he gives rise to doubt and uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how, moreover, are the four noble truths to be seen?
The Blessed One replied: "Mañjuśrī, by one who has seen that all phenomena are unarisen, suffering has been fully understood."
For one by whom all phenomena are seen as unarisen, origination has been abandoned;
for one by whom all phenomena are seen as utterly extinguished, [origination has been abandoned].
By him cessation has been realized;
by him who has seen all phenomena as absolutely empty,
the path has been cultivated.
Mañjuśrī, one who has thus seen these four noble truths does not conceptualize: "These phenomena are wholesome; these phenomena are unwholesome."
These phenomena are to be abandoned;
these phenomena are to be realized;
suffering is to be fully understood.
The origin is to be abandoned,
cessation is to be realized,
and the path is to be cultivated.
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive nor apprehend that phenomenon which one might conceptualize;
yet foolish ordinary people, conceptualizing these phenomena, become attached, hostile, and deluded.
He neither constructs nor deconstructs any dharma whatsoever. Because he thus neither constructs nor deconstructs, his mind does not become attached to the triple world;
he perceives the entire triple world as unborn, like an illusion, like a dream, and like an echo.
Seeing all phenomena as having such a nature, he becomes free from attachment and aversion toward all sentient beings.
Why is that?
Because he does not perceive those phenomena in which he might become attached or repelled.
With a mind equal to space, he does not perceive even a Buddha,
he does not perceive even the Dharma,
and he does not perceive even the Saṅgha.
Perceiving all phenomena as empty, he does not give rise to doubt regarding any phenomenon.
Being without doubt, he becomes free from grasping.
Being free from grasping, he attains parinirvāṇa without further clinging; such is the detailed explanation. // 40 //
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Examination of the Noble Truths," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Nirvāṇa, the twenty-fifth chapter.
Here it is said:
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away.
Through the abandonment or through the cessation of what is nirvāṇa intended? // 1 //

For here, the Blessed One has described two kinds of nirvāṇa for those persons who have lived the holy life, who have entered upon the teaching of the Tathāgata, and who are engaged in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma:
that with a remainder of substrate and that without a remainder of substrate.
Among these, nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate is intended through the abandonment of the entire mass of afflictions, such as ignorance, passion, and so forth, without exception.
In this context, "substratum" (*upadhi*) refers to that in which self-attachment is deposited.
By the word "substratum," the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which are the causes for the conceptual designation of a self, are meant.
"Remainder" (*śeṣa*) means that which remains.
The "remainder" is the substratum itself;
that which exists together with this remainder of the substratum is called "with remainder of substratum.
What is that? It is nirvana.

And that remains as nothing but the mere aggregates (*skandha-mātra*), entirely devoid of the thieves of afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); it is analogous to the remaining of a village alone after the entire band of thieves has been slain. That is *nirvāṇa* with a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
But in that *nirvāṇa* where even the five aggregates do not exist, [it is *nirvāṇa* without remainder].
That is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
It is so called because the remainder of the substrates (*upadhi*) has departed from it;
this is by way of analogy with the destruction of even a mere village whose entire band of thieves has been slain.
And with reference to that very state, it is said:
"The body was broken, perception ceased, and all feelings were consumed; mental formations were stilled, and consciousness reached its end."
Likewise:
"With the body not drawn inward, he dwelt upon the feeling;
like the extinguishing of a lamp was the liberation of his mind. Thus it is said.
Thus, this nirvana without remainder is attained through the cessation of the aggregates.
But how is it logical that there are these two kinds of nirvana if there is a cessation of both the afflictions and the aggregates?
For when all this is empty, [how can there be such a distinction]?
When nothing at all arises and nothing at all ceases, then from where could afflictions come, or from where could the aggregates come?
In the cessation of what would there be nirvāṇa?
Therefore, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities certainly exists. // 1 //
To this it is replied: But even so, if one accepts that things possess intrinsic nature—If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
through the abandoning or the cessation of what, then, is nirvāṇa intended? (2)
For since the afflictions and the aggregates, being established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), possess an intrinsic nature that is non-perishing, from what could there be their cessation,
such that through that cessation there might be *nirvāṇa*?
Therefore, for those who maintain the doctrine of intrinsic nature, *nirvāṇa* is simply not tenable.

Furthermore, the proponents of emptiness do not assert that nirvana has the characteristic of the cessation of the aggregates or the characteristic of the cessation of the afflictions, such that this fault would apply to them;
therefore, this criticism is entirely unfounded against the proponents of emptiness. // 2 //
If indeed those who propound emptiness do not accept that nirvana has the characteristic of the cessation of the afflictions or the aggregates, then what characteristic do they accept? It is said:
"Neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal."
Unceasing and unarisen—this is called nirvāṇa. // 3 //
For that which is neither abandoned like passion and so forth,
nor attained like the fruits of asceticism,
nor cut off like the aggregates and so forth—

Furthermore, that which is not eternal, unlike the non-empty, is said to be nirvana— by its very nature unceased and unarisen, characterized by the subsiding of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
How, then, could there be any conceptualization of afflictions (*kleśa*) within such a state free from proliferation, the abandonment of which would constitute nirvana?
Or from where could there be the conceptualization of the aggregates therein, such that through the cessation of those aggregates it [the state of peace] would come to be?
For as long as these conceptualizations proceed, [so long does that state remain unattained].
Until then, there is no attainment of nirvāṇa,
because its attainment occurs only through the complete exhaustion of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
Now, it might be argued: although neither the afflictions nor the aggregates exist in nirvāṇa,
nevertheless they do exist prior to nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, through their complete exhaustion, there will be nirvāṇa.
It is said: "Let this grasping be abandoned."
Because it is impossible to bring about the non-existence of things that exist by way of their own nature prior to nirvāṇa,
this conceptual construction must be abandoned by one who desires nirvāṇa.
For he will say:
"The limit of nirvāṇa and the limit of saṃsāra—
between these two, not even the slightest difference is found.
Thus, it should be understood that in nirvāṇa there is neither the abandonment of anything nor the cessation of anything.
And therefore, nirvāṇa is precisely the nature of the total exhaustion of all conceptual construction.
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"There is the cessation of phenomena, yet there are no phenomena that exist here; those which do not exist here never exist at all."
"For those who possess the conceptual constructions of 'it exists' and 'it does not exist,' suffering does not cease for them while they practice in this way.

This is the meaning of this verse: In cessation, the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), there is the total disappearance of all phenomena—namely, the aggregates (*skandhas*) characterized by afflictions, karma, and birth; thus, their non-existence is indeed accepted by all proponents of philosophical views.
Those phenomena which do not exist here in the state of cessation— just as the fear of a snake in a rope perceived due to darkness is [dispelled] by the arising of a lamp— those never exist at all.
Those phenomena characterized by afflictions, karma, birth, and so forth do not exist in reality at any time, even during the state of saṃsāra.
For a rope does not exist as a snake by way of its own nature even in the state of darkness;
like a truly existent snake, it is not perceived by the body or the eye either in darkness or in light.
If it is asked, "How then does cyclic existence (saṃsāra) come to be? it is said:

To foolish ordinary people who are seized by the false grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, entities that lack an existent nature nevertheless appear as real, just as non-existent hairs, mosquitoes, and the like appear to those with cataracts. As it is said:
"For those who possess the conceptual constructions of 'it exists' and 'it does not exist,' and who move in this way, suffering is not stilled."
The notion that "it exists" belongs to those who conceive of the existence of entities, such as the followers of Jaimini, Kaṇāda, Kapila, and others, up to the Vaibhāṣikas.
The notion that "it does not exist" belongs to the nihilists (*nāstika*) who are intent upon rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*).

Furthermore, there are those other than these who deny the existence of the past, the future, and the formations dissociated from consciousness (*vijñapti-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), while asserting the existence of things other than those.
For those who assert the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
and for those who assert the existence of the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures—
thus, for those who maintain such views of existence and non-existence and act accordingly, the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) does not subside. Likewise:
"Just as one who suspects [something] perceives it as poison, yet it does not enter the stomach nor take hold there;
even so, the fool who is devoid of... is always born and dies, being unreal.
Thus, it should be understood that in this way, for no one is there abandonment in nirvāṇa, nor is there cessation for anyone.
And therefore, nirvāṇa is precisely the nature of the exhaustion of all conceptual construction.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnāvalī*:
"Nirvāṇa is not even non-existence; how much less could there be its cultivation?"
The cessation of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is called nirvāṇa.
Thus [ends the third].

However, for those who, failing to realize that nirvāṇa is of the nature of the cessation of all conceptual construction, instead imagine nirvāṇa to consist of existence, non-existence, both, or neither— it is said in response to them:
"Nirvāṇa is certainly not an entity, for it would then possess the characteristics of old age and death."
For it would follow that there exists an entity without old age and death. // 4 //

In this regard, some who are attached to *nirvāṇa* as a real entity (*bhāva*) declare: "Here, *nirvāṇa* consists of cessation (*nirodha*), which acts like a dam that obstructs the flow of water; it is that which brings about the definitive obstruction of the continuous progression of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth. Furthermore, no phenomenon (*dharma*) lacking an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is ever seen to perform such a function."
But surely it has been said that the destruction, fading away, cessation, and nirvana of this craving accompanied by delight and passion is [nirvana];
and mere destruction cannot be an existing entity. Thus:
"The liberation of his mind is like the extinguishing of a lamp."
Thus it has been said. And it is not tenable that the cessation of a lamp is an existent thing.
It is replied: this should not be understood in that way; "the destruction of craving" (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*) means the exhaustion of craving.
Rather, it should be said that "the destruction of craving" exists when there is the phenomenon called nirvana, because within it the destruction of craving occurs;
and the lamp is merely an illustration.
In that case as well, it should be understood that liberation of the mind occurs when this [condition] is present.
When nirvāṇa is thus established as an existent entity (bhāva), the Master examines it: first of all, nirvāṇa is not an existent entity.
What is the reason?
Because [if it were], it would follow that it possesses the characteristics of old age and death.
Because an entity is never dissociated from the characteristics of aging and death;
consequently, that [nirvāṇa] would not be nirvāṇa at all,
because it would possess the characteristics of aging and death, just like consciousness.
This is the intended meaning.
Clarifying that very fact of the non-deviation from the characteristics of aging and death, he says: "For there is no entity without aging and death.
For that which is devoid of aging and death cannot possibly exist as an entity at all.
It is like a flower in the sky, because it is devoid of old age and death. // 4 //
Furthermore:
If nirvāṇa were an entity, nirvāṇa would be conditioned; for no entity whatsoever exists anywhere that is unconditioned. (5)
If nirvāṇa were an existent entity, then that nirvāṇa would be conditioned, because it would possess the nature of an entity, like consciousness and so forth.
But that which is unconditioned is not an entity, just like the horn of a donkey; thus, demonstrating the negative concomitance (vyatireka), he says:
For no unconditioned entity exists anywhere;
"anywhere" refers to the locus— whether in space, time, or philosophical tenet—
and "any" refers to the thing contained therein.
The meaning is: whether internal or external. // 5 //
Furthermore:
If nirvāṇa were an existent entity, how could it be non-dependent? For indeed, no existent entity whatsoever exists that is not dependent. (6)

If, according to your view, nirvāṇa were an existent thing (bhāva), it would exist by depending upon something; that is to say, it would exist by relying on its own collection of causes (svakāraṇasāmagrī).
And nirvāṇa is not intended in this way as being dependent;
rather, it is independent.
Therefore, if nirvāṇa were an entity that is independent, [it would follow that it is a conditioned thing].
How, then, could there be nirvāṇa?
It could not exist without appropriation, because it would be an entity.
Like consciousness and so forth.
He states the reason for their distinction: "For no entity whatsoever exists without depending [on something else]. (6)
Here it is said: If nirvāṇa is indeed not an existent thing, because of the consequence of the faults already mentioned, then what is it? Is nirvāṇa simply a non-existent thing?
Is it because it is merely the cessation of afflictions and birth? It is replied:
this too is incorrect, because— if nirvāṇa is not an entity, what will non-entity be?
In that which is nirvāṇa, neither being nor non-being exists. // 7 //
If nirvāṇa is not accepted as an existent thing,
and if nirvāṇa is not accepted as being an existent thing, then will nirvāṇa be a non-existent thing?
The meaning is that even non-existence will not exist.
If it is argued that the non-existence of afflictions and birth is nirvāṇa, then in that case, (Pp_231)
Nirvana would be the impermanence of afflictions and birth;
for impermanence itself is the non-existence of afflictions and birth, and nothing else.
Therefore, impermanence itself would be nirvana.
And this is not accepted, because it would entail the consequence that liberation occurs without effort; this has already been stated. // 7 //
Furthermore:
If nirvana were a non-entity, how could it be non-dependent? For there exists no such thing as a non-entity that occurs without dependence. (8)
In that regard, non-existence or impermanence is designated in dependence upon existence,
because impermanence is not perceived in things such as the horns of a donkey;
and the characterized object is designated in dependence upon its characteristic.
And the characteristic depends upon the characterized object;
therefore, since the operation of the characterized object and its characteristic is mutually dependent, how could impermanence exist in dependence upon an existent characterized object?
Consequently, even non-existence is designated dependently.
Therefore, if nirvāṇa were non-existence,
how could nirvāṇa exist without depending [on something]? It would exist only by depending [on something].
Because it is a non-entity, like destruction.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "For there is no such thing as a non-entity that exists without depending [on something else]."
If, then, non-existence does not exist without a basis,
on what basis will non-existents such as the son of a barren woman now come to be?
By whom was it said that the son of a barren woman and so forth are non-existents?
For it was said previously:
"If an entity is not established, then non-existence is certainly not established;
for people describe the alteration of an entity as non-existence."
Therefore, the son of a barren woman and such things do not possess the status of non-existence.
As for what is also said:
"Space, the horn of a hare, and the son of a barren woman..."
"And just as non-existent things are spoken of, so too is conceptualization regarding entities";
even in that case, there is merely a negation of the conceptualization of existence, not a conceptualization of non-existence.
It should be understood that this is precisely because its existence is unestablished;
the expression "son of a barren woman" is a mere word, for no referent for it is perceived.
Regarding that object which might possess either existence or non-existence:
how could the conceptualization of existence or non-existence be appropriate for something whose intrinsic nature is not perceived?
Therefore, it should be understood that the son of a barren woman is not a non-entity.
And therefore, it remains established that there is no non-existence which exists without depending [on something]. // 8 //
Here it is asked: if nirvāṇa is neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing, then what is nirvāṇa? It is said in reply:

For here it has been taught by the Blessed Tathāgatas: "That which is the state of coming and going, whether by way of grasping or dependent origination—that is taught to be Nirvana when there is no longer grasping and no longer dependent origination. (9)
In this context, "the state of coming and going" (ājavaṃjavībhāva) means the succession of births and deaths consisting of the process of arriving and departing.
Furthermore, this state of coming and going is sometimes designated as "existing" by depending on the totality of causes and conditions, like the relationship between long and short;
and it is sometimes designated as "arising," like the light of a lamp or a seed and its sprout.
In every respect, whether this is established as being designated by way of appropriation (*upādāya prajñapyate*), or as arising dependently (*pratītya jāyate*),
the non-occurrence of this continuous succession of birth and death— either without dependence or without appropriation— is its nirvāṇa. (Pp_232)
It is established that mere non-occurrence cannot be conceptualized as either an entity or a non-entity;
thus, nirvāṇa is neither an entity nor a non-entity.
Alternatively, for those who hold the position that it is the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that transmigrate,
that which is their arising and perishing through successive dependencies, when it no longer proceeds through such dependencies, is called *nirvāṇa*.

However, for those who maintain that a person (pudgala) transmigrates, since that person is inexpressible as either permanent or impermanent, the state of coming and going (ājavañjavībhāva) occurs by depending upon various respective appropriations (upādāna).
That very process, while proceeding through successive appropriations, is designated as "nirvāṇa" when it no longer proceeds without appropriation at this present time.
Furthermore, it is not possible to conceptualize the mere non-occurrence of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) or of the person (*pudgala*) as either existence or non-existence.
For this reason as well, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence. (9)
Furthermore:
The Teacher has taught the abandonment of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence. (10)

Regarding this, it is said in the Sūtra: "O monks, whatever recluses seek liberation from existence through further existence, or through non-existence, that is for them a lack of full comprehension."
For both of these must be abandoned: craving for existence and craving for non-existence. Yet this nirvana was not said by the Blessed One to be something to be abandoned;
rather, it is that which is not to be abandoned.
Therefore, if nirvana were of the nature of an entity or of the nature of a non-entity,
it too would have to be abandoned;
yet it is not to be abandoned.
Therefore, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence.

To demonstrate that for those who hold that nirvāṇa is of both natures— being of the nature of non-existence because afflictions and birth are absent therein, yet being of the nature of existence because it itself is of the nature of existence— their position that nirvāṇa is of both natures is untenable, he says:
If nirvāṇa were both existence and non-existence, then liberation would be both existence and non-existence; and that is not tenable. (11)
If nirvāṇa were of the nature of both existence and non-existence, then it would follow that both existence and non-existence constitute liberation;
and consequently, there would be both the acquisition of a self-nature by conditioned phenomena and their subsequent disappearance.
That itself would be liberation;
however, it is not tenable that the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) alone are liberation.
Therefore, he says: "And that is not tenable. (11)
Furthermore:
If nirvāṇa were both an existent and a non-existent, then nirvāṇa would not be non-dependent; for that [pair] is dependent upon both. (12)
If nirvāṇa were of the nature of existence or non-existence, then it would exist by depending upon and relying on a collection of causes and conditions, not without such dependence.
What is the reason?
Because both of those exist dependently;
that is, non-existence exists in dependence upon existence.
And since existence depends upon non-existence,
both of these— existence and non-existence— come to be only by depending [on each other],
not without depending.
In this way, nirvāṇa would consist of both existence and non-existence;
but since this is not the case, it is not tenable. // 12 //
Furthermore:
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
Nirvāṇa is unconditioned, whereas existence and non-existence are conditioned. (13)

For an existent thing (*bhāva*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) because it arises from the totality of its own causes and conditions; likewise, a non-existent thing (*abhāva*) is also conditioned because it arises in dependence upon an existent thing,
and because of the scriptural statement that "aging and death have birth as their condition."
If, therefore, nirvāṇa were to have the nature of existence or non-existence, then it would not be unconditioned; rather, it would be precisely conditioned.
Since it is not accepted as conditioned, therefore it is not logical for nirvāṇa to have the nature of either existence or non-existence. // 13 //
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Nirvana is certainly not of the nature of existence or non-existence;
rather, existence and non-existence are within nirvana.
Even so, this is not tenable.
Why? Because:
How could both non-existence and existence exist in nirvāṇa? Their coexistence in a single place is impossible, just like that of light and darkness. (14)

Since existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, cannot both occur in a single place such as nirvāṇa, it follows that how could both existence and non-existence exist in nirvāṇa? The intended meaning is that they simply could not exist. // 14 //
Now, demonstrating how it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence, he says:
"The teaching that nirvāṇa is neither non-existence nor existence..."
And both in non-existence and in existence, that [emptiness] is established when these two are established. // 15 //
For if there were such a thing as an entity,
then by its negation this conceptualization— that nirvana is not an entity— would be possible; likewise,
if there were some non-entity, [then its negation would be possible].
In that case, by the negation of that [existence], nirvāṇa could not be non-existence;
and when both existence and non-existence do not exist, then their negation also does not exist.
Therefore, even the conceptualization that "nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence" is not tenable;
thus, this [position] is not logical. // 15 //
Furthermore:
If nirvana exists as neither non-existence nor existence, by what means is it characterized as "neither non-existence nor existence"? (16)

If it is conceived that this nirvāṇa exists neither as a non-entity nor as an entity, then by what means is it indicated, grasped, or manifested that such a nirvāṇa, which possesses neither form, exists?
Is there some such cognizer present within that nirvāṇa, or is there none?

If it exists, then even in nirvāṇa your self would exist; but this is not accepted, because a self devoid of appropriation does not exist. If, on the other hand, it does not exist, by whom is it determined that such a nirvāṇa exists?
If it is argued that one who abides in saṃsāra discerns,
then if one who abides in saṃsāra discerns, does he discern by means of consciousness?
Or by knowledge?
If it is conceived that it is by consciousness (*vijñāna*),
that is not tenable.
What is the reason?
Because consciousness has a sign as its object,
and there is no sign whatsoever in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, that [object] is not apprehended by consciousness;
it is not even known by cognition.
What is the reason?
Since knowledge must indeed have emptiness as its object, and that [emptiness] is of the very nature of non-arising,
how can nirvana— which is neither non-existence nor existence— be grasped by means of that [knowledge] whose own nature is non-existent?

Because knowledge has a nature that transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), therefore nirvāṇa is not designated by anyone as being neither non-existence nor existence. Since it is thus uncharacterized, unmanifested, and ungraspable, it is not tenable to say that "it exists. // 16 //

Demonstrating that just as these four conceptual constructions do not occur in any way whatsoever regarding *nirvāṇa*, so too these conceptual constructions do not occur at all regarding the Tathāgata who has attained *nirvāṇa*, he says:
"It is not conceived that the Blessed One exists after cessation."
It is not both, nor is it neither; thus it is not conceived.
For it was said previously:
"But one who is seized by the dense grasp of conceptualization, imagining that the Tathāgata exists or does not exist, would be conceptualizing regarding the one who has attained parinirvāṇa."
Thus, first of all, it is not conjectured that the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after cessation.
Because of the non-existence of these two, it is also not conjectured that he is both.
Precisely because of the non-existence of both, it is not conjectured nor apprehended that he is neither. // 17 //

And it is not only after his final cessation that the Blessed One cannot be conceived in four ways; moreover—even while remaining, the Blessed One is not conceived as "existing," nor as "not existing," nor as "both," nor as "neither. // 18 //
Just as clarified butter is neither to be poured nor to be offered, so it has been demonstrated in the *Tathāgataparīkṣā*. // 18 //
Therefore:
There is no distinction whatsoever of saṃsāra from nirvāṇa;
there is no distinction whatsoever of nirvāṇa from saṃsāra. (19)

Because the Blessed One is not conceived as "existing" even while remaining [in this world], nor is he conceived as "existing" and so forth even when he has entered final nirvana, for that very reason there is no distinction whatsoever between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Because the two, when investigated, are of an identical nature;
and as for that which was said by the Blessed One— "O monks, the saṃsāra of birth, old age, and death is indeed without beginning or end"— that too is established for this very reason.
Because there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. // 19 //
For it is thus:
"The limit of nirvāṇa and the limit of saṃsāra—between these two, not even the slightest difference exists. (20)

And it is not only because cyclic existence is indistinguishable from nirvāṇa that the conceptualization of prior and posterior limits is impossible; for those views as well—namely, the views concerning what is beyond cessation, the extremes, and eternalism and so forth—which rely upon the future limit [of nirvāṇa] and the prior limit [of cyclic existence]. (21)
These [distinctions] also do not hold for this very reason,
because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are of a single flavor due to their being quiescent by nature.
In this context, by the phrase "beyond cessation" (*paraṃ nirodhāt*), four views are included as illustrations:
namely, that the Tathāgata exists after death,
or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
these four views proceed from the grasping of nirvāṇa.
There are also views concerning the finite and so forth,
such as: "the world is finite," or "it is infinite."
"The world is finite," "the world is infinite," "the world is both finite and infinite," and "the world is neither finite nor infinite"—
these four views proceed by relying upon the future limit (*aparānta*).

In that regard, not seeing the future arising of either oneself or the world, one proceeds by taking hold of the future limit while conceptualizing, "The world is finite. Likewise, seeing the future arising, one proceeds [with the thought], "The world is infinite.
Thus, both seeing and not seeing, one engages in both ways.
By the negation of both, one realizes that it is neither finite nor infinite;
[namely,] "the world is eternal" and "the world is non-eternal."
"The world is eternal and non-eternal; the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal"— these four views proceed by relying upon the prior limit.
In that regard, seeing the past arising of either oneself or the world, one concludes that the world is eternal;
not seeing it, one concludes it is non-eternal; and both seeing and not seeing it, one concludes it is both eternal and non-eternal.
Neither seeing nor not seeing, one does not maintain that "it is neither eternal nor non-eternal" by relying on the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
How, then, are these views tenable?
If some entity possessed some intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [these views would be possible].
From the conceptualization of its existence or non-existence, these views would arise.
But when it has been established that there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, then— since all phenomena are empty— what is infinite and what is finite?
Is it both infinite and finite? Or is it neither infinite nor finite? 22.
Is it that very same thing, or is it something else? Is it eternal, or is it non-eternal? Or is it both non-eternal and eternal, or neither of these two? // 23 //
These fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) are not at all tenable if the intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvarūpa*) of things does not exist.
However, for one who superimposes an intrinsic nature onto things and, based on their disappearance or non-disappearance, gives rise to these views and becomes attached to them,
this attachment blocks the path leading to the city of Nirvāṇa.
And it should be understood that it subjects one to the sufferings of saṃsāra. // 23 //
Here he says: If even *nirvāṇa* has been thus refuted by you,

then surely that which was undertaken by the Blessed One— who follows the infinite multitudes of beings in their various conducts, who knows the nature and intentions of the entire world without error, who is dependent upon great compassion, and whose love for all people of the three worlds is like that for an only beloved son— [was it not] in accordance with the remedies for their conduct?
The Dharma has been taught for the sake of attaining nirvāṇa for the world;
if that were so, it would become utterly futile.
It is said in response: if there were such a thing as "Dharma" by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [it would be futile].
And some beings might be hearers of that Dharma, or perhaps the Buddha, the Blessed One, who teaches it, might be an entity possessing an intrinsic nature;
this might indeed be so. But when—
The cessation of all apprehension, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, is auspicious.
Nowhere, to no one, has any dharma been taught by the Buddha. (24)
In that case, how could the aforementioned consequence of faults apply to us?
For here, nirvāṇa is the subsiding—that is, the non-occurrence—of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and signs (*nimitta*).
And that very subsiding is auspicious (*śiva*), because it is by its very nature already quiescent.

It is "peaceful" (*śiva*) because of the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) due to the non-occurrence of speech, or because of the non-occurrence of the mind; it is "peaceful" because of the non-occurrence of afflictions (*kleśa*), or because of the non-occurrence of birth; or it is "peaceful" as the cessation of conceptual proliferation through the abandonment of afflictions when the latencies (*vāsanā*) have been abandoned without remainder.
Through the non-apprehension of the knowable, there is the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); through the non-apprehension of knowledge, there is peace (*śiva*).

And when the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, abide in that peaceful Nirvana—the nature of which is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation—by means of the yoga of non-abiding, like king swans in the sky, or like [birds] in the wind-sky driven by the wind of the accumulation of their own merit and wisdom, because of the sky’s state of possessing nothing;

Then, because no signs whatsoever are perceived, it should be understood that nothing has been taught—neither among gods nor among humans, nor for any god or human, nor any dharma, whether pertaining to affliction (*saṃkleśika*) or to purification (*vaiyavadānika*).
As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, from the very night the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."

And during the interval between the night he attained [enlightenment] without grasping and the night he will enter final nirvana, not even a single syllable has been uttered, spoken, or pronounced by the Tathāgata, nor will it ever be pronounced; yet,
according to their inclinations, all sentient beings— with their various elements and dispositions— perceive those diverse words of the Tathāgata as they issue forth.
To each of them it occurs individually: "The Blessed One teaches this Dharma to us, and we hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma.
In that regard, the Tathāgata neither conceptualizes nor discriminates.
"For, Śāntamati, the Tathāgata is indeed free from the conceptual proliferation of the latencies of all nets of discursive thought and mental construction," thus it is said at length.
Likewise:
"Those who know that all phenomena are inexpressible, beyond syllables, entirely empty, peaceful, and pure from the beginning— they are called a Buddha, a youth."
If, then, no dharma whatsoever has been taught by the Buddha to anyone anywhere, how is it that these various conventional expressions of the teaching are perceived? It is said:

for embodied beings who are pursued by the sleep of ignorance and are as if dreaming, this is merely the arising of their own conceptual constructions—[namely], "This Blessed One, the lord of all the gods, asuras, and humans of the three worlds, [has taught] this Dharma to us..."
"He teaches" means as it was said by the Blessed One:
"For the Tathāgata is the reflection of wholesome, untainted phenomena."
"Neither suchness nor a Tathāgata exists here; yet an image is seen throughout the entire world.
This has been explained in detail in the *Tathāgataguhyaka-parivarta*.
Consequently, since there is no teaching of the Dharma for the sake of nirvāṇa, how could the existence of nirvāṇa come to be through the existence of the teaching of the Dharma?
Therefore, it is established that even nirvāṇa does not exist.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "Indeed, non-nirvāṇa is what has been taught as nirvāṇa by the Lord of the World."
"A knot tied by space is released by space alone.
Likewise: "O Blessed One, those who seek nirvāṇa as a substantial entity do not transcend saṃsāra.
For what reason?"
“Blessed One, that which is called ‘nirvāṇa’ is the pacification of all signs and the cessation of all mental agitation and movement.

Blessed One, those deluded persons who, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, fall into the views of the non-Buddhists and seek nirvāṇa as a substantial entity— just as one seeks oil from sesame seeds or clarified butter from milk— are truly deluded.”
"Blessed One, since all dharmas are already in a state of ultimate parinirvāṇa, those who seek nirvāṇa—I call them conceited heretics.
Blessed One, a practitioner of yoga who has correctly entered the path does not bring about the arising or the cessation of any dharma;
nor does he desire the attainment of any dharma, nor its realization," and so forth in detail.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Examination of Nirvāṇa," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of the Twelve Links, the twenty-sixth chapter.
Here it is said:
"That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness."
"That dependent designation is itself the middle way.
But what is this dependent origination which is called emptiness?
Alternatively, as it has been said:
"He who sees dependent origination sees this:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path itself."
What, then, is this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)?
Therefore, with the intention of explaining its specific divisions, it is said:
"For the sake of renewed existence, one who is obscured by ignorance performs threefold formative forces (saṃskāra)."
Whatever actions one performs through volitional formations, it is by those karmas that one goes to a [particular] destiny. // 1 //
In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is non-knowing, darkness that obscures the reality of things as they are, and a state of stagnation.

A person (*pudgala*) who is shrouded—that is, covered—by ignorance performs (*abhisaṃskaroti*) and brings about (*utpādayati*) specific volitions, such as wholesome ones, for the sake of renewed existence (*punarbhava*), for the purpose of renewed existence, and for the sake of the arising of renewed existence; because these perform the formation of renewed existence, they are called "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*).
And these are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable;
or alternatively, bodily, vocal, and mental.
A person, obscured by ignorance, performs those three types of formative forces characterized as karma.
And by means of those conditioned formative forces, which are designated as karma, one goes to a destination caused by them. // 1 //
Then, his consciousness descends into a state of existence conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

For this person who has performed and accumulated formative forces, consciousness—which has formative forces as its cause—descends, enters, and arises in a state of existence corresponding to those formative forces, such as the realm of the gods; it becomes the seed for the misfortunes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Thereafter, once consciousness has become established, name-and-form is infused. (2)

In this context, it is called "name" (*nāma*) because, impelled by karma and afflictions, it bends (*namayati*) toward this or that place of rebirth; or, it is called "name" because it bends toward objects by means of perception (*saṃjñā*). The four formless aggregates (*skandha*) are designated as "name."
It is called "form" (rūpa) because it is affected (rūpyate); the meaning is that it is afflicted.
And this form, together with the aforementioned name, [constitute the aggregate of form].
These two taken together are established as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
In this regard, according to the analogy of a reflection in a mirror, or the analogies of recitation, a lamp, a seal and its impression, and so forth,
when the aggregates at the moment of death cease, in that very same instant, by the analogy of the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale, the factors pertaining to rebirth arise.
The aggregates arise through the projection of karma;
and thus dependent origination is established by way of the analogy of the reflection and its image, or the seal and its impression.
However, as for what was stated regarding consciousness "descending" by way of the analogy of the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale:
That is said in accordance with the understanding of the world of the ignorant,
that the reconnection of existence occurs at the very same time;
likewise, for the world, suffering and the arising of happiness occur simultaneously.

"May there always be the power to both take away and to create, just as the sun possesses both darkness and light. However, it is not appropriate for those who are discerning of the true nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) to speak in this way— claiming that [arising and ceasing] exist simultaneously in a single moment through association, using the analogy of the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale— for if this [entity] were not yet existent while tending toward birth, and even if it were existent while tending toward destruction, it would be that which is currently ceasing.
In that case, how could this [world] be equal to that which is desired [as the cause], since it lacks an agent? Furthermore, this production [of the world] would not be logical.
Because of such statements as these:
just as you do not accept momentariness according to the logic of the original object and its reflection, or the seal and its impression,
so too it is not logical for any other entity that perishes immediately after arising to possess momentariness.

For the scriptural teaching of the Abhidharma states that the four conditioned characteristics—known as birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—occur in a single moment for any entity, whether external or internal, as it arises.

In this regard, since birth and aging are mutually contradictory, and since duration and impermanence cannot coexist in a single entity at the same time, the wise do not accept their simultaneous occurrence.
Furthermore, if everything were momentary, how could there be any state of antiquity, given that [the entity] would have ceased to exist entirely?
Furthermore, if [the entity] were non-momentary due to its stability, how could there be any antiquity whatsoever?
Just as there is an end to a moment, so too should its beginning and middle be conceived;
since the moment itself has an end, the world does not endure for even a single moment.
The beginning, middle, and end must further be considered as being like a moment;
for the state of having a beginning, middle, and end exists neither from itself nor from another.

Thus, from the reading of the Madhyamaka tenets, it should be understood that because momentary entities are not established, [the opponent's argument] is unestablished. Furthermore, birth and death, which possess mutually distinct characteristics, cannot possibly occur in a single moment— just as, for example, doubt and certain knowledge, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, seed and sprout, or the state of death and the state of rebirth, all of which possess distinct characteristics.

Coexistence is logical only for two things that are mutually independent and established by their own causes and conditions, such as the left and right horns of a cow, a youth and his son, or the ears of a donkey;
it is never possible, however, for two mutually contradictory states, such as destruction and arising.
As it was said in the *Rāgaraktaparīkṣā*:
Furthermore, it is not logical for passion and the impassioned one to arise simultaneously; for if they were to exist thus, passion and the impassioned one would be independent of each other.
In identity there is no coexistence, for a thing does not exist together with itself;
if there were separateness, how indeed could coexistence arise?
Thus, the establishment of passion through that which is impassioned occurs neither together with it nor apart from it;
as with passion, so too for all phenomena, their establishment occurs neither together with them nor apart from them.
Since there is such a prohibition, how could there be simultaneity between the existence at death and the existence at rebirth for living beings?
Therefore, it is observed that the notion of their coexistence proceeds solely out of consideration for the understanding of those to be trained.
Consequently, the lowering and raising of a scale do not occur in a single moment, because there is a difference in time between the lowering and the raising.

According to the scriptural passage stating that sixty-five moments pass with the mere snap of a strong man's fingers— just as when piercing a hundred thousand lotus petals with the point of a needle—
it should nevertheless be understood here that the piercing of a hundred thousand lotus petals by the point of a needle occurs sequentially, because moments are exceedingly subtle.
In a single moment, like the illustration of the syllables and words of a verse.
Furthermore:
neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal,
not a unity nor a plurality, neither coming nor going.

By the reading, "That which is dependent origination, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, the auspicious," the absolute impossibility of arising and ceasing is established in the *Madhyamaka* treatise.
In the *Āgama* sūtras—
The world is undestroyed and unarisen, equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
yet he teaches it as the realm of sentient beings—this is his conformity with the world.
"In the three times, one does not perceive the intrinsic nature of sentient beings;
yet one teaches the realm of sentient beings—this is conformity with the world," and so forth.
Likewise:
Form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a bubble; perception is similar to a mirage, mental formations resemble a plantain tree,
and consciousness is like an illusion— thus it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun.
"Beholding phenomena in this way, a monk who has initiated vigor— whether by day or by night— being clearly comprehending and mindful,
shall penetrate the peaceful state, the auspicious stilling of all conditioned formations. Thus it is said.
These verses are recited in all the Nikāyas, Śāstras, and Sūtras.

Therefore, regarding things such as a mass of foam—which have arisen dependently upon the assembly of causes and conditions and are devoid of any substantial essence—how can there be any consideration of whether they are momentary or non-momentary?
And in the Mahāyāna Sūtras:
All states of existence are like a dream; indeed, no one is born and no one dies.
Yet, an action once committed never perishes; whether dark or bright, it yields its fruit for one wandering in saṃsāra.
It is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation; there is no further accumulation of karma, nor is there any persistence.
One who has performed an action does not experience its result again, nor does another who did not perform it experience it.
Just as a young girl might see in a dream her own son born and then dead—
exceedingly joyful at his birth and distressed at his death— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as various auspicious and inauspicious actions proceed from seeing a letter in another village,
yet no transfer of that letter occurs through speech, know all phenomena to be like that.
From a seal, a counter-seal is seen, yet no transfer of the seal is perceived; it is not there, nor is it from anywhere else.
In this same way, conditioned phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Just as when a seed exists there is a sprout, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout;
it is neither different from it nor is it exactly that—such is the nature of phenomena, characterized by neither annihilation nor permanence.

Just as a rope is fashioned from muñja grass and balbaja grass through the power of exertion, and the water-wheel with its mechanism turns, yet within each of those individual parts there is no turning; so it is here.
Likewise, that which exists within all factors of existence depends upon mutual accumulation;
though it proceeds through each of these factors individually, neither a beginning nor an end is perceived.
Therefore, it has been said by the venerable master Nāgārjuna:

"The reconnection of the aggregates and the absence of transmigration are to be understood by the wise through the analogies of recitation, a lamp, a seal, a mirror, a sound, a sun-gem, a seed, and sourness."
And in the *Śatakaśāstra*, the venerable Āryadeva, established in the firm setting of the practice of great awakening,
stated: "Existence is like a whirling firebrand, a magical creation, a dream, an illusion, the moon reflected in water,
mist, an echo, a mirage, and a cloud."

Thus, by the analogy of the reflection and its original object, when consciousness has coalesced (*saṃmūrcchita*) in the mother’s womb, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is infused (*niṣicyate*), meaning it flows forth or manifests, conditioned by consciousness.
If consciousness were not to coalesce here in this state of existence, [name-and-form would not arise].
Then the manifestation of name-and-form would not occur.
If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, that embryo (kalala) would not develop into the state of an embryo.
Because of this statement. // 2 //
Thus, when name-and-form has been infused, the six sense bases arise:
through the nature of being doors for the production of suffering, the six sense bases— known as sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and mind— originate with name-and-form as their cause.

Having seen forms with the eye, he becomes attached to those things that are a basis for mental pleasure; being thus attached, he performs actions born of attachment, hatred, and delusion. In this way, through such a process, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) serve as the gateway for the arising of suffering. Thus, once the six sense bases have come into existence, at a subsequent time—
Dependent upon the six sense bases, contact comes into being. // 3 //
Explaining what this contact is and how it arises, he says:
"Depending upon the eye, visible forms, and attention..."
In this way, consciousness proceeds in dependence upon name-and-form. // 4 //
That which is the contact (*sparśa*) resulting from the conjunction of these three— the eye, form, and consciousness— is the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

Depending upon the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), forms (*rūpa*), and attention (*manaskāra*)— which is distinct from the object and so forth and serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) that constitutes the seed of consciousness— visual consciousness arises.
In this context, the eye and the sphere of visible form constitute "form" (rūpa),
while the mental attention (samanvāhāra) characterized by the four aggregates constitutes "name" (nāman).
Eye-consciousness, which arises in dependence upon these three, arises in dependence upon name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Thus, the conjunction of these three— the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness— which is their simultaneous arising and their equal engagement through mutual assistance,
is contact (*sparśa*) characterized by touching.
Following that, in subsequent time—
From that contact, feeling arises. // 5 //
The experience of objects—whether desirable, undesirable, or neither—is called *vedanā*, *vitti*, or "feeling.
It is threefold: painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
And just as this [occurs] by depending on contact (*sparśa*), which is characterized by the coming together of these three—the object, consciousness, and the eye—(Pp 243)
Feeling has been explained;
in the same way, feeling—characterized by the conjunction of the remaining triad of faculty, object, and consciousness—should be understood as having contact as its cause. // 5 //
Thereafter,
it continues: "With feeling as condition, craving arises."
That craving for which feeling is the condition is "conditioned by feeling. But what is the object of that craving?
It has feeling alone as its object.
What is the reason?
Because that one who is thirsty thirsts for the sake of feeling.
The meaning is that one forms a longing for the very sign of feeling. How so?
First, if a pleasant feeling arises for him...
He thirsts again and again for the sake of union with that [pleasure];
if it is suffering,
then he thirsts for the sake of separation from it.
Then there is that which is neither painful nor pleasant;
one also craves for the sake of never falling away from that. Craving in this way, he grasps the fourfold grasping. (6)

Thus, being thus attached and clinging to sensations, he grasps the fourfold cause that projects karma—known as the grasping of desire, views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self—which has craving as its condition.
In this way, for him, grasping occurs with craving as its condition. 6.
Thereafter, when there is grasping, existence proceeds for the grasper.
For if one were liberated without grasping, existence would not come to be. (7)
Those five aggregates are "existence" (bhava); they are the appropriator, the grasper, and the producer of the four kinds of appropriation as previously described.
For that appropriator, existence arises with appropriation as its condition.
What is the reason? Because he who has not produced craving for sensation, by the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) refusing to accept craving,
and having abandoned the fourfold grasping (*upādāna*), would indeed be liberated if, through the manifestation of stainless non-dual gnosis (*jñāna*), he were to become a non-grasper.
At that time, there would be no further becoming for him.
What, then, is this existence (bhava)?
It is the five aggregates; and that existence is that which proceeds from grasping (upādāna).
It should be understood that its intrinsic nature consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Furthermore, because bodily, vocal, and mental karma of all three types give rise to the future pentad of aggregates, it is designated as "existence" (*bhava*).
Among these, bodily and vocal karma have the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature, because they are informative actions (*karmavijñapti*).
The mental [existence], however, has the four aggregates as its intrinsic nature. Thus, that existence should be understood as consisting of the five aggregates. From that existence, birth proceeds.
Birth is the arising of the future aggregates;
and that proceeds from existence (*bhava*).
Thereafter—
The suffering of old age, death, and so forth, as well as grief together with lamentation. // 8 //
Mental distress and despair proceed from this birth;
these factors, such as old age, death, and so forth, proceed with birth as their cause.
Their explanation should be understood exactly as it is in the Sūtra.
In that context, the maturation of the aggregates is aging; the disintegration of the aged aggregates is death;
and the heart-rending anguish of one who is dying, departing, and deluded, accompanied by attachment, is sorrow.
Lamentation is the outpouring of words arising from sorrow. Suffering is the onset of affliction for the five sense faculties. Mental distress is the onset of affliction for the mind.
"Distractions (upāyāsas) arise from the abundance of suffering and mental distress.
Thus, by the principle as it has been described:
In this way, there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering, which is nothing other than this alone. // 9 //
"Of the solitary" means of that which is devoid of the nature of self and what belongs to self, being merely imagined by foolish ordinary people;
the meaning is that it consists solely of suffering, unmixed with pleasure.
"In this way" means solely through the power of causes and conditions.
"Of the mass of suffering" means of the accumulation of suffering, the collection of suffering, the heap of suffering; such is the meaning. // 9 //

And since the activity of the factors of existence proceeds precisely from ignorance and so forth as described above, therefore: "Because the ignorant person forms the volitional formations which are the root of saṃsāra, the ignorant one is the agent; the wise one is not, because of his vision of reality. (10)
In this context, the root—the primary cause—of saṃsāra, which is characterized by the activity of consciousness and so forth, is the formative forces (*saṃskāras*).
Consequently, the ignorant person constructs those formative forces that are the root of saṃsāra.
Monks, a person who is followed by ignorance performs meritorious formations,
performs non-meritorious formations, and also performs imperturbable formations.
Thus, according to the word of the Blessed One, since it is the ignorant one who is the agent,
therefore it is the ignorant person alone who becomes the agent of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The wise one who perceives reality has abandoned ignorance. Why is this?

Because of the perception of reality; for when reality is perceived, since no entities whatsoever are apprehended, there is nothing at all that one could take as an object and perform an action toward. // 10 //
And since it is thus that formations proceed only when ignorance exists and do not proceed when it does not exist, therefore:
when ignorance has ceased, there is the non-arising of formations.
Because the cause would otherwise be purposeless.
To the question, "From what, then, does that ignorance cease? he says:
"But the cessation of ignorance comes from the cultivation of the very knowledge of this [truth]. (11)
Through the cultivation of this very dependent origination exactly as it is and without error, ignorance is abandoned;
for he who correctly perceives dependent origination does not perceive the intrinsic nature of even the subtlest entity.
Just like a reflection, a dream, a firebrand wheel, or a mirage, he enters into the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena.
Having thus entered into the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, he does not perceive any entity whatsoever, whether external or internal.
Not perceiving anything, he is not deluded regarding any phenomenon.
And one who is undeluded does not perform [unwholesome] action;
thus, through the cultivation of dependent origination, one enters into reality.
For the yogi who perceives reality, ignorance is necessarily abandoned.
For one whose ignorance has been abandoned, the formative forces cease. // 11 //

And just as through the cessation of ignorance the formative forces cease, so too—through the cessation of each respective factor, that respective factor no longer proceeds; in this way, this entire mass of suffering is completely ceased. (12)

It should be understood that through the cessation of each preceding factor, there occurs the cessation of each subsequent factor. By this sequence, this practitioner— having abandoned attachment through the vision of neither self nor what belongs to a self— correctly brings about the non-arising and total cessation of the mass of suffering, which is devoid of an agent or an experiencer and empty of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, as it is stated in the *Ārya-Śālistamba-sūtra*:
In this way, internal dependent origination also arises from exactly two causes.
From which two? From causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) and from conditional connection (*pratyayopanibandha*).
In that regard, what is the causal connection of internal dependent origination?
It is this: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
If ignorance did not exist, volitional formations would not be discerned;
and so on, until: if birth did not exist, aging and death would not be discerned.
Alternatively, when ignorance exists, the manifestation of the formative forces occurs;
likewise, up until when birth exists, the manifestation of old age and death occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to ignorance: "I am bringing about the formative forces."
Nor does it occur to the formative forces (saṃskāra) that "we have been produced by ignorance.
Likewise, up to birth, it does not occur to birth that "I am producing old age and death.
Nor does it occur to old age and death that "I have been produced by birth."
And yet, when ignorance exists, there is the production and manifestation of the formative forces;
likewise, up to: when birth exists, there is the production and manifestation of aging and death.
In this way, the causal connection of internal dependent origination is to be understood.
How is the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination to be viewed? It is through the coming together of the six elements. Through the coming together of which six elements?
That is to say, the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination should be seen as arising from the conjunction of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
In that regard, what is the earth element of internal dependent origination?
It is that which, through the cohesion of the body, brings about its solid state.
This is called the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
That which performs the function of maintaining the body is called the water element (*abdhātu*).
That which digests what has been eaten and consumed by the body is called the fire element;
that which performs the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body—
This is called the wind element;
that which produces the internal cavities of the body is called the space element.

"Monks, that which brings about name-and-form— consisting of the five groups of consciousness in conjunction with the mental consciousness accompanied by outflows, like the joining of bundles of reeds—
is called the consciousness-element.
In the absence of these conditions, there is no arising of the body."

But when the internal earth element is complete, and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are complete, then from the conjunction of them all, the production of the body occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to the earth element: "I produce the solid state of the body.
It does not occur to the water element: "I perform the function of cohesion for the body.
It does not occur to the fire element: "I digest what has been eaten, drunk, and consumed by the body."
It does not occur to the wind element: "I perform the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body.
It does not occur to the space element: "I produce the internal cavities of the body.
It does not occur to the consciousness element: "I produce name-and-form for the body."
The body, too, does not think, "I am produced by these conditions.
Nevertheless, from the coming together of these existing conditions, the arising of the body occurs.

In that regard, the earth element is not a self, not a sentient being, not a living soul, not a creature, not a human, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a neuter, nor is it "I," nor "mine," nor belongs to anyone else.
Thus, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are not the self,
not a sentient being, not a living soul, not a creature, not a human, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a neuter, nor am I, nor mine, nor anyone else's.

In this context, what is ignorance (*avidyā*)? It is that which, regarding these very six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), consists of the notion of unity, the notion of a mass, the notion of permanence, the notion of stability, the notion of eternity, the notion of pleasure, the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), the notion of a living soul (*jīva*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), a human (*manuja*), or a descendant of Manu (*mānava*), and the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*).
The notion of "mine" and other such various forms of ignorance are called *avidyā*.
When such ignorance exists, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise toward sense objects.
In that context, those attachments, aversions, and delusions regarding sense objects are called "formations" (saṃskāra);
the distinct cognition of an object is "consciousness" (vijñāna).
The four formless aggregates that arise simultaneously with consciousness are called "appropriation" (*upādāna*); that is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
These consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the form derived from them (*upādāyarūpa*).
That name and form, condensed together into a unity, is "name-and-form.
The sense-faculties based upon name-and-form are the "sixfold base" (ṣaḍāyatana).
The coming together of the three factors is contact;
the experience of contact is feeling;
the attachment to feeling is craving.
The expansion of craving is grasping (*upādāna*).
The action born from grasping that produces renewed existence is becoming (*bhava*).
The manifestation of the aggregates caused by becoming is birth (*jāti*).
The maturation of the arisen aggregates is aging;
the destruction of the aged aggregates is death;
and the internal burning of one who is dying, deluded, and possessed of attachment is sorrow.
Lamentation is the utterance arising from sorrow.
Suffering is the experience of the unpleasant associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness. Mental distress is the mental suffering associated with the mind.
And whatever other secondary afflictions there are of this kind, they are called *upāyāsas*.
In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is so called in the sense of being blinded by delusion;
formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in the sense of volitional construction;
and consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the sense of making known.
Name-and-form exists in the sense of mutual support;
the six sense bases exist in the sense of being gateways for arising;
contact exists in the sense of touching.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is so called in the sense of experiencing;
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the sense of parching thirst;
grasping (*upādāna*) in the sense of seizing.
Existence (*bhava*) is so called in the sense of renewed becoming;
birth (*jāti*) in the sense of being born;
and aging (*jarā*) in the sense of maturation.
Death is so called in the sense of destruction;
sorrow (*śoka*) in the sense of grieving;
lamentation (*parideva*) in the sense of wailing; and suffering (*duḥkha*) in the sense of physical affliction.
Dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is so called in the sense of afflicting the mind;
the despondencies (*upāyāsāḥ*) are so called in the sense of being secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Alternatively, ignorance (*avidyā*) is non-comprehension regarding reality, or false comprehension; it is lack of knowledge.
When such ignorance exists, three kinds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are produced: those leading to merit, those leading to demerit, and those leading to the imperturbable.
Among these, from formative forces leading to merit, there arises consciousness leading to merit.
For volitional formations leading to demerit, consciousness leads only to demerit;
for volitional formations leading to the imperturbable, consciousness leads only to the imperturbable.
This is called consciousness.

"Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness": the four formless aggregates, beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), are called "name" (*nāma*) because they cause one to bend (*namayanti*) toward this or that state of existence. Together with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), these are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Through the growth of name-and-form, functional activities proceed and become manifest via the six doors of the sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
That which is conditioned by name-and-form is called the six sense bases.
And from these six sense bases, the six groups of contact proceed;
this is called contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
"Monks, whatever kind of contact arises, a feeling of that same kind proceeds;
this is called 'feeling conditioned by contact.
One who specifically relishes that feeling, delights in it, becomes attached to it, and remains fixed in attachment—"
That is called "craving conditioned by feeling.

Monks, because of relishing, delighting in, and being attached to it, there arises this prayer: "May I not be separated from what is dear and pleasant to me; may I never be parted from it. This is called "clinging conditioned by craving.
Regarding whatever object one has craving for, one takes up clinging for the sake of acquiring and securing that object.
In this and that [object] he makes a request; making such requests, he brings forth karma that produces renewed existence through body, speech, and mind.
That is called "existence" (bhava) conditioned by grasping (upādāna).
The manifestation of the aggregates produced by that karma is called "birth conditioned by becoming.
From the accumulation and maturation of the aggregates manifested through birth, their destruction occurs;
this is called "old age and death conditioned by birth."

Thus, this twelve-linked dependent origination is mutually causal and mutually conditional; it is neither impermanent nor permanent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither causeless nor conditionless, neither an experiencer nor a non-experiencer, neither dependently originated nor not dependently originated,
neither subject to the nature of exhaustion nor not subject to the nature of exhaustion, and neither subject to the nature of destruction nor not subject to the nature of destruction.
It is neither subject to cessation nor not subject to cessation; it has proceeded from beginningless time, uninterrupted, and continues on like the flow of a river.
Although this twelvefold dependent origination proceeds uninterruptedly like the flow of a river, nevertheless,
four members of this twelvefold dependent origination function as the causes for the act of conjunction.
Which are the four?
Namely: ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.
Among these, consciousness is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a seed;
karma is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a field.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), by virtue of having the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), are the cause.
Karmic actions and afflictions produce the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Among these, karma performs the function of a field for the seed of consciousness.
Craving moistens the seed of consciousness;
ignorance sows the seed of consciousness.
In the absence of those conditions, the production of the seed of consciousness does not occur.
In this regard, it does not occur to karma: "I perform the function of a field for the seed of consciousness.
Nor does it occur to craving: "I perform the function of moisture for consciousness.
Nor does it occur to ignorance: "I sow the seed of consciousness."
Nor does the seed of consciousness think: "I am produced by these conditions."
Moreover, the seed of consciousness, established in the field of karma, moistened by the moisture of craving, and covered with the soil of ignorance, sprouts as it develops.
In the linking of successive births at various places of rebirth, it produces the sprout of name-and-form within the mother’s womb.
