And that sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, nor made by another, nor made by both; it is not created by a Lord (Īśvara), nor transformed by time, nor produced from primordial matter (prakṛti); it is not dependent on a single cause, nor has it arisen without a cause.

And yet, through the union of mother and father, the coincidence of the season, and the convergence of other conditions, the seed of consciousness— pervaded by craving— brings forth the sprout of name-and-form within the mother’s womb.

For among phenomena that are ownerless, without appropriation, without "mine-ness," equal to space, and having the nature of the characteristic of illusion, there is no deficiency of causes and conditions.
For example, visual consciousness arises through five causes.
What are these five?
Namely, depending on the eye, and depending on form, light, space, and the attention produced therefrom, visual consciousness arises.
In that regard, the eye performs the function of being the basis for visual consciousness;
visible form performs the function of being the object;
and light performs the function of illumination.
Space performs the function of non-obstruction;
the attention arising from that performs the function of mental engagement.
In the absence of these conditions, visual consciousness does not arise.

But when the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired, and likewise when visible form, light, space, and the attention arising from them are unimpaired, then, through the conjunction of all these factors, visual consciousness arises.
In this regard, it does not occur to the eye: "I perform the function of being the basis for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to light: "I perform the function of illuminating for visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to space: "I perform the function of non-obstruction for visual consciousness."
The mental attention born thereof does not think, "I perform the function of attending to visual consciousness," nor does the visual consciousness think, "I am produced by these conditions.
Nevertheless, through the coming together of these existing conditions, the arising of visual consciousness occurs.
In this same manner, the same should be applied to the remaining faculties as appropriate.
In this regard, no dharma whatsoever transmigrates from this world to the next;
yet there is the discernment of the fruit of karma due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
It is just as, monks, the reflection of a face is seen in a perfectly pure mirror-surface.
And yet, the face does not actually transfer into that mirror-disk,
and there is nevertheless the cognition of the face due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions;
in the same way, no one has passed away from this world, nor has anyone been reborn elsewhere.
And yet, there is the discernment of the fruit of karma because of the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
For example, monks, the lunar disk travels forty thousand yojanas above,
and yet the reflection of the moon is seen even in a small vessel of water.

And yet, it does not fall from that place in space and enter into a small vessel of water; nevertheless, there is the perception of the moon's disk because of the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
In the same way, no one has passed away from this world nor been reborn elsewhere, and yet there is the perception of the fruit of karma because of the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
Just as fire burns when there is the condition of fuel,
but does not burn due to a lack of fuel,
even so, monks, the seed of consciousness produced by karma and afflictions [continues] at each respective point of rebirth in the various spheres of existence.

In the mother’s womb, it brings about the sprout of name-and-form among phenomena that are ownerless, without possession, characterized by illusion, devoid of "mine-ness," and artificial, due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
In this regard, internal dependent origination should be viewed through five reasons.
Which five?
Not as eternal, not as annihilated, not as transmigrating, as the production of a vast fruit from a small cause, and as a continuous succession of similar [states].
How is it not eternal? Because the aggregates at the end of death are one thing, and the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth are another.
But it is not that the very same aggregates which are at the end of death are themselves the aggregates belonging to rebirth;
rather, the aggregates at the end of death cease, and at that very same moment, the aggregates belonging to rebirth appear.
Therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not subject to annihilation?
The aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth do not appear when the aggregates at the end of life have already ceased, nor do they appear when they have not yet ceased.

Rather, at the very moment the aggregates of the time of death cease, the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear— like the rising and falling of the arms of a scale, or like the reflection of the moon's disk;
therefore, it is not through annihilation.
How is it not by way of transmigration?
Sentient beings of dissimilar classes produce birth within a homogeneous class of birth;
therefore, it is not by way of transmigration.
How is it that from a small cause there is the production of a vast fruit?
A small action is performed,
yet a vast ripening of fruit is experienced.
Therefore, because a vast fruit is produced from a limited cause,
how is it that there is a continuity of what is similar to that? It is according to the way the karma is to be experienced that the action is performed.
In that way, the ripening (vipāka) is experienced as being to be felt accordingly;
therefore, it is because of its similarity and its continuous succession—
thus is the detailed explanation.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Examination of the Twelve Links," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.
The Examination of Views, the twenty-seventh chapter:
He who thus correctly perceives dependent origination as it really is does not resort to a prior limit.
"One does not pursue the future limit," and so forth is recited in the Sūtra; therein,
what is the "prior limit"?
What is the future limit (aparānta), and how does one not rely upon it?
This [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of explaining that.
In this context, with reference to the present personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), past personal existences are called the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*).
For the prior portion of the succession of births is the prior limit;
one does not resort to that.

One does not apprehend [objects] through various types of views, because one perceives the reality of dependent origination as it truly exists; thus, one does not adhere to a thing that exists in one way as being otherwise. In this regard, eight views function erroneously by taking the past limit (*pūrvānta*) as their object, as follows:
The views that "I existed in past time" and "I did not exist," as well as those concerning the eternity of the world and so forth, are all based upon the prior limit [of existence]. (1)
In this context, the word "iti" has the sense of "and so forth.
Alternatively, the mention of these two views is intended as an illustration;
for there are actually four such views.
Namely: "Did I indeed exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past?
Did I both exist and not exist in the past?"
"I neither existed nor did I not exist"—
these four views are based on the past limit (*pūrvānta*).
He further says there are another four:
Those views concerning an eternal world and so forth, which were previously described in the context of the discussion, are likewise dependent upon the prior limit.
In this regard, although the latter four views do not differ significantly from the former four views, they are nevertheless presented separately based on their specific distinctions;
we shall explain this further below.
In that regard, the statement "the world is eternal" does not differ significantly from the statement "I existed in past time."
Alternatively, this is the distinction: the view of those who hold that "the world is eternal" generally relies upon the prior limit [of existence];
however, the view "I existed in past time" proceeds specifically by referring to the prior limit of the self alone.
"Not in a general sense"—in this way, a specific distinction must also be stated regarding the other views.
Thus, for now, these eight views are based upon the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). (1)
The past limit has been explained together with those views that take it as their object;
now the future limit is being discussed.
In this context, future states of existence in relation to the present state of existence are called the "future limit" (*aparānta*).
For the "future limit" (aparānta) is that portion of the succession of births which follows; he does not pursue it, nor does he grasp it through various types of views.
Because one sees the reality of dependent origination as it truly exists, one does not misapprehend an object that exists in one way as being otherwise.
In this regard, eight views proceed erroneously by taking the future limit (*aparānta*) as their object. They are as follows:
The views such as "I shall not exist" and "Shall I be something else in the future time," as well as those beginning with "an end," are based upon the future limit. (2)
Here too, the mention of two views is intended as an illustration;
for these views are fourfold, namely:
"Shall I indeed exist in future time?"
"I shall not exist," "I both shall and shall not exist," and "I neither shall nor shall not exist" in the future time.
Thus, these four views rely upon the future limit (*aparānta*).
Are there only these four views that rely upon the future limit? No, he says.
What then? There are also another four [views] beginning with finitude (*anta*) that rely upon the future limit.
In this regard, while the first four views among those concerning the extremes generally proceed by relying upon the future limit (*aparānta*),
these [specific ones] proceed by relying upon the future limit of the self alone— namely, "Shall I exist in the future time?"—
thus one should understand that such is the distinction between this set of four views. // 2 //
In this regard, demonstrating how the four views that take the prior limit as their object are impossible, he says:
"It is not tenable [to say] 'I existed in past time.'"
For he who existed in previous births is not this very same person.
In that regard, if he who existed in past births were indeed this very same person now, then it would be logical for him to apprehend: "I existed in the past."
And this is not possible, because it would entail the consequence of permanence; and because transmigration is untenable for that which is permanent;
and because it would entail the consequence that even one situated in a single state of existence would be comprised within multiple states of existence.

For if one who was previously in a state such as the hells were now reborn among humans due to the variety of karma, and were to conceive the thought, "I myself was that hell-being," that would not be logical for him.
How indeed could one who is currently a human have been a hell-being and so forth?
As for that which is recited in the Sūtra— "At that time, on that occasion, I myself was the universal monarch named Māndhātṛ"—
how is this to be understood?
It should be known that such a statement is intended to negate difference, not to establish identity.
For this very reason, it is recited that "he was not someone else at that time and on that occasion.
However, if there were identity between the former and the present, such that "this is indeed he," what fault would there be?
The fault in this case has already been stated: that there would be permanence. // 3 //
Nevertheless, it is stated further:
"If that very same prior self were this [present] one, then the appropriation would be distinguished [as being the same].
That is to say, if that very former self were now this [self], then the appropriation would be specifically characterized as identical.
In that case, there would be no distinction in the appropriation characterized by the five aggregates, because the appropriator remains undifferentiated, just as in the prior state.
But such non-distinction of appropriation does not exist for this self;
rather, the appropriation is indeed differentiated from the appropriator due to the difference in actions and the difference in causal agents.
And therefore, because of the distinction in the substratum of appropriation, it is not tenable that "this very thing is the self."
Now, you might think: "Let the appropriation be differentiated, but the self is indeed one;
therefore, because the self is undifferentiated, it will certainly follow that [the self] has passed through the past time. To this, it is said:
Furthermore, what is this self of yours that is completely liberated from appropriation?
For if the appropriation were one thing and the self another,
then even when there is a distinction in the appropriation, this [consequence] would indeed follow, since the self would remain undifferentiated.
Furthermore, it is impossible to demonstrate this through a distinction such as, "This is the self;
this is its appropriation," because the self would then result in being causeless, since its very nature is defined by its appropriation.
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of having to apprehend [the self] as something distinct.

And since a self cannot be demonstrated as being liberated from its appropriation (*upādāna*), one cannot then postulate that the self remains undifferentiated even when there is a difference in its appropriation. // 4 //
Furthermore, someone might imagine: "True, it is not possible that [the self] exists as something separate from appropriation;
rather, is it not the case that appropriation itself is conceptualized as the self?"

Demonstrating that this too is not tenable, he says: "If it is established that there is no self apart from the appropriation, then the appropriation itself would be the self; yet for you, there is still no self. (5)
Demonstrating how it is impossible for the appropriation itself to be the self, he says:
"The appropriation itself is not the self, for it passes away and it arises.
How indeed could the appropriation be the appropriator? (6)
In this regard, that which is called the appropriation consisting of the five aggregates of appropriation arises and perishes at every moment;
however, the self does not arise and perish in this way at every moment.
The self (ātman) cannot indeed be described as either identical to or different from the aggregates (skandhas), nor as eternal or non-eternal, because that would entail numerous logical fallacies.
For if the self were eternal, it would result in the doctrine of eternalism (śāśvatavāda).
Furthermore, if there were impermanence, it would entail the consequence of the doctrine of annihilationism;
consequently, since both of these—known as eternalism and annihilationism—are productive of great harm, they should not be accepted.
Therefore, first of all, it is not tenable that the appropriation itself is the self.
Furthermore— how indeed could appropriation be the appropriator?
In this context, that which is appropriated is "appropriation," which is an object (karman).
And that [appropriation] must necessarily have an appropriator who performs the act of appropriation;
if the self-nature of that appropriation is admitted, then it follows that the appropriation itself is the appropriator.

Furthermore, if there were identity between the agent and the object, there would also have to be identity between the cutter and the thing to be cut, as well as between the potter and the jar, fire and fuel, and so forth.
Demonstrating that neither this is observed nor is it logical, he says:
"How indeed could the material cause be the appropriator?"
Rather, the intention is that this position is absolutely impossible.
Here it is said: "It is true that the self is not tenable as being merely the appropriation;
rather, the self will exist as something distinct from the appropriation.
This also is not tenable.
What is the reason? Because:
Furthermore, a self that is distinct from the appropriation is not at all tenable; for if it were distinct, it would be perceived as being without appropriation, yet it is not so perceived. (7)
If the self were distinct from the appropriation,
it would be perceived as separate from that appropriation,
just as a cloth is distinct from a jar.
And yet it is not apprehended in this way;
therefore, even as something distinct from the appropriation, it does not exist.
Being without appropriation, it does not exist because it is not apprehended apart from appropriation, like a flower in the sky.
This is the intended meaning. // 7 //
Now, concluding the point as it has been established, he says:
"Thus, the self is neither other than appropriation nor is it the appropriation itself;
there is no self that exists without appropriation."
Now, it might be argued: if the self were not of the same nature as the appropriation, it would follow that the appropriation and the appropriator are one and the same;
furthermore, it would follow that [the self] is subject to arising and passing away.
For it is not something other [than the appropriation], because that would entail the consequence of its being perceived as distinct from it;
nor is it without appropriation,
because that would entail the consequence of its being perceived independently of appropriation.
If that is so, then let it be that there is no self. It is said in reply:
nor is there this certainty that [it] does not exist. (8)
For how could that which is designated in dependence upon the aggregates be said not to exist?
Indeed, the son of a barren woman, who does not exist, is not designated in dependence upon the aggregates.
How is it logical that when appropriation exists, there is no appropriator?
Therefore, even its non-existence is not tenable;
consequently, this certainty that "the self does not exist" is also untenable.
The detailed systematic presentation of this self (ātman) should be understood from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*;
since a systematic presentation has already been made here at various points, no further effort is exerted here toward such a presentation. // 8 //
Thus, first of all, the conceptualization that "I existed in past time" is not tenable.
Now, demonstrating how the notion that "I did not exist in past time" is likewise untenable, he says: "The claim that 'I did not exist in past time' is not tenable."
For this person is not other than that [person] in previous births.
If this present self were different from the previous self, then one would not have said, "I existed in past time.
But this is not possible.
Therefore, the claim that "I did not exist in past time" is not tenable. // 9 //
If, however, this [self] were different from the previous self, what fault would there be? It is said:
For if this were other, it could exist even after having rejected that [previous self].
In that very same way, he would remain there, or he would be born there as an immortal. // 10 //
For if this present self were other than the previous self, then, having rejected and abandoned that previous self, it would be independent of it and would not have that as its cause.
Furthermore:

And it would likewise remain exactly as it was; for if there were a difference between this [subsequent] self and the prior self, then, due to that difference, just as a cloth is not destroyed when a pot is produced, there would be no cessation even when the subsequent self arises from the prior self.
And because of this non-cessation, wherever one was previously born among gods, humans, and so forth, [one would remain there].

In whatever manner—by way of color, shape, and so forth—it was previously perceived, in that very same way and in that very state it would have to remain there; it would have to remain exactly as it was.
Therefore, the claim that "I did not exist in past time" is untenable.
To this, he says: Regarding what was stated there—
"If indeed this were other, it would exist even after having rejected that"—
if, on the other hand, this [present self] were to exist here after having rejected the prior self, [then...]
What fault would there be?
There would be many faults therein.
If you ask how:

Because, this being the case, it would follow that there is the annihilation of actions—that is, their destruction—and that actions performed by one person would be experienced by another; such [absurdities] and others like them would result. // 11 //
If this self were to exist by rejecting the previous self, then,
because the previous self would have perished there and another distinct self would be produced here, there would be the annihilation of the previous self.

And if that self were annihilated, there would be total destruction [of karma], because actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced would be severed by the severance of their substratum, and because the experiencer would no longer exist.
Alternatively, if it is postulated that the enjoyment of the fruit of an action performed by a prior self occurs through a subsequent self—
Nevertheless, the fruit of an action performed by one would be experienced by another;
and consequently, there would arise the fear of encountering what was not done, if the action were uncreated.
In this way, such undesirable consequences as these would follow. // 11 //
Furthermore, if this self were something entirely different from the previous self that has arisen here,
then it would follow that it did not exist previously and was produced later.
To demonstrate that this is not tenable, he says:
Nor has it arisen without having previously existed, for in that case a logical fault would follow:
either the self would be something produced, or it would have come into being without a cause. (12)
Thus: for if the self were to arise after having previously not existed, then the self would be merely something produced;
yet a produced self is not accepted.
Because it would follow that [the self] is impermanent,
and since there is no separate agent to produce it, how could "being produced" be attributed to the self? Furthermore,
if the self were imagined to be produced, saṃsāra would necessarily have a beginning.
And there would be the manifestation of a previously non-existent being;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, the self is not something produced.
Moreover, even if it were produced, it would be without cause;
for if the self, having not existed previously, were to arise, it would necessarily follow that it arises without a cause.
For if the self did not exist previously, it would be uncreated and without cause.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative:
either the self would have to be created, or else one must not accept the proposition that "I did not exist in past time."
Whether [the self] has arisen without a cause, or else that "I did not exist in past time"—this is not tenable;
thus let it be accepted. 12.
Now, concluding the very point as it has been described, he says:
"Thus, regarding the past, the view that 'I existed,' 'I did not exist,' 'both,' or 'neither'—none of these is tenable. (13)
Thus, by the reasoning already described, the view that "I existed in past time" is also not tenable;
and because of the non-existence of these two [extremes], both [views] together are likewise not tenable.
What is the reason?
Because this "both" is conceived as a combination of two;
and since each one does not exist individually, how could there be their combination? Thus, even "both" is not possible.
Since both [existence and non-existence] are absent, how could there be "neither" by means of their negation?
Therefore, even the claim "I neither existed nor did I not exist" is not tenable. // 13 //

Thus, having demonstrated the impossibility of the fourfold set of views based on the past limit (*pūrvānta*), he now states the refutation of those based on the future limit (*aparānta*): "What indeed shall I become in the future time?"—this view, as well as "I shall not become," is the same as [the analysis] regarding the past time. (14)

For just as the fourfold set of views was refuted regarding the past time, so too must the fourfold set of views regarding the future time be refuted by means of a modification of the stated formula. That is to say:
"In the future time, will I exist?"—this is untenable.
That which is the state in a future birth is not this very same [state].
In this manner, all [arguments] should be applied equally to the negation of identity;
likewise, they should also be applied equally to the negation of difference:
"It would not exist in the future time"—this is not tenable.
This [present] state is not other than the state that existed in the future birth.
Thus, by means of such a modification of the reading of the preceding verse. // 14 //
Now, for the purpose of refuting the fourfold set of views such as eternalism which rely upon the prior limit, he says:
"If that god were that human, then it would be eternal;
but the god would be unarisen, for what is eternal is not born. (15)
For in this case, someone situated in the human realm, having performed wholesome karma, goes to the divine realm.
If that very same being were the god and that very same being were the human— such that there were identity between the two— then it would be eternalism (*śāśvata*).
And it is not the case that one remains exactly the same as a human being;
therefore, nothing whatsoever is eternal. Moreover:
If the doctrine of eternalism were true, the deity would be unarisen.
Why?
Because that which is eternal is certainly not born.
For whatever entity is eternal, because it already exists, it is not born at all;
consequently, the deity would be unarisen.
It is not tenable that an unarisen deity exists.
Thus, for now, permanence is not tenable. // 15 //
Now, demonstrating how even impermanence is not possible, he says:
If the human were other than the divine, then there would be impermanence;
if the human were other than the divine, then continuity would not be established. (16)

For if the deity were one thing and the human another, then, because the previous human self would have perished there and another [self] would arise here, that previous human self would have been destroyed there, and thus [the self] would be non-eternal (*aśāśvata*).
If it is argued that it is not non-eternal because of the continuity of its stream (*saṃtāna*), it is said in reply:
If a human were other than a god, a continuum would not be possible;
for if a human were other than a god,
then just as there can be no mango-tree continuum from a neem tree, [so too there could be no continuity between them].
In this way, the god would not belong to the same continuum as the human;
and consequently, because the former [human] has perished, it would be non-eternal.
Or else:
If a human were different from a deity,
then there would be no continuity of the continuum;
yet this continuity of the continuum exists, in that a human belongs to the same continuum as a deity.
Therefore, because it would follow that there is no continuity of the stream [of existence], a human being is not other than a god;
and since this is so, there is also no non-eternalism. // 16 //
Now, for the purpose of refuting both the eternal and the non-eternal, he says:
If one part were divine and one part were human, it would be both non-eternal and eternal; and that is not tenable. (17)

If this person were to abandon humanity in one part and, having abandoned humanity in that part, were to assume a divine self-existence, then, because of the destruction of one portion, it would be non-eternal.
And because one part would remain [in the world], it would be eternal;
and this is untenable, that one part of a single being should be comprised within the divine realm while another part should be human.
Therefore, both "eternal" and "non-eternal"—neither of these two is tenable. // 17 //

Now, in order to refute the views of both non-eternalism and eternalism, he says: If both the non-eternal and the eternal were established, then it would indeed be established that there is neither the eternal nor the non-eternal. (18)
If there were any entity that was eternal, then, because it would later be seen as non-eternal, it could not be eternal.
Likewise, if anything were non-eternal...
In that case, because of its subsequent arising as eternal, it would follow that it is "non-eternal.
But when both "eternal" and "non-eternal" are themselves unestablished,
how could there be "neither eternal nor non-eternal" through their negation?
Therefore, this too is incorrect. // 18 //
Now, it might be argued: having observed the continuous succession of birth and death proceeding in an unbroken sequence from beginningless time, we postulate an eternal self;
for there exists some eternal entity which, indeed, is still perceived even today as wandering through this beginningless saṃsāra.
It is said:
even this is not tenable.
What is the reason? For indeed—
If someone who has come from somewhere were to go again to some place, then saṃsāra would be beginningless; yet such a person does not exist. (19)

For if there were a movement from some other state of existence to another state of existence for conditioned phenomena or for a self, and if there were then a further movement from that other state of existence to somewhere else, only then would saṃsāra be beginningless.
Nor is the arrival of anything from anywhere possible, because the arrival of either a permanent or an impermanent entity is untenable;
nor, moreover, is the departure of anything from here to anywhere else possible.
Because movement is impossible for either what is permanent or what is impermanent,
and since this is not possible,
how could there be a beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) due to the extreme length of the succession of births and deaths, given that no beginning is perceived?
Since there is no transmigrating being, how could beginninglessness or having a beginning possibly belong to saṃsāra?
And when that is not possible,
then as for what was said— that there exists some eternal entity— [that too is untenable].
For it is not logical to say that someone who has indeed been wandering thus through beginningless saṃsāra is still being perceived even today.

And therefore, according to the reasoning thus stated: If nothing eternal exists, what could there be that is non-eternal? Nor can there be anything both eternal and non-eternal, nor anything excluded from these two. (20)
And when an eternal entity is thus impossible, then from the departure of what could there be the non-eternal?
Since neither the eternal nor the non-eternal is perceived, how could there be both, and how could there be neither?
Therefore, in this way, the fourfold set of views beginning with eternalism is not possible regarding the prior limit of cyclic existence. // 20 //
Now, demonstrating how the fourfold set beginning with "finite" and "infinite" cannot possibly exist in the future limit, he says:
If the world were finite, how could there be a future life?
Moreover, if the world were infinite, how could there be a future life?
For if the world were finite, then after its destruction the prior world would no longer exist;
in that case, there would be no future world (paraloka). Yet, since there is a future world, it is not tenable to say that the world is finite.
Moreover, if the world were infinite, how then could there be a future life?
The intended meaning is that there would simply be no future life at all.
And yet, the next world does not not exist;
therefore, because the next world exists, the world is also not finite. // 21 //
Now, demonstrating how both finitude and infinity of the world are impossible, he says:
"Because this continuum of the aggregates is like the flame of a lamp..."
Therefore, it proceeds; thus, neither finitude nor infinitude is tenable. // 22 //

Since this continuum of aggregates proceeds as an uninterrupted sequence, characterized by the constant succession of the relationship between preceding causes and subsequent effects—just like a lamp—it follows that, because the activity of cause and effect is observed, it is neither logical for it to be finite nor for it to be infinite. // 22 //
How so?
If these aggregates were to perish first and yet not arise [again] in dependence upon these [present] aggregates, then the world would be finite. (23)

If the preceding aggregates of a human being were to perish, and if, dependent upon them, the subsequent aggregates comprised within rebirth in the divine realm did not arise, then the world would be finite, like a lamp extinguished by the exhaustion of its oil and wick.
Because there is the arising of a future personal existence, there is no state of being finite. // 23 //
If these aggregates were not destroyed in the past, nor were they produced, then this world would be infinite because of these aggregates that arise in dependence upon [the previous] aggregates. (24)

Now, if the preceding aggregates were not to perish, then the subsequent aggregates, which constitute the fruit, would not arise in dependence upon them; in that case, the world would be infinite and indestructible, because it would never deviate from its own nature.
However, when the preceding aggregates cease, other aggregates caused by them are born at a later time.
In that case, since there would be no prior limit, how could the samsara be infinite? // 24 //

Now, demonstrating the third possibility—that of being both—he says: If one part were finite and another part were infinite, then the world would be both finite and infinite; but that is not tenable. (25)
For if there were the destruction of one part [of the world] and the movement of another part to another location, then the world would be both finite and infinite.
And this is not possible—that one part should perish while another part does not perish.
Therefore, it is not tenable that the world is both finite and infinite. // 25 //
Furthermore, demonstrating why it is not tenable for one part to perish while another part remains, he says:
"How, first of all, could one part of the appropriator perish while another part does not perish? Thus, this is not tenable. (26)

In this case, when the destruction of one part and the persistence of another part are being postulated, is it the destruction or the persistence of one part of the appropriator that is being postulated,
or rather that of the appropriated object? If, first of all, the destruction of one part and the persistence of another part of the appropriator are being postulated, [then...]
That is not tenable.
Why? Because:
how, first of all, could one part of the appropriator perish?
Nor will one part perish;
for there is no logical justification whatsoever here by which we might conceive of the destruction of one part and the non-destruction of another part.
Precisely because he sees no such justification, the Master says:
And thus, this is not tenable.
Alternatively, that which is called the "appropriator" is the self;
yet, when sought in the five aggregates in five ways, it does not exist.
And how could that which does not come into being have one part perish while another part does not perish?
For this very reason, he says: "And thus, this is not tenable.

Alternatively, if one part of the appropriator were to perish while another part did not perish, then that single appropriator would simultaneously possess divinity through one portion and humanity through the other.
And this is not accepted; thus he says: "In this way, this is not tenable.
Thus, first of all, it is not tenable that the appropriator is either finite or infinite. // 26 //
Now, demonstrating how grasping (upādāna) likewise cannot possibly exist, he says:
"How indeed could one part of grasping perish, while another part does not perish? This too is not tenable. (27)
This should also be explained in the same manner as the appropriator. // 27 //
Having thus established the impossibility of perceiving both [the finite and the infinite], he now says, demonstrating how neither of the two is possible:
"If both the finite and the infinite were established, then it would be established that it is neither finite nor indeed infinite, as you desire. (28)
Since the entity to be negated is impossible, the negation itself is also impossible.
Therefore, when both finitude and infinitude are unperceived, for what could there be a negation such that the view "the world is neither finite nor infinite" might arise? // 28 //
Thus, having first established that even by accepting a conventional appropriator in the form of a reflection and an appropriation, views such as eternalism and so forth are impossible,

[the author] now says— desiring to demonstrate that views such as eternalism are impossible in every respect because the intrinsic nature of entities is not perceived, just like the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman:
Alternatively, since all phenomena are empty, where, for whom, which, and from what cause could views such as eternalism and so forth possibly arise? (29)
In this work, the emptiness of all phenomena has been established throughout the entire treatise because they are dependently originated.

Consequently, since all phenomena are empty, what views— such as eternalism and so forth— could there be that exist outside of all phenomena, which someone might grasp such that we would undertake their refutation?
Likewise, what could that object be which is not included within all phenomena (*sarvabhāva*), wherein these views will arise, and wherein we shall restrain these views?
And what is that entity or person (*pudgala*) outside of all phenomena, for whom these views will arise, and whom we shall restrain from those views?

Or what is the causal sign (*nimitta*) as an objective support (*ālambana*) for the arising of views—something external to all phenomena—from which sign views such as eternalism and so forth arise, and which we shall restrain?
For indeed, because all things whatsoever are included within the totality of existence, they are empty;
and because they are empty, none of those things are perceived.
Where, for whom, which, and from what source could views possibly arise?
Not at all anything, not at all anywhere, not at all for anyone.
The intention is that they will not exist in any manner whatsoever.
And since they are impossible, even the conceptualization of them does not arise; thus, these views are indeed untenable. // 29 //
Thus,
I pay homage to Gautama, who, out of compassion, taught the true Dharma for the sake of abandoning all views. (30)
In this context, it is called *dharma* because it sustains one from falling into the precipice of apprehending saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, abandonment, or attainment.
It is the *saddharma* (True Dharma) because it is the *dharma* of the virtuous, the noble ones, who have accomplished their task;
or alternatively, it is the *saddharma* because it is a beautiful (*sat*) *dharma*.
Because it is worthy of praise for bringing about the destruction of all the sufferings of saṃsāra.
That which is the true Dharma— neither ceasing nor arising, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither a single entity nor diverse entities, without coming and without going.

Out of compassion for the world, relying solely upon great compassion— the object of which is all beings in the three realms of existence who are more worthy of love than even an only beloved son— he taught the auspicious cessation of conceptual proliferation by means of the designation "dependent origination" for the sake of abandoning all views,
and not out of a desire for gain, honor, or reciprocal benefit.
I pay homage to that unsurpassed, peerless Teacher.
What is his name? Gautama;
the meaning is that he is born of the lineage of the supreme ṛṣis.

As it was said by the noble Maitreya, the great bodhisattva, in the *Ārya-śālistamba-sūtra*: "He who, with right wisdom, constantly and continuously perceives this very dependent origination as it truly is— without a living soul (*ajīva*), devoid of a life-principle (*nirjīva*), as it really is, unerring, unborn, unbecome, uncreated, unconditioned, non-obstructive, unimpeded, auspicious, fearless, unassailable, inexhaustible, and whose nature is not subject to cessation."
He perceives it as non-existent, as empty, as hollow, as insubstantial, as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as an evil, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self;
he does not pursue the past, wondering,
"Did I indeed exist in the past?"
Or did I not exist in past time? Who indeed was I in past time?
How indeed was I in past time?
Or again, one does not look back toward the future limit, thinking: "Shall I exist in the future time?
Or shall I not exist in the future time?
Who indeed shall I be in the future time?"
"How indeed shall I be in the future?
Or again, one does not rely upon the present, wondering: 'What is this? How is this? Who were we? Who shall we be? From where has this being come?
Having passed away from here, where will it go?'—these are the various speculative views held by certain recluses and brahmins in the world."
They will be as follows: those associated with the doctrine of a self, those associated with the doctrine of a living soul, and those associated with omens and auspicious signs;
at that time, these have been abandoned by him, fully understood, cut off at the root, made like the stump of a palm tree, and rendered subject to non-arising and non-ceasing in the future.
Then the venerable Śāriputra, having rejoiced and greatly delighted in what the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya had spoken, rose from his seat and departed; and those monks also departed.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Examination of Views," in the *Prasannapadā*, a commentary on the *Madhyamaka* composed by the venerable master Candrakīrti.

And thus is completed this *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, which is skilled and proficient in explaining the definitive and interpretable meanings of all mundane and supramundane teachings, and which bestows the seat at the terrace of enlightenment for the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Buddhas.
